The classical bound θ_pr(x)−x=O_ε(x^{Θ+ε}) for x≥2 comes from the explicit formula truncated at height comparable with x (Σ_{|γ|≤O(x)}1/|ρ|≪log²x, and removing powers costs O(√x log²x)); if Θ=1 Chebyshev suffices. For y≤X integrate by parts with the primitive θ_pr−x. On [2,X], |h_v(x)|≪_c x^(-1/2) and |h_v′(x)|≪_c x^(−3/2) for v≥1 since 0≤v−log x≤v. The mass in (0,2] is O_c(1) by integration of x^(−1/2) and the atom at 2. Since Θ≥1/2, B_X≪_{c,ε} X^{2Θ−1+2ε} results. The use of ε avoids any assumption that the supremum is attained.

Floor. Write b=limsup log(1+B_X)/log X≥0. Choose a smooth partition of unity χ(x/X) into dyadic blocks, with compact support inside (1/4,1) in the variable x/X: a non-negative function positive on an interval of ratio >2 is normalized by the sum of its dilates. For x∈[X/4,X], h_v(x)≍_c X^(−1/2)/√v and |h_v′/h_v|≪_c 1/X. By integration by parts without boundary terms and Cauchy–Schwarz, on any compact set K of complex s, σ=Re s,
|∫χ(x/X)x^(−s)(dθ_pr−dx)|=|∫F_X(y)(χ(y/X)y^(−s)/h_v(y))′dy|≪_{c,K}√v X^{1/2−σ}√B_X.
Indeed, the first L² factor is √(XB_X), and the second ≪√v X^(−σ). The sum of the large pieces converges normally for σ>(1+b)/2. Completing with an initial part entire in s (restricting the Mellin transform to x≥1), this continues P(s)−1/(s−1) from σ>1. On σ>1/2 the difference −ζ′/ζ−P comes from the powers ≥2 and is holomorphic by absolute convergence. Therefore there are no zeros with real part >(1+b)/2. This inequality gives b≥2Θ−1. The argument uses neither Selberg's bound nor presupposes that an individual prefix has a determined sign.

Provenance: it is a weighted localization of the classical link between θ_pr−x and the abscissa of the zeros via Mellin. It is not a new bound for Θ. The pending step, in this formulation, is to prove B_{2^n}=2^{o(n)} for a fixed c without assuming RH; a small subsequence is not enough in the continuation proof.

The same equality of exponents holds even after subtracting the mean of F_X on [X/4,X]. In the proof of the floor, the derived factor integrates to zero; therefore any constant can be subtracted from F_X and its norm optimized. The variance so normalized is ≤B_X and keeps the same ceiling. By the two-copy identity one writes exactly
[2X·(3X/4)]⁻¹ ∫_{X/4}^X∫_{X/4}^X |F_X(y)−F_X(z)|²dy dz.
Now only increments of the centred count on intervals contained in [X/4,X] intervene. All dependence on the primes below X/4 at that scale disappears. Nor is it necessary that the energy of the prefix and the variance be equivalent up to a constant factor: the conclusion is the equality of their upper exponents.

**Cross-check and improvement via 231-A.** The audit identified the direct antecedent: ROUND_231_A already proves for the unweighted local prime count, even fitting an arbitrary line, the ordinary limit of exponent 2Θ−1. It is transferred to the previous boundary. On I=[X/4,X] let G=θ_pr−id. Since dG=h_v⁻¹ dF_X, a primitive of dG, up to a constant, is h_v⁻¹(F_X−m)−∫_{X/4}^y(h_v⁻¹)′(F_X−m)dx. Since sup|h_v⁻¹|≪√(Xv) and sup|(h_v⁻¹)′|≪√(Xv)/X, its L²(I) norm is ≪√(Xv)||F_X−m||₂. On the sub-band [X/2,X] the optimal fit of 231 (length log 2) thus costs, with its normalization, ≤O(v) times the boundary variance. The floor at each X of 231 and the previous ceiling turn both limsups into ORDINARY LIMITS. Hence a single subsequence of subpower variances does suffice when using 231. The isolated Mellin proof only gave the limsup. Classify this branch as an application of 231, without opening an independent route by change of weight.

**Cross audit: the density of negative eigenvalues does not transfer from the shifted moments to POWER.** Substantive antecedent 21-A.1 (two negative indices per distinct off-line orbit) and POWER bridge 001/014. For the nested blocks of derivatives at a single real rate u>1/2, if hypothetically there were a finite number m of distinct off-axis quartets, their determinants would be strictly POSITIVE at every sufficiently large size, even with 2m negative directions. In particular neither the eventual sign of the determinants nor the o(1) fraction of negative eigenvalues would by themselves exclude the finite defect. By contrast an unbounded subsequence of blocks with index ≤1 would suffice. It is a consequence of the known index, not a new sign mechanism.

Verification directly on the kernel of 001. Centre λ=ρ−1/2 and put Jλ=−conj λ. On the space of sequences over distinct zeros, with weight their multiplicity m_λ, the index inversion J is a self-adjoint unitary involution. Let h_z(λ)=1/(z−λ). The Pick form is ⟨h_z,Jh_w⟩: in the partial-fraction sum of the logarithmic derivative of the centred ξ, λ is grouped with −λ (the completed function is even), and on dividing L(z)+conj L(w) by z+conj w one gets Σ m_λ/[(z−λ)(conj w+λ)]. This last series converges absolutely by the zero count. The factors ζ(a) of 001 are invertible congruences; for derivatives at one rate the non-vanishing analytic factor still gives an invertible triangular change.

The derivatives of h_z at u are total: for a vector orthogonal to all of them, the scalar series pairing it with h_z is meromorphic, with normal convergence away from the poles by Cauchy–Schwarz and Σ m_λ/(1+|λ|²)<∞. Its germ at u is zero, hence each residue is zero. The derivatives of orders 0,…,n−1 are independent, being consecutive powers of 1/(u−λ) evaluated at infinitely many distinct points. Complexification preserves the inertia of real matrices. Each 2-cycle of J contributes one negative dimension, each fixed point a positive one; the two signs of the height give two cycles per quartet. The multiplicity only weights the norm. By density any finite-dimensional negative subspace is approximated in some block, preserving its strict margin. This includes the case of infinite index for the criterion ≤1.

If the total index κ=2m is finite, once attained in a block it is preserved by inclusion. Every negative subspace of dimension κ has a form-orthogonal complement that is strictly positive: if a non-zero neutral vector were in that complement, non-degeneracy of the complement would provide a second vector with non-zero pairing; their plane would have an additional negative direction. Non-degeneracy follows from the direct decomposition by the finite negative subspace and the invertibility of J. Therefore all later blocks are non-singular and have determinant sign (−1)^κ=+1. This obstruction concerns tail determinants; it does not authorize ignoring the initial minors in the positivity criterion.

**Shifted blocks of fixed width in the normalized POWER kernel.** Fix a centred rate u>1/2 and form the matrix of mixed derivatives of the kernel K of 001 at (u,u), of orders n,…,n+d−1 in each variable, normalizing order j by (−1)^j/j!. Let S be the set of distinct centred zeros λ with |u²−λ²|<R, where R is not a boundary value and S is non-empty. If d=|S|, for ALL sufficiently large n the matrix is non-singular and its negative index is exactly the number of λ∈S with Re λ>0. This localizes the count of 21-A.1 even when the defect outside S is infinite. The width is fixed before taking n to infinity. The precedent GRAM §19.10 keeps the start fixed and requires all final sizes; its tail criterion does not compute this local inertia.

Proof. Put x_λ=(u−λ)⁻¹, Jλ=−conj λ and w_λ=x_λ conj(x_{Jλ})=1/(u²−λ²). For the coefficient vector of the polynomial P of degree <d the form is Σ m_λ w_λ^{n+1}P(x_λ)conj(P(x_{Jλ})). On S the evaluation P↦(P(x_λ)) is a square invertible Vandermonde matrix independent of n. Before that congruence, each fixed point gives the positive weight m_λ w_λ^{n+1}, and each exchanged pair gives a Hermitian block with two conjugate cross entries, with eigenvalues ±m_λ |w_λ|^{n+1}. Therefore, after the congruence, the distance of its spectrum to zero is ≥s_min(Vandermonde)² min_S |w_λ|^{n+1} (apply the norm bound to the inverse). This does not require the phases to converge. Outside S the norm of the matrix is ≤C_{u,d} max_{λ∉S}|w_λ|^n Σ_{λ∉S}m_λ |w_λ|, since x_λ is uniformly bounded and the zero count gives convergence. The exponential base of the tail is strictly less than min_S |w_λ| by discreteness and divergence of |u²−λ²| with the height. The perturbation preserves the inertia from some n on.

In particular, if S lies within the verified zone and contains only zeros on the axis, the late blocks are positive definite at every width ≤|S| by principal restriction. Conversely, if there were a single off-axis quartet, there is some finite R containing it, and the fixed width |S| detects at least two negative directions for ALL large initial orders. It would therefore suffice to prove that at each fixed width there are arbitrarily late starts with index ≤1. That uniform bound over the widths is not known; nor is an effective start given. To use the verified zone R<u²+G²−1/4 suffices, since |u²−λ²|≥u²+γ²−(Re λ)². The jets are those of the normalized kernel K, equivalent to differentiating the generators normalized by ζ(a) before choosing the block. Multiplying by a non-constant analytic function mixes lower orders and does not in general give an internal congruence on a shifted block of fixed width.

**First partial cut of a quartet: the determinants change sign at an odd width.** Unlike the cut that includes the four nodes, the first degree exceeding the number of interior nodes on the axis leaves a single new direction. Under failure of RH there is a rational centred rate u∈(1,2) and a fixed odd width d for which the determinant of the normalized block of orders n,…,n+d−1 is strictly negative with lower density ≥1/4, and strictly positive with lower density ≥1/4. The densities are taken in the integer n. Neither simple zeros nor rational independence of ordinates are needed.

To select u, fix a candidate exterior quartet. On [1,2] its radius |u²−λ²| is bounded, while those of all high ordinates grow uniformly. Only finitely many quartets or pairs on the axis can precede it or tie with it. Among those distinct groups, the functions |u²−λ²|²−u⁴ are lines in u²; coinciding identically requires equal Re(λ²) and |λ²|, hence the same group up to conjugation and sign. Remove the finitely many crossings and choose an interior rational. The first off-axis group is isolated, with modulus q=|(u²−λ²)⁻¹|. Before it there are r distinct nodes on the axis, in conjugate pairs, r even. The real monic polynomial P₀(x)=∏_{interior}(x−x_λ) has degree r and is non-zero at the four nodes of the group. Take d=r+1.

In the real basis 1,…,x^{r−1},P₀, the upper-left block has minimal value ≥const·α^{n+1} for large n, with α=min_{interior}|w_λ|>q, by Vandermonde and the previous tail estimate. The cross term with P₀ is O(q^{n+1}) because all interior terms vanish. The correction to the last pivot by the Schur complement is thus o(q^{n+1}). If r=0 the single entry is used directly. In that entry the first group contributes
4m Re[w_λ^{n+1} P₀(x_λ)P₀(x_{−λ})],
since λ and −λ contribute the same complex expression and the other two nodes its conjugate. The later groups cost o(q^{n+1}) by the radial gap. Since the initial block is positive, the sign of the determinant is that of the pivot. Divided by q^{n+1}, the latter is a cosine of non-zero amplitude plus o(1). The angle arg w_λ is not a multiple of π, since Re λ and Im λ are non-zero. For irrational rotation, equidistribution gives density 1/2 of each sign by excluding neighbourhoods of the zeros. For rotation of finite order l≥3, take the points strictly in each semicircle; there are at least (l−1)/2 if l is odd or l/2−1 if l is even. Their strict margins survive the o(1); the uniform floor 1/4 results. The exact zeros of the cosine are not assigned to any sign in this argument.

Under RH every matrix of this type is positive definite by independence of the evaluations at infinitely many zeros on the axis. Therefore it would suffice that for each rational u in (1,2) and each fixed odd d the lower density of negative determinants be <1/4. Formulating the criterion does not require computing r or locating the first quartet. Nor has the density bound been proved for the arithmetic data. The distinction from the late positive determinants under finite defect is that there the size of a complete prefix is increased (or a complete group is included), whereas here the start of a fixed partial width is shifted. The mechanism is the classical separation of dominant poles already indexed; the conclusion specifies which cut of POWER retains the sign.

**Three shifts: a phase-free sign and an unconditional positive range.** Let D_n be the determinant of the normalized POWER block of the previous paragraph, of fixed width d and consecutive orders from n. Define T_n=D_n D_{n+2}−D_{n+1}², always without dividing by a determinant. The antecedent POWER 046/055 records the Turán mechanism for moment sequences. Here it is applied to the determinant of the first partial cut, and it is verified separately when the second layer in the expansion of the determinant guarantees the inequality for ζ.

At the odd witness width of failure of the previous paragraph, let S be the r interior nodes and W=∏_{λ∈S}w_λ>0 (empty product 1). The determinant of the upper-left block equals C W^{n+1}(1+o(1)), C>0: the interior part is a congruence of the diagonal m_λ w_λ^{n+1} by a fixed Vandermonde, and the relative error in norm, after normalizing by its inverse square root, is O((q/α)^{n+1}). In fixed dimension the relative determinant tends to 1. The change to the monic basis has determinant one. Multiplying the previous pivot gives D_n=A R^{n+1}(cos((n+1)φ+β)+o(1)), with A>0, R=Wq and non-zero sine of φ. By the identity cos x cos(x+2φ)−cos²(x+φ)=−sin²φ one obtains
T_n/[A² R^{2n+4}] → −sin²φ < 0.
This holds for all sufficiently large shifts, even when some cosine is arbitrarily close to zero.

Under RH, Cauchy–Binet gives D_n=Σ_S c_S t_S^{n+1} over all subsets of d distinct nodes, with t_S=∏w_λ>0 and c_S=|det V_S|²∏m_λ>0. Hence T_n≥0 by Cauchy–Schwarz. Consequently, that for each rational 1<u<2 and each odd d one has T_n≥0 for arbitrarily large shifts n is equivalent to the global sign. Estimating a frequency of sign changes is not required.

Even without RH there is late strict positivity of T_n in a verifiable band of widths. Let N be the number of distinct nodes of a safe radial cut that contains only zeros on the axis (for example R_cut<u²+G²−1/4). For 1≤d≤N−2, enumerate its nodes by decreasing moduli of w_λ. Fix the first d−1, with product L. At least three candidates remain in the cut, containing at least two distinct moduli because each distinct positive height of the zeros on the axis contributes exactly two nodes and its modulus 1/(u²+γ²) decreases strictly in γ. Two distinct positive products are obtained, both larger than the modulus of any product of d nodes containing a node outside the cut (such a product has modulus ≤L·max_exterior|w|).

To justify the comparison, Cauchy–Binet remains exact outside RH with coefficients c_S=det V_S·conj(det V_{JS})∏m_λ, ordering JS by the images of the same list S. The products of moduli of determinants are bounded at fixed d and Σ_S |c_S t_S|<∞ by Σm_λ|w_λ|<∞. For every positive threshold there are only finitely many subsets with product of modulus above the threshold, because |w_λ|→0. The two largest distinct products U>V in this case come only from nodes on the axis and on grouping them have positive coefficients C_U,C_V. In the two-copy identity for T_n each pair of bases t,t′ contributes c_t c_t′(tt′)^{n+1}(t−t′)², summing unordered pairs. Coinciding bases cancel exactly. The maximum UV is isolated and the previous absolute convergence dominates the rest by a strictly smaller exponential base. Thus T_n/(UV)^{n+1}→C_U C_V(U−V)²>0. The previous positivity of the blocks by itself did not imply this comparison between orders. The statement provides neither an effective start nor covers the arbitrary widths required by the criterion.

**Even and odd splitting of the block and scalar differences with certified sign.** For t=u², w=(t−λ²)⁻¹, put a=2u/(u−λ)−1. Then a_{−λ}=1/a_λ and (a+1/a)/2=2tw−1. At width 2l+1, rewrite P(x_λ) as a polynomial in a and multiply it by a^(−l); the bilinear product evaluated at a,1/a remains unchanged. Every real Laurent polynomial with exponents between −l and l is written uniquely as A(w)+(a−1/a)B(w), with degrees ≤l,≤l−1 respectively, by the Chebyshev identities. On evaluating the product with the inverse argument the cross terms cancel and −(a−1/a)²=16tw(1−tw). The normalized block is thus congruent over the reals to the sum of two Hankel forms:
Σ_λ m_λ w^{n+1} A(w)²  + 16t Σ_λ m_λ w^{n+2}(1−tw) B(w)².
The paired sums are real even if w is complex. The factorization by symmetry of a Toeplitz form is classical. A separate question is the sign of the scalar differences that intervene when evaluating those moments.

For n≥0 define M_n(t)=Σ_λ m_λ w(tw)^n. It is proved for ALL t>0, ALL n≥0 and all 0≤j≤10⁹ that
Σ_{h=0}^j (−1)^h binom(j,h) M_{n+h}(t)>0.
Only the critical strip, the Z2 control, γ₁<15 and the bound Σm_λ/γ²<.049 already used above (γ₁>14) are used. The computation does not assume RH. Define S(y)=Σ m_λ exp(λ²y) for y>0. Each derivative of fixed order converges normally on interior real compact sets by the zero count. In (−1)^j S^(j) the zeros on the axis contribute positively. For the others, |γ|>G=3·10¹², and |arg(−λ²)|≤2 arctan(|Re λ|/|γ|)≤1/|γ|. For j≤10⁹, a summand with negative real part requires |γ|y>1, since |Im(λ²)y|≤|γ|y and j/|γ|<.001. Relative to a contribution γ₁^{2j}exp(−γ₁²y), the modulus of such a term, without multiplicity, is at most
exp(2j log(2|γ|)−.99|γ|) ≤exp(−.96|γ|).
Indeed (γ²−1/4−γ₁²)y>.99|γ| and log(2z)/z decreases for z≥G. Summing all adverse terms and their multiplicities, the relative cost is ≤.049 sup_{z≥G} z² exp(−.96z)<1. This proves (−1)^j S^(j)(y)>0 on the whole open half-line for those orders.

The difference written above is Σ m_λ t^n(−λ²)^j/(t−λ²)^{n+j+1}. It is the integral of (−1)^j S^(j)(y) against t^n y^{n+j} exp(−ty)/(n+j)!, strictly positive. The interchange is absolute: integrating the moduli separately produces in the tail O_{t,n,j}(|γ|^{−2n−2}) per zero. The M_n are recovered from real data of ξ: M_0=L(√t)/√t by parity and centred partial fractions, and M_n=t^n(−1)^n M_0^(n)(t)/n!.

If the inequality held at ALL orders j for a single t>0, the classical Hausdorff theorem would give a positive measure on [0,1] with moments M_n. Its generating function would be holomorphic outside the real cut [1,∞). The effective generating function near zero is Σ m_λ/[t(1−z)−λ²], meromorphic with non-real poles if there are zeros off the axis. The residues of nodes with equal λ² add with the same sign, without cancellation. The continuation excludes such poles. Under RH the measure exists directly at the points tw∈(0,1). The index already records the finite-order heat/Hausdorff barrier (phase-101, 033/037); the classical criterion is not proposed as a new solution. What is certified here is the explicit band in this POWER sequence, simultaneous in n and t. Positivity of individual differences of bounded order does not by itself provide the sign for every polynomial square of the two sectors.

**Difference orders without limit: a fixed row and the variation of a complete diagonal.** Write A(n,j;t)=Σ_{h=0}^j(−1)^h binom(j,h) M_{n+h}(t). For FIXED n≥0 and t>0 one has, unconditionally,
A(n,j;t) ∼ Γ(n+1/2) j^(−n−1/2) log j /(4π√t) as j grows.
Thus control of the tails of each row separately can hold even if RH fails. The antecedent 255 on a decisive row refers to another observable.

Indeed, put z=−λ² and Y=√(jt). The summand of A is m t^n(t+z)^(−n−1)[z/(t+z)]^j. For |γ|=Yv, on each compact subset of 0<v<∞, divided by m t⁻¹ j^(−n−1) it converges uniformly to v^(−2n−2)exp(−1/v²); it suffices to expand log(1+t/z), since z=γ²+O(|γ|) uniformly. By Riemann–von Mangoldt, the counting measure of |γ|/Y with multiplicities and both signs, divided by Y log j, converges on those compact sets to dv/(2π). To justify the step in the tails, |t+z|≳γ² and |z/(t+z)|≤exp(−c_t t/γ²) by Re z≥γ²−1/4. On the intervals v∈[2^l,2^{l+1}] the count O(Y2^l log(2+Y2^l)) gives, after normalizing, a majorant C_{n,t} 2^{−(2n+1)l}(1+max(l,0))exp(−c'_t 2^{−2l}), summable in l∈ℤ (if Y2^{l+1}<14 there are no nodes). The remaining integral is Γ(n+1/2)/2 by substitution. This proves the equivalent, without uniformity in n.

To keep the information lost at fixed n, use only t=1 and the binomial variation of the diagonal n+j=N:
V_N=Σ_{n=0}^N binom(N,n)|A(n,N−n;1)|.
Then the ordinary limit exists
lim V_N^(1/N) = sup_{λ=b+iγ} (1+|z|)/|1+z| = sup_{λ} √(1+4b²/|1−λ²|²).
The sum WITHOUT moduli equals exactly M_0(1)>0 by the binomial formula. Under RH, V_N=M_0(1) for all N. Outside RH, the total binomial mass of negative entries, (V_N−M_0(1))/2, grows exponentially on ALL large diagonals. A subsequence with V_N=exp(o(N)) would suffice. It is a collective variation criterion, not one of tails row by row.

Proof. Let x=1/(1+z); the summand of A at t=1 is m x·x^n(1−x)^j. The triangle inequality gives V_N≤(Σm|x|)L^N, L=sup(|x|+|1−x|). The second expression for L follows from |z|−Re z=2b². If L>1 it is attained, since the ratios tend to 1 in height. Choose a maximizer z₀ and θ=arg z₀. The modulus of the sum of the diagonal with factors exp(inθ) is ≤V_N, and its complex value is Σ m x[(z+exp(iθ))/(1+z)]^N. At z₀ the modulus of the base is L. Equality at another node would require arg z=θ and the same ratio (1+|z|)/|1+z|. On the half-line z=v exp(iθ), with sin θ≠0, the square of the ratio is 1+2v(1−cos θ)/(1+2v cos θ+v²), strictly decreasing for v>1, the range of all nodes. Hence equality requires z=z₀. The preimages λ,−λ have the same coefficient x and their multiplicities add. All other bases have modulus ≤L′<L by discreteness and their limit 1 in height. The remaining sum is O((L′)^N Σm|x|), while the dominant group has constant modulus times L^N. If L=1 all nodes are on the axis and the real summands are positive. This proves the limit in both cases. The direction θ is used to prove the floor; the arithmetic definition of V_N does not need to know it. Z2 gives L²≤1+(G²+3/4)^(−2) but does not give L=1.

**Positivity in a region of growing rows.** In the same table at t=1 there exist δ>0 and finite J such that A(n,j;1)>0 for j≥J and 0≤n≤δ√j. The proof does not use the verification up to G; it only uses the critical strip, the initial height >14 and Riemann–von Mangoldt with remainder O(log T). Numerical values for δ,J are not given here.

More precisely, if n→∞ and a=n+1=o(√j), put Y=√(j/a), W=Y/√a and B(y)=y^{2j}/(1+y²)^{j+a}. Then
A(n,j;1) ∼ B(Y) W log(Y)/√(2π).
At this scale W→∞ and W/Y→0. The summand of the centred zero b+iγ is B(γ−ib), understanding B as a rational function (by parity one can consider positive heights and their conjugates). On the real axis B attains its maximum at Y. With r=y/Y,
d log B(y)/d log r = 2a(1−r²)/(r²+Y^(−2)).
For y=Y+vW and v in a compact set, integrating this identity gives log(B(y)/B(Y))=−2v²+o(1) uniformly. The imaginary shift of modulus ≤1/2 leaves the same equivalent: on the vertical segment the logarithmic derivative 2a(Y²−y²)/(y(1+y²)) is O(a(|γ−Y|+1)/Y²)=O((|v|+1)/W). The count of |γ| by Riemann–von Mangoldt, divided by W log Y, on [Y+v₁W,Y+v₂W] tends to (v₂−v₁)/π for fixed v₁,v₂. The remainder O(log Y) disappears precisely because W→∞.

Absolute control outside compact sets. For y=√(γ²+b²) and z=−(b+iγ)² the exact modulus of the summand is B(y)(1−4b²/(1+y²)²)^{−(j+a)/2}. On Y/2≤y≤2Y the additional factor is exp(O(j/Y⁴))=1+o(1). The previous real derivative gives B(y)/B(Y)≤exp(−C((y−Y)/W)²) on that band with C absolute; y−|γ|=O(1/|γ|). By the count on intervals of length W, each cell weighs O(W log Y) zeros. Therefore the cells more than K widths away contribute, normalizing by B(Y)W log Y, O(Σ_{l≥K−2}exp(−C′l²)).

For y<Y/2 use y≥14, log(1+y⁻²)≥.99/y² and the additional factor ≤exp(.01j/y²) for large j. Dividing by B(Y) one gets at most exp(a[2log(1/r)+1.01−.98/r²]), exponentially small in a for r≤1/2. There are O(Y log Y) zeros in this zone, so their relative contribution is o(1). For y≥2Y the modulus correction is 1+o(1) and the quotient is ≤(1+o(1))exp(1.01a)r^(−2a), using (j+a)log(1+Y⁻²)≤1.01a. Summing dyadically with O(2^lY log(2^lY)) zeros per block gives o(1) again. Integrating the central profile exp(−2v²)/π produces the indicated constant.

Finally, if there were no eventually positive strip δ√j, for each integer l one could choose j≥l and some n≤√j/l with A≤0. If the n have a bounded subsequence, this contradicts the fixed-row equivalent already proved. Otherwise a subsequence with n→∞ contradicts the present estimate. Thus the hypothetical negativities of the large diagonals must escape at least from this common strip; the joint negative mass outside it still has no subexponential bound.

**Pointwise positivity on the opposite side of the diagonal and localization of a possible failure.** At t=1, N=n+j and G=3·10¹², put S=1/(1+(G−40)²). For ALL sufficiently large N, each entry A(n,N−n;1) with n/N≥S is strictly positive. This second sector differs from the previous one n≤δ√j: here the comparison is with a verified zero near the upper end of the verification. It is not claimed that the initial N is computationally reachable.

Detail. With z=−λ², x=1/(1+z), define L_λ=|x|+|1−x| and p_λ=|x|/L_λ=1/(1+|z|). For an exterior zero, p_λ≤P=1/(1+G²) and log L_λ≤1/(2G⁴) by the identity of the previous variation. There is a critical ordinate γ_A between G−40 and G−20: Z3 of paper 46 gives an increment of the main term ≥20 log((G−40)/(2π))/(2π)>80 and the sum of the two errors <16; Z2 identifies the axis. Write p_A=1/(1+γ_A²); then P+30/G³<p_A≤S<2/G². For s=n/N compare the product |x|^n|1−x|^{N−n} with p_A^n(1−p_A)^{N−n} of the critical zero. The logarithm of the quotient per factor is
log L_λ+s log(p_λ/p_A)+(1−s)log((1−p_λ)/(1−p_A)).
It is decreasing in s, and at p_A it equals log L_λ−D(p_A||p_λ), with D the binary divergence. By Taylor with respect to the first argument, D(p_A||p_λ)≥(p_A−p_λ)²/(2p_A), since D′′(v)=1/[v(1−v)]≥1/p_A on the range. Thus for s≥S the quotient over the N factors is ≤exp(−N/G⁴). Even summing the exterior ones with their prefactors m|x| (summable), their total modulus is less than the term of the single chosen critical zero, with prefactor p_A, for N large uniformly in s. The other critical zeros contribute positively. This argument proves the sign of the individual entry, not just a bound on the total mass of that region.

If RH fails, an exponential negative excess can be localized in a window of a BOUNDED number of entries per diagonal. There exist a rational slope 0<s<S and a fixed integer K such that, for all sufficiently large N, between ⌊sN⌋ and ⌊sN⌋+K there is an n with binom(N,n)A(n,N−n;1)≤−c_s Λ^N/√N, for some Λ>1. To see this, fix a node z₀ maximizing L_λ=L>1 and take p₀=1/(1+|z₀|). At s=p₀ the rate per weighted entry is L_λ exp(−D(s||p_λ)). Only z₀ and its conjugate maximize: imposing simultaneously L_λ=L and p_λ=p₀ fixes |z| and cos(arg z). The coincidences from λ and −λ add with equal coefficient. The tail of rates tends to zero uniformly on a small compact set around p₀>0, because |x|→0; a strict gap to the rest remains. Dominance and a rate Λ>1 are preserved at some rational slope s close to p₀, chosen in (0,S).

At n=⌊sN⌋+l for 0≤l≤K fixed, the two conjugate contributions give a cosine whose phase advances in steps −arg z₀. This quantity is not zero and its modulus is <π/2. Within a fixed number of steps one enters the arc cos≤−1/2, for any initial phase (it suffices to run through one full turn plus one step). The exponential ratio between the other contributions and the dominant one is uniformly less than one in that window; they are summed using Σm|x|<∞. Stirling, for fixed interior s and bounded shifts, provides the prefactor ≍N^(−1/2) and the rate with the entropy indicated before. The exponential bound refers to the entry multiplied by the binomial coefficient.

Consequently a subexponential bound along a subsequence of diagonals for the largest weighted negative part in ⌊sN⌋≤n≤⌊sN⌋+⌈log N⌉, for each rational 0<s<S, would suffice. This does not require knowing K or a hypothetical zero when defining the test. Those bounds are missing for arbitrarily small positive slopes. The tools of binomial concentration and dominant poles are classical; the pointwise range in this table uses Z2 and Z3.

**Exact transport to round 207 by a positive average of scales.** The central candidate does not constitute an independent route: for z=−λ², a=n+1, b=j≥1 and k_{a,b}(v)=v^a/(1+v)^{a+b} one has t A(n,j;t)=Σm k_{a,b}(t/z). In particular 4^K t A(K−1,K;t)=b_K(√t) is literally the packet of 207 (its spectral expression is used, well defined also for 0<u≤1/2). Moreover, any interior entry is an EXACT positive average of that packet for a single order K, varying only the scale. For K≥max(a,b), let U,V be independent with beta laws of parameters (a,K−a),(b,K−b), using the constant 1 if the second parameter vanishes. Then
t A(n,j;t) = B(a,b)/(4^K B(K,K)) · E[b_K(√(tV/U))].
As K varies the support of scales does not in general stay within a bounded band. This links the two routes directly on the whole interior, beyond identifying their growth rates.

Proof. For x>0, the Mellin transform of k_{a,b} is B(a+s,b−s) on −a<Re s<b. That of E[k_{K,K}(xV/U)] is B(K+s,K−s) E[U^s] E[V^(−s)]. The gamma quotients of the two expectations give exactly B(K,K) B(a+s,b−s)/B(a,b). Tonelli on the real line and Mellin uniqueness prove the kernel identity. It extends holomorphically to Re x>0: there |1+x|≥(1+|x|)/√2, also after any positive dilation, and the kernel remains uniformly bounded at fixed K. The same bound and the real positive identity majorize the integrated sum of moduli by a constant depending on K,a,b times Σm k_{a,b}(t/|z|), finite because a≥1. This justifies applying the identity to each complex node and summing.

**Concrete simultaneous bound.** At ALL parameters t>0 one has A(n,j;t)>0 if max(n+1,j)≤⌊πG/2⌋. In particular b_K(u)>0 for every scale u>0 and every 1≤K≤⌊πG/2⌋. At an exterior node |arg z|≤2 arctan(1/(2|γ|))<1/G. As t>0 varies, arg(t+z) lies between 0 and arg z. The unreduced phase of the summand of A is j arg z−(a+j)arg(t+z); its modulus is bounded by max(a,j)|arg z|<π/2 on that square. All real parts are positive separately. For critical nodes the summands are real positive. The edge j=0 is included directly by the same argument. This adds to the strip j≤10⁹ with no bound on n, which had other quantifiers. The explicit ceiling is of order 4.7·10¹² in each index, but remains finite. The identification with 207 and the positive transport do not provide the inequality for all orders of the packet.

**From the central packet to a uniform square of order 10¹⁸.** For K=10¹⁸ one has b_K(u)>0 for ALL u>0. By the beta transport above, A(n,j;t)>0 for all t>0 and max(n+1,j)≤10¹⁸ (for j=0 use the difference-free row already proved). Moreover b_K(u)>0 for K≥10¹⁸ and u≥10⁴√K, with no upper bound on K. Nearby references: 205 proved rows and cones at a fixed rate; 207–210 contain the packet and its concentration. The step here is to pay uniformly for the adverse terms with the local mass guaranteed by Z3, so that all scales can be mixed in the square.

Write y=|λ|, z=−λ², s=log(y/u), φ=arg z and h=4u²z/(u²+z)². Then h=sech²(s+iφ/2), |tan(φ/2)|=|Re λ|/|γ|. One may take |arg h|≤|tanh s|/|γ| and sech²s≤|h|≤sech²s(1+1/γ²), by the complex cosh formula. On the axis h is real positive. At a node with Re(h^K)<0 one needs √K|s|≥|γ|/√K, since if K|arg h|≤1 the real part is positive.

First K=10¹⁸ and u≥G/2. Set D=u/√K≥1500. By Z3 there are at least .01D log u positive ordinates in [u,u+D/2], counted with multiplicity: the derivative of the main term is log(v/(2π))/(2π) and each endpoint error is <log(2u) in that range. There |s|≤.6/√K since y−|γ|<1/|γ|, and K|arg h|≤.6√K/|γ|<.001. Each contributes Re(h^K)>.1 by log cosh s≤s²/2. The adverse mass can only come from √K|s|≥3000, since the off-axis nodes have |γ|>G. For them |h|^K≤2 sech^{2K}s.

To make the cost explicit, the cell l≤√K|s|<l+1 contains at most 10⁵ D log(2u)(1+l)exp(2(l+1)/√K) nodes of both signs. Indeed the two intervals in y have length ≤2D exp((l+1)/√K) each; to count in |γ| they are enlarged by one unit, and 175 is used, ≤100 log(3+|j|) per integer cell. Moreover log(3+y)≤log(4u)+(l+1)/√K. The inequality log cosh x≥min(x²,|x|)/4 gives sech^{2K}s≤exp(−l/2) for l≥1. Hence the cells l≥2999 cost less than .0001 D log u: it suffices to sum (1+l)exp(−l/3) from 2999 with the previous prefactor. This leaves a positive margin even discarding all the other favourable terms.

For u<G/2, Z3 and Z2 give an axis zero at .6G≤γ_A≤.61G. With H(y)=4u²y²/(u²+y²)², the quotient H(G)/H(γ_A) is <.75: it increases with u up to G/2, and there the bound holds even with γ_A=.61G, since H decreases after u. The absolute total of the exterior nodes divided by H(γ_A)^K is ≤exp(K/G²)(.75)^K Σ_{exterior}4u²/(γ²H(G)), since H(y)≤H(G) and H(y)≤4u²/γ². The last sum is ≤.049(u²+G²)²/G² using Σm/γ²<.049, with multiplicities in all sums. The result is less than one for the K considered, at every u of this band. A single critical term suffices here.

Finally, for K≥10¹⁸ and u≥10⁴√K, the count and the mass of the central interval above remain valid. In y<u/2 one has H(y)≤.64, |h|^K≤(.64 exp(1/196))^K and by Z3 there are O(u log(2u)) nodes (by 175 the constant 1000 suffices). This is negligible against the floor .001D log u. In y≥u/2 we have |γ|≥u/3, so that K/γ²≤9·10⁻⁸ and every adverse contribution requires √K|s|>3300. The same explicit cell-by-cell sum applies. Positivity has not been proved for unbounded orders at EVERY scale: when u is fixed and K→∞ the new band does not cover it.

**From positive entries to a bound for all real coefficients.** For t>0 write ℒ(x^i)=M_i(t), extended linearly, and L(F)=ℒ(x^h(1−x)^l F) for integers h,l≥0. Let N≥2m≥2 with h+N+1≤10¹⁸ and l+N≤10¹⁸. For real coefficients c₀,…,c_m define P(x)=Σ_i c_i binom(m,i)x^i(1−x)^{m−i} and P₂ with the same weights but coefficients c_i². With ε=m/(N−m), one obtains
L(P²) ≥ (1+ε)L(P)²/L(1) − ε L(P₂).
Here L(1)>0 and L(P₂)≥0. The inequality controls every square with mixed signs, including coefficients with zero weighted sum. For the two sectors of the odd POWER decomposition one applies, up to positive scale factors, the pairs (h,l)=(n,0) and (n+1,1): the polynomial variable is x=tw, and ℒ already includes the weight w. It is a lower bound with a corrector term, not a PSD certification of the uncorrected block.

Direct proof. Assign to each word of N bits with k ones the probability L(x^k(1−x)^{N−k})/L(1). All are positive by the certified square and the sum is one by the binomial theorem. The law is invariant under permuting the positions. For a subset S of m positions put f(S)=c_{number of ones in S}. If S and T are uniform samples of size m forced to be disjoint, the mean over words and samples of f(S)f(T) is L(P²)/L(1): with S,T fixed, summing over the remaining positions only multiplies by (x+(1−x))^{N−2m}. Analogously the means of f and f² are L(P)/L(1) and L(P₂)/L(1).

For each fixed word, on the space of functions of S with uniform measure, the operation Kf(S) that averages over disjoint T is symmetric and preserves constants. Its smallest eigenvalue is −m/(N−m). Indeed, the indicator functions e_U(S)=1_{U⊂S} of the sets U of size ≤j generate nested subspaces V_j up to the whole space at j=m. For |U|=j,
K e_U = [(m)_j/(N−m)_j] Σ_{W⊂U, including U} (−1)^|W| e_W,
with falling factorials (the sum is over all subsets). This is counting the T that contain U when S avoids it. On V_j modulo V_{j−1} one gets the scalar (−1)^j(m)_j/(N−m)_j, and by symmetry it is the same on the corresponding orthogonal complement. The moduli for j≥1 do not exceed m/(N−m), attained at j=1. Separating the mean of f for that word gives ⟨f,Kf⟩≥(1+ε)(mean f)²−ε mean f². Averaging over the word and applying Jensen to its conditional mean gives the statement.

The corrector is optimal if the only information is positive N-bit data and binomial consistency. Fix exactly 0<k<N ones, distribute them uniformly and take c_i=i−mk/N. The function of S lies in V₁ perpendicular to the constants and is nonzero; there is equality with zero mean and positive second moment. This law defines a functional up to degree N through the probabilities in the degree-N Bernstein basis (without the binomial factor). If strict positivity on each word is required, mixing with an arbitrarily small proportion of independent fair bits preserves a negative value by continuity. Therefore eliminating the ε term requires additional information from the real moments of ξ. This argument uses the elementary spectrum of the average over disjoint subsets (Kneser graph); it does not presuppose a positive measure on [0,1].

**Localisation of the corrector by total number of ones.** In the preceding certificate the first-order loss can be measured with a one-dimensional table, before applying a cubic-order bound to the remainder. Let q_k=binom(N,k)L(x^k(1−x)^{N−k})/L(1). For each k take I hypergeometric (N,k,m), μ_k=E[c_I], v_k=Var(c_I), d_k=Cov(c_I,I)^2/Var(I), with d_k=0 if Var(I)=0. Write ε₃=(m)_3/(N−m)_3 for m≥3 and zero for m<3. Then
L(P²)/L(1) ≥ Σ_k q_k [μ_k²−ε d_k−ε₃(v_k−d_k)].
To verify it, with the word fixed, the projector onto V₁ minus the constants commutes with the permutations preserving the ones. Its image of c_I is a centred linear function of I: averaging any combination of position indicators under these permutations leaves two coefficients, one per colour, and the sample size is fixed. Its squared norm is exactly d_k by one-variable regression. Degree two has a nonnegative eigenvalue and the remaining odd degrees have modulus at most ε₃. The orthogonal decomposition and the average with q_k give the formula. For m=1 it is an equality. In particular the linear cost depends exclusively on the local regression, and the favourable term Σq_k μ_k² keeps the dispersion between compositions that Jensen discarded. It remains to compare both quantities for the specific laws of ξ uniformly in the degree. Mere positivity of q_k admits the fixed-composition obstruction of the previous section.

**Falsifier in the moments of ξ themselves for the truncated comparison.** Choose t=γ₁² with the first critical ordinate 14<γ₁<15, h=1000, l=0, m=2 and c_i=(−1)^i. For every 4≤N≤10¹⁸−1001 the right-hand side of the NORMALISED refined bound is strictly negative. This excludes even choosing the elevation degree N adaptively within the proved square to force that comparison. The verified locations of the first two ordinates (γ₂>21) are used.

In the pure evaluation at x=1/2, P(x)=(1−2x)² and the square vanishes. The only contribution omitted at m=2 is degree two of the disjoint operator, with eigenvalue 2/((N−2)(N−3)). Its mean energy is (N−3)/(N−1): under independent fair bits the vector over pairs has coordinates that are products of two independent signs, with identity second-moment matrix. The trace of the degree-two projector is binom(N,2)−N (the N position indicators are independent as functions on pairs, since a_i+a_j=0 for all pairs implies a=0). Dividing the trace by binom(N,2) gives the energy. Hence the truncated side in the fair urn is exactly −2/((N−1)(N−2)).

To transfer it to ξ, the unnormalised composition masses are proportional to Σ_λ m_λ x_λ^1001 binom(N,k)x_λ^k(1−x_λ)^(N−k), x_λ=t/(t−λ²). The first pair contributes mass B≥(1/2)^1001 with fair binomial law. At the other nodes |x|<.35 using Re(−λ²)≥21²−1/4 and t<225. Moreover Σm|x|<12 by Σm/γ²<.049 and |x|≤225/γ². At the critical nodes |x|+|1−x|=1; at the exterior ones this factor is ≤sec(1/G) by the angle between t and −λ² and projection onto the bisector. Its N-th power is <2. The sum-of-moduli norm of the remainder divided by B is thus ≤48(.70)^1000. After normalising, the distance in sum norm from the fair binomial is less than 10^(−150). The function of k being averaged, μ_k²−ε d_k, has modulus at most one. The error is smaller than the explicit loss even at the maximal admissible N. The failure is due to having discarded the favourable degree two. It is not a negative value of the square for ξ.

**Exact sign for the whole sequence of powers of the falsifier.** At the same tilt h=1000 and t=γ₁² one has L((1−2x)^{2d})>0 for EVERY integer d≥0. For d=2 even the second ordinate suffices: 21<γ₂<22 gives .28<x₂<.35 and the second term contributes more than .28^1001·.30^4 on the scale of the unnormalised sum. The exterior ones cost at most 12(225/G²)^1000, since |1−2x|<1 by Re z>0.

For general d write g=|γ|, z=−λ², R=(z−t)/(z+t). The terms are x^1001 R^{2d}, up to the same positive factor. Those on the axis are nonnegative. For g≥G and w=dt/g², one has |arg x|≤2/g, |arg R|≤4t/g³ (the real part of the numerator of R after rationalising is |z|²−t², the imaginary part 2t Im z), and |R|^{2d}≤exp(−2w), because 1−|R|²=4t Re z/|z+t|²≥2t/g². Hence any term with negative real part requires w≥g/10: otherwise its phase has modulus ≤2002/g+.8. In particular w≥G/10.

Set H=G+sqrt(dt). Z3 guarantees some ordinate in [H,2H] by difference of the main term and endpoint errors less than log(3H) each. In that band |x|≥t/(5H²), the phase is ≤2002/H+8/H and |R|^{2d}≥exp(−10), since 1−|R|²≤5t/g² and log(1−v)≥−2v for v≤1/2. That term has real part at least B=(t/(5H²))^1001 exp(−10)/2, even if its zero were off the axis. For each adverse term H≤10w+10w^{3/2}≤20w^{3/2}. Thus exp(−2w)/B≤2 exp(10−2w)(2000w³)^1001<1/24 for w≥3·10¹¹ (by logarithms and monotonicity). Since Σm|x|<12 and |x|≤1, the entire adverse mass is below B/2. This covers d without ceiling, including the transition from the second ordinate towards the tail. The even exponent identifies squares of an individual power; the argument does not control the cancellations in linear combinations of distinct powers.

**Complete shifted block in the variable R.** Fix any t>0, an integer h≥0 and a degree m. For d sufficiently large (depending on t,h,m), the spectral form Σm_λ x^{h+1}R^{2d}P(x)^2 is positive definite simultaneously for every nonzero real polynomial of degree ≤m. This controls all the cancellations among R^d,...,R^{d+m}, since R=1−2x. Z2 is not required. The threshold is asymptotic.

Indeed, let a=h+1 and H=√(dt). In polynomial coordinates y=dx the matrix, multiplied by d^a/(H log H), converges entrywise to the moment matrix of the density y^{a−3/2} exp(−4y)/(2π) on y>0. For the moment of order r≤2m the rescaled summand before dividing by H log H is (dx)^{a+r}R^{2d}. On each compact set of 0<v=g/H<∞ we have dx→v^(−2) and R^{2d}→exp(−4/v²) uniformly, also off the axis, since |Re λ|≤1/2. By Z3 the counting measure of both ordinates in v, divided by H log H, converges on compacts to dv/π. Substituting y=v^(−2) gives the stated density.

Control of tails. For g above a fixed constant depending on t, the modulus of the summand is ≤C v^(−2(a+r)) exp(−c/v²) by 1−|R|²=4t Re z/|z+t|² and |x|≤C t/g². The remaining nodes are finite in number, each |R|<1, and they vanish even after multiplying by a power of d. In each annulus V≤v<2V reaching the range of large g there are at most C HV log(3+HV) nodes by Z3. Summing over dyadic V, after normalisation, near zero the exponential exp(−c/(4V²)) dominates; for V≥1, C V^{1−2(a+r)}(1+log V) dominates, summable even with a=1. Matrix convergence follows for fixed m. The limit matrix is positive definite because the density is strictly positive on every interior interval and a nonzero polynomial has only finitely many roots. Its smallest eigenvalue is positive; stability in fixed dimension and the invertible change x↔dx prove the claim for arbitrary coefficients, even if they depend on d. The order of quantifiers allows d≥d₀(m,t,h); it gives no uniformity as m grows at fixed d.

**Sublinear width sufficient to detect any exterior zero.** Fix t=1,h=0. It would suffice to prove semidefiniteness along an unbounded sequence of integer shifts d with width m(d)=⌈10^(−24)d/log d⌉ (d≥2). If an exterior zero exists, ALL those blocks are indefinite for d sufficiently large (the constant positive direction in P follows from the preceding limit). The deduction uses the discreteness of the spectrum in addition to its density.

Indeed choose its non-real node x₀ and the conjugate, with R₀=1−2x₀ nonzero. Write b=−log|R₀|. Since |x₀|≤1/G² and |R₀|≥1−2/G², one has b<3/G². Choose b/2<c<10^(−24). Put Y=d/(log d)^4. Form the real polynomial B_d having as simple roots all the distinct nodes with g≤Y except the chosen pair, and normalise its modulus at x₀ to one by a positive scalar. Its degree k=O(Y log Y)=o(d/log d). For any node x one has |B_d(x)|≤C^k with C fixed: the distance from x₀ to the rest of the distinct nodes is positive since they only accumulate at zero, and the diameter of the set is finite. Multiplicities do not affect the vanishing.

Take j=⌊cd/log d⌋ and F_d(x)=R^d B_d(x)(x/|x₀|)^j (A_d+D_d x), with A_d,D_d real. Choose them so that F_d(x₀)=i/√x₀ (any fixed root). Evaluation of the linear factor at x₀ is a real isomorphism onto ℂ, so that |A_d|+|D_d|≤C₀ exp(bd) uniformly in the phases. The two nodes each contribute −1 per unit of multiplicity to the sum Σm_λ x F_d(x)^2. At the remaining nodes with g>Y, use |x|≤Y^(−2), |R|≤1. Then log sup|F_d|≤bd+O(k)+j log(Y^(−2)/|x₀|)+O(1)=(b−2c)d+o(d). That whole tail tends to zero in the form because Σm_λ|x|<∞. The extra degree over R^d is k+j+1≤m(d) eventually. Under RH each term of the form is positive or zero, so the equivalence is proved. The explicit coefficient uses Z2; the width is asymptotic and its semidefiniteness was not obtained.

**Growing width effectively proved.** At the same scale t=1,h=0, for every d sufficiently large the shifted matrix is positive definite with m=⌊(log d)/(32 log log d)⌋. Here and in the sublinear detection the logarithms are natural. The form is compared directly with the one obtained by moving each zero horizontally to the axis, keeping its ordinate and multiplicity.

Write u=d/(1+g²), y=dx, r=1−2u/d. Normalise the real polynomial p in the variable y by sup_[1,2]|p|=1, which runs through all directions of the block. One has |p(s)|+|p′(s)|≤(C(1+|s|))^{m+1} for complex s with an absolute constant: expand in T_j(2s−3), whose expansion coefficients are bounded by 2 by orthogonality of the cosine, use the Chebyshev recurrence and Cauchy on the circle of radius one. By Markov on [1,2], |p′|≤2m² there. Hence there is an interior interval of length ≥1/(8m²) on which |p|≥1/2. Its preimage in g has length ≫√d/m² at height comparable to √d. Z3 by difference at the endpoints gives ≫√d log d/m² ordinates in that preimage, since the counting error is O(log d). There r^{2d} is bounded below by a positive constant. The projected sum Σm_λ (u/d) r^{2d}p(u)^2 thus has floor ≫log d/(√d m²), uniform in p.

To compare the sums put U=(log d)². When u≤U one has g≫√(d/U), |x−u/d|≤C(u/d)/g by |z−g²|≤g+1. Also |R|,|r|≤1, so that |R^{2d}−r^{2d}|≤4d|x−u/d|. On the segment [u,y] the bounds for p,p′ are ≤(C(1+U))^{m+1}. By differences of products the error per node is ≤(u/d) d^{−1/2+1/8+o(1)}: the polylogarithmic factors are absorbed into o(1) and 2(m+1)log(C(1+U))≤(1/8+o(1))log d. The sum of u/d in that band is O(log² d/√d) by Z3 summing dyadic annuli in g from ≍√d/log d. Thus the aggregate error is o(the floor).

For u>U, at every g≥14 one has |y|≤2u and |R|^{2d}, |r|^{2d}≤exp(−c u) with absolute c>0, by 1−|R|²=4 Re z/|1+z|². The bound (C(1+2u))^{2(m+1)}≤exp(cu/2) holds uniformly from U for d large, since log(C(1+2u))/u decreases there. Using Σm_λ/(1+g²)<∞, both tails are O(exp(−cU/2)). Strict positivity of the original form remains. The choice 1/32 leaves slack and does not claim optimality. The asymptotic gap between this width and 10^(−24)d/log d persists.

**Polynomial width by normalisation with the weight.** Under the same hypotheses, for each 0<α<1/13 and every d sufficiently large there is definite positivity up to m=⌊d^α⌋. Keep u,y,r from above. Take U=A m with A a large constant and normalise sup_[0,U] exp(−2u)|p(u)|=1. On every unit interval of [0,U] containing u, iterated Markov gives |p^(j)(u)|≤exp(2u+2)(2m²)^j. Thus the derivative of exp(−2u)p(u) is O(m²) and there is a subinterval J of length ≍m^(−2) where its modulus exceeds 1/2. Trimming J by a constant fraction we may assume u≍v on J for some v between c/m² and U (take the upper half). In the preimage the heights are ≍√(d/v), and its length is ≫√d/(m² v^(3/2)). This length tends to infinity even for v=U. Z3 gives ≫√d log d/(m² v^(3/2)) ordinates there. Since r^d exp(2u)=1+O(U²/d) uniformly, the projected form has floor ≫log d/(√d m²√U).

Let δ=CU^(3/2)/√d, a bound for |y−u| on [0,U]. By Taylor and the preceding derivatives, exp(−2u)|p(y)−p(u)|=O(m²δ) since m²δ=o(1). Likewise R^d exp(2u)=1+O(δ+U²/d) by expanding the logarithm around 1. With |x/(u/d)−1|=O(√(U/d)), the absolute error of each term against its projection is O((u/d)(m²δ+U²/d+√(U/d))). The sum of u/d here is O(√U log d/√d) by dyadic counting. Dividing by the floor yields O(m⁴ U^(5/2)/√d + m² U³/d + m² U^(3/2)/√d)=o(1) for the stated choice.

To justify the tail without implicit constants depending on A, fix c>0 such that |R|^{2d},|r|^{2d}≤exp(−cu) for every node, as above. First choose a constant B>16/c. On [0,U/B] we have |p|≤exp(2U/B). By the Chebyshev expansion after rescaling that interval, for |y|≤2u and u≥U one has |p(y)|≤exp(2U/B)(C B u/U)^{m+1}, C absolute (also for y=u). Now choose A so large that 2(m+1) log(C B u/U)≤cu/4 for all u≥U and m large, using that log(C B s)/s decreases for s≥1. There remains a bound exp(−cu/2) for the product of the weight and the square, and summability of |x| and u/d gives an exponential error. This improvement uses the same comparison with projection; the substantive change is to prevent an unweighted global bound from amplifying the error at all nodes.

**Exact detection threshold if the exceptions are finite.** Suppose there is a finite nonempty set E of off-axis nodes and define b*=min_E(−log|R|)>0 at t=1,h=0. For m=⌊c d/log d⌋, c>0 fixed, the shifted blocks are eventually positive definite if c<b*/2 and eventually indefinite if c>b*/2. Equality is not decided. The second part is the isolation construction above, taking a node realising the minimum and a power coefficient strictly between b*/2 and c.

For the first, by Z3 one chooses a large fixed constant D such that every interval [s,s+D] contains an ordinate for s sufficiently large (the main increment is asymptotic to D log s/(2π) and the endpoint error is O(log s)). Pick an ordinate g_i in each [2D(m+i),2D(m+i)+D], 0≤i≤m. For m large all are critical under the finiteness hypothesis. Their real nodes x_i are ≍m^(−2) and |x_i−x_j|≥c₁|i−j|/m³ by the derivative of 1/(1+g²) and the separation. Normalise max_i |p(x_i)|=1, possible for every nonzero real p of degree ≤m. At a node of maximum the weight x_i R_i^{2d} is ≥c₂ m^(−2) exp(−C d/m²). All the remaining critical terms are nonnegative.

At each exterior node Lagrange interpolation bounds |p(x)| by (C m³)^m Σ_i 1/(i!(m−i)!) ≤(C′m²)^m (the spectral diameter is bounded). The joint absolute contribution of E is ≤C_E exp(−2b*d+4m log m+O(m)), multiplicities included. For c<b*/2 its exponent is ≤−η d for some η>0, while the preceding critical floor has logarithm o(d). Thus a positive sign holds simultaneously for all coefficients. By inclusion it also holds for any width o(d/log d), even bounded. This is a genuine conditional barrier: extending the proved width only up to d^α for every α<1 would still be compatible with a finite number of exceptions. It neither presupposes nor asserts that such exceptions exist for ξ.

**The boundary belongs to the positive regime and the inertia counts the visible pairs.** Under the same hypotheses and for the exact width m=⌊cd/log d⌋, the eventual number of negative eigenvalues is the number of DISTINCT conjugate pairs of exterior nodes with b=−log|R|<2c. The multiplicity of a node weights its contribution but does not increase the rank. Indeed, for b≥2c the previous per-node bound is O(exp(−4c d+4m log m+O(m))). Since log m=log d−log log d+log c+o(1), the exponent is ≤−4c d log log d/log d+O(d/log d), even at equality. This is smaller than the logarithm of the critical floor, which is −O(log d+d/m²). Hence the form composed of the axis and all pairs with b≥2c is eventually positive definite. Each of the remaining pairs adds a form of negative index at most one: its contribution is a positive multiple of Re(w²), with w=√x R^d p(x). Requiring Im w=0 imposes only one real linear equation. This proves the upper bound and in particular settles the equality c=b*/2.

For the opposite bound apply the isolation construction simultaneously to the r pairs with b<2c, choosing a common c′ between max(b/2) of those pairs and c (if r=0 there is nothing to do). Each polynomial constructed annihilates the other chosen pairs and contributes a strictly negative diagonal at its pair. The cross Gram elements in the tail tend to zero by the uniform isolation bounds and Σm|x|<∞. For fixed r one obtains a negative definite compression of dimension r. This last argument works for any finite selection even if E is infinite: then b→0 along a sequence, and for each c>0 the negative index of these blocks tends to infinity with d. If E is empty the form is positive definite directly. The criterion quantifies the spectral defect; to obtain the global sign an unconditional inertia bound is still needed.

**Precise exponential tolerance in coefficient norm.** Fix explicitly the basis 1,x,…,x^m of the factor multiplying R^d and the Euclidean norm of those coefficients. Let D_d=max(0,−λ_min) of the real matrix with entries Σm_λ x^{i+j+1} R^{2d}, 0≤i,j≤⌊cd/log d⌋. If E is nonempty finite and b*=min_E b<2c, then lim (log D_d)/d=−2b*. If E is infinite the limit is 0 for every c>0. This measures the size, in addition to the preceding index.

Indeed |x|<1/100 on the whole spectrum for t=1. On the coefficient sphere |p(x)|²≤1/(1−|x|²)≤2. Discarding the axis one obtains D_d≤2Σ_E m_λ |x| exp(−2b_λ d). Conversely, for any target node with b<2c the preceding isolating test has quadratic value ≤−1 eventually. Its coefficient norm is ≤exp(bd+o(d)): in the sum norm, which is submultiplicative, each normalised linear factor of B_d costs at most a constant depending on the chosen node, since the denominators are away from zero. The normalised power costs |x₀|^(−j)=exp(O(j)), and the last factor costs O(exp(bd)); k+j=o(d). The Euclidean norm does not exceed that sum norm. By Rayleigh, D_d≥exp(−2bd−o(d)). Take the finite minimum or, if there are infinitely many, apply the inequality to each fixed b of a sequence tending to zero and then take the limit. The limits in height and shift are not interchanged.

In particular, with c=10^(−24), a matrix lower bound −exp(−10^(−24)d) I along an unbounded subsequence would ALREADY suffice: Z2 and b<3/G² give 2b<10^(−24) for every exterior one. If there are no exceptions, D_d=0. A fixed multiplicative constant or exp(o(d)) in the error is allowed. The tolerance depends on the specified basis; that unconditional estimate at this width is not known.

**Unconditional bound on the defect for ALL widths in the preceding normalisation.** Write M_{d,m} for the matrix in the basis 1,x,…,x^m. If M_{d,k} is positive semidefinite, then for every m≥k one has
λ_min(M_{d,m}) ≥ −C ((k+1)/(2 e d))^{k+1}
with C absolute. In particular, for each α∈(0,1/13), taking k=⌊d^α⌋, for every d sufficiently large and any m the defect is at most exp(−(1−α+o(1))d^α log d). The same lower bound holds for the continuous form on ℓ² coefficient sequences. It is an estimate of the sought matrix even at its sufficient width; the exponent obtained remains sublinear.

Indeed, q=|x|, x=(1+z)^(−1), z=−λ². Since g≥14 and |Re λ|≤1/2, |Im z|≤g, Re z≥g²−1/4 and Re x/q=(1+Re z)/|1+z|>.99. Together with q<.01 this gives 1−|R|²=4(Re x−q²)≥2q. Hence |R|^{2d}≤exp(−2dq). For p with coefficient norm one and its truncation p_k, geometric Cauchy–Schwarz gives |p|,|p_k|≤(1−q²)^(−1/2) and |p−p_k|≤q^{k+1}(1−q²)^(−1/2). The error of both squares, even at the complex nodes, is ≤3q^{k+1}. Summing with the weight and using Σm_λ q<∞, it suffices to maximise q^{k+1}exp(−2dq) over q≥0, whose maximum is the one stated. This proof also gives an operator-norm bound for the difference between M_{d,m} and M_{d,k} extended by zeros, by real symmetry. For m<k inclusion is used. The extension to ℓ² follows by the same bounded evaluation and density. Even if positivity were proved up to k of order d/log d, this truncation estimate for larger widths would only give an exponent of order d log log d/log d; it must not be confused with the isolation implication that uses the sign of the sufficient block itself.

**Stable transfer of the defect to all of ℓ² via interpolation at the nodes.** Let D_{d,k} and D_{d,∞} be the defects in coefficient norm. Uniformly in d, for k large,
D_{d,k} ≤ D_{d,∞} ≤ C k³ D_{d,k} + exp(−2k log k + 2k log log k + O(k)).
Unlike truncation at zero, here for k=⌊cd/log d⌋ the transfer exponent is −2cd+o(d). Hence the sufficient error exp(−cd+o(d)) in the block is preserved at the same rate in the whole operator.

Proof. Order the distinct nodes ξ_j=x_λ by decreasing modulus, keeping conjugate pairs together in case of ties. Choose the first n=k or k+1 so that the set is closed under conjugation (if the cut at k+1 splits a pair, k is used). By Z3 and |x|≤1/g² one has |ξ_j|≤C(log(2j)/j)²: the number of nodes of modulus ≥q is O(q^(−1/2) log(2/q)). Also Σ_j |ξ_j|<∞. For p with real coefficients of ℓ² norm one, let I p be its Newton interpolant at those n nodes. It is real and of degree ≤k. The Newton coefficient of order l<n is the Cauchy integral of p(ζ)/∏_{j≤l+1}(ζ−ξ_j) over |ζ|=1−1/n, divided by 2πi. There |p(ζ)|≤√n and the inverse of the product is bounded by an absolute constant: the radial factor is ≤(1−1/n)^(−n), and the factors (1−|ξ_j|/(1−1/n))^(−1) have product bounded by summability. Each polynomial of the Newton basis has coefficient sum norm ≤∏(1+|ξ_j|)=O(1). Consequently ||I p||₂≤C n^(3/2), with no dependence on the minimal separation.

At each remaining node ξ, the Cauchy remainder formula introduces an additional denominator ζ−ξ, with bounded inverse, and a numerator ∏_{j≤n}(ξ−ξ_j). Its modulus is ≤∏_{j≤n}2|ξ_j|≤exp(−2n log n+2n log log n+O(n)) by factorials. Hence the error in values, including the O(√n) prefactor, satisfies the stated bound. Since |p|≤2 at the nodes, the difference of squares is also controlled at that rate. Sum using |R|≤1 and Σm_λ|x|<∞. At the interpolated nodes the error is zero. Applying the definition of D_{d,k} to I p and taking the supremum proves the transfer. The bound uses the localisation of the nodes without needing to compute them; it does not prove the exponential error of the decisive block.

**Discrimination test of the finite data and of the expansions in d.** For any fixed integer L one can construct two symmetric model spectra in the strip that agree below G, have exactly the same first L moments Σm x^r (1≤r≤L) and whose shifted matrices differ in operator norm, uniformly in the width, by O(exp(−ηd)) for some η>0. One has positive global sign and the other exhibits a negative direction in all sufficiently shifted decisive blocks. The moment agreement is exact even with integer multiplicities. The model preserves the asymptotic count with error O(log H), without claiming to realise the Euler product of ξ.

Construction. Start from the ordinates projected to the axis, keeping multiplicities, and add above G a double positive ordinate and its symmetric one. Choose in addition L distinct real positive ordinates above G, distinct from the added one, and reserve one copy of each together with its symmetric one. Work at t=1. At the double height shift the two copies horizontally with parameters +δ and −δ, together with their images at negative height. The change in each power sum is real and tends to zero with δ. To compensate, vary the heights of the reserved copies using as coordinates their real nodes u_j=1/(1+g_j²). The Jacobian of the L moments in those L parameters has entries 2r u_j^{r−1}, 1≤r,j≤L, invertible by Vandermonde. The local inverse function theorem gives exact compensation for every δ sufficiently small, with heights still above G and symmetries intact. The heights differ only on a finite set. The comparison of operators is a finite sum of removed and added contributions, each of norm ≤2m|x||R|^{2d} by evaluation on the coefficient sphere. All those nodes have |R|<1, whence η>0. Isolation of the non-real pair proves indefiniteness of the second model for c=10^(−24), and the first contributes positive real squares. In particular any prescribed finite collection of entries M_{d,k} can be matched by choosing L sufficiently large, since each entry is a polynomial in x without constant term. Agreement to all algebraic orders as d tends to infinity is uniform in the width and does not require a complete expansion to exist. Deducing the sign using only those finite data and a comparison O_A(d^(−A)) for each A is excluded; for ξ the arithmetic information that the models do not satisfy remains available.

**Reproduction of 213-412-A: the primitive of the defect under horizontal projection has a sign per orbit.** Here I(U)=D(U)/2 exactly: the integrand of 412, after subtracting the normalisation constant, sums one Δ per orbit and is even. Round 413 already contains the rectangular representation and the density bound. For g>0 and a=|Re λ|>0 take an orbit of four zeros, with its common multiplicity. In the centred real coordinate u define f_g(u)=log(u²+g²) and Δ_{a,g}(u)=f_g(u+a)+f_g(u−a)−2f_g(u). It is the logarithm of the quotient of the monic factors of the orbit and of its projection, including the doubling of the projected pair. For U≥1 one has
(4/9) U Σ a²/(U²+g²) ≤ ∫₀ᵁ Σ Δ_{a,g}(u) du ≤ 12 U Σ a²/(U²+g²).
The sums are over orbits with multiplicity. In particular it suffices to show that the integral is o(1/U) along a subsequence to exclude even a single exterior orbit. The quantity U times the integral converges to 2Σa² if the sum is finite and diverges to +∞ if it is infinite.

Proof. The second difference is the integral of f_g″(u+s) with the triangular weight a−|s| on [−a,a]. On integrating in u the term f_g′(s) cancels by oddness. What remains is the mean with that weight of 2(U+s)/((U+s)²+g²). Since U/2≤U+s≤3U/2, this kernel lies between (4/9)U/(U²+g²) and 12U/(U²+g²), and the weight has mass a². The interchange of sums is justified on each compact set by |f_g″|≤2/g² and Z3. Multiplying by U, each orbit tends to 2a²; dominated convergence or Fatou give the stated limit.

Arithmetic connection and limitation. In a finite modification preserving the archimedean factors, the change in the logarithmic derivative is the logarithmic derivative of a monic rational quotient of spectral factors. A nontrivial change of that kind cannot be O(2^(−u)) as u→+∞: it has a nonzero Laurent term of finite order. By contrast the difference of two logarithmic derivatives of ordinary normalised Dirichlet series, absolutely convergent sufficiently far to the right, is O(2^(−u)), by absolute convergence of the derivatives on a fixed half-line. This explains why the two model surgeries cannot share that arithmetic requirement with identical completion factors. Applying it to ξ and its projection would require an independent estimate for the projected object. The Euler product of ξ only informs about the original side; the bound on the primitive has not been proved.

**Adversarial test with genuine Euler values, on a finite list of abscissae.** Assume RH only to construct the positive control model. For every finite list of distinct real points s_i>1 one can modify finitely many zeros of the true ξ, above G, obtaining an entire completed function with the same symmetries, one exterior orbit and EXACTLY the same values of ξ′/ξ at all the s_i. In particular both functions satisfy there the numerical identities with the prime series of the true ζ and the same archimedean terms. The modification does not presuppose any multiple zero.

Write w_i=s_i−1/2. A pair on the axis at height √v contributes 2w_i/(w_i²+v) to the logarithmic derivative. To vary v the derivative vector has coordinates −2w_i/(w_i²+v)². Evaluating those vectors at all existing distinct heights greater than G generates the whole space of the list: any orthogonal vector would give a rational function with infinitely many zeros and with distinct double poles at −w_i², so all its coefficients would vanish. Reserve as many pairs as points with invertible Jacobian. At two distinct heights tending to infinity remove one pair from each and add a symmetric exterior quartet at an intermediate height, with fixed horizontal shift 1/4. At the fixed abscissae the perturbation tends to zero, since each conjugate pair removed or added contributes O(1/g²). Apply the inverse function theorem to the reserved pairs to compensate it exactly by small real changes of their heights. Multiplying ξ by the monic quotient of the added and removed factors implements the changes: the denominators cancel existing zeros, the centred parity and reality are preserved, and the quotient tends to one at infinity. All alterations lie above G. By isolation the altered model has negative sign in the decisive block eventually. It is a falsifier of the sufficiency of Euler SAMPLES, not of the Euler identity on an interval. It complements the previous rational obstruction, which precisely distinguishes both models if the whole half-line is imposed.

**Arithmetic realisation with uniform error in the decisive matrix.** For integers d≥1 and 0≤m≤d, write w=√(1−v), s=1/2+w on the branch w(0)=1 and F(v)=(ξ′/ξ)(s)/w. By the even Hadamard product, F(v)=Σ_λ m_λ x/(1−vx) (each pair ±λ contributes 2/(w²−λ²)). Let F_X be the result of keeping in F the exact archimedean and polar term and replacing ζ′/ζ by −Σ_{n≤X}Λ(n)n^(−s). Define a computable real symmetric matrix by
H_{ij}=Σ_{l=0}^{2d} binom(2d,l)(−2)^l [v^{i+j+l}]F_X(v),  0≤i,j≤m.
With X=⌈exp(40d)⌉, one has ||M_{d,m}−H||_op = O(exp(−2d)) uniformly in m≤d.

In |v|≤1/2, Re w≥1/√2 and |1/w|≤√2. The Euler tail is O(X^(−.19)) by Λ(n)≤log n, Re s≥1/2+1/√2>1.20 and integral comparison (the logarithm is absorbed with the margin down to .19). Cauchy majorises the error of the degree-j coefficient by C 2^j X^(−.19). The binomial gives error per entry ≤C 2^{2m}5^{2d} X^(−.19) and in norm an additional factor m+1. For m≤d the exponent before that factor is ≤(2log 10−7.6)d<−2.99d. The identification with M is the exact expansion of (1−2x)^{2d}. Consequently at m=⌊10^(−24)d/log d⌋ it would suffice to prove H≥−exp(−10^(−24)d)I along an unbounded subsequence. This step uses growing Taylor orders and prime cut-offs; the surgery that preserved fixed finite samples does not invalidate this reduction. The proved estimate controls only the cut-off error: it does not provide the lower bound of H. The cost of the cut-off is exponential in d.

Corpus audit: POWER_CONFLUENT_BRIDGE_014 §7 already reduces all numerators of V_N(u) to a cut-off exp(40N/u) with exponential precision. Hence the preceding realisation transfers a known mechanism to the coordinates of the decisive block. Rounds 208–212 also treat cut-offs for balanced packets. Do not record the exponential cut-off as a new method.

**Cost of the pole and how to remove it in the decisive block itself.** In the entry (0,0) the polar summand of F is 2/(3/4−v), so that it contributes exactly (8/3)(5/3)^{2d}. The complete spectral value is O(1) by Σm|x|<∞ and |R|≤1. The archimedean term is O(1) uniformly in d. Indeed, for real v near zero the Poisson formula in Re w>0 writes [ψ(1/4+w/2)−log π]/(2w) as the integral of [Re ψ(1/4+iγ/2)−log π]/(2π(w²+γ²)) over the line. It is applied to the real part, harmonic of growth O(log(2+|w|)) by Stirling, with the real value at w>0. On extracting the binomial the weight (1+γ²)^(−1)((γ²−1)/(γ²+1))^{2d} remains, dominated by (1+γ²)^(−1). Likewise each e^(−w log n)/w has the same representation with density cos(γ log n)/π, by the Fourier transform of the resolvent. Extracting the coefficients is justified by analyticity and domination near v=0. Each prime term without its factor Λ(n)/√n therefore has modulus ≤1. Thus a cut-off X with error O(1) in that single entry requires √X log(2X) ≳ (5/3)^{2d}; in particular liminf log X/d ≥4 log(5/3). The need for an exponential cut-off has a precedent in 014 §§8–9; here the exact polar direction is identified.

To separate that cancellation before estimating, restrict P(x)=(1−3x/4)Q(x). The matrix of the form in Q is M'_{ij}=M_{ij}−(3/2)M_{i+1,j}+(9/16)M_{i+1,j+1}; the pole disappears identically for each d. This step DOES preserve the detection criterion at the same rate: for each exterior node x₀ the isolating interpolation is repeated choosing as the value of R^d Q(x₀) the old value divided by 1−3x₀/4, which is nonzero. The cost changes by a constant depending on the node and in the tail the factor is uniformly bounded. The Rayleigh bound and the sufficiency of the error exp(−10^(−24)d+o(d)) survive at the same width in Q. On the axis the new terms are squares with positive weight. File 47 already removes poles in its own space; here the linear factor specifies the restriction for these blocks and their tolerance. The cause of the previous NECESSARY bound is removed; it is not inferred that a subexponential cut-off attains the required precision in the restricted form.

**Obstruction to the short cut-off even in the pole-free block.** To obtain error o(d^(−1/2)) in the single direction Q=x of the preceding restricted block, log X/√d→∞ is necessary. Indeed, fix any finite C. For X≤exp(C√d) and every d sufficiently large the truncated form in that direction is ≤−c₀/√d, with c₀>0, while the complete value is O(d^(−2)). RH is not presupposed.

In the previous cosine representation the weight is W_d(g)=x³(1−3x/4)²R^{2d}, with x=1/(1+g²) and R=1−2x on the real line of integration. For K_d(u)=π^(−1)∫_ℝ W_d(g)cos(ug)dg one has uniformly in |u|≤C√d
√d K_d(u)=exp(−u²/(16d))/(32√π)+o(1).
In |g|≤1/2 change g=y/√d: d log(R²)→−4y², the prefactor tends to 1/16 and an integrable Gaussian dominates. L¹ convergence controls all frequencies uniformly in absolute error. In 1/2≤|g|≤2 there is geometric decay, and in |g|≥2 it is dominated by C g^(−6) exp(−c d/g²), with integral O(d^(−5/2)). The same computation with the archimedean multiplier a(g)=[Re ψ(1/4+ig/2)−log π]/2 gives √d times the archimedean contribution tending to a(0)/(32√π)<0; the logarithm at infinity only costs O(log(2d)) in the tail. The sign a(0)<0 follows from the monotonicity of ψ on the positive axis and ψ(1)=−γ_E. Each retained prime contributes −Λ(n)K_d(log n)/√n≤0, since the minimum of the Gaussian profile over |u|≤C√d is strictly positive. The polar term vanishes exactly.

At the true nodes q=|x|<.01 and |R|^{2d}≤exp(−2dq), as before. The absolute sum in this direction is O(Σm_λ q ·sup_{q≥0} q² exp(−2dq))=O(d^(−2)). Thus the entry fails even in sign at precision d^(−1/2), for any fixed C and large d (its eventual exact positivity follows moreover from the fixed-width block). This imposes a minimal scale for the direct cut-off after polar elimination, without deciding whether an exponential cut-off in d is necessary.
Independent cross-check of scope: 211-A, final section, already detects cut-off failure at the Gaussian scale with peaks at ±u and oscillating phase along a subsequence; 212-A takes it up again and POWER 014 §9 already has a pole-free falsifier. In this direction the central phase is zero and the failure holds for every d sufficiently large.

**One-sided separation of the prime remainder after suppressing the central peak.** Keep the polar annihilation and multiply the test in addition by (1−x)^d: the new carrier is [R(1−x)]^d. At width m=⌊10^(−24)d/log d⌋ the complete modified form still detects every exterior node, even with tolerance exp(−10^(−24)d+o(d)). Indeed |1−x|=|z/(1+z)|≤1 at every node and, at each exterior node, b′=−log|R(1−x)|≤−log(1−2/G²)−log(1−1/G²)<4/G². Hence 2b′<10^(−24). In the isolating construction it suffices to replace b by b′, adjust the prescribed complex value by the fixed polar factor and use |R(1−x)|≤1 in the tail. The cost in norm is exp(b′d+o(d)).

For this carrier the FIXED cut-off X=2 already satisfies by itself the lower bound −O(exp(−10^(−13)d)) I for m≤d and d large. In the Poisson representation its density is a(g)−(log 2)/√2 cos(g log 2) and the weight is x(1−3x/4)² [R(1−x)]^{2d}Q(x)^2, with x=1/(1+g²) real. The density is positive for |g|≥10⁶. To check this in the series of ψ(1/4+ig/2), the first hundred summands contribute at least H₁₀₀−10⁴/(g/2)² and the tail has lower bound −Σ_{k≥100}(1/(k+1/4)−1/(k+1))≥−.02. Subtracting Euler's constant leaves a margin even after log π and the prime atom. In |g|≤10⁶ the density is bounded and 1−x≤1−1/(1+10¹²). For Q of coefficient norm one, |Q(x)|²≤m+1 on [0,1]. The integral of the negative part is O((m+1) exp(−2d/(1+10¹²))), which implies the bound. The Poisson identity is applied here only to the finite cut-off.

Thus, for the modified reduction it would suffice to bound FROM ABOVE the contribution subtracted by the prime terms n>2 by exp(−10^(−24)d+o(d)) on the coefficient sphere, or to compare it with the positive margin of the cut-off if that turns out larger. That one-sided control is not proved. The weight (1−x)^d has antecedents in the table of differences; the specific statement is its simultaneous compatibility with the detector and with a fixed cut-off satisfying the tolerance from below.

**All exponents ≥3 are paid with only half of the archimedean term.** In the same modified carrier, separate the half A/2 of the archimedean form A and the contribution S₃ of ALL the powers p^k, k≥3, with the sign of a positive sum before subtracting it. For m≤d one has A/2−S₃≥−O(exp(−10^(−22)d))I. It also holds for any subset of those powers. Thus the other half of the archimedean term remains available for comparison with the primes and their squares.

Indeed, the cosine density of S₃ is bounded in modulus by Σ_p log p/[p^(3/2)(1−1/√p)]<5.3. For p<16 the six terms sum to less than 2 (by direct evaluation); from 16 on use all integers and (4/3)∫₁₅^∞ log u/u^(3/2) du=(8/3)(log 15+2)/√15<3.25. Absolute convergence allows the sum to be moved inside the integral. For |g|≥10¹¹ half of the archimedean density a(g)/2 exceeds 5.3. In detail, with b=|g|/2, N=⌊b⌋, the digamma series gives Re ψ(1/4+ib)≥−γ_E+H_N−Σ_{k<N}(k+1/4)/b²−Σ_{k≥N}(1/(k+1/4)−1/(k+1))≥log b−2 for b≥10¹⁰. Hence [Re ψ−log π]/4≥(log(5·10¹⁰)−2−log π)/4>5.3. On the remaining compact set the density is uniformly bounded, and the factor (1−x)^{2d} reduces it as before at rate 2/(1+10²²)>10^(−22); the polynomial factor m+1 is absorbed asymptotically. In particular for the target it suffices to prove the required lower bound for A/2−S₁−S₂ at the decisive width, where S₁ and S₂ are the prime and square terms defined by the arithmetic formula (or by the limit of the Taylor extractions). The argument does not interpret their cosine series as absolutely convergent.

**Falsifier of the preceding sufficient condition: the remaining half fails, even without assuming RH.** At the decisive width m=⌊cd/log d⌋, c=10^(−24), the block A/2−S₁−S₂ has for every large d a direction with Rayleigh quotient ≤−exp(−2bd−o(d)), with 0<2b<c fixed. Therefore do NOT attempt to prove the sufficient bound of the previous paragraph. The floor of A/2−S₃ proved there remains valid; what fails is discarding its positive mass before controlling the other terms.

Proof. Write H(x)=(1−2x)(1−x), V(x)=1−3x/4. Choose a fixed real height g₀>10¹³ that is not an ordinate, x₀=1/(1+g₀²), b=−log H(x₀)<4/g₀². The distance from x₀ to the set of spectral nodes is positive by discreteness. With Y=d/(log d)^4, construct B as the product of (x−ξ)/(x₀−ξ) over ALL distinct nodes of height ≤Y, closed under conjugation. It has real coefficients, B(x₀)=1, degree k=o(d/log d), sum norm ≤exp(O(k)). Choose b/2<c′<c and j=⌊c′d/log d⌋. The polynomial Q=exp(bd)B(x)(x/x₀)^j satisfies ||Q||₂≤exp(bd+o(d)) and H(x₀)^d Q(x₀)=1. The value of the complete form at Q is exponentially small in modulus: all nodes up to Y are roots, and in the rest |H^d Q|≤exp((b−2c′)d+o(d)) using |ξ|≤Y^(−2), |H(ξ)|≤1 and Σm_λ|ξ|<∞.

On the other hand A/2−S₃ in this direction contributes at least a positive constant times d^(−2) for d large. In |g−g₀|≤d^(−2), H(x)^d Q(x)=1+O(1/d) uniformly: the logarithmic derivative in g is bounded by O(d+j+k) by separation of x₀ from the roots and from the zeros of H. There xV² and the density a/2 minus the series of S₃ are strictly bounded below by positive constants independent of d. Outside that window, only |g|≤10¹¹ can contribute negatively and its cost is O(exp(−10^(−22)d)||Q||₂²) by the previous proof. Subtracting A/2−S₃ from the complete form produces the stated negative quotient. Choosing g₀ arbitrarily high makes b arbitrarily small. The defect comes from a direction localised between nodes, not from an exterior zero. Closure requires keeping the compensation with the continuous form that was meant to be reserved.

**The cost of restricting the search to numerators with all roots real.** Antecedent: R160_X_C1, corollary R2, restricts the physical minimum to transforms with real roots. In the shifted block another norm and an exponential tolerance are relevant. For any real functional L on polynomials of degree ≤2m, if L(q²)≥−ε||q||₂² for all real polynomials of degree ≤m with all their roots real (constants included), then L(p²)≥−4^m ε||p||₂² for EVERY real p of degree ≤m. Here the norm is the Euclidean coefficient norm. The factor is exp(o(d)) at the decisive width and therefore preserves the sufficient exponent. L may include the carrier and the WHOLE arithmetic contribution, without splitting it.

Proof. Factor p with leading coefficient A. Each pair a±ib introduces into p² the factor (x−a)^4+2b²(x−a)²+b⁴, a positive sum of three squares of polynomials with only real roots. Multiplying out one obtains p²=Σ q_j², with positive coefficients absorbed into q_j. To estimate Σ||q_j||₂² use the sum norm, which is submultiplicative. Each real root r costs (1+|r|)² in the quadratic sum, and each pair costs ((1+|a|)²+b²)²≤(1+|a+ib|)^4. Thus Σ||q_j||₂²≤|A|²∏_r(1+|r|)²≤4^m||p||₂²: in the last step, |A|∏max(1,|r|) is the geometric mean of |p| on the unit circle by Jensen, and this is at most the quadratic mean by Parseval. The case of roots on the circle is obtained by a limit. Applying L to the identity gives the transfer. This proof also produces real-rooted witnesses from the gap and isolation interpolants: among the branches of the expansion some branch keeps the negative quotient, up to the factor 4^m. It is not deduced that all roots can be placed in the spectral interval nor that a prescribed choice of roots suffices.

**A second explicit shift reduces the FREE degree to log d.** Fix H=(1−2x)(1−x), V=1−3x/4, c=10^(−24), j=⌊d/log log d⌋ and k=⌈log d⌉ for d large. It would suffice to establish, along an unbounded subsequence, the floor −exp(−cd+o(d)) in the norm of the coefficients of p, degree ≤k, for
Σ m_λ x V(x)² H(x)^{2d} x^{2j} p(x)².
