It is a doubly shifted block. It is not a subblock of the previous width starting at degree zero: j eventually exceeds cd/log d. Only k+1 coefficients remain free; the additional shift is fixed by the formula and is incorporated into the arithmetic moments.

Proof. If there is an exterior node x₀, put b=−log|H(x₀)|<4/G². With Y=√(log d), construct B by annihilating all distinct nodes of height ≤Y except the target pair, as in the previous isolation. For d sufficiently large the target lies below Y. The degree K is O(√(log d) log log d)=o(k); normalising |B(x₀)|=1 costs at most exp(O(K)) in sum norm by separation of the fixed target. Put p=B(A+D x), with A,D real chosen so that V H^d x^j p at x₀ equals i/√x₀. This is possible by Im x₀≠0 and |A|+|D|≤C exp(bd)|x₀|^(−j). Since j=o(d), ||p||₂≤exp(bd+o(d)). The pair contributes a fixed strictly negative value; the rest of the head vanishes. In the tail |x|≤Y^(−2)=1/log d, so j log|x|≤−d+o(d), uniformly. Summability of Σm_λ|x| and |H|≤1 make the total contribution O(exp(−2(1−b)d+o(d))). The negative quotient is ≤−exp(−2bd−o(d)), incompatible with the floor since 2b<c. Under RH all summands are nonnegative. The arithmetic remains intact. The positive estimates for small free degree at fixed weight h do not transfer: here h=2j grows and changes the band of heights that predominates.

**Two-dimensional alternative, paying for the family of slopes.** With H,V as above fix a rational slope α>0, j=⌊αd⌋ and define S_l=Σm_λ x^(1+2j+l)V² H^{2d}, l=0,1,2. Put B(α)=max_{0≤u≤.01} H(u)u^α. If there is an exterior node, there exists a fixed rational slope 0<α<4/G² such that for EVERY d sufficiently large
(S₀S₂−S₁²)/B(α)^{4d} ≤ −exp(ηd)
for some η>0. Thus, for each rational slope in that interval it would suffice to prove nonnegativity of the determinant along some unbounded subsequence, even one depending on α. Under RH the determinant is nonnegative by Cauchy–Schwarz with positive weights. This alternative keeps two free coefficients but no longer uses a single predetermined shift.

Indeed take any exterior node ξ and a=Re ξ, 0<a≤|ξ|≤G^(−2). The slope α₀=a[2/(1−2a)+1/(1−a)] lies in the stated interval and makes a the unique real maximum, by strict concavity of log H(u)+α₀ log u. At ξ each of |1−2ξ|, |1−ξ| and |ξ| exceeds its value at a, giving a rate larger than B. This gap persists on a small compact interval of slopes around α₀. The tail of nodes tends to zero in rate uniformly there, so only finitely many pairs compete. Their lines log|H(x)|+α log|x| are distinct: given |x|, the moduli of 1−2x and 1−x are strictly decreasing in Re x; hence the two moduli |H|,|x| determine the conjugate pair. Avoiding the finitely many crossings choose a rational α with a unique winning pair ξ₁, conjugate, of rate L>B. The others stay below L by a uniform factor <1 (the rounding factors in the tail are controlled by reserving a small interval of α, applying the separation to j/d). Write A_d=m ξ₁ V(ξ₁)² H(ξ₁)^{2d} ξ₁^{2j}. Its modulus is ≍L^{2d}; the dominant matrix is A_d (1,ξ₁)^t(1,ξ₁) plus its conjugate. The determinant is exactly −4|A_d|²(Im ξ₁)², with no phase dependence. The contribution of the rest to each entry is O(L^{2d}θ^d) for some θ<1 by Σm|x|<∞. This proves the statement. Antecedents: the same file already contains rational-slope domination for Bernstein entries, and the Prony pivot for matrices. What is made precise here is the three-adjacent-moment inequality and its eventual sign for the pole-free carrier. It does not supply the arithmetic inequality at those slopes.

**Effective sign by range of slopes in the 2×2 criterion.** Put P=G^(−2). For every fixed real slope α≥(3+1000/G)P the preceding matrix is positive definite for every d sufficiently large (threshold not quantified). Thus, inside the sufficient interval (0,4P), the upper segment is closed. The idea of comparison with a verified zero already appeared in the Bernstein table; here two are needed to obtain a matrix floor.

By Z3 there is an ordinate in each interval [G−100,G−80] and [G−60,G−40]: on each length 20 the main increment exceeds 80 and the sum of errors is less than 16 by the bounds already used in this round. Z2 places both on the axis. Their distinct real nodes u_i satisfy P+70/G³≤u_i≤P+210/G³ by the formula 1/(1+g²). At the exterior ones q=|x|≤P and |arg x|≤2/G. The series log(1−z)=−z+O(|z|²) with remainder ≤|z|² for |z|≤1/2 gives log|H(x)|≤−3q+11P² (angular error ≤6q/G² and remainder ≤5q²). At the two real nodes log H(u_i)≥−3u_i−5u_i². Put β=⌊αd⌋/d, which eventually exceeds (3+999/G)P. The function −3q+β log q increases up to P. Thus the logarithmic ceiling of the exterior rate is E=−3P+β log P+11P². At each u_i the advantage over E is at least
(u_i−P)(β/u_i−3)−5u_i²−11P²,
by log(u_i/P)≥(u_i−P)/u_i. Given β/u_i−3≥300/G, this advantage exceeds P². All these margins are independent of d once the condition on β is past.

The norm of the exterior matrix is bounded by C exp(2dE), by Σm|x|<∞ and boundedness of V and (1,x). The two critical contributions together have smallest eigenvalue ≥c₀ exp(2d(E+P²)), since their two fixed vectors (1,u_i) are independent and their prefactors u_i V(u_i)² are positive. The other critical nodes only add positive semidefinite matrices. Eventually the floor dominates, even with c₀ very small. This argument does not reach slopes arbitrarily close to zero, which would correspond to heights without a verified ceiling.

**Height localisation of the two-moment test.** Let U be sufficiently large, u=1/(1+U²) and α=u[2/(1−2u)+1/(1−u)]. If all zeros with | |γ|−U |≤1000 are on the line, the 2×2 block for this α is positive definite for every d sufficiently large depending on U. Verification in that band suffices, even if there are exceptions both below and above. Equivalently, failure of positivity along an unbounded sequence for this slope requires at least one exception in that band.

Write f(q)=log H(q)+α log q for real positive q<.01. By concavity of log H and f′(u)=0 one has f(u)−f(q)≥α(y−1−log y), y=q/u. For a non-real node of modulus q, the angular gain log|H(x)|−log H(q) is ≤20q²: |arg x|≤2/g, q≍1/g² with qg²→1 uniformly for g=|γ| large, and for t=1,2 one uses |1−tx|²/(1−tq)²=1+2tq(1−cos(arg x))/(1−tq)². Z2 places all exterior ones at g>G.

In 1/2≤y≤2 the deficit is ≥α(y−1)²/8. For g outside [U−1000,U+1000] in that region, |y−1|≥1900/U for U large: uniformly q=(1+g²)^(−1)(1+O(g^(−2))), and (1+U²)/(1+g²) is monotone with boundary differences (2000+o(1))/U. The net deficit after the angular gain exceeds 10⁶ u². For y≤1/2 the deficit is ≥α(log 2−1/2), which also suffices. For y≥2 one has y−1−log y≥0.15y, so the deficit is ≥.45q; for exterior nodes q≤1/G² and this eventually dominates 20q² and 10⁶u². Consequently there is uniform strict separation in rate between f(u)−10⁶u² and the exterior ones (with margin, by the same constants).

By Z3 there are two distinct ordinates in [U−40,U−20] and [U+20,U+40], since the main term over twenty units grows like (20/(2π))log U against two endpoint errors of size less than log(2U) each. They are critical by hypothesis. Their nodes q_i have |q_i−u|≤(81/U)u and f(u)−f(q_i)≤30000u² by Taylor, since |f″|≤5/u on the segment for U large. Their independent vectors give a rank-two floor, as in the previous paragraph. The rounding j/d→α preserves the separation of rates: on every compact set of q>0 there is uniform convergence and as q approaches zero the rates tend uniformly to zero using j/d≥α/2. The claim follows. The 1000 is a comfortable bound, without optimisation. This principle localises the required information; it does not certify new bands above G.

**Unconditional mean bound on the rate excess at the unverified slopes.** In the notation of the preceding saddle define
E(U)=U⁴[max_ξ log(|H(ξ)| |ξ|^α)−log B(α)]_+.
For T large, T⁻¹∫_T^{2T} E(U)dU ≪1/(log T)². This is a bound on the rate above the real continuous maximum, not on the sign of the determinant. It uses the uniform density of 413, not the local verification of each band.

To see it write F(v)=log H((1+v²)⁻¹)−α log(1+v²) with real branches at U. At v=g+iδ its real part is exactly the logarithmic rate of the node of ordinate g and horizontal shift δ (conjugation does not affect the modulus). For |v−U|≤1001, F′(U)=0, F″(U)=−12/U⁴+O(U⁻⁶), F‴(v)=O(U⁻⁵), uniformly. Indeed F=log(1−v^(−2))−(2+α)log(1+v^(−2))−2α log v, and α=3/U²+O(U⁻⁴); the convergent series in v^(−2) are differentiated term by term there. By Taylor, the rate minus log B is 6[δ²−(g−U)²]/U⁴+O(U⁻⁵) in the fixed band. The exterior ones outside the band are strictly below B by the previous estimate, independently of the zeros inside, and the real nodes never exceed it.

Therefore E(U)≤O(1/U)+6Σ_g [δ²−(U−g)²]_+, restricting the sum to g in [T−1000,2T+1000] when integrating. The error O(1/U) is taken only once since we control a maximum. Each parabola contributes integral 4|δ|³/3. By symmetry and the uniform density bound used in 413, Σ_{0<g≤3T}|δ|³=6∫₀^(1/2) v² N(1/2+v,3T)dv ≪ T/(log T)². This proves the statement. In particular, for fixed positive ε, the fraction of heights with normalised excess greater than ε is O(1/(ε log²T)). The estimate leaves an isolated orbit unexcluded and also does not force the excess to be exactly zero where it is small.

**The rate excess can be exactly zero on a whole interval with negative determinant.** Discrimination test on model spectra, not a statement about exterior zeros of ξ. Start from the ordinates projected to the axis and add a double ordinate g₀>10¹³ in a gap, with the symmetries. At the saddle slope of g₀ the node x₀ is the unique maximum among distinct nodes and realises B. There is strict separation from the second node: the tail tends to zero and the head is discrete. In a neighbourhood of that slope the node keeps winning. Choose inside it a compact interval J of positive length not containing the central slope. There the continuous maximum B is strictly GREATER than the rate of the winner, since the real saddle is unique and distinct from x₀. Both gaps are uniform on J by compactness and by the uniform decay of the tail.

Replace the double node by the conjugate pair obtained from g₀±iδ with small δ>0, without altering the heights or the total multiplicities at each height. Uniformly on J the pair stays strictly below B and above all other nodes. Consequently E(U)=0 on the whole corresponding interval of heights, while the determinant is strictly negative there for every d sufficiently large (uniformly on J for each fixed δ). The rank-two identity above gives the sign. This prevents converting local control of E, even exact, into a sign estimate at the same slopes.

When the change appears is quantified. Fix α interior to J, L the rate of the double node before splitting it, L₂ the maximum of the rest and Δ=log(L/L₂)>0. For d=⌊κ log(1/δ)⌋, κ>0 fixed, the determinant is positive if κ<1/Δ and negative if κ>1/Δ, for δ sufficiently small. Indeed, by the pair formula for the determinant, the internal term of the pair is negative of size ≍δ²L^{4d}: Im x_δ≍δ and L_δ/L=1+O(δ²) by conjugation. The cross term between the pair and the rest is positive of size ≍(LL₂)^{2d}. To see it, the complex weight of the node is its original real weight times 1+O(dδ) (the variation of x^j and H^{2d} is estimated by their local logarithms), and (x_δ−y)²/(x₀−y)²=1+O(δ) uniformly at the real and remaining nodes by separation. The original sum is positive and is bounded above and below at that rate, using a node attaining L₂ for the floor. For the ceiling despite the rounding of αd, separate a finite head and bound the tail at a strictly smaller rate with α in a small interval. The pairs entirely in the rest cost O(L₂^{4d}) and are nonnegative. The ratio of magnitudes internal/cross is ≍δ² exp(2Δd), which gives the two signs without deciding equality. The detection scale thus depends on the gap BETWEEN nodes, even when the excess over the continuous saddle is identically zero.

**Duplicate check: aggregating all normalised slopes rediscovers the Bernstein variation.** For a node x, q=|x| and H=(1−x)(1−2x), the largest possible rate advantage on optimising the slope is |H(x)|/H(q): always B(α)≥H(q)q^α and equality is attained at α=q[2/(1−2q)+1/(1−q)]. For exterior ones that slope lies in the interval examined. If L=|x|+|1−x|, then for all nodes
L ≤ |H(x)|/H(q) ≤ L^5.
Indeed e=L−1≥0 and |1−x|/(1−q)=1+e/(1−q). Moreover |1−2x|²−(1−2q)²=2e[2(1−q)+e]. Since q<.01 and e≤2q, the square root gives |1−2x|/(1−2q)≤1+3e; the first factor is ≤1+1.02e. Their products are bounded by (1+e)^5 by Bernoulli, and the floor comes from the first factor. L is exactly the factor of the diagonal variation theorem in this same round. Hence attempting to suppress the signs by summing or maximising the normalised rates of the slopes, and using only their spectral envelope, changes the logarithmic size of the same defect by at most a factor five. This audit does not identify the finite sums or their possible arithmetic cancellations. Aggregation by envelope is discarded as an independent mechanism; the obligation with the phases and the real coefficients remains.

**What the Euler determinant with fixed cut-off measures: the limit in d produces the square of the density.** For a fixed finite X write h_X(g)=a(g)−Σ_{n≤X}Λ(n)n^(−1/2)cos(g log n). At the saddle slope α of a fixed large U, the truncated determinant D_X=S₀S₂−S₁² satisfies, with β=⌊αd⌋/d, u=x(U), κ=−∂²_g log[H(x(g))x(g)^α] at U,
d² D_X / B(β)^{4d} → (2/π) u² V(u)^4 h_X(U)² x′(U)² /κ².
Here only small slopes of the preceding criterion are taken. In particular if h_X(U)≠0 the determinant of the cut-off is eventually positive even when h_X(U)<0. For a single height U outside an at most countable set, this happens for EACH fixed integer X (the threshold in d may depend on X). It is not a uniform floor for the complete determinant.

Detail. The Poisson representation gives S_l as the integral over g>0 of (2/π)x V² h_X x^l |H(x)x^β|^{2d}. The global saddle in modulus is unique: in x<1/2 this follows from strict concavity, and in x≥1/2 one has |H|≤1/8 while B(β)>1/2 for the slopes considered. On compacts away from a neighbourhood of the saddle there is a gap, also in the tails since β≥α/2 and x V² h_X is integrable. Centre the moments at u_β=x(U_β), which preserves the determinant. With g=U_β+y/√d one obtains the Gaussian weight exp(−κy²), by Taylor and local Gaussian domination. The three centred moments, divided by B(β)^{2d}, have orders d^(−1/2), o(d^(−1)), d^(−3/2), with extreme constants (2/π)uV²h_X(U) times √(π/κ) and times x′(U)²√π/(2κ^(3/2)) respectively. Multiplying gives the limit. The density is real analytic and does not vanish identically because of its logarithmic growth against a bounded trigonometric sum.

At a simple zero of h_X the conclusion is reversed: D_X<0 eventually at the corresponding slope. Indeed U_β−U=O(1/d). In the same centred moments the first is O(d^(−3/2)), the third O(d^(−5/2)) and the second is asymptotic to d^(−3/2) times (2/π)uV²h′_X(U)x′(U)√π/(2κ^(3/2)), nonzero (in all of them one has divided by B(β)^{2d}). The improved orders of the even moments follow by oddness of the linear term in y and a Taylor remainder of order d^(−1) with Gaussian polynomial majorant, including the cubic term of the exponent. The negative of the second centred moment squared (moment of index one) dominates. This dependence distinguishes the sign of the cut-off from the zero criterion of the exact form; the sign must not be deduced by first taking d→∞ on a list of fixed cut-offs.

**Moving cut-off log X=λ√d: threshold forcing a negative determinant independently of the phase.** Keep a fixed saddle slope of a large U and κ>0 from the previous paragraph. If λ>√(2κ) is fixed, the determinant of the cut-off X=exp(λ√d) is strictly negative for EVERY d sufficiently large. This holds even for slopes in the verified range where the complete determinant is eventually positive. The Gaussian/PNT edge mechanism has an antecedent in 211-A; in the determinant a negative phase-independent contribution appears.

Indeed by partial summation and ψ(X)=X+o(X) (here ψ is the von Mangoldt sum), locally uniformly in real g,
Σ_{n≤X} Λ(n)n^(−1/2+ig)/√X = exp(ig log X)/(1/2+ig)+o(1).
For uniformity it suffices to integrate the error function against O((1+|g|)v^(−3/2)) and divide by √X. Moreover the normalised sum is globally bounded in modulus by the same computation at g=0. Hence the density h_X/√X at g=U_β+y/√d has, on compacts of y, profile −cos(θ_d+λ y)/|1/2+iU|+o(1), where θ_d=U_β log X−arg(1/2+iU). The archimedean term divided by √X disappears (for global domination its logarithmic majorant suffices). The localisation and domination of the fixed cut-off proof still apply to these bounded profiles.

Write C=(2/π)uV(u)² √(π/κ) exp(−λ²/(4κ))/|1/2+iU|. For the three moments centred at x(U_β), of indices l=0,1,2, divide by √X B(β)^{2d} d^{−(1+l)/2}. Integrating 1,y,y² against the modulated Gaussian (differentiate its transform twice), the three results are, with additive errors o(1), −C cos θ_d, C x′(U) λ sin θ_d/(2κ), and −C x′(U)² (1/(2κ)−λ²/(4κ²)) cos θ_d. It follows that
d² D_X/(X B(β)^{4d}) = C² x′(U)² [cos² θ_d/(2κ)−λ²/(4κ²)] + o(1).
The bound cos²≤1 gives a strictly negative sign uniform in phase under the hypothesis. The computation does not treat λ growing with d and does not decide the sign of the cut-off linear in d whose exponential precision is indeed controlled (with cut-off constant sufficiently large for the degree of the carrier).

**Compensating the continuous main term cancels the edge, but leaves detectable prime jumps.** For the same cut-off add to the truncated series of Λ(n)n^(−s) the continuous tail X^(1−s)/(s−1), before applying the Taylor functional (with the corresponding sign of ζ′/ζ). In the block with V the contribution of the TOTAL continuous integral is a bounded Poisson piece: 1/[w(w−1/2)]=2/(w²−1/4)−1/[w(w+1/2)], and the first summand vanishes. The second has a cosine representation with bounded density, integrating exp(−t/2)cos(gt) for t≥0. Thus a sum remains with centred head density dψ−dn, plus fixed terms. PNT and the same partial summation imply that this density divided by √X is o(1) on compacts of g, globally dominated by O(1) for the truncated part. By Gaussian domination, the compensated determinant, multiplied by d²/(X B(β)^{4d}), tends to zero in the regime log X≈λ√d. This does eliminate the previous false main term, but does not determine the residual sign.

There is a finer obstruction to UNIFORM precision at the endpoint. Fix λ>0 and choose a prime p between exp(λ√d) and 2exp(λ√d), possible for every large d by PNT. Compare the limits of the compensated matrix as X approaches p from below and from above. The continuous corrector has zero jump. The prime jump is −(log p)/√p times the matrix obtained by using only the density cos(g log p). In the polynomial coordinates 1 and x−u_β (a uniformly bounded and invertible change), its entry of index zero, after dividing by B(β)^{2d}/√d and omitting the prime multiplier, is C₁ cos(U_β log p)+o(1); the one of index one after dividing by B(β)^{2d}/d is −C₁ x′(U) λ sin(U_β log p)/(2κ)+o(1). Here C₁=(2/π)uV²√(π/κ)exp(−λ²/(4κ))>0. It is obtained by the same Gaussian transformation, without invoking PNT for the size of the atom. Since sine and cosine do not vanish simultaneously, the norm of the jump is ≥c_U,λ B(β)^{2d}(log p)/(d√p). At least one of the two limits is at half that distance or more from the complete matrix. In particular no continuous corrector in X for the sharp cut-off gives a uniform error B(β)^{2d}exp(−ηd) with η>0 in that band of endpoints. This does not exclude arithmetically chosen endpoints, a cut-off smoothed at each atom, or a one-sided sign proof. The subtraction of dx has an antecedent in 211–212; here the obstacle persists after compensating it and is measured at the scale of a single prime.

**Sign of the COMPLETE determinant in the moving band j→∞, j=o(√d).** For any such sequence, the matrix of the three moments is eventually positive definite, without verification of zeros at new heights or prime cut-off. Unlike the previous control of individual entries at square-root scale, here the local variance that decides the determinant is retained.

Take β=j/d, u the saddle of H(x)x^β and U²=1/u−1, W=U/√j. Then U²∼3d/j and W→∞. In the basis 1, √j(x/u−1), divide the matrix by B(β)^{2d}u W log U/π. The limit is the Gram matrix of 1,−2y in the measure exp(−4y²)dy on the whole line. It is positive definite. Indeed, for g=U+Wy, y bounded, and any |δ|≤1/2, write x=1/(1+(g+iδ)²). One has √j(x/u−1)→−2y, x/u→1, V→1 and 2d(F(g+iδ)−F(U))→−4y². This follows from F′(U)=0, F″(U)∼−12/U⁴ and F‴=O(U^(−5)) in |g−U|≤U/4, with dW³/U⁵=O(1/√j). The imaginary shift costs o(1) in the variable y. Z3 gives convergence of the count in y, with both ordinates and normalisation W log U/π, to dy on each compact: the endpoint error is O(1/W).

Domination detail. Let q=|x|, v=q/u. The modulus of the carrier divided by its maximum, raised to 2d, is ≤exp(−2j(v−1−log v)+40dq²), by the angular bound and concavity above (for real nodes the correction is omitted). For U/2≤g≤2U, dq²=O(j²/d)=o(1), and v−1−log v≥c(v−1)²; here √j|v−1| is comparable to |y| up to an o(1) error, and √j|x/u−1|≤C(1+|y|). Each unit cell in y has count O(W log U) by Z3. A summable polynomial-times-Gaussian majorant results. In g>2U the ratio v is ≤.26 and in the annulus 2^l U≤g≤2^(l+1)U, l≥1, the deficit is ≥c(1+l), while dq²=o(1). The factors of the normalised matrix grow at most polynomially in j times a factor O(2^l(1+l)) from the count, dominated by exp(−cj(1+l)). In g<U/2, v≥3.9 eventually and v−1−log v≥.38v. At the exterior ones q≤G^(−2), so that 40dq²≤.1jv by du/j→1/3; on the axis there is no angular penalty. The factors outside the exponential are O(j(1+v)^3) per node after extracting u, and there are O(U log U) nodes. Dividing by W log U only loses √j, so this tail also disappears. The convergence proves the sign with all arithmetic terms. The slopes β tend to zero simultaneously with d; this limit is not interchanged with that of d→∞ at fixed positive slope.

**At the boundary j=⌊λ√d⌋, the complete determinant is positive in density one for each fixed λ>0.** More precisely the proportion of integers d∈[D,2D] where the matrix is not positive definite tends to zero. Here W→√3/λ may be a small constant. It is not assumed that the zeros of the local bands are all on the axis.

Compare with the matrix obtained by projecting each node to its real ordinate. Use the same centred basis as above and normalise by B(β)^{2d}u log U. The projected matrix has floor c_λ I>0 for all large d. Indeed the two intervals [U−40,U−20] and [U+20,U+40] each contain ≫log U ordinates by Z3. There the normalised weight per node, before dividing by log U, is bounded below by a positive constant depending on λ by the local expansion. The coordinate √j(x/u−1) runs over two separated compacts on the two intervals, one positive and the other negative. Each pair, with one vector from each interval, gives a Gram matrix with uniform positive minimum (determinant equal to the squared separation, bounded trace). Pairing ≫log U terms counting multiplicity proves the floor.

For a fixed H sufficiently large depending on λ, the contribution in norm of |g−U|>H to both matrices is less than c_λ/4 each for d large. In the preceding domination bounds the angular term dq² is now O_λ(1) in the comparable region and W is bounded above and below. The cell majorant remains C_λ(1+|g−U|)^2 exp(−c′_λ(g−U)²) after the local count; the two far regions still tend to zero. Within H the normalised error of replacing each g+iδ by g is O_{λ,H}(|δ|/log U): in the complex strip |Im v|≤1/2 the rescaled functions and their first derivative in v are uniformly bounded, by Taylor at the saddle with d/U⁴=O_λ(1), √j/U=O_λ(1) and |v−U|≤H+1. There are O_H(log U) zeros. Fixing ε>0 sufficiently small depending on λ,H, the block keeps a positive floor unless there is a zero with |δ|>ε and |g−U|≤H.

It remains to count the affected shifts. For d∈[D,2D], U=√(3/λ)d^(1/4)+O_λ(D^(−1/4)), by the saddle equation and the floor error in j. Write T=D^(1/4); each height in the band of order T affects O_{λ,H}(D/T) integers by monotonicity and the derivative of the main term. The density bound of 413 and symmetry give O_λ,ε(T log T · T^(−ε/4)) relevant zeros up to C_λ T. The exceptional proportion is therefore O_λ,ε,H(log T · T^(−ε/4))=o(1). The constants may be very unfavourable for large λ. The sign proved is that of the real determinant of ξ; the statement leaves open the exceptional d and the fixed positive slopes.

**Classification of what decides extending the 2×2 block to ALL sublinear indices.** The following are equivalent: (i) there are at most finitely many non-real spectral nodes; (ii) there exist ε>0 and finite D such that for d≥D and all integers 0≤j≤εd the complete 2×2 matrix of H^{2d}x^{2j}V² is positive definite; (iii) for every sequence d→∞, j→∞ with j/d→0 its determinant is eventually nonnegative. In particular, not even eventual strict positivity on the WHOLE sublinear region excludes a single exterior orbit. This concerns the matrix of two free moments; the double-shift criterion with growing free degree has different quantifiers.

For (i)⇒(ii), if the non-real set E is nonempty finite, r=max_E|H(x)|<1 and |x|<1. Choose two fixed distinct critical nodes u₁,u₂ so close to zero that H(u_i)>r (they exist by Z3 and finiteness of E). By continuity choose ε>0 and r′>r so that H(u_i)u_i^ε≥r′ for both. In 0≤j≤εd their joint positive contributions give a floor c₀(r′)^{2d} by independence of (1,u_i). The whole exterior matrix has norm ≤C_E r^{2d} and the other real nodes contribute semidefinitely. If E is empty two distinct nodes suffice directly. (ii)⇒(iii) is immediate.

For the contrapositive of (iii)⇒(i), with infinitely many non-real nodes take ξ_n→0. The proof of the 2×2 alternative gives a rational slope α_n with a dominant exterior pair and strictly negative sign for every d sufficiently large at j=⌊α_n d⌋. One can choose α_n→0: the strict advantage of the node ξ_n over the real saddle is obtained at the slope of a_n=Re ξ_n→0; the perturbation avoiding rate crossings can be chosen smaller than half of that slope. Choose d_n increasing past each threshold and with α_n d_n≥n+1. Thus j_n→∞, j_n/d_n→0 and all the determinants are negative. No uniformity in the thresholds is required. This classification advises against pursuing exclusively the extension j=o(d) in dimension two as a global closure; even if achieved in full, it would only give finiteness.

**Bridge with C_B and the precision Euler really contributes in the finite case.** The implication «finitely many exterior orbits ⇒ none» is recorded as C_B in R162_2501_FINITE_OFFLINE (§§0,5); it would be a mistake to propose it again as a new mechanism. One can identify the single coefficient that would have to be controlled in this comparison. Let P(w) be the projected product of 412, and A(w)=1/s+1/(s−1)−(log π)/2+ψ(s/2)/2 with s=w+1/2. If Σ_orb m a²<∞ (in particular, if there are finitely many exceptions), then
lim_{w→+∞} w³ [A(w)−P′(w)/P(w)] = 4 Σ_orb m a².
For finite E the error before multiplying by w³ is O_E(w^(−5))+O(2^(−w)). Thus under finiteness a nonpositive liminf of the rescaled side would suffice. P′/P counts ALL heights with multiplicity: it cannot be replaced by the sum over the known zeros on the line.

Proof. In the logarithm of the quotient of the products, an orbit contributes up to a constant the centred second difference of f_g(w)=log(w²+g²) from the paragraph identified with 412. Its derivative is ∫_{−a}^a(a−|h|) f_g‴(w+h)dh, with f_g‴(v)=4v(v²−3g²)/(v²+g²)^3. For w≥2 the modulus of w³ f_g‴(w+h) is uniformly bounded in g,h and for each fixed g tends to 4. With summability of m a² one can pass to the limit; the differentiation comes from the normally convergent paired product. In the finite case the rational expansion and the symmetry in h leave error O_E(w^(−5)). Finally (ξ′/ξ)(s)=A(w)+ζ′(s)/ζ(s), and by the von Mangoldt series the last term is O(2^(−w)). The order-three coefficient, if an exception exists, belongs to the projected side and not to an Euler truncation remainder. Without an independent estimate of P′/P, C_B is not obtained. This is a differential consequence of 412 under summability, not a new route to closure.

**Compatibility with paper 46: physical size needed to transfer the window directly to the fixed-slope test.** Fix a small positive slope of the 2×2 criterion and the carrier H,V. On the Fourier line, any factor f whose spectral power is
|f̂(g)|²=x V² |H(x)|^{2d} x^{2j}|p(x)|²,  x=1/(1+g²), j=⌊αd⌋, deg p≤1,
satisfies, for every interval I of length L,
∫_I |f|² / ||f||₂² ≤ C_α L/√d
if p is nonzero and d sufficiently large. The bound is uniform even if the phase of f̂ or the polynomial is chosen afresh at each d. Hence a fixed physical window with proved sign captures a fraction tending to zero of the norm in these tests. It includes any translation of the window and any choice of spectral factor with that modulus.

Proof with the unitary Fourier convention. Write p=A+B√d(x−u_β), with β=j/d and u_β the real saddle. By Laplace at the two peaks ±U_β one has
||f̂||₁ ≤ C B(β)^d (|A|²+|B|²)^(1/2)/√d,  ||f̂||₂² ≥ c B(β)^{2d} (|A|²+|B|²)/√d
(distinguish the coefficient B from the maximum B(β)). For the floor it suffices to integrate over g=U_β+y/√d with |y|≤1: the linear factors in y converge to A+B x′(U)y and their Gaussian Gram matrix on that interval is positive definite. For the ceiling, at both peaks an integrable Gaussian times (1+|y|) dominates. Outside them there is a uniform geometric gap, and for integrability in the tail one factor x of x^j is reserved (β is bounded below), leaving the integrable weight √x·x. More explicitly, in the tail one may reserve a complete factor |H|x^β for each of a fixed number of powers sufficient for x^{Nβ}≤x, without altering the geometric gap. Using ||f||∞≤||f̂||₁/√(2π) and Plancherel concludes. The order L/√d for fixed positive L is attainable up to a constant depending on L and α: with p=1 and zero phase, on a fixed interval around the origin the inverse transform divided by B(β)^d/√d converges uniformly to a positive constant times cos(Ut), by the same local computation. Its normalised energy there is ≍1/√d.

This limitation concerns direct norm truncation of a single factor. It does not prove that a decomposition controlling the cross terms between windows separately is impossible. Antecedents of the mechanism: Gaussian peaks of 211-A and physical bridges at the beginning of this round; the estimate is for the whole plane and for arbitrary phases at this slope.

**Two copies of a fixed primitive pulse: polynomial sampling of the separation.** There exists a real even f supported in (−1,1), independent of the zeros, such that for the crossings C(h)=W(f,T_h f) of the polarised form of paper 46,
RH ⇔ |C(n^(1/4))|≤exp(o(n^(1/4))) (as an upper bound as n→∞).
The sufficient implication allows one to check only the fourth power of the scale in number of separations up to h. It does not use a bound on the sign of each piece to control its crossing. The general antecedent is detection by translations in this round; the point of the construction is subexponential alias-free sampling through quantified regularity.

Take φ the infinite convolution of uniform laws on [−a_k,a_k], a_k=A/k² with Σ a_k<1. It exists as the distribution of the absolutely convergent sum of independent variables. Its bilateral transform is the product of sinh(a_k z)/(a_k z), normally convergent and without zeros off the imaginary axis, since Σa_k²<∞. In |Re z|≤1/2 each factor has modulus ≤exp(a_k/2), and also ≤exp(a_k/2)/(a_k|z|); taking the first ⌊√(A|z|)/2⌋ one obtains O(exp(−c√|z|)). By Fourier inversion φ is smooth. Put f=φ″−φ/4. It keeps the support and annihilates the two polar evaluations; its transform F does not vanish at any exterior node. By the zero sum of P46 and symmetry, C(h)=Σm F(z)^2 exp(hz), z=ρ−1/2 (with the same normalisation of W). Under RH it is bounded. In general |C^(k)(h)|≤exp(h/2)C₁^{k+1}(k!)² for h≥0 by the preceding decay and Z3 (integrate powers against exp(−c√g), absorbing polynomial factors). If C(h) grows at most subexponentially, its Laplace transform is holomorphic in Re s>0. For Re s>1/2 it coincides with Σm F(z)^2/(s−z), which continues meromorphically to Re s>0 by normal convergence away from poles. A right exterior node would have nonzero residue; therefore it does not exist.

To pass from the samples to large real h interpolate at the k consecutive nodes immediately to its right, with k=⌈2h/log h⌉. The steps h_n=n^(1/4) are comparable to h^(−3) with absolute constants throughout the packet. The sum of the moduli of the Lagrange weights at h is ≤C₂^k: for the weight of index i, 1≤i≤k, the products of distances are bounded in ratio by C^k k!/[(i−1)!(k−i)!], and one sums. Extrapolation of the subexponential datum preserves exp(o(h)) because k=o(h). The remainder is bounded by exp(h/2+O(k))(k!)² h^(−3k): the product of distances costs ≤C^k k! h^(−3k) and the remainder divides by k!. Its logarithm is ≤h/2−k log h+O(k)=−Ω(h). Thus the sampling implies the required continuous bound. The arithmetic inequality on these samples remains unproved.

**Realisation inside the certified window of the two-copy pulse with square bias.** Direct antecedents in this round: «A fixed test with negative square bias», «Completely explicit eight-box test» and «One-sided sampling ... H^(−3)». Reducing to ordinary primes or the order of the number of samples is not new. What is made compatible here is centred support within T=2.7695, both polar annihilations, numerical control of the margin and the preceding sampling with no exterior zeros of the filter.

Let U be the uniform law on [−1/4,1/4], η the convolution of boxes of radii 1/(20k²), k≥1, as in the interpolation paragraph, and φ=U^{*10}*η. Put f=φ−4φ″, k=f*f, and F its bilateral transform. The radius of f is 5/2+π²/120<2.59. F(0)=1, F(±1/2)=0, and the other zeros of F are purely imaginary. For any ordinate g≥14, |F(ig)|≤(1+4g²)(4/g)^10. Hence over ALL projected nodes Σm |F(ig)|² ≤17·4^20·14^(−14)·.049<.000083, using the sum over both ordinates proved in this round. The same bound holds unconditionally for the contribution of all nodes that are indeed critical.

With V=n^(1/4), form with primes only B(V)=Σ_p (log p)/√p k(V−log p). Under RH, limsup |B(V)+1/2|≤.000083. Indeed, the explicit formula cited in the antecedent gives for the sum over Λ the negative of the spectral crossing plus o(1). The square powers sum to (1/2)∫k+o(1)=1/2+o(1) by PNT with the change t=V−2log p. The exponents ≥3 cost O(poly(V)exp(−V/6)) by fixed support and trivial counting up to exp((V+O(1))/3). Conversely, it would suffice that |B(n^(1/4))+1/2|≤.001 for all n sufficiently large: this bounds the samples of the crossing and the preceding Gevrey interpolation applies without modification because η retains its decay in strips and the additional factors only add polynomial growth there. This does not verify the prime inequality; the window certificate controls the individual pulse, not its translation.

**Unconditional sign for two copies of the explicit pulse at ALL separations 0<h≤10⁶.** In the plane of f and T_h f the matrix has diagonal C(0) and cross terms C(h), real by symmetry. One has C(0)>|C(h)| throughout that interval; h=0 gives the positive line. The individual support has radius <2.59. The result does not cover other pulse shapes on the long interval.

Exterior bound. For z=b+ig with |g|>G=3·10¹², the first N=193600 boxes of η satisfy a_k |g|≥4 with a_k=1/(20k²). By the sinh bound used in the sampling, |F(z)|²≤exp(3) (1+4|z|²)² (4/|g|)^20 4^(−2N), using the total radius <2.59. Thus Σ_ext m(1+|z|²)|F(z)|²≤exp(−530000), by |g|≥G and Σm/g²<.049. For both signs, the error of the exterior ones in C(0)±C(h) is ≤2 exp(h/2−530000), and for the minus sign it is moreover ≤h² exp(h/2−530000) by the integral formula for cosh(zh)−1 and the symmetry ±z. On the axis each term of both forms is nonnegative.

Critical floor. At the first two ordinates γ₁,γ₂ one has |F(iγ_i)|²>10^(−40): both values of |sin(γ_i/4)/(γ_i/4)| exceed .05 and the product of η exceeds .7 by sinc(t)≥1−t²/6 and Σ_k (γ_i/(20k²))²/6<.23. Let r=γ₂/γ₁. At 128 bits Arb, acb.zeta_zero(i).imag, gives |64794022 r−96365687|<4·10^(−9); the integers are coprime. For 1≤n≤5000000, the distance from nr to the nearest integer is therefore ≥(1−5000000·4·10^(−9))/64794022>10^(−8). Take n the nearest integer to γ₁h/π; for h≤10⁶ one has n≤5000000. If n≥1 the two distances from γ_i h/π to integers cannot both be less than 10^(−9), since r<2. One of the two nodes then contributes to both forms ≥10^(−40)·2·10^(−18) using 1−|cos πt|≥2 dist(t,ℤ)². This dominates the uniform exterior error. If n=0, cos(γ₁h)≥0 and the first node alone gives floors 10^(−40) and 2·10^(−40)(γ₁h/π)² for the plus and minus signs respectively. This covers the limit of small separations without losing the margin against the quadratic exterior error. At h=0 the same node dominates the tail in C(0).

**Three equally spaced translations up to diameter 10⁶.** For all 0<h≤500000, W is positive definite on span(f,T_h f,T_{2h} f) with the same f. The guarantee includes the second difference mode as h→0. It is not deduced from the sign on each pair.

Let g₁,…,g₄ be the first four ordinates. For each one |F(ig)|²>10^(−62): the sinc factor of the large box has modulus >.001 and that of η as a whole exceeds .5 using Σ(31/(20k²))²/6<.5. The six positive gaps g_j−g_i lie between 3 and 17. For two gaps a<b, r=b/a, there is a reduced fraction p/q with 2000000<q≤10⁸ and |qr−p|<1/4000000. Verification run with python-flint, 160 bits:

    from flint import acb, arb, ctx
    from fractions import Fraction
    from itertools import combinations
    ctx.prec = 160
    g = [acb.zeta_zero(i).imag for i in range(1,5)]
    ds = sorted(b-a for a,b in combinations(g,2))
    assert ds[0]>3 and ds[-1]<17 and g[-1]<31
    for a,b in combinations(ds,2):
        r = b/a
        p,q = Fraction(float(r)).limit_denominator(100000000).as_integer_ratio()
        assert q>2000000 and abs(r*q-p)<arb(1)/4000000
    assert all(abs((v/4).sin()/(v/4))>arb('0.001') for v in g)

For .01≤h≤500000 at most one gap has dist(ah/(2π),ℤ)<10^(−10). If two had it, the integer n near ah/(2π) would be positive and <1500000, with dist(nr,ℤ)<7·10^(−10). But dist(nr,ℤ)≥(1−n/4000000)/q>6·10^(−9). Hence one can choose three of the four nodes Y_i=exp(ihg_i) with mutual distances ≥4·10^(−10), discarding one end of the unique close pair if there is one. For a real polynomial p of degree ≤2 with coefficient norm one, Lagrange interpolation at those three nodes gives max |p(Y_i)|≥(4·10^(−10))²/12. On the axis the form is the sum of m|F(ig)|²|p(exp(igh))|². The positive contribution exceeds 10^(−105). Off the axis p(exp(zh))p(exp(−zh)) costs in modulus at most 3 exp(2|Re z|h), so that the total error is ≤3 exp(500000−530000).

For 0<h<.01 use the coefficients in Z=(exp(zh)−1)/h, which remain invertible coordinates on the same space. At the first three ordinates |Z|≤31 and the mutual distances exceed 1 by the sine bound and the separation of the g_i. Lagrange gives max |p(Z_i)|≥1/(3·32²) with norm one. At the exterior ones |Z(±z)|≤|z|exp(h max(±Re z,0)), by the integral of the exponential. The error remains ≤3 exp(h) Σ_ext m(1+|z|)^4 |F(z)|²; the box bound of the previous paragraph still gives <exp(−529000) for that sum (the net exponent in g after extracting the first N boxes is at most −12, integrable by Σm/g²). The critical floors dominate in both regimes. The window length for general data does not change.

**Undoing exact aliasing in the finite case with a single perturbed lattice.** For the crossing C of the explicit pulse and any fixed step h>0 take t_n=nh+1/n. If there is a nonzero finite number of right exterior nodes, with b*=max Re z, then
limsup_n log(1+|C(t_n)|)/t_n=b*.
More generally it suffices that the nodes of the front Re z=b*>0 be finite and the rest lie in Re z≤b*−η for some η>0. The step h may cause exact phase coincidences. The result needs neither Baire nor the choice of a generic h. Antecedents 089–090 already study aliasing and families of steps; the modification here is the decreasing deterministic shift.

Group the distinct nodes of the front by the same phase θ=h Im z modulo 2π. Their contribution divided by exp(b* t_n) is Σ_θ exp(inθ) A_θ(1/n), where A_θ(t)=Σ_{z in class} m F(z)² exp(it Im z). No A_θ is identically zero: the frequencies of the class are distinct and the coefficients do not vanish. By Vandermonde, its order of vanishing at zero is at most the size of the class minus one. Let l be the minimum of those orders. Multiplying the sum by n^l gives Σ c_θ exp(inθ)+O(1/n), with at least one c_θ nonzero. Its Cesàro mean square tends to Σ|c_θ|²>0 by distinctness of phases. The spectral remainder after the same normalisation is O(n^l exp(−ηt_n)) by summability of the coefficients. Hence the lower exponent, and the upper one follows from the triangle inequality. Under RH the crossing remains bounded.

Consequence for the two obstacles already identified: (1) eventual nonnegativity of the 2×2 determinant along every sublinear sequence j→∞ with j/d→0, and (2) subexponential growth of the crossing along the single sequence t_n=n+1/n, TOGETHER are equivalent to RH. The first would reduce to finitely many exterior ones and the second would exclude exactly the finite case, without needing a mesh of order V⁴ for (2). In terms of ordinary primes |B(t_n)+1/2|≤.001 eventually suffices, by the pulse identity. Neither of the two global obligations is established. For infinitely many exterior ones without an isolated maximum the alias proof by finite polynomials does not apply.

**A pulse with residues in an acute sector eliminates aliasing at any attained front.** Let v(t)=exp(−6t)1_[0,1](t), ṽ(t)=v(−t), φ=(v*ṽ)*(v*ṽ), f=(1/4−∂²)φ. It is real, even, primitive, supported on [−2,2], and defines a function in H¹ (its transform decays like O((1+|g|)^(−2))). The zero formula of P46 applies at this regularity, also by compact smoothing and dominated convergence in the series. In the bilateral convention,
F(z)=(1/4−z²) [(1−exp(−6+z))(1−exp(−6−z))/(36−z²)]².
In C_f(t)=W(f,T_t f) the coefficient of each distinct node is c_z=m_z F(z)². It satisfies Re c_z ≥ |c_z|/2>0 on the WHOLE divisor. Indeed for |Re z|≤1/2, |Im z|≥14, both arguments of 1/4−z² and 36−z² have modulus ≤1/14 since their real part is ≥g² and their imaginary part ≤|g|. Each factor 1−exp(−6±z) has argument of modulus ≤arcsin(exp(−5.5))<.005. The unreduced argument of F² therefore has modulus ≤2/14+4(2·.005+1/14)<.48. The bounds are independent of the sampling step and Σ|c_z|<∞ by Z3.

If b*=sup Re z>0 IS ATTAINED, then for EACH h>0 one has limsup_n log(1+|C_f(nh)|)/(nh)=b*, even if infinitely many nodes attain the supremum or if smaller nodes approach it. Indeed exp(−b*nh)C_f(nh)=Σ_{Re z=b*} c_z exp(inh Im z)+o(1). The remainder is o(1) by dominated convergence for the absolutely convergent sum, without spectral gap. Group by phase modulo 2π: each class present keeps a nonzero coefficient by the sectorial bound. By Cesàro orthogonality (first truncate the series uniformly) the average of the squared modulus tends to the sum of the squared moduli of the grouped coefficients, which is strictly positive. Thus there is even a positive lower proportion of indices where |C_f(nh)|≥c_h exp(b*nh) for some c_h>0. Under RH all crossings are bounded. The modification n+1/n was sufficient for the previous pulse and an isolated finite front; here the step is exactly fixed and the attained front needs no isolation. The non-attained positive supremum remains uncovered by this proof, and the arithmetic ceiling on the integer samples has not been proved.

**Compact average of crossings that does see the non-attained supremum.** For the sectorial pulse of exponential boxes, let μ be the uniform probability on [−1,1], M(z)=sinh(z)/z. For integers h≥2 and n≥1 define D_n(h)=∫ C_f(nh+t) dμ^{*n}(t). It is a single crossing by bilinearity, with the second copy convolved n times. One has the rate formula
limsup_n |D_n(h)|^(1/n)=R_h=max_z exp(h Re z)|M(z)|.
It therefore suffices to obtain R_h≤1 arithmetically for an unbounded sequence of integer speeds h, even when the supremum of the abscissae of the zeros is not attained. More precisely lim_{h→∞} log R_h/h=sup_z Re z. This changes the observable: it does not claim detection on a single lattice without averaging.

Proof. Integrating the absolutely convergent series of the crossing over the compact gives Σ c_z [exp(hz)M(z)]^n. The modulus of the base tends to zero in height at fixed h because |sinh z|≤cosh(1/2) in the strip. The positive maximum is attained at finitely many nodes (for example M does not vanish at the first ordinate), with a gap to the rest. If several maximal bases coincide, Re c_z≥|c_z|/2 prevents cancellation in each class. The same Cesàro mean square as in the previous paragraph gives equality of rates. If Re z>0, M(z)≠0 and h Re z+log|M(z)| grows with h. In general the ceiling log R_h≤h sup Re z+O(1) and the floor given by any node with M≠0 give the limit (under RH use the first ordinate). Compactification by a decreasing multiplier has precedents in 207 and in the Gaussian profiles of this round; here phase grouping works without selecting generic steps and with a real positive compactly supported convolution.

**Unconditional segment of the arithmetic average.** For ALL integers 2≤h≤56 one has R_h≤max(1/14,exp(28)cosh(.5)/G)<.55. On the axis |M(ig)|≤1/14, and off the axis Z2 applies. Consequently |D_n(h)|≤(Σ|c_z|)·.55^n for all n. If B_f(V)=Σ_p log(p)k(V−log p)/√p with k=f*f, the same average around nh converges to −F(0)^2/2 without the RH hypothesis, for each h in that range. Indeed, the polarised explicit formula for this compact pulse expresses B_f(V)=−C_f(V)−F(0)^2/2+o(1): the square powers give the constant term by PNT and fixed support, the higher ones are o(1), and the archimedean part of the crossing at disjoint supports decreases exponentially by the kernel of P46. The o(1) error is uniform on the support of the average since V≥n(h−1). The ceiling for arbitrarily large speeds remains open; the bound .55^n refers only to the crossing, not to the PNT error in the prime average.

**Unconditional sign of the mixed plane for separations growing without bound.** Let f be the preceding sectorial pulse and g_n=μ^{*n}*f. For EVERY n sufficiently large and simultaneously for every real t with |t|≤51n, W is positive definite on span(f,T_t g_n). It is a plane of distinct functions; the support radius of the second can reach n+2. The sign refers to combinations with arbitrary coefficients, even chosen depending on n and t.

Indeed, let r=M(iγ₁)=sin(γ₁)/γ₁>.069 by the preceding Arb enclosure. The first critical pair has total mass A₁=2m₁F(iγ₁)²>0. All the other critical ordinates are ≥21 in modulus and hence |M|≤1/21. At the exterior ones |M|≤cosh(.5)/G. Thus W(g_n,g_n)/r^{2n}→A₁ by the explicit sum with multiplier M^{2n}. Moreover, uniformly in the stated range,
W(f,T_t g_n)/r^n=A₁ cos(γ₁ t)+o(1),
because both 1/21 and exp(25.5)cosh(.5)/G are less than .069. The diagonal of the translated copy is preserved by translation invariance.

There remains a strict separation between W(f,f) and A₁. At every exterior node |F(z)|≤2/g² by the box formula (|36−z²|≥g² and the numerator factors are ≤1+exp(−5.5)). Thus Σ_ext m|F|²≤4·.049/G². The second ordinate lies between 21 and 22, and there F(ig)=(1/4+g²)|1−exp(−6+ig)|⁴/(36+g²)²>10^(−3). That single critical contribution exceeds the tail, and the rest are nonnegative. Hence the determinant of the plane matrix divided by r^{2n} has uniform liminf ≥A₁[W(f,f)−A₁]>0, and the first diagonal is positive. The margin takes into account that the energy of g_n also tends to zero. This inequality is not obtained from the absolute bound .55^n for the crossing.

For fixed speed h there is also a necessary barrier: if R_h>r, the rate formula of the crossing gives |W(f,T_{nh}g_n)|/r^n unbounded along a subsequence, while both normalised diagonals are bounded. Then there are indefinite planes along that subsequence. Hence, establishing an eventual sign of these planes for unbounded speeds h would be sufficient for RH. The proved domain |t|≤51n does not have that uniformity in speed.

**Speeds of the order of the verified height with the same averaging radius.** Replace the uniform box by the symmetric probability ν of radius one whose transform is
K(z)=cosh(√(A²+L²z²))/cosh A · sinh(z/G)/(z/G), with G=3·10¹², L=1−1/G, A=LG.
The first factor is entire by its series. To see positivity of the corresponding measure take half the trace of exp(diag(Lz,−Lz)+[[0,A],[A,0]]). Expand in ordered insertions of the off-diagonal matrix: the trace keeps only paths with an even number of jumps, with positive weights A^{2k} integrated over the simplex of times of total length one. The z-dependent exponential is exp(zL∫ sign(t)dt), with displacement in [−L,L]. The trace divided by two equals cosh(√(A²+L²z²)) by the square of the matrix. Normalising at zero and convolving with the box of radius 1/G gives ν and K.

For g_n=ν^{*n}*f, with the same fixed sectorial pulse, W is positive definite on all of span(f,T_t g_n) for n sufficiently large and |t|≤(2G−5√G)n. The physical radius of each convolution remains at most one. Justification: on the axis up to G both factors are positive and strictly decreasing in g>0 (sinc on [0,1]); r=K(iγ₁)>.99 since A−√(A²−L²γ₁²)≤L²γ₁²/A and γ₁<15. Beyond G the first factor on the axis does not exceed 1/cosh A in modulus. Hence the first critical pair dominates the others with a fixed gap. At the exterior ones write g=|Im z|, |b|=|Re z|≤1/2. For G≤g≤2G, the real part of G²+z² is ≤1/4 and the modulus of its imaginary part ≤2G; the formula for the root gives |Re √(G²+z²)|≤2√G. For g≥2G, the real part is ≤−g²/2 and the same rationalised formula gives |Re √(G²+z²)|≤1. Hence |K(z)|≤3 exp(−A+2√G) using the majorant cosh(1/(2G)) of the last box. Even multiplied by exp((2G−5√G)/2) it stays strictly below r. The preceding proof of the normalised determinant applies, with the same margin W(f,f)−A₁>0. Finally K has no exterior zeros and tends to zero in height in the strip by the box factor. Hence it remains sufficient to prove an eventual sign for an unbounded sequence of speeds with THIS fixed kernel.

**Limit of the uniform suppression mechanism using only the strip.** For any symmetric probability supported on [−1,1] with transform J, sup_{|g|≥G}|J(1/2+ig)|≥exp(−πG/2). Indeed fix b=1/2 and consider the function bounded by one on Re z≥0 given by e^(−z)J(b+z)/J(b). If on the tail of the boundary the modulus is ≤s≤1, the two-constants principle in the half-plane gives at z=a>0 log|e^(−a)J(b+a)/J(b)|≤(2/π)arctan(a/G) log s, by the harmonic measure of the two half-lines. The left-hand side is ≥−a by symmetry and monotonicity of J on the positive axis. Let a↓0 and use J(b)≥1. In particular one cannot guarantee by a uniform majorant on the WHOLE exterior strip that exp(h/2)|J(1/2+ig)|<r≤1 for h>πG. The boundary b=1/2 can be approximated from inside by continuity. This limits the envelope technique independent of the location of the zeros, not the sign of the real planes.

**The optimal leading constant of the uniform comparison is 2, not π.** For every symmetric probability of radius one with bilateral transform J, every real b and G>0,
sup_{|g|≥G}|J(b+ig)| ≥ exp(−G) J(b).
In the vertical strip |Re ζ|≤π/2 use the function J(b+iG sin ζ)exp(−G cos ζ). It is entire and bounded there by exp(|b|): |Im(G sin ζ)|=G cos(Re ζ)|sinh(Im ζ)|≤Re(G cos ζ). On each vertical side the argument G sin ζ is real of modulus ≥G and the outer exponential has modulus one. The three-lines theorem gives the inequality on evaluating at ζ=0. Thus, since J(1/2)≥1, a uniform domination exp(h/2)|J(1/2+ig)|<r≤1 above G cannot have a uniform margin for h≥2G. The limit on the boundary line also binds any uniform estimate valid on the whole open strip.

**Construction at distance O(G^(1/3)) from that barrier.** In the preceding trace kernel use a=G^(1/3), L=1−1/G and A=L(G−a). Same positive probability supported in radius one and same box factor. For |g|≥G, |b|≤1/2, write A²+L²(b+ig)²=−X+iY. One has X≥L²g² a/G since ((G−a)²+1/4)/G²≤1−a/G, and |Y|≤L²|g|. Rationalising the root, |Re√(−X+iY)|≤|Y|/(2√X)≤a/2. It follows that |K(b+ig)|≤3exp(−A+a/2). For h≤2G−4a its product with exp(h/2) is ≤3exp(1−a/2)<.99. On the axis up to G−a the filter is positive decreasing, with r=K(iγ₁)>.99, and above G−a the cosh part is oscillatory of modulus ≤1/cosh A. The whole mixed-plane argument holds. For G=3·10¹², 4G^(1/3)<57700. This improvement in the gap settles the leading constant of the method for large G. The barrier corresponds to dominating the modulus on the WHOLE exterior using only support and symmetry, not to the specific values at the zeros.

**Periodic sampling with open gaps: any fixed interval of separations per period suffices, even without an attained front.** For the crossing C_f of the sectorial pulse, any h>0 and nonempty open interval I⊂(0,h), it suffices to prove sup_{s∈I}|C_f(nh+s)|≤exp(o(n)) to obtain RH. Under RH the bounded estimate holds. The proportion |I|/h may be arbitrarily small but fixed. The additional mechanism is to use Selberg density to make the relevant front finite through a positive average with support as short as desired. It is not assumed that the sampling operator reconstructs every smooth function from those intervals.

Fix a right target node b₀+iγ₀, b₀>0, and choose 0<ε<b₀. For each orbit with b>ε and ordinate g>H use the symmetric probability on {−l,0,l}, l=π/g, whose transform is
J_{b,g}(z)=[cosh(lz)+cosh(lb)]/[1+cosh(lb)].
It vanishes on the orbit. Its only zeros have imaginary parts (2k+1)g and real parts ±b. The cost in support radius is π/g. By the density of 413 and partial summation, the sum of these costs for g>H is O_ε(H^(−ε/4)(1+log H)), even counting multiplicity, and tends to zero. Convolve all those factors (one copy per orbit suffices). The resulting law exists as a sum of variables absolutely bounded by a summable series. Its transform J is the normally convergent product; on a compact set each factor differs from one by O(l²), so no additional zeros are introduced by the limit. In particular J preserves the target if H>|γ₀|. Choose H so that the total radius is less than |I|/4.

The average C_J(t)=∫ C_f(t+y)dν(y) has weights c_z J(z) and an absolutely convergent sum, since |J(z)|≤exp(rad(ν)/2). Every surviving node with Re z>ε has height ≤H. There is a nonempty finite right front, above ε and separated from the rest by a positive gap. Let s₀ be the centre of I. Apply to the average at t=nh+s₀+1/n the perturbed lattice proof: the fixed factor exp(s₀z) annihilates no coefficient and the Vandermonde proof tolerates any phase. Along a subsequence the average grows exponentially. But for large n all separations involved lie in nh+I; the assumed bound prevents it. The node-dependent filter only appears in the proof by contradiction; the inequality to be proved involves exclusively the explicit pulse and the intervals fixed in advance. That arithmetic inequality has not been proved. Unlike 090, no set of steps is required and no half-line is covered by overlap.

**Exact rate on each short interval, even after subtracting a local polynomial.** Fix any compact interval I of positive length and any integer degree k≥0. With the preceding sectorial pulse let
E_k(t)=inf_{deg P≤k} ∫_I |C_f(t+s)−P(s)|ds,
with real polynomials chosen afresh for each t. Then the ordinary limit t^(−1)log(1+E_k(t))→Δ=sup_ρ(Reρ−1/2) exists. The same result holds replacing C_f by the sum over ordinary primes B_f, and also without subtracting any polynomial. In particular a subexponential ceiling for this local oscillation along ONE subsequence of real centres t→∞ suffices, even though the length of I is fixed and small. Close antecedent: the mean-subtracted variance earlier in this round uses another scale and another observable.

The ceiling comes from the absolutely convergent series with maximal upper exponent Δ and P=0; under RH it concludes immediately. If Δ>0, choose any right target b₀+iγ₀. Use the preceding Selberg filter with radius less than |I|/4 and target preserved, obtaining a surviving maximum b≥b₀, attained on a finite set, separated from the rest. On the central subinterval I′ of length |I|/2,
exp(−bt) C_J(t+s)=Σ_{Re z=b} a_z exp(iγ_z t) exp(zs)+o(1)
uniformly in s and for EVERY large t. The o(1) uses the gap and summability. The L¹(I′) distance from the finite sum to the space of polynomials of degree ≤k has a positive floor independent of t: allow all phases on the compact torus, apply continuity of the distance to the closed subspace, and observe that no combination can be a polynomial. Indeed, differentiating a supposed identity k+1 times on the interval and applying independence of the distinct exponentials leaves a_z z^{k+1}=0, impossible. The same argument works in the complex space, so it suffices for the real one.

By positivity and unit mass of ν, the integral over I′ of the modulus of the convolution of the residue C_f(t+·)−P with ν is at most its L¹ norm on I. The convolution of P is another polynomial of degree ≤k. Hence E_k(t)≥c exp(bt) for every large t, with c depending on the target, I and k. Passing to the liminf and then to the supremum over b₀ proves the formula even without an exterior maximum. For B_f, the identity in the paragraph on averaged crossings gives B_f(t+s)=−C_f(t+s)−F(0)^2/2+o(1) uniformly in s∈I, which preserves the conclusion. The arithmetic estimate of this local oscillation remains open.

**How much trend can be subtracted without erasing the sign.** In the preceding local E_k(t) allow an integer k=k(t)≥0. If k log(k+2)=o(t), the exact limit Δ is preserved, even with infinitely many exceptions. More generally, if k log(k+2)/t→c finite then liminf log(1+E_k(t))/t ≥ max(0,Δ−c). When there are only finitely many exterior orbits the limit exists and IS exactly max(0,Δ−c). It holds for C_f and for B_f. Thus the order t/log t is a genuine boundary if polynomial fitting is to be used to rule out finitely many exceptions.

Proof of the floor when Δ>c. Choose a target z with b=Re z>c and 0<ε<b−c. Devote less than |I|/8 to the positive Selberg filter annihilating the tail Re z′>ε, preserving the target. Also eliminate the remaining distinct nodes z′ with Re z′>ε other than z, now finitely many, by translation factors with transform exp(lw)−exp(lz′). Each step l>0 can be chosen arbitrarily small outside the discrete set that would annihilate the target. The sum of the steps is chosen less than |I|/8. It is an auxiliary complex measure of finite total variation K fixed depending on the target, independent of t and k. It may also eliminate the conjugate. The averaged crossing on any available interior subinterval is then A exp(z(t+s))+O(exp(εt)), with A≠0. The average of any P still has degree ≤k.

Now apply the difference of order m=k+1 with step l₀=|I|/(8m) and normalisation 2^(−m). It has variation one, total displacement radius |I|/8, and annihilates every polynomial of degree ≤k. By translation and the triangle inequality, the L¹ norm of the result on a central interval of fixed length is bounded by K E_k(t). On the isolated exponential the multiplier is [(exp(l₀z)−1)/2]^m, of modulus ≥ exp(−m log m−O_z(m)): for large m use the expansion at zero and for bounded m the real part of z is positive. The processed tail is still O(exp(εt)). Hence E_k(t)≥exp((b−c−o(1))t) and one lets b↑Δ. If c=0 the general ceiling from the complete series gives equality. The uniformly o(1) errors on replacing C_f by B_f remain harmless in distance to any degree.

For the ceiling with finitely many exceptions, the critical nodes give a bounded function and so do the left ones. In each of the finitely many right terms exp(z(t+s)) approximate exp(zs) by its Taylor polynomial of degree k on the fixed interval. The error is ≤ exp(bt) C_z^{k+1}/(k+1)! up to a fixed multiplicative constant; summing conjugates yields a real polynomial. Stirling gives the ceiling max(0,Δ−c), with the case of bounded degrees included by the trivial ceiling. This proves both the robustness and its limit without requiring the prime inequality to be solved.

**Exact localisation of the primes that decide the oscillation: nine short bands and eight boundary parameters.** For the sectorial pulse, fix I=(0,l), 0<l<1, and the family of trends H=span{s^j exp(±6s):0≤j≤3}. In the L¹(I) norm, the best-fit error of B_f(t+·) by H can be computed exactly using only primes with log p in the nine disjoint bands t−r+(0,l), r=−4,…,4. The limit of the logarithm of one plus this error, divided by t, is Δ. Thus the arithmetic obligation can be proved in bands of width l chosen beforehand, omitting exactly the primes of all gaps.

Detail. Put D=∂_s, q=exp(−6) and define the nine coefficients a_r by (1−qY)^4(1−q/Y)^4=Σa_rY^r. By the explicit transform F, the distributional identity is
(36−D²)^4 B_f(t+s)=(1/4−D²)^2 Σ_r a_r Σ_p (log p)/√p · δ_{log p+r−t}(s).
The symmetry a_r=a_{−r} makes the sign of the bilateral convention irrelevant. It is justified term by term locally by the compact support of k=f*f. Let K_c be the causal kernel whose Laplace transform is (1/4−z²)^2/(36−z²)^4 in Re z>6 (partial fractions, locally integrable function, zero for s<0). Form
J_t(s)=Σ_r a_r Σ_{0<y=log p+r−t<l} (log p)/√p · K_c(s−y).
On the open I the right-hand side of the equation is identical for J_t and B_f(t+·). Their difference belongs exactly to H by the homogeneous constant-coefficient equation, also in distributions. The atoms at the endpoints only modify boundary data. In particular inf_{P∈H}||J_t−P||₁=inf_{P∈H}||B_f(t+·)−P||₁; there is no PNT error in this equality.

For the rate, H is finite-dimensional, closed, invariant under translations and under convolution with the auxiliary filters. The preceding local isolation argument applies because no z of the front, with nonzero imaginary part, is ±6: applying (36−D²)^4 to a supposed coincidence between a sum of exponentials of the front and an element of H contradicts it by independence. The constant term from squares, although not in H, has bounded norm and changing it alters the distance by O(1). The same limit Δ follows. The decomposition does not bound the error in the nine bands. The antecedent of boxes and discrete differences in this round produces polynomial splines; here the differential equation of the concrete sectorial pulse is used to eliminate the boundary data from the arithmetic test.

**Cross-check of the reduction to a single band and effective gain from counting only the targets.** Round 231-A ALREADY obtains a criterion with a single band of ordinary primes, even of logarithmic width h=(log X)^(−o(1)) and subtracting a line. Do not record the step from nine bands to one as a novelty. Instead, for h=(log X)^(−a) with FIXED a>0 a calibrated conclusion is obtained. With the same quadratic error D(X,h) of 231 and Δ=sup(Reρ−1/2), if Δ>3a/(4+6a) then log(1+D)/log X→2Δ. Hence a ceiling X^o(1) along some subsequence of such bands would exclude EVERY zero with Reρ>1/2+3a/(4+6a). If there are only finitely many exceptions, the limit is 2Δ for any fixed a without the restriction.

Indeed t=log X and σ intermediate between 1/2 and the abscissa β₀ of the target. Put q=3(1−σ)/(2−σ)<1, the Ingham exponent used in 230–231. For G=t^v, the tail of the support cost is O(G^(q−1)log^5 G) and the head has only O(G^q log^5 G) targets, since only zeros to the right of σ are annihilated (plus two boundary terms). Choose a/(1−q)<v<1/q. Then the cost of the tail is o(h) and the number M of finite targets satisfies M log t=o(t). With the common step l=h/[10(M+1)(G+|ρ₀|+3)] of 231, log(1/l)=O(log t); the head factors cost exp(o(t)) in variation and the final smoother costs only powers of t. The whole residue extraction of 231 is preserved, including the two annihilations for the best line and the transfer ψ→θ. The interval of v is nonempty exactly if a<(1−q)/q; writing σ=1/2+δ this becomes δ>3a/(4+6a). Choosing σ and then targets with abscissa approaching the supremum proves the limit together with the ceiling on a larger band already proved. If the exceptions are finite for each σ>1/2, a fixed list without tail is kept, with cost only t^O(1) for every a. In this last argument it actually suffices that the list be finite for each intermediate σ used. The ceiling X^o(1) along a subsequence is not proved.

**What resolution measuring the defect of 231 requires.** Let L=X(exp(h)−1), with 0<h≤1, and divide the band into equal cells of length H≤√(X²/L). Linearly interpolating the values of θ at the endpoints gives a function S. By monotonicity, both θ and S lie between the two endpoint values on each cell. Their pointwise difference costs at most (H+1)log(eX), counting integers. The L² distance to the lines is 1-Lipschitz, so the change in √D costs at most √L(H+1)log(eX)/X = O(log X). In particular log(1+D)/log X changes by o(1), in both directions, using 1+(a+b)²≤2(1+a²)(1+b²). The cost is uniform even for the unknown best slope. The defect of the interpolant only requires the cumulative counts on the mesh: for nodal residues u,v against a line, the cell integral equals H(u²+uv+v²)/3. Thus an excess of positive exponent must survive forgetting the internal positions of the primes. What remains is exactly the joint control of the cumulative profile across cells. It is a resolution estimate for the 231 criterion, not a new route; 235 already detects the exponent on a fixed band with fewer statistics.

**Adversarial test for the mesh.** A nearly optimal mass ceiling in EACH cell and the correct total mass do not imply the affine ceiling of 231. In [X,2X] with X=N², fix 1/2<β<1 and use the target profile M(x)=x−X+X^β v((x−X)/X), v(t)=t(1−t). Construct a subset of integers weighted by log n, starting with S(X)=0: include n if S(n−1)+log n≤M(n). For X large, 0<M(n)−M(n−1)<2<log n. By induction 0≤M(n)−S(n)<log n: if n is included the previous ceiling plus the increment is used, and if it is omitted the rule applies. For real x the error is O(log X). In each cell of length √X the mass is √X+O(X^(β−1/2)+log X) and the total is X+O(log X). However √D(S)=X^(β−1/2)/√180+O(log X/√X), since the projection of v onto the lines is the constant 1/6 and its variance equals 1/180. The local hypotheses hold simultaneously with relative error tending to zero. For this comparison, a uniform ceiling of absolute error X^o(1) in each cell of length √X would indeed be sufficient: the cumulative partial errors would be ≤√X X^o(1) and the interpolation error of the previous paragraph costs O(log X). The example allows any arbitrarily small positive power in the error per cell (β arbitrarily close to 1/2), and shows why size bounds alone lose the cancellation between cells. The chosen integers model only those hypotheses and do not satisfy any imposed primality condition.

**What order information a local inventory still loses.** Two ideal profiles can share exactly the multiset of all strings of up to m consecutive cells, for growing m, and have different defect exponents. Put N=4m², X=N², split [X,2X] into N cells of length N. Each mass is N+e. The positive and negative blocks carry respectively m zeros followed by m errors +m or −m. Use m blocks of each type, first alternating, then grouped by sign. In the linear count of strings of length r≤m, the internal ones depend only on the block type. Those crossing a boundary only read zeros of the incoming block, so they depend only on the outgoing one. Both orders end with a negative block and give the same exact counts.

Interpolate linearly. After removing the line x−X, the alternating profile has height ≤m², hence √D≤m²/√X=1/4. For the grouped one, divide the height by m³ and rescale the domain to [0,1]. The profile converges uniformly to v(t)=1−|2t−1| with error ≤1/m (interpolation between block boundaries). The L² distance from v to the lines is 1/√12 by symmetry and variance. Thus √D=(m/4)(1/√12+O(1/m)). Even an exhaustive inventory of local patterns of reach mN in the original variable sees only the same data. The exact equality of inventories refers to ideal masses. The rounding of the previous paragraph realises both profiles with weights log n and alters their heights by O(log X), but only approximately preserves the cell masses. This test identifies the information that any use of local statistics to estimate the defect must supply.

**When the mode list of 235 can be fixed once.** Suppose there is a finite nonempty set of distinct zeros ρ_j with real part β>1/2 and that all the others have real part ≤σ with 1/2≤σ<β. Then there exist fixed K and c>0 such that max_{1≤m≤K}|S_q(m)|≥c q^β for all q sufficiently large. The parameters may depend on the zeros. To prove it, the truncated formula cited in 235, retaining the terms of those zeros, gives θ(x)=x−Σ_j d_j x^{ρ_j}/ρ_j+O(x^σ log²x) with multiplicities d_j, also after removing prime powers. Integrating by parts on [q,2q], for each nonzero integer m one obtains S_q(m)=−Σ_j d_j q^{ρ_j} A_{mj}+O_m(q^σ log²q), where A_{mj}=∫₁²u^{ρ_j−1}exp(2πim(u−1))du. The rows with 0<|m|≤K reach full column rank for some finite K: a vector in the kernel of all of them would give a combination of u^{ρ_j−1} constant by Fourier uniqueness; passing to log u, independence of exponentials with distinct exponents (zero included) forces the vector to be zero. The kernels decrease in finite dimension. The smallest singular value of the finite matrix is positive, while the vector (d_j q^{i Imρ_j}) has constant norm. The negative modes are conjugates of the positive ones. This eliminates the choice of scales and the logarithmic loss under the stated spectral hypothesis. It does not suffice for a non-attained supremum or for infinitely many zeros on the extreme line; the arithmetic bound for the low modes remains open.

**Elimination of the gap and of finiteness on the extreme line.** It suffices that the supremum β>1/2 be attained by a zero ρ₀. Fix 1/2<σ<β. Use the test of 235 with fixed n sufficiently large (Z_n≠0 and regularity at least C⁵), in coordinates u=x/q∈[1,2]. Its mean is zero, its support interior, its Mellin moment at ρ₀ equals one and it eliminates the other zeros with real part ≥σ. By the explicit formula of 235 its prime-weighted sum is −mult(ρ₀)q^ρ₀+O(q^σ+√q log²q).

For g with zero mean, C² on [1,2] and vanishing at both endpoints, the weighted sum of g(p/q) costs ≤C q^β ||g||_{C²} for all large q, with C independent of g. Indeed, two integrations by parts in the moment ∫u^(ρ−1)g(u)du, the first without boundary term, give O(||g||_{C²}/(1+|γ|²)); the boundary term of the second satisfies the same ceiling. The sum of these bounds converges by Z3 and q^Reρ≤q^β. The continuous term vanishes, the trivial terms cost O(||g||∞) by geometric sum for q≥2 and removing prime powers costs O(||g||∞√q log²q). The distributional formula for the test extended by zero is also obtained by smoothing in log u: the extended first derivative has bounded variation, giving the same summable majorant to pass to the limit.

Approximate the fixed test W in C² by its zero-mean Fourier partial sums P_K. Subtract P_K(1)cos(2πu) to keep zero mean and annihilate both endpoints. The approximation still converges in C² by the regularity and interior support of W. Fix K such that the error in the sum is less than mult(ρ₀)q^β/4 by the preceding bound. The sum of the moduli of the coefficients of the corrected polynomial is fixed. The triangle inequality gives max_{1≤m≤K}|S_q(m)|≥c q^β for EVERY large q, even if there are infinitely many zeros on the extreme line or zeros approaching it from the left. The decisive step is to annihilate the endpoints before summing over zeros. If the supremum is not attained, the cost q^β of the approximation error may exceed the signal of any fixed target.

**Converse for the floor with fixed constant.** If β=sup Reρ>1/2 is not attained, there is a single sequence of integers q→∞ such that S_q(m)=o(q^β) for EACH fixed integer m≥1. Indeed, fix g_m(u)=exp(2πimu)−cos(2πu). It has zero mean over [1,2] and vanishes at both endpoints. In the formula of the previous paragraph, after dividing by q^β, the term of each zero tends to zero because Reρ<β, and its modulus is dominated by C_m/(1+|Imρ|²). By dominated convergence and the o(q^β) cost of higher powers, S_q(m)−Re S_q(1)=o(q^β) at ALL integers q→∞. By 236 there are integers q→∞ with |Re S_q(1)|≪log q. The sequence is chosen only with that cosine, so it serves simultaneously for any fixed list without additional extraction. Together with the previous paragraph, this characterises exactly, for β>1/2, when there exist fixed positive K and c with max_{1≤m≤K}|S_q(m)|≥c q^β at every sufficiently large integer q: if and only if β is attained. The converse treats integers and does not claim that the crossings are prime. The little-o only loses a factor tending to zero, which may be subpolynomial; detection with floor q^(β−ε) remains open.

**The simultaneous crossings also transfer to prime scales.** For 1/2<β=sup Reρ<1 and (1+β)/3<a<β, every sufficiently high [x,x+x^a] contains a prime. Indeed put H=x^a, T of order x^(1−a+η) with η>0 so small that 1−a+η<(2−β)/3. In the difference of the truncated explicit formulas of 235 (endpoints rounded to interior half-integers and the same good height) the error O(x log²x/T) is o(H). Use |((x+H)^ρ−x^ρ)/ρ|≪H x^(Reρ−1). The zeros with Reρ≤1/2 contribute in units of H at most x^(−1/2)T log T=o(1). For the rest, by layer integration, the sum costs that same term plus log x times the integral over [1/2,β] of x^(s−1)N(s,T). By Ingham from 230 the exponent in x of the integrand is (1−s)[−1+3(1−a+η)/(2−s)], uniformly negative since β<1. The higher powers cost O(√x log²x)=o(H). Thus the increment of θ is H(1+o(1)). For β=1 it suffices to take a=2/3 by the estimate already cited in 238.

For each integer crossing n of 237 choose a prime q in [n,n+n^a]. In each fixed mode, changing from n to q costs O_m((1+n^a)log n) from entries/exits and phase change at the common primes (Chebyshev). This cost is o(n^β). If β is not attained, the preceding converse then gives S_q(m)=o(q^β) along a SINGLE sequence of PRIMES for each fixed m. Hence the characterisation by the floor c q^β remains exact when all scale quantifiers are restricted to prime numbers, as in the original formulation of 235. The transfer uses the strict margin β−(1+β)/3 and degrades as β descends to 1/2.

**Crossings forced exactly at a prime by the direction of the jumps.** For the original cosine f(u)=cos(2πu), the continuous part of F'(x) between events equals −x⁻¹Σ_{x<p≤2x}log p (p/x)f'(p/x)→−∫₁² u f'(u)du=−1 by PNT and partial summation. The convergence holds uniformly for all large x (the error is bounded by C sup_{x≤y≤2x}|θ(y)−y|/x). The only positive jumps are the entries at x=p/2, of size log p. By the unconditional excursions of 237 each sufficiently high upward crossing occurs through one of those jumps. Hence 0≤F(p/2)≤log p for infinitely many primes p, with prime UPPER endpoint and no gap cost.

For the prime LOWER endpoint use f(u)=(2−u)cos(2πu), of zero mean by symmetry, and call F_f the corresponding sum. The same computation gives continuous derivative tending to +1, entries without jump and exits at x=p of size −log p. If there is an exterior zero, there are excursions of both signs by Landau as in 236: H_f(s)=∫₁²u^(s−1)f(u)du has H_f(1)=0 and sH_f(s)=−1+O(1/|s+1|) by two integrations by parts. In the strip 1/2≤Re s≤1 the numerator of the error is bounded by 4|f'(2)|+|f'(1)|+4 sup|f''|<300, smaller than the exterior heights by Z2. Thus all exterior poles survive. The downward crossings give −log p≤F_f(p)≤0 at infinitely many primes under that hypothesis. The comparison holds for a single component in each construction; it does not make distinct filters simultaneous. A pointwise ceiling of logarithmic size for this component along a prime subsequence is therefore compatible with exterior zeros.

**Between consecutive entries the full envelope is preserved.** With F from 236 and p<r large consecutive primes, for all p/2≤x<r/2 one has
    F(r/2)−log r ≤ F(x) ≤ F(p/2).
Indeed F decreases on that segment, including all exit jumps, and the left limit at r/2 is F(r/2)−log r. The consequence combines the drift already proved with the energy of 236: for M(X)=max_{2X≤p≤4X}|F(p/2)| with p prime, log(1+M(X)/√X)/log X→B. For the floor, every x in [1.2X,1.5X] is flanked by two entries in [X,2X] for X large by PNT (primes in [2X,2.4X] and [3X,4X] suffice). The envelope majorises |F(x)| by M(X)+log(4X). The energy of 236 with start 1.2X and ratio 1.25 gives the lower exponent 2B, and the pointwise ceiling of 236 gives the upper one B. For B=0 the trivial floor suffices. Thus, even if the abscissa is not attained, it is sufficient to find a sequence X with ceiling X^(1/2+o(1)) for a SINGLE cosine measured only at the entry of each prime, uniformly over all entries of that band. A single cheap crossing per band does not satisfy this condition. The use of the cube to integrate jumps is already in 232; the envelope only needs the direction of the variations.

**The average over prime entries preserves the exponent without weighting by gaps.** Let P(X)=X⁻²Σ_{2X≤p≤4X}(log p)|F(p/2)|². Then log(1+P(X))/log X→2B with B from 236. For B>0 put β=1/2+B. Choose a between (1+β)/3 and β when β<1, or a=2/3 if β=1. The preceding short-interval proof gives θ mass comparable to X^a in each cell of length comparable to X^a inside [2X,4X] (constant factors do not affect the proof). Split [1.2X,1.5X] into equal cells of length comparable to X^a. In each cell I there is mass Σ_{p/2∈I}log p comparable to |I|. Moreover for all x,y of the cell |F(x)−F(y)|≪X^a log X by counting entries and exits and phase change. Average |F(x)|²≤2|F(p/2)|²+O(X^(2a)log²X) over those entries and integrate in x. One gets X⁻²∫|F|²≪P(X)+X^(2a−1)log²X, with the integral over [1.2X,1.5X]. By 236 the left-hand side is X^(2β−1+o(1)), and a<β strictly absorbs the error. The ceiling P(X)≤X^(2B+o(1)) follows from the pointwise ceiling of 236 and Chebyshev, also for B=0. This allows individual exceptions and does not require measuring gaps: a subsequence with P(X)=X^o(1) (or smaller) suffices. As a consequence for each δ>0 and B>0, the entries with |F(p/2)|≥X^(β−δ) number at least X^(1−o(1)) in each band: the rest contribute O(X^(2B−2δ)) and each normalised summand costs ≤X^(2β−2+o(1)). The cardinality exponent does not ensure positive density.

**Necessary cancellation among triples of distinct primes.** Under RH the average P(X) of the previous paragraph is O(1). To see it, on each logarithmic interval of fixed length the explicit formula of 236 for F_ψ(e^t)e^(−t/2) is, up to a bounded remainder from trivial zeros, the series of exponentials with coefficients −H(ρ), of modulus O(1/(1+|γ|)) by parts. It has local L² norm uniformly bounded in the position of the interval. Indeed majorise its indicator by a translate of a positive compact smooth cut-off; on expanding the square of a finite sum, the pairs of ordinate blocks [n,n+1),[k,k+1) cost C(1+|n−k|)⁻² b_n b_k, with b_n≪log(2+|n|)/(1+|n|) by Z3. Young gives CΣ b_n² and the same argument in the tails ensures L² convergence to the distributional object of 236.
