The modulus of the target moment is ≫_{ρ,A} X^b independently of the list, and the integral inequality transfers it to the absolute mean. The extreme abscissa need not be attained.

If RH holds, for the positive ordinates γ≤T=3√log X round π/(2γ) down to the nearest multiple of X^(−2). Use, for example, one entry per zero counted with multiplicity. The number is O(T log(2T))≤ceil(log X) eventually and the sum of squares fits in a fixed A by Σ_γ γ^(−2)<∞. At each of those zeros, the chosen factor costs at most γ/X² by the Lipschitz inequality of the cosine, while the other factors have modulus ≤1 on Re s=1/2. This also holds at the conjugate. After summing the residues, the Gaussian leaves a cost O(√X/X²) by the zero count. For |γ|>T, the Gaussian tail, even using only exp(−T²/4) and summing the rest exp(−γ²/4), costs O(√X exp(−T²/4)) on the band. Adding the remainder O_A(1/X) proves the ceiling. It remains to produce by arithmetic arguments lists with small mean in arbitrarily high bands without using RH.

**The minimum over convex mixtures stops detecting exterior zeros.** With the same admissible lists, consider a distribution over them, fixed for the whole band, and take the absolute value AFTER averaging the balances F_a. For some fixed budget A this problem has error O(1/X) uniform on [X,2X] unconditionally. Hence the convex relaxation admits the favourable result whatever the position of the zeros. The original selection of a single list remains open.

For each zero ρ=b+iγ with 0<γ≤T=3√log X take d=π/γ. In C_d(s)=cosh(d(s−1/2))/cosh(d/2) one has C_d(ρ)=−cosh(d(b−1/2))/cosh(d/2)<0. If this factor is activated with probability p=1/(1−C_d(ρ)), the mean factor 1−p+pC_d(ρ) is zero. It also vanishes at the conjugate. Make the activations independent for all zeros below the cut. In each outcome use as admissible parameter d'=floor(X²d)/X². Every resulting list fits in a fixed integer budget larger than Σ_{γ>0}π²/γ² and has o(log X) entries. The averaged transform is the common Gaussian times the product of 1−p+pC_d'(s), where C_d' here denotes C with rounded parameter, not a derivative. The combination uses the real parts of the zeros only to prove their existence in the convex hull.

In the strip 0≤Re s≤1, |C_u(s)|≤1 for u≥0. At the target zero the change of parameter degrades the exact zero by O((1+γ)/X²) by differentiation in u on a fixed compact, with the other mean factors of modulus ≤1. For y≤2X each residue below the cut thus costs O(X^(−1)(1+γ)exp(−γ²/2)/|ρ|); the sum converges with multiplicity. Above the cut, the tail is O(X exp(−T²/4))=O(X^(−5/4)). The shift to −1 contributes O_A(1/X) uniformly also for the mixtures, by linearity and the previous bounds. This proves the result without assuming RH. On the other hand averaging the already formed absolute errors has exactly the same minimum as choosing a single list, by linearity in the probabilities.

**Finite prime data for both problems.** The Gaussian introduces unbounded arguments of ψ, even though the family of lists is finite. On [X,2X] every sum can be truncated to prime powers ≤U=2X exp(C_A√log X), with uniform error O_A(X^(−2)) both for lists and for mixtures. Indeed for t≥1 one has E exp(tv)=K_a(t)≤exp(C'_A t²) by the cosh bound and the budget. For v>u=C_A√log X, the moment E[exp(v)1_{v>u}] is ≤exp(C'_A t²−(t−1)u), with t=u/(2C'_A) for large X. Choose C_A generously and use ψ(y exp v)≪y exp v. The same estimate applies to the lower endpoint. In particular the distinction between the two problems persists with truncated prime data; the integral over y and the Gaussian weights remain analytic objects.

**Safe independent mixture and scalar fitting by median.** Let C_a(s)=cosh(a(s−1/2))/cosh(a/2), a>0, and B_{a,p}=1−p+pC_a for 0≤p≤1. The factor has some zero in 0<Re s<1 off the critical line if and only if
    1/2 < p < p_*(a),    p_*(a)=cosh(a/2)/(1+cosh(a/2)).
Indeed, for p>0 solve cosh(a(s−1/2))=−d, d=(1−p)cosh(a/2)/p. If d≤1 all roots lie on the line. If d>1 their real parts are 1/2±arcosh(d)/a, inside the open strip precisely if d<cosh(a/2). For p=0 the factor is constant. In particular one can work entirely in the box p_*(a)≤p≤1 and mix INDEPENDENT activations before the absolute value. The probability of the construction that erased an exterior zero fell inside the forbidden interval.

Fixed agenda without knowing ordinates. For large X take T=3√log X, j from 0 to ceil(log₂ T), a_j=2^(−j). At each scale reserve m_j=ceil(C 2^j(j+1)) slots with independent probabilities in [p_*(a_j),1]. C absolute and sufficiently large by the zero count up to height π 2^j. Thus there are O(T log(2T)) slots, O(log log X) distinct scales and Σ m_j a_j²≤A_C fixed. The mean factors multiply, with the same Gaussian N(−1/2,1). The whole agenda, even the unadjusted slots, keeps the budget. The minimum of the mean absolute error on the band over this single box also characterizes RH, with threshold 1 in arbitrarily high bands. A mesh can be imposed on the probabilities by rounding up to the nearest multiple of X^(−2) (including 1).

If RH holds, for each positive γ≤T choose j with π/2≤a_jγ≤π (the ordinates start above π). The number at each scale fits in its slots. Adjust one of them with p=cosh(a_j/2)/(cosh(a_j/2)−cos(a_jγ)), which belongs to the box and gives a zero factor at 1/2+iγ. Use p=1 in the leftover ones. Rounding costs ≤2/X² in the target factor and the remaining ones have modulus ≤1 in the strip. The preceding Gaussian proof gives error O(1/X). Conversely, for every exterior zero ρ no factor of the box vanishes there. Uniformly in p, B_{a,p}(ρ)=1+O_ρ(a²) near zero; by compactness for a away from zero and Σa²≤A_C, the product has modulus ≥c_{ρ,C}>0. The uniform vertical Gaussian bound and the isolation of 230 give the same floor ≫X^Reρ in each high band, independently of the selection of probabilities.

With the other parameters fixed, the balance in y is U(y)+pV(y), where U and V are obtained by evaluating the slot off and on and taking the difference. An exact minimizer of the absolute mean over p in the allowed interval is a median of −U/V with weights |V|dy, clipped to the interval (if V=0 almost everywhere any value works). On the mesh it suffices to compare its admissible neighbours and the admissible endpoints. It is a convex optimization in one coordinate at a time; averaging whole products with each other does not necessarily preserve the class, and it has not been shown that the successive medians reach the global minimum or the required threshold. The internal novelty relative to the failed convexification is the exact classification of each factor and the box of prescribed scales.

**Local convexification with spectral guarantee and test by finite linear programs.** Keep the dyadic agenda of the previous entry. Each level X requires a disjunction of linear feasibility problems; the total number of vertex occurrences is X^o(1) and O(log X) arithmetic observations per vertex suffice. RH is equivalent to the feasibility of at least one of the problems at arbitrarily large integer levels X. The mixtures in each problem are joint, not a sequence of coordinate updates.

Split each admissible probability interval into subintervals of width ≤δ=1/log log X using O(1/δ) pieces per slot. In each small box allow any convex combination of the outputs of its vertices. By multiaffinity, the output of every point of that box is exactly a combination of the vertices through successive linear interpolation. The hull of the vertices is therefore exactly the hull of the outputs of the whole box. Different boxes are not mixed. With D=O(√log X log log X) slots there are at most (O(1/δ))^D·2^D=X^o(1) vertex occurrences in total.

Let ρ be any fixed exterior zero. On every safe interval of scale a, |∂_p log B_{a,p}(ρ)|=|(C_a(ρ)−1)/B_{a,p}(ρ)|≤C_ρ a². For small a uniform Taylor is used; for the rest compactness and the absence of zeros. Integrate this logarithmic derivative along the segment from a base vertex p₀ to p. Since Σ a²≤A_C is fixed, the transform satisfies |K_p(ρ)/K_{p₀}(ρ)−1|≤exp(C_ρ A_C δ)−1. The disc so obtained is convex and its relative radius tends to zero. Every mixture in that box therefore keeps, for high X, at least half the modulus of the base vertex, which has a uniform positive floor. The vertical Gaussian bound also survives the mixture. The isolation of the variational proof forces absolute mean ≫_{ρ,C}X^Reρ in each box, uniformly over its weights. Under RH the favourable list of exact probabilities of the previous entry falls in some box, and its output, of uniform norm O(1/X), belongs to the admissible hull.

The test can be implemented mathematically with finite linear constraints. Take k=ceil(c log X) Chebyshev nodes of the first kind in v∈[0,log 2]. For a box with vertices i, look for λ_i≥0, Σλ_i=1, such that |Σλ_i F_i(X exp v_j)|≤1 at each node. The truncated prime data of the preceding entry can be used there, with error O_A(X^(−2)) per observation. To check that the nodes suffice, continue each complete output as a function of v by Mellin on Re s=2. On a fixed Bernstein ellipse, for example the one of parameter 2 for that interval, the Gaussian dominates exp(|Im v|·|Im s|); one obtains O_C(X²) uniformly, also after centring and mixing. Truncating the Chebyshev series before degree k approximates with error O_C(X² 2^(−k))=O_C(X^(−2)) choosing c sufficiently large, by Cauchy's formula for the coefficients. If the truncated data pass the test, that polynomial has modulus ≤1+O_C(X^(−2)) at the nodes. By discrete orthogonality of cosines each coefficient of the polynomial costs O(1), so its supremum on the interval is O(k). This contradicts the exterior floor. Under RH the favourable mixture passes all constraints eventually even with truncation. The count X^o(1) measures vertices; it does not include the cost of generating prime data nor certify a total numerical complexity. It has not been shown that there are arbitrarily high feasible boxes without assuming RH.

**A single linear program per band through moving reflection and common weights.** Keep the boxes and nodes of the previous construction. As columns take ALL ordered pairs (p,q) of vertices of one and the same box, then gather the columns of all boxes into a single simplex of weights λ. For each u of a mesh of [1/2,1] of step ≤1/log log X, the column uses the multiplier
    M_{p,q,u}(s)=K_p(s)K_q(2u−s).
It is the transform of a finite positive measure: convolve the law of p with the image under v↦−v of exp(2uv)ν_q(dv). In the cell count the main term of EACH column is subtracted, (1−r)y M_{p,q,u}(1). Require error between −1 and 1 at each pair (u, Chebyshev node), using the same λ for all. Feasibility of this single program at arbitrarily high integers X is equivalent to RH. There are X^o(1) columns (at most 4^D per box) and O(log X log log X) observation pairs. The validity of the global mixture is not extended to the previous single-copy test.

Indeed, under RH let t be the favourable choice of exact probabilities. In its box, K_t(s)=Σ_p c_p K_p(s) by multiaffine interpolation, with c_p≥0 summing to one and independent of s. Hence λ_{p,q}=c_p c_q represents simultaneously K_t(s)K_t(2u−s) for ALL u. The zeros below the cut are cancelled by the first factor; for the remaining ones and for the contour on the left the Gaussian bounds are uniform in u. The main term has been centred according to the tilted mass. One obtains error O_C(1/X) and eventual feasibility. This explains why pairs within a box, including off-diagonal ones, are admitted.

Conversely, given any exterior zero ρ=b+iγ and any column, at u=b one has
    M_{p,q,b}(ρ)=K_p(ρ)·conj(K_q(ρ)).
The quotient K_p(ρ)/K_q(ρ) lies in a disc of radius o_ρ(1) around one because the two vertices of THIS column are close. Since |K_q(ρ)|≥c_ρ>0 uniformly, the real parts of all columns are ≥c_ρ²/2 at high levels, even if they come from very distant boxes. Choose u in the mesh closest to b. On a compact disc around conj(ρ), the K_q and their derivatives are uniformly bounded by the strip bounds and Cauchy. Hence the change in M is O_ρ(1/log log X); a common positive floor remains. Consequently an arbitrary mixture of columns keeps the target pole in that SAME channel u, with uniform margin. The isolation of 230 gives mean absolute error ≫_ρ X^b in that channel for all mixtures. The previous Gaussian interpolation arguments at O(log X) nodes contradict it if the constraints pass. They are uniform in u because the second argument 2u−s varies in fixed strips. The prime powers can also be truncated as before: the moments of the new measure are bounded by exp(O_C(1+t²)) uniformly in u. The conclusion remains a reduction; it is unknown how to prove that the arithmetic system is feasible in arbitrarily high bands.

**An LP of polylogarithmic size without enumeration of boxes or lists.** Keep the dyadic agenda a_j=2^(−j), 0≤j≤J=ceil(log₂(3√log X)), with its m_j fixed slots. All sums of shifts of a filter before the Gaussian belong to the grid z_i=i2^(−J), |i|≤2^J Σ m_j a_j=O(2^J(J+1)²). Use one real variable μ_ij per ordered pair of points, without independence or rank constraints. Require μ≥0, Σμ=1 and Σμ exp(4(|z_i|+|z_j|))≤C₀ for a fixed constant sufficiently large depending on the agenda. Put D(s,t)=Σμ exp(sz_i+tz_j) and G(s)=exp((s²−s)/2).

Protection constraints. Take R=(log log X)^(1/4) and meshes with endpoints and maximal step (log X)^(−2) in [1/2+1/R,1] and [0,R] for X sufficiently large. At each pair (u,v) impose
    Re D(u+iv,u−iv) ≥ 1/log X.
Arithmetic constraints. For each u of the first mesh, use the multiplier M_u(s)=G(s)G(2u−s)D(s,2u−s) and centre by (1−r)yM_u(1). Impose error between −1 and 1 at the same O(log X) Chebyshev nodes as before. Everything is linear in μ: a column corresponds to the two shifted Gaussians and to the tilt-reflection of the second. The program has O(log X (1+log log X)^4) variables, O(R(log X)^4) protection constraints and O((log X)^3) arithmetic observations, in addition to the basic constraints. These bounds do not account for the cost of evaluating the coefficients.

Feasibility under RH. Take for w_i the discrete distribution preceding the Gaussian of the favourable dyadic filter already constructed and μ_ij=w_i w_j. The budget Σm_j a_j²≤A implies E exp(±4z)≤exp(CA) by the cosh bound; thus C₀ is fixed in advance using the agenda, also for E exp(4|z|). In the protection constraints D(s,conj s)=|∏B_{a,p}(s)|². Check uniformity as the mesh grows: for |Im s|≤R, 1/2+1/R≤Re s≤1, the factors with small a(1+R) have log|B|≥−C a²(1+R)² by Taylor. There are O(A(1+R)²) remaining factors. In each one write B=p(cosh(a(s−1/2))+cos θ)/cosh(a/2), 0≤cos θ≤1 by the safe branch. Factor the sum as 2cosh((a(s−1/2)+iθ)/2)cosh((a(s−1/2)−iθ)/2). Each modulus is at least sinh(a(Re s−1/2)/2). Hence |B|≥c a²/R²≥c'/(1+R)^4 for those factors. The squared product is ≥exp(−C_A(1+R)²log(2+R))>1/log X eventually. The arithmetic constraints pass because the first factor of the favourable filter kills the critical zeros below the cut and the second keeps the Gaussian bounds.

Necessity without a maximum hypothesis. If ρ=b+iγ, γ>0, exists, the mesh approaches (b,γ) within O((log X)^(−2)) for all large X. In the strip |Re s|,|Re t|≤3, D and its first derivatives have a uniform ceiling by the imposed moment. For u of the mesh closest to b, transferring the constraint of the neighbouring point (u,v) to D(ρ,2u−ρ) gives real part ≥1/log X−O((log X)^(−2)). The factors G keep modulus ≥c_ρ>0. Thus |M_u(ρ)|≫_ρ1/log X even for matrices that do not decompose as products of filters. On the line −1 and on the initial line 2 the arguments of D have real parts between −1 and 3. Therefore the uniform Gaussian bounds, the isolation and the interpolation of 230 and of the preceding entry are kept. The mean floor ≫_ρ X^b/log X contradicts the ceiling O(log X) implied by the nodes. No positive semidefinite matrix is needed for this direction.

Even for the enlarged matrices, the discrete shifts have modulus O((1+log log X)^2) and the remaining Gaussian noise has fixed variance and bounded mean under the tilts u considered. Hence truncating the prime powers at X² costs less than X^(−2) uniformly, using the moment bound for the tilted mass and the Gaussian tail. The result is a single LP per band with finite prime data. The improvement is one of representation: no feasible matrix in arbitrarily high bands has been constructed without RH, nor has a polylogarithmic bound for the complete computation time been established.

**Both families of constraints are feasible separately; dual cost of making them incompatible.** In the compact LP fix C₀ sufficiently large depending on the agenda and write η=1/log X. Let F be the matrix of centred and truncated arithmetic observations, P that of protection and H_ij=exp(4(|z_i|+|z_j|)). There exists unconditionally a distribution μ⁰ on the original grid with H·μ⁰≤C₀, Pμ⁰≥0 and ||Fμ⁰||∞=O(1/X). Therefore replacing the positive floor η by zero makes the test feasible without any hypothesis. The construction is used as an existence witness, not as a computation from the primes alone.

For each zero ρ=b+iγ, 0<γ≤T, use a dyadic slot d of the agenda with π/2≤dγ≤π. At the points −d,0,d put masses proportional respectively to e^(2db), −2e^(db)cos(dγ), 1. They are nonnegative and the discrete transform is proportional to e^(−ds)(e^(ds)−e^(dρ))(e^(ds)−e^(d conj(ρ))). It annihilates exactly the zero and its conjugate even though b≠1/2. For any of these distributions the mean has modulus O(d²): the normalization denominator is ≥1 and the difference of the extreme weights is O(d) before multiplying by d. Thus the exponential moments at ±4 are ≤exp(C d²) by uniform Taylor for d≤1. On convolving the support stays on the prescribed grid and all necessary moments are uniform by the quadratic budget. Use a single slot per positive zero, enough by the same local count. Call w the product distribution of summed shifts and take μ⁰_ij=w_i w_j. In P it gives squared moduli, while the first factor of D(ρ,2u−ρ) vanishes for each zero below the cut. The Gaussian and the shift to −1 of the previous entries give O(1/X) at each observation, including truncation. C₀ can be enlarged once for this family; the protection of the complete LP and its converse test remain intact for any fixed C₀. The mass e₀₀ at the origin, for its part, satisfies P e₀₀=1 and H·e₀₀=1.

Consequence for any infeasible band. By finite separation (or Farkas), there exist a real vector v of arithmetic rows, a vector λ≥0 of protection rows and τ≥0 such that
    min_ij [(Fᵀv)_ij−(Pᵀλ)_ij+τ H_ij] > ||v||₁−ηΣλ+τC₀ .
Indeed one separates the image of the simplex (Fμ,Pμ,H·μ) from the box ||f||∞≤1, p≥η, h≤C₀; the former is compact and the latter closed. Conversely such a test proves infeasibility. Evaluating at e₀₀ excludes v=0 for η<1, so normalize ||v||₁=1. Then evaluating at μ⁰ and at e₀₀ respectively forces
    ηΣλ>1−O(1/X),
    v·F e₀₀ > 1+(1−η)Σλ+τ(C₀−1).
In particular no certificate with protection mass o(log X) can separate the system. On the primal side, (1−η)μ⁰+ηe₀₀ already satisfies all constraints except, possibly, the arithmetic ones, and its maximal error is ≤η||F e₀₀||∞+O(1/X). This identity locates the remaining obligation, without providing a ceiling O(log X) for the unfiltered error nor the feasibility of the complete system.

**Finite localization of a possible infeasibility.** With R=(log log X)^(1/4) and e=R^(−2), call a protective row (u,v) marked if there is a zero b+iγ with
    |b−u|<e,   0<γ≤v+e.
For all sufficiently large X, the ternary matrix μ⁰ of the previous entry satisfies the floor 1/log X in ALL unmarked rows and keeps ||Fμ⁰||∞=O(1/X). In particular, if the LP is infeasible there must exist a zero with b≥1/2+1/R−1/R² and 0<γ≤R+1/R². It is not claimed that γ is close to v from below: the harmonics of a smaller height can also affect a row.

Indeed, the normalized factor of the ternary shift for the target b+iγ at s=u+iv has modulus
    exp(−du) |exp(ds)−exp(d(b+iγ))| |exp(ds)−exp(d(b−iγ))| / (1−2exp(db)cos(dγ)+exp(2db)).
The denominator is bounded by an absolute constant, d≤1. For γ≤CR, C fixed and large, one has d≥π/(2CR). In an unmarked row, if |u−b|≥e, each difference is bounded below by the difference of radii, ≫de. In the remaining case γ>v+e. The angles d(γ−v) and d(γ+v) lie in [de,2π−de] because dγ≤π. Using |r₁exp(iθ)−r₂|²=(r₁−r₂)²+4r₁r₂ sin²(θ/2), the two differences are again ≫de. Each low-height factor therefore has modulus ≫R^(−6). Their number is O(R log(2R)) by the usual count.

For γ>CR, d≤π/γ makes d(1+R) small. If Z is the corresponding ternary shift, |Z|≤d, E Z=O(d²); by Taylor |E exp(sZ)−1|≪d²(1+R)². Increase C so that the right-hand side is <1/2. The product of the high moduli is ≥exp(−C'(1+R)²Σ d²), not depending on T. Hence in the unmarked rows Pμ⁰, which is the square of the total modulus, is ≥exp(−O(R²+R log²(2R)))>1/log X eventually. If no row is marked, μ⁰ is a witness for the complete LP. Moreover, in the previous dual inequality one obtains
    (1/log X) Σ_{marked rows} λ > 1−O(1/X):
the unmarked rows cannot contribute positively to Σ λ(η−Pμ⁰), and Pμ⁰≥0 in the others. The statement does not give an effective numerical threshold for certifying a concrete band nor exclude the zeros of the growing rectangle. It does identify which local spectral information suffices for feasibility and where the protective part of a separator must concentrate.

**Localization in both coordinates; test with a single row.** With e=R^(−2), now mark (u,v) only if there is a zero b+iγ, γ>0, with |u−b|<e AND |v−γ|<e. There exists one and the same matrix satisfying the arithmetic constraints with error O(1/X), Pμ≥0 on the whole mesh and Pμ≥1/log X in all unmarked rows. Therefore the same dual mass floor of the previous entry is concentrated in these squares, without marks due exclusively to higher harmonics.

The agenda constant and C₀ can be fixed from the start with absolute slack as follows. For γ≤C R (C fixed and large), choose independently a uniform d among the multiples of h=2^(−J) falling in [1.8/γ,2.6/γ]; for larger heights up to T use the previous dyadic d. For every d build the three ternary weights with the exact zero as before: cos(dγ)<0 on the new interval. Each distribution w of the sum of shifts lives on the original grid: the maximal shift is ≤πΣ_{0<γ≤T}1/γ=O((log(2T))²) by partial summation. The slot constant is taken sufficiently large to cover this multiple in the allowed support. The exponential moment is uniform because Σd² is bounded. Take μ as the average of wwᵀ over the choices. For each choice all zeros below T are annihilated exactly in the first factor, so the arithmetic error remains O(1/X) also for μ. In the protective rows Pμ is the product of the expectations of the squared moduli of the individual factors, by independence of the scales (in each outer product the SAME choice is used on both sides).

The radial distance |u−b|≥e gives the previous floor for every choice of d. To account for the distance in height, put t=dγ and λ=(v±γ)/γ. In [1.8,2.6] a proportion larger than 3/4 of the values of t on the grid of step γh satisfies |sin(λt/2)|≥c min(1,|λ|), with c absolute and sufficiently small and X high. For 0<|λ|≤1/4 it holds on the whole interval by the elementary bound for the sine near zero. For |λ|>1/4, the exceptional intervals have total length O(c) and number O(1+|λ|), counting neighbourhoods of the multiples of π. The error of counting those intervals on the grid, in proportion to the total, is O((1+|λ|)γh)=O((R+CR)h)=o(1). When |v−γ|≥e both signs apply and at least half of the scales are good at once. On them the two exponential differences cost in modulus at least c min(1,e/γ) and c respectively, since v+γ≥γ. The expectation of the squared modulus is thus ≥c'R^(−6); in the radial case the square floor c'R^(−12) suffices. There are O(R log R) low targets. For the high ones the joint exponential floor of the previous entry still holds. Again Pμ≥exp(−O(R²+R log²(2R)))>1/log X outside the marked squares.

For a local test keep only ONE protective row (u,v), the arithmetic rows of its channel u and the basic constraints on μ. If the local program fails at sufficiently high X, the square centred at that row contains an exterior zero. Conversely, given a specific exterior zero, the mesh row closest to it fails at all sufficiently large X: the constraint of that row itself and the exponential moment force |M_u(ρ)|≫_ρ 1/log X for any candidate, and the isolation in its channel contradicts the ceiling of the nodes. The threshold in this direction may depend on the zero. It is not claimed that all rows of its square fail, nor that separate feasibility of each row implies joint feasibility at a given X. No infeasible local program has been found.

**Quadratic order of the optimal margin near a fixed exterior zero.** Variant of the local LP: keep ALL arithmetic observations and require floor ZERO on the WHOLE protective mesh. On that nonempty set of matrices maximize f_μ(s)=Re D(s,conj s) at a free point s. Call m_X(s) the maximum. Let η=1/log X. For each fixed exterior zero ρ of the upper half-plane there exist a fixed disc around ρ contained in the exterior strip and positive constants such that, on that whole disc and for X sufficiently high,
    c_ρ |s−ρ|² ≤ m_X(s) ≤ C_ρ (|s−ρ|²+η²).
The constants are local. The zero is not assumed simple. These estimates describe the modified test, which observes all arithmetic channels and keeps auxiliary nonnegative floors.

Floor. Repeat the previous random witness using exactly one factor per DISTINCT zero of positive ordinate, even if multiple. The logarithmic derivative has only simple poles; the residue counts the multiplicity, so exact annihilation still suffices. Shrink the disc to separate ρ from all other distinct zeros, including its conjugate. For the factor of ρ, in the ternary notation the term exp(ds)−exp(dρ) has modulus ≥c_ρ|s−ρ| for every scale of the interval [1.8/γ,2.6/γ], by uniform Taylor on that compact interval of positive d. The conjugate term stays away from zero: at s=ρ its angular difference is 2dγ∈[3.6,5.2]. This persists on a small disc. For each of the other targets of bounded height, separation in at least one coordinate, together with the two-angular-differences lemma of the previous entry, gives a positive floor of the expectation of the squared modulus, uniform on the disc and for high X. There are only finitely many targets up to a fixed height C times the maximum of 1+|s| on the disc. For the higher ones, even if the scale is random, |E exp(shift·s)−1|≪_ρ d² for the ternary shift (the expectation here is over its three weights). The quadratic budget and the smallness of each d at large heights give a positive floor for their whole product. The average matrix of the outer products is admissible; hence the floor for m_X.

Ceiling. For any admissible matrix choose the arithmetic channel u closest to b=Reρ. In that channel the Chebyshev argument gives a uniform ceiling O(log X) on the band for the complete output. Apply the isolation test of 230 to ρ with 1/2<σ<b. Without presupposing positive protection one obtains X^b |M_u(ρ)|≪_ρ X^σ+log X, since all other surviving terms lie to the left of σ and the strip bounds are uniform. The Gaussian factors do not vanish and u→b. Moving the second argument of D from 2u−ρ to conj(ρ) costs O_ρ(η²) by the mesh step. The result is |f_μ(ρ)|≪_ρ η².

The imposed exponential moment uniformly bounds the gradient and the Hessian of f_μ on a somewhat larger disc. That whole region eventually lies inside the mesh and the zero floors imply f_μ≥−C_ρ η² also between nodes. If the gradient at ρ is not zero, advance a distance η in the direction opposite to it; Taylor and the floor give |∇f_μ(ρ)|≤C'_ρ η. Taylor again at the free point s proves the ceiling, also after maximizing.

In this variant, requiring protection η at s produces an infeasibility core of radius c'_ρ√η around each fixed exterior zero; outside a radius C'_ρ√η but inside the same disc the additional row is feasible. It is a local order in both directions, not an effective threshold for a numerical band. It does not supply a positive bound for the margin at the possible centres ρ.

**Conditional annihilation imposed by the arithmetic rows and minimal dispersion cost.** Consider any sequence X→∞ and probability matrices of the compact LP satisfying the moment bound and all arithmetic observations; impose no protection. View them as laws of (Z₁,Z₂) in R². If there is an exterior zero ρ=b+iγ, γ>0, every weak limit law μ satisfies
    E_μ[exp(ρ Z₁) | Z₂]=0   almost surely.
In particular, tilting μ by exp(bZ₁) and normalizing, the mean squared error in predicting Z₁ from Z₂ is ≥π²/(4γ²), even for the best measurable predictor (here the MEAN OF THE SQUARE is meant, without taking a root).

Proof. The exponential moment bound gives sequential compactness and allows passing to the limit in D(s,t)=E exp(sZ₁+tZ₂) on compacts of |Re s|,|Re t|<4, by uniform truncation of tails. Fix u in (1/2,1) and observe the closest mesh channel. The isolation and Chebyshev argument of the margin ceiling gives D_X(ρ,2u_X−ρ)=O_{ρ,u}(X^(σ−b)+X^(−b)log X) for 1/2<σ<b (the Gaussians have a fixed floor). Hence D_μ(ρ,2u−ρ)=0. The segment so obtained has accumulation points inside the strip of holomorphy in t. By analytic identity D_μ(ρ,t)=0 for all |Re t|<4. For purely imaginary t this is the Fourier transform of the finite complex measure B↦E_μ[exp(ρZ₁)1_{Z₂∈B}]. Fourier uniqueness proves the conditional annihilation. This uses all arithmetic channels, not only the channel closest to b.

Under the indicated tilt, the conditional law of Z₁ given Z₂ has phase moment E[exp(iγZ₁)|Z₂]=0. For any measurable centre c=c(Z₂) the conditional expectation of cos(γ(Z₁−c)) also vanishes. For every real v one has v²≥π²/4−π cos v. Indeed the difference is even, decreases on [0,π/2] by sin v≥2v/π and increases from π/2 on by 2v≥π≥π sin v; its minimum is zero. Applying this inequality conditionally proves the floor, even on almost every fibre. The constant is optimal for a single phase condition: the symmetric law at c±π/(2γ) attains it. It is not claimed that this law passes the remaining rows of the LP.

Verifiable arithmetic consequence on the sequence of matrices: for the fixed predictor c(z)=z, if the zero exists then
    liminf_X E_X[exp(bZ₁)(Z₁−Z₂)²] / E_X[exp(bZ₁)] ≥ π²/(4γ²).
To prove it take a subsequence realizing the liminf, extract a limit and use continuity of those two observables under the exponential budget. The same conclusion holds for each fixed continuous predictor of at most linear growth. The limit is not interchanged with a minimization over predictors that may change arbitrarily with X. The inequality gives a quantitative condition that any arithmetic construction concentrated near the diagonal would have to overcome in order to exclude a zero; it does not prove that such matrices exist.

### Unconditional obstruction to concentrating the two coordinates

Under RH, let μ be any weak limit of arithmetically feasible matrices in bands X→∞ with the fixed exponential budget. For each zero ρ=1/2+iγ one has Eμ[exp(ρZ₁)|Z₂]=0. In particular, the variance floor of the preceding subsection applies under RH with b=1/2 and with the ordinate of the first zero.

Proof. In the subsequence converging to μ, extract by diagonalization a subsequence where X^(iγ) converges to a phase pγ for each ordinate. Fix u in (1/2,1) and take the closest channel u_X. In the preceding explicit formula put y=X exp(v) and divide by √X exp(v/2). Under RH the limit sum for real v is the series in exp(iγv) with coefficients
    −mult(ρ)(1−r^ρ)pγ G(ρ)G(2u−ρ)Dμ(ρ,2u−ρ)/ρ.
The convergence of D for each ordinate follows from the exponential budget. The two Gaussian factors give a summable majorant even after multiplying by exp(A|γ|) for each fixed A, using the usual count of zeros with multiplicity. The limit series is entire in v. The arithmetic bound O(log X) on the whole band forces its vanishing on (0,log 2), and hence on the whole line. Averaging against exp(−iγv) on [−H,H] and letting H→∞ extracts each coefficient by absolute convergence. Under RH each ordinate identifies a single distinct zero. Since the factors other than D are nonzero, Dμ(ρ,2u−ρ)=0. The extraction of phases was independent of u. Continuation in the second variable and Fourier uniqueness give the conditional statement as in the previous subsection.

Consequence without assuming RH. The liminf as X grows of the infimum of E[(Z₁−Z₂)²] over the arithmetically feasible matrices is strictly positive for a fixed budget. If it were zero, an almost minimizing sequence would have a weakly convergent subsequence and its limit would lie on the diagonal by lower semicontinuity. Under RH choose the first critical zero and apply the previous result. If RH fails, symmetry provides an exterior zero and the preceding subsection applies. In either case the conditional annihilation is impossible on the diagonal, where the conditional expectation is exp(ρZ₂). The argument does not compute the unconditional constant.

More precisely, put t=−ρ in the identity for D and d=Z₁−Z₂. Then 1≤E|exp(ρd)−1|≤|ρ| (E d²)^(1/2) (E exp(2b|d|))^(1/2) by integration along the segment and Cauchy–Schwarz. The last moment is ≤C₀ because 2b≤2 and |d|≤|Z₁|+|Z₂|. Thus the floor is at least 1/(C₀|ρ|²) for the zero chosen in each branch. The budget ensures uniform integrability of d², so this floor passes to the liminf of the matrices.

### Quantitative test on the projection of an exterior zero

Symmetry of the tilted law alone was already discarded by the unsafe mixture of this round (line 2979). A more precise consequence for an arithmetic observable is the following. Let ν be the marginal of Z₁ tilted by exp(Z₁/2), normalized and symmetric, of a feasible limit. Put f(v)=Eν cos(vZ₁). If ρ=1/2+δ+iγ is exterior, 0<δ<1/2, the following hold simultaneously
    |f(γ)| ≤ (δ²/2) Eν[Z₁² cosh(δ Z₁)],
    |f'(γ)| ≤ (δ²/6) Eν[|Z₁|³ cosh(δ Z₁)].
Indeed, the marginal annihilation already proved implies Eν cosh(δ Z₁)cos(γ Z₁)=Eν sinh(δ Z₁)sin(γ Z₁)=0 by symmetry. Subtract respectively 1 and δ Z₁ from the hyperbolic factors and use the integral Taylor remainder. The moments on the right-hand side are uniformly bounded with the fixed budget: the denominator of the tilt has a positive floor by Jensen and the numerator is dominated by the exponential moment. On the other hand a zero on the line only imposes f(γ)=0; the factor cos(hv) admits nonzero slope there. This last point illustrates the distinction for a single factor. To use the test globally one still has to obtain, from the prime data, a symmetric feasible law with sufficiently large value or slope at the relevant ordinates. The test by itself does not supply such a law.

### Which slope is compatible with RH itself

Under RH, every feasible limit with symmetric tilted marginal satisfies f(γ)=0 at each critical ordinate, by the previous simultaneous rigidity. The budget fixes M with Eν exp(|Z₁|)≤M, and hence sup |f^(m)|≤m! M for all m. On an interval I of length 1/2 with m distinct ordinates γ₁,…,γ_m, real interpolation with those nodes gives for all v in I
    |f(v)| ≤ M ∏ⱼ |v−γⱼ|,
    |f'(γᵢ)| ≤ M ∏ⱼ≠ᵢ |γᵢ−γⱼ| ≤ M 2^(1−m).
Indeed for v outside the nodes subtract from f the multiple of the nodal polynomial that interpolates f(v). Applying Rolle m times gives the first inequality; dividing by |v−γᵢ| and passing to the limit gives the second, including endpoints by one-sided limit.

There are infinitely many integers n with at least c log n distinct ordinates in [n/2,(n+1)/2), for some constant c>0: otherwise, summing up to 2R would contradict N₀,simp(R) ≫ R log R taking c small. The necessary classical input is already audited in P122_003_CRITICAL_DENSITY_DEPENDENCY_AUDIT. Consequently there are blocks at arbitrarily large heights where, simultaneously for ALL these laws with fixed budget, each slope at the nodes is O(n^(−c log 2)). Even choosing a different law for each node does not avoid this ceiling. The obstruction affects requiring a uniform floor or one with decay slower than every power. It does not exclude a test that explicitly uses local separation or that applies only at previously selected heights.

### Two witnesses with exact intersection of zeros under RH

Under RH there exist two feasible limits of the arithmetic matrices whose tilted averages f₁,f₂ are entire, have only simple real zeros and have as common zeros exactly the signed ordinates of the distinct nontrivial zeros. This includes a single law with nonzero slope at ALL ordinates simultaneously. The construction uses the ordinates as input.

For each distinct ordinate γ>0 choose d in (1.8/γ,2.6/γ). The factor of the tilted transform is
    F(v)=(cos(dv)−cos(dγ))/(1−cos(dγ)).
It is the characteristic function of a symmetric ternary probability because cos(dγ)<0. All its complex zeros are real and simple and form the two progressions ±γ+2πk/d. When choosing d, forbid a term with nonzero k from coinciding with any signed ordinate, or with any zero of an already chosen factor. Only countably many values are discarded, since each coincidence equation fixes at most one d. Interleave the choices of the two families, once per target in each family. The only coincidences will be the intended ones between the two factors of the same target, at ±γ. The rule that protects all ordinates from the start also covers targets not yet processed.

For each family the product converges uniformly on complex compacts since F(v)−1=O_K(d²) and Σγ⁻²<∞. Outside the individual zeros the product is nonzero, and at each zero the remaining product is nonzero, which keeps simplicity. The finite symmetric laws have uniform exponential moments of any fixed order by the same quadratic budget. Untilting by exp(−Z₁/2) and normalizing recovers the original law of shifts. To realize it on the finite mesh, truncate as in the localization in both coordinates, replace each d by a nearby interior dyadic point, and recompute the central weight with cos(dγ) at the new point. The mesh step times the cutoff height tends to zero, so such points exist for all truncated targets. The exact annihilation at the cutoff and the support and moment budget of that entry give arithmetic feasibility of each outer product wwᵀ. For each fixed factor the dyadic values converge to the chosen one and the tail is uniformly summable on compacts. Thus the two claimed limits are obtained. The slope result remains qualitative; a construction based only on prime data with quantitative control remains pending.

### Explicit arithmetic witness without spectral input, on a refined grid

Take the positive density p(z) proportional to exp(−z/2)Φ(z), with the complete even theta kernel of POWER_GLOBAL_ROUTE_REVIEW. By the representation of ξ its normalized two-sided transform is K(s)=ξ(s)/ξ(0). In particular K(0)=1. For large X put h=1/ceil(4 log X), L=2 log log X and take w_j proportional to h p(jh) for |jh|≤L. Use μ=wwᵀ. Only values of theta at real points enter. The original mesh is explicitly changed. The matrix uses O(log² X (log log X)²) entries. For a sufficiently large fixed budget it satisfies, unconditionally, the arithmetic constraints of all channels, with error O(1/X) uniform on the band. The positive protection floors are not imposed here.

Detail of the error. For −1≤Re s≤3 and |Im s|≤3√log X, the Poisson formula applied to p(z)exp(sz) gives the transform of the infinite sum as Σ_k K(s+2πik/h). Stirling and the polynomial growth of ζ in this fixed strip give |K(σ+it)|≪exp(−|t|/2) uniformly (absorbing the power into the decay of the gamma). Hence the sum over nonzero k is O(X^−8), since π/h≥4π log X. In both tails p(z)≪exp(−c exp(2|z|)) by the parity of Φ and its theta series on the positive half-line; the cost of truncating at L is O(X^−8) even with real tilts of modulus up to 8, by comparison with the integral of a decreasing majorant. Normalizing the mass keeps the error. Thus K_X(s)=Σw_j exp(sjh)=K(s)+O(X^−8) on the rectangle. The exponential moments for the budget are uniform by dominated Riemann sum. In the explicit formula, for each zero below the cut the first transform K_X(ρ) is O(X^−8), and the second is bounded by the moments. The Gaussians make the residues summable with multiplicity and the total cost below the cut is O(X^−7). Above it the previous Gaussian ceiling O(X exp(−(3√log X)²/4)) is used; the contour remainder is O(1/X). This certifies the witness in the refined model. Its limiting protection multiplier in the conjugate channel is exactly |ξ(s)/ξ(0)|², so proving its exterior floor requires a lower bound for ξ itself. Arithmetic feasibility alone was already known from the ternary witness.

### Multiplicity cannot be forced through symmetry and feasibility

Without RH there is an entire transform H of a positive probability, H(0)=H(1)=1 and H(1−s)=H(s), that has a simple zero at each distinct nontrivial zero of ζ. It is obtained as a limit of feasible arithmetic witnesses. For an orbit with target b+iγ, γ>0, b≥1/2, take the factor
    (cosh(d(s−b))−cos(dγ))/(cosh(db)−cos(dγ)),
with 1.8<dγ<2.6. Its coefficients at exp(−ds),1,exp(ds) are positive and sum to one. If b>1/2 multiply by the factor with centre 1−b and the same d. Reflection exchanges the numerators and leaves the normalized product fixed. At b=1/2 a single factor is taken. Each factor has simple zeros exactly at b+i(±γ+2πk/d); the two distinct centres never collide. Choose one scale per orbit avoiding accidental coincidences with future targets or roots of earlier orbits as in the preceding countable selection. The product converges locally because each factor is 1+O_K(d²) uniformly in b∈[0,1]. Thus H keeps all targets with multiplicity one. The refined grid of the theta witness can be used: truncate the orbits at 3√log X, approximate the d on the fine grid inside the admissible interval and recompute the coefficients. Take support O((log log X)²), as in the ternary witness. This allows both witnesses on a common mesh by enlarging the sampling support, and the exact annihilation below the cut keeps the error O(1/X) of the channels.

Moreover K=ξ/ξ(0) can be approximated locally by feasible symmetric transforms with ALL their zeros simple. Take H_ε=(1−ε)K+εH for ε∈(0,1). The marginal law is the mixture of the two probabilities. Its outer product on the common grid is admissible for the arithmetic observations by the same residue estimate: the first factor is O(X^−8) at the truncated targets and the second is bounded by the moment. At each common zero K=H=0, H′ is nonzero and at most one ε cancels the derivative. Outside the common zeros, a multiple zero of H_ε would require K/H to have zero derivative and value −ε/(1−ε), since H cannot vanish there. If the quotient is nonconstant, there are only countably many critical values; in the constant case K=H already has all zeros simple. Hence one can take ε↓0 avoiding the exceptions. The limit reproduces K and its derivatives on compacts. Neither arithmetic feasibility nor symmetry requires reproducing the multiplicity of ξ, even arbitrarily close to the theta witness. Additional zeros of the approximants are allowed. This perturbation is existential and uses the zeros of ζ in building H.

### A single law, a single channel and only a ceiling at scales n^A

Antecedent 213-060/073/074: one-sided sampling at powers was already used for another balance. Here the variant identifies unconditionally the WHOLE set of common zeros of stationary laws, including the critical ones even if RH fails. Let A>0 be fixed, r=1/2, w a probability on R with E exp(4|Z|)≤C₀, K_w(s)=E exp(sZ). Use in the centred cell count the single multiplier G(s)K_w(s), with the same Gaussian and centring (1−r)yG(1)K_w(1). Write E_w(y) for its error. Then
    sup_n E_w(n^A)<∞   if and only if   K_w(ρ)=0 at every distinct nontrivial zero.
In that case E_w(y)=O(1/y) for all y≥1. A single fixed w is required for all n.

Proof. The previous explicit formula with a single Gaussian shift (same shift to Re s=−1, with no contribution from s=0 by the cell factor) gives E_w(y)=Σ a_ρ y^ρ+O(1/y), where a_ρ=−mult(ρ)(1−r^ρ)G(ρ)K_w(ρ)/ρ. The coefficients decay like a Gaussian with height. For Re z>1, summing against n^(−1−Az) gives Σ a_ρ ζ(1+A(z−ρ)) plus a remainder holomorphic in Re z>−1. The sum continues meromorphically there, by the polynomial growth of ζ in fixed strips and the Gaussian ceiling; on compacts there are only finitely many nearby poles. The residue at each ρ is a_ρ/A. If there is a ceiling M, the series with nonnegative coefficients (M−E_w(n^A))/n has Dirichlet transform Mζ(1+Az) minus the previous one. This is holomorphic on the whole real half-axis z>0, since there are no real zeros of ζ there contributing poles in the expansion. By Landau's theorem for nonnegative coefficients its abscissa of convergence is ≤0 (or −∞); hence it is holomorphic in Re z>0. All residues a_ρ must be zero. The converse is direct from the explicit formula.

In particular the envelope sup_w |K_w(s)| over these laws with one-sided ceiling and sufficiently large fixed budget has zero set in the strip 0<Re s<1 exactly at the zeros of ξ, by the theta witness. Near each zero ρ it is comparable to |s−ρ| even if ρ is multiple: the upper bound follows from the moment and common vanishing; for the lower one the symmetric witness with simple zeros of the previous subsection suffices. The two continuous laws pass the ceiling at all powers by the converse. There is no lower estimate independent of ρ nor a proven way to locate the envelope without solving the infinite feasibility.

### Minimal cost of the shifts that annihilate the residues

Use N_d(t) for the number of DISTINCT nontrivial zeros in |ρ|<t, counting both signs. For every stationary law w of the preceding test and R>0 one has
    log(K_w(R) K_w(−R)) ≥ π ∫₀ᴿ N_d(t) dt/t.
If some moment is infinite the inequality is interpreted in the extended sense. The bound is invariant under translation of the shift. It is also valid for a law that annihilates only a finite subset, counting only those points in N_d.

Proof. With finite moments apply Jensen on a disc of radius r<R, where the transform is holomorphic and K_w(0)=1. For σ=Re s≥0, Hölder gives log|K_w(s)|≤(σ/r)log K_w(r); for σ≤0 it gives (−σ/r)log K_w(−r). Integrate over both semicircles: the mean of the bound is log(K_w(r)K_w(−r))/π. The Jensen side counts, with weight log(r/|ρ|), at least one copy of each imposed zero. Let r↑R through radii avoiding zeros, using one-sided continuity of the moments. This is the classical Jensen argument applied to the stationary test.

By P122.003 and Riemann–von Mangoldt, the integral is ≫R log R. Counting by ordinate up to t−1 can be used for a lower bound in the disc. The theta witness attains the same order: by functional symmetry and Stirling, log(K(R)K(−R))=R log R+O(R). Hence the infimum of this cost among stationary witnesses with a fixed budget containing theta is Θ(R log R). If all multiplicities of ξ are also required, Jensen counts the complete count, N(t)=(t/π)log t+O(t), and the minimal cost even has leading term R log R with error O(R). The multiplicity requirement is additional to the arithmetic test.

Consequence for finite constructions: any positive law supported on an interval of length L that annihilates exactly all zeros of height |Im ρ|≤H satisfies L≥(π/H)∫₀ᴴ N_d(t)dt/t ≫ log H, because K(H)K(−H)≤exp(HL). This prevents an exact construction with uniformly bounded support. For arithmetic constraints that are only approximate at finite height the same bound has not been established here.

### Positive quadrature with asymptotically optimal diameter up to height H

For large H there is an atomic probability w, with O(H log H) real atoms and diameter ≤log H+O(log log H), that reproduces the zeros of ξ up to height H even with their multiplicity. It also reproduces the moments of the theta law at s=±8, so that its exponential budget stays bounded independently of H. With imposed multiplicities the optimal diameter divided by log H tends to one. For distinct zeros alone the order Θ(log H) is established.

Proof. Take the real space spanned by 1, exp(±8z) and the real and imaginary parts of z^j exp(ρz), for 0≤j<mult(ρ), 0<Imρ≤H. Also use the conjugate roots when counting exponents. Let m be the number of complex exponents with repetition, including 0,±8; m=O(H log H). For every exponential polynomial P of the space and each fixed x, u_k=P(x+k/m) satisfies the recurrence with characteristic polynomial ∏(t−λ), λ=exp(ρ/m), also counting the three real exponents. The polynomial blocks of degree j are annihilated by the power j+1 of the corresponding difference operator. The same statement holds moving to the left, with λ inverted. In both cases |λ|≤exp(8/m).

With S=max_{0≤i<m}|u_i|, the generating series Σ_{k≥0}u_k t^k has denominator ∏(1−λt) and numerator of degree <m with coefficients of modulus ≤S(1+exp(8/m))^m. The degree-l coefficients of the reciprocal of the denominator are bounded by binom(l+m−1,m−1)exp(8l/m), by expansion of the geometric factors. Hence
    |u_k| ≤ S exp(Cm log(2+k/m)+8k/m)
with C absolute (use binom(k+m,m)≤[e(1+k/m)]^m). Integrate in x∈[0,1/m] to the right and in its reflection to the left. The integral of the initial maximum is dominated by I=∫_{−1}¹|P|, summing the integrals of the m cells. The result, for each cell at distance y=k/m from the origin, is a bound for its absolute integral by I exp(Cm log(2+y)+8y).

Let p be the untilted theta density of the previous witness. It is strictly positive on [−1,1] and in the tails p(z)≤C₁ exp(−c exp(2|z|)). Take L rounded up to the step 1/m from (log m)/2+2 log log(m+3)+C₂. For y≥L, c exp(2y)/2 dominates Cm log(2+y)+8y uniformly for large m (the quotient grows in y). The sum over those cells of exp(−c exp(2y)/2) is o(1), by comparison with the integral multiplied by m. Thus ∫_{|z|>L}p|P|=o(1)I uniformly. If P≥0 on [−L,L], one concludes ∫pP≥(min_{[−1,1]}p−o(1))I≥0.

By convex separation in finite dimension, the moment vector of p belongs to the convex hull of the evaluation vectors of the compact interval: otherwise there would be an affine combination P≥0 there with negative integral. Carathéodory provides at most m+1 atoms. Matching those moments reproduces the prescribed derivatives of ξ/ξ(0) at the zeros. The diameter is ≤2L≤log H+O(log log H). With multiplicities, Jensen at radius H gives the inverse bound L_diam≥log H−O(1), using the complete count in the disc and K(H)K(−H)≤exp(H L_diam). This existence uses the locations of the zeros and admits free real nodes; it does not provide an exact quadrature on the dyadic grid nor protect the multiplier away from the zeros.

### Which zeros the finite quadrature forces exactly

On the same interval of diameter log H+O(log log H) there are TWO positive quadratures with O(H log H) nodes each that reproduce the previous moments. The only common zeros of their transforms in the whole plane are the targets of height ≤H, with the minimum of the two multiplicities exactly equal to the prescribed one. Moreover the second quadrature can be chosen nonzero at every zero of ζ of height >H simultaneously.

The strict inequality of the previous proof gives relative interiority of the theta moment vector in the compact hull: an affine support function not identically zero on the curve would be P≥0 on the interval with zero theta integral, impossible by ∫pP≥c∫_{−1}¹|P|. This allows reserving a small positive mass at any finite list of points of the interval. Indeed, if v is the desired vector and u the average of the evaluations of the list, (v−ηu)/(1−η) belongs to the hull for η>0 sufficiently small. The residual moment is represented with ≤m+1 atoms.

Fix a first quadrature w₀ of the previous subsection. Let Λ be the list of exponents with repetitions used there. For h∈(0,1/m) define Q_h(Y)=∏_{λ∈Λ}(Y−exp(hλ)); its coefficients are real by conjugation. The roots of Q_h(exp(hs)) are exactly λ+2πik/h. Choose h avoiding coincidences between distinct exponents under the exponential and avoiding that a harmonic with k≠0 reaches any zero of K₀, any target or any non-imposed zero of ζ. These are only countable exceptions. Then the multiplicity of the composite polynomial at each λ is exactly the prescribed one.

Reserve positive mass at 0,h,…,mh and build the residual quadrature as above. To the resulting law add ε times the signed measure which at jh has as mass the coefficient of Y^j in Q_h. Its transform is Q_h(exp(hs)); all moments are preserved, including the prescribed derivatives, the total mass and the moments ±8. For |ε| sufficiently small the law stays positive. At every zero of K₀ other than the targets and at every omitted zero of ζ, the perturbation has nonzero value (the real exponents 0,±8 are never zeros of a probability). Each point forbids at most one real ε. Similarly at each target one avoids cancelling the first non-prescribed derivative, since the perturbation has exact order there. Choosing ε outside the countable union ends the proof. The part about omitting the high zeros is existential, without computing ε from a prefix. A single spectral cutoff, even with multiplicities, positivity, moments and asymptotically optimal diameter, leaves freedom to omit simultaneously all the rest of the divisor of ζ.

### Quantitative rigidity immediately after the cutoff

Let η be a signed redistribution with total variation ≤2 supported in [c−D/2,c+D/2]. Suppose its transform vanishes with the multiplicities of ξ at the zeros up to height H. Let F(s)=∫exp(s(x−c))dη(x). For 0≤b≤1, R=H/2 and 0≤u≤R one has uniformly
    log|F(b+i(H+u))| ≤ DR/π − (R log H)/(2π) g(u/R) + O(H+D),
    g(v)=1−v+v log v,   g(0)=1.
For example D≤0.19 log H gives |F|≤exp(−κ H log H) on all of H≤Im s≤9H/8 for H sufficiently large and an absolute κ>0, since g(1/4)/2>0.20. If c=O(log H), removing the centring costs only a factor exp(O(log H)). The estimate concerns the difference between two witnesses that coincide outside the redistribution interval, not any pair of quadratures of optimal diameter.

Proof. Centre the Jensen disc at s₀=b+i(H+u). If F(s₀)=0 the bound is immediate. On its circle of radius R the mean of log|F| is ≤log 2+D/2+DR/π using the variation and the mean of |cos θ|. For u+4≤t≤R, the zeros with heights between H−(t−u)+3 and H lie inside the disc of radius t independently of their abscissa. By Riemann–von Mangoldt between heights ≥H/2 their number, with multiplicities, is at least (t−u)log H/(2π)−O(t−u+log H). On integrating the count with dt/t, the errors are O(R+log² H), including the omitted initial stretch of length ≤4 (the main integral there costs O(log H)). The main integral from u to R is Rg(u/R)log H/(2π). Jensen subtracts that quantity from the boundary mean. Radii with zeros on the boundary are handled by continuity. In the example u/R≤1/4 and g is decreasing. The result uses only the imposed multiplicities and the support of the modification; it certifies no new sign.

### Attainable size of a positive modification on a fixed interval

Let p be the previous theta density. Modify it on [0,1] keeping positivity, mass, moments ±8 and the zeros with multiplicities up to H. Put Λ={0,±8} together with those zeros with their repetitions, m=|Λ|=(H/π)log H+O(H). For fixed B>1 and 0≤Re s≤1, |Im s|≤BH, the envelope E_H(s) of the modulus of the change in the transform satisfies, with positive constants depending at most on B,
    (c_B/m)^m ∏_{λ∈Λ}|s−λ| ≤ E_H(s) ≤ (C_B/m)^m ∏_{λ∈Λ}|s−λ|.
A single positive modification attains the lower bound simultaneously on that rectangle. The constants exponential in m do matter when the product does not contribute a larger scale.

Upper. Each signed difference η has variation ≤2 and entire transform F with |F(z)|≤2exp(max(0,Re z)). Jensen on the disc of centre s and radius m subtracts at least Σ log(m/|s−λ|), since for H sufficiently large all distances are <m. The mean of the logarithm on the boundary is O(m). This proves the upper bound, the case of a centre that is a zero being immediate.

Lower. Take h=1/(2m) and Q(Y)=∏(Y−exp(hλ)). Divide its real coefficients by their ℓ¹ norm and use them as signed masses at 0,h,…,mh. The norm before dividing is ≤∏(1+exp(h Re λ))≤C^m. On the whole rectangle h|s−λ|=O_B(H/m)=o(1); the expansion exp(w)−1=w(1+O(|w|)) gives |exp(hs)−exp(hλ)|≥c h|s−λ| for each factor. Convolve with the uniform probability on [0,ℓ], ℓ=1/(10(B+1)H). The transform of this box has modulus ≥1/2 on the whole rectangle by |s|ℓ<1/5, and the resulting signed density has modulus ≤1/ℓ. Multiply by ℓ min_{[0,1]}p/2 and add to p. Positivity is kept, the support of the change fits in [0,1] and all annihilations with jets persist. The factor of order 1/H is absorbed in c_B^m. The conditions at ±8 and 0 keep the indicated moments. The construction uses the zeros up to H and does not use the later ones.

Consequence: at s=b+iαH with fixed α>1, all distances are Θ_α(H). Thus log E_H(s)=−m log log H+O_α(m), uniformly in 0≤b≤1. The leading term is −(1/π)H log H log log H. This gives the optimal scale of the change for redistributions in [0,1] at a height proportionally above the cutoff. It does not carry over to redistributions with growing diameter nor establish a protective margin independent of the zeros.

### Global rigidity by domination of the real moments

Let K=ξ/ξ(0). Let W be the two-sided transform of a probability with all exponential moments, vanishing at each zero of ξ at least with its multiplicity. If W(x)≤C(1+|x|)^d K(x) for all real x, with fixed d≥0, then W(s)=P(s)K(s) for a real polynomial P of degree ≤⌊d⌋, P(0)=1 and P(x)>0 on R. In particular for any d<2 the only possible witness is theta. Neither RH nor symmetry of W is assumed. In the arithmetic single-law criterion, requiring the multiplicities is an additional hypothesis.

Proof. Q=W/K is entire. The circular mean of log⁺|Q| is O(r log r): use log⁺|Q|≤log⁺|W|+log⁻|K|, Jensen at K(0)=1, and the bounds of order O(r log r) for log⁺|W| and log⁺|K| that follow from two-sided positivity, the real hypothesis and Stirling. Poisson applied to log⁺|Q| at radius 2r gives the same ceiling for the maximum at radius r.

For σ≥2, |t|≤σ/2, uniform Stirling and the two-sided bounds on the Euler product in Re s≥2 give
    log(K(σ)/|K(σ+it)|) ≤ C t²/σ+C.
Indeed the gamma part contributes (t/2)arctan(t/σ) minus a nonnegative logarithmic term for σ≥2, plus O(1). The quadratic prefactor and π^(−s/2) do not worsen this bound. For σ≤−1 use K(s)=K(1−s). Since |W(σ+it)|≤W(σ), in both horizontal cones one gets log|Q|≤C t²/(1+|σ|)+O_d(log(2+|s|)). On the rays θ and π−θ for small θ>0, the linear coefficient is O(θ²) with constant independent of θ. In the sector between those rays, apply Phragmén–Lindelöf to Q(s)exp(iAθs), with A absolute and sufficiently large: the term −Aθ Im s dominates on both edges, and the growth order is at most one, strictly smaller than π/(π−2θ). One obtains log|Q|≤Aθ|s|+O_θ(1) there. Conjugation gives the same below; the remaining cones are already controlled. Letting θ↓0, Q is of exponential type zero.

For n=ceil(d), Q(s)/(s+i)^n is holomorphic in the upper half-plane, of type zero and bounded on the real axis. The minimal-type Phragmén–Lindelöf principle in the half-plane bounds it there. In the lower one use (s−i)^n. Cauchy implies that Q is polynomial and the bound on the line reduces its degree to ⌊d⌋. Strict positivity of Q on the line excludes odd degree. A constant polynomial equals one by normalization. Uniqueness of the law follows by Fourier. Hence to obtain a global witness different from theta that keeps the whole divisor, its moment quotient cannot have subquadratic real growth in the sense of a bound by a power d<2.

The threshold d=2 is attained with a positive modification symmetric in transform. Take p_ε=p+ε(p″+p′). The quotient (p″+p′)/p is continuous and tends to +∞ at both ends: in the positive tail the first summand n=1 of the theta kernel is a factor exp(−π exp(2z)) times a finite combination of exponentials with positive leading term, and the n≥2 are exponentially smaller even after two derivatives. Thus (log p)′ is asymptotic to −2π exp(2z) and (log p)″=O(exp(2z)); in the negative tail Φ is reflected and the linear tilt is kept. So the square of the logarithmic derivative dominates in p″/p. For ε>0 sufficiently small p_ε is positive. The derivatives integrate to zero by their tails. Two integrations by parts give W_ε=(1+εs(s−1))K, symmetric under s↦1−s and different from K. This shows that the subquadratic exclusion is optimal.

### Uniqueness with vanishing of values: exact equivalence with simplicity

In the class of laws with W(x)≤C K(x) on the whole real axis, the stationary one-sided ceiling test has theta as unique solution if and only if all nontrivial zeros of ζ are simple. One can even require symmetry W(s)=W(1−s). If all are simple, the ceiling forces reproducing the complete divisor and the rigidity of the previous entry with d=0 applies. The converse direction requires building a positive law, not only a formal meromorphic quotient.

Division lemma. If a complex density g satisfies |g|≤A p, with p the theta density, and its transform G vanishes at λ, define
    q(x)=exp(−λx) ∫_x^∞ exp(λu)g(u)du.
It can also be written with the negative integral from −∞ to x. Then |q|≤A C_λ p and its transform is G(s)/(s−λ) by q′+λq=−g and integration by parts. For the bound, in the right tail the derivative of log p tends to −∞, so p(x+v)/p(x)≤exp(−(|Re λ|+1)v) for large x and v≥0. In the left tail the alternative expression and the same bound for p(x−v)/p(x) apply. On compacts p has a positive minimum. In particular the division can be repeated as long as a zero remains at the chosen point.

For each orbit O of multiple zeros under conjugation and reflection, of multiplicity m_O>1, let D_O(s)=∏_{λ∈O}(s−λ). It has even degree, real coefficients and symmetry D_O(1−s)=D_O(s). Dividing successively one obtains a density g_O, |g_O|≤C_O p, with transform K/D_O^(m_O−1). It is real by conjugation and Fourier uniqueness. It has a simple zero at each member of O and keeps the multiplicities of the other zeros of ζ. A small positive perturbation of p by g_O, normalized at zero, provides a different law that keeps all null values and passes the ceiling at the powers. This proves the equivalence, without assuming that any multiple orbit exists.

Moreover, all multiple orbits can be treated simultaneously: enumerate them and choose ε_j>0 with Σ ε_j C_j<1/2. Normalize p+Σ ε_j g_j. The resulting density is bounded between positive multiples of p and its transform is symmetric. The series converges on complex compacts with all its derivatives by domination. At each multiple orbit only its own summand contributes to the first derivative. To avoid possible cancellation at the already simple zeros, multiply the whole perturbation by a single τ∈(0,1), excluding at most one value per simple zero (at τ=0 the derivative is nonzero). Thus, unconditionally, there is a witness with density comparable to theta in both directions and order exactly one at ALL distinct zeros of ζ. Additional zeros are allowed. This construction uses the divisor as input; the equivalence indicates that uniqueness of the law of values alone in this class would decide simplicity, and by itself does not locate the zeros on the critical line.

### Uniqueness defect when imposing only the zeros on the line

Let V be the REAL space of signed densities g with |g|≤C_g p, entire transform F symmetric under s↦1−s, F(0)=0, and such that F/K is locally bounded along the line Re s=1/2 (local on each compact interval, without a bound uniform in height). The latter is equivalent to annihilating the jets of K at its critical zeros up to the required order, by the Taylor expansion even when approaching only along the line. The definition uses only the theta density and values on the line; it does not need the locations of exterior zeros.

If there are k exterior orbits counted with multiplicity, each orbit consisting of four points, then dim_R V=2k for finite k. If k is infinite, V contains subspaces of arbitrarily large dimension. In particular V={0} is equivalent to RH and would detect even a single simple quartet. Each element of V produces positive densities p±εg for small ε, with mass and symmetry preserved. This test is distinct from the stationary arithmetic ceiling: it omits the exterior zeros and imposes multiplicities at the critical ones.

Proof for finite k. Let D be the monic polynomial of all exterior zeros with their multiplicities, of degree 4k, taking D=1 if k=0. D(1−s)=D(s). Then P=DF/K is entire. The proof of domination by real moments of the previous subsection applies literally in the modulus estimates: |F(σ+it)|≤C_g K(σ), the polynomial D adds O_k(log(2+|s|)) to the growth in the cones, and the bound on R is O((1+|s|)^(4k)). Thus P is a real polynomial of degree ≤4k. By symmetry it is a polynomial in y=s(s−1) of degree ≤2k; by zero mass its constant term is zero. This gives the upper bound on the dimension.

Conversely, for any P of that class write P/D as a constant plus partial fractions in (s−λ)^(-j), with j at most the multiplicity in D. The previous two-sided division represents K/(s−λ)^j as the transform of a density dominated in modulus by a constant times p. Summing, KP/D is the desired transform, real by conjugation, with all critical jets and zero mass. Fourier uniqueness gives injectivity. If k is infinite the lower construction applies to any finite subset of orbits, without dividing by the others. Moreover, for finite k, fixing l additional real moments F(x_j)=0 with x_j(x_j−1) distinct and nonzero leaves dimension max(2k−l,0), by polynomial interpolation. In particular a single additional moment does not hide a simple quartet. The computation translates localization into an exact linear problem; it does not prove that V is zero.

### A single approximation problem with uniform cost per quartet

Take the even measure ν(dx)=exp(x/2)p(x)dx without normalizing. In real even L¹(ν) consider the distance Δ of cosh(3x/2) to the closed space spanned by cosh(x/2) and by the functions ∂_t^j cos(tx)|_{t=γ} for each critical zero 1/2+iγ and 0≤j<mult(1/2+iγ). For any exterior quartet of height γ one has
    Δ ≥ 2 K(2) / [(2+γ)^4 A² (1+(2+γ)A)^2],
with A≥1 depending only on p. In particular the constant does not degenerate when the abscissa of the zero approaches 1/2 at fixed height. Under RH, Δ=0. This gives an approximation target with a single fixed function and a computable sufficient threshold for excluding quartets up to a given height. No approximant improving the existing verifications has been obtained here.

Uniform detail. The two-sided division operator T_λ of the previous entry has norm ≤A from the ball |g|≤p to |T_λg|≤A p, when G(λ)=0, simultaneously for 0≤Re λ≤1. In both tails it suffices to choose a common threshold with logarithmic derivative of p of modulus ≥2 and sign towards the centre; on the compact use the positive minimum of p and the integrals of (1+exp(x))p(x) for the bound. A does not depend on Im λ. For the four distinct roots λ₁,…,λ₄ of the orbit, apply to K the factors
    [1+λ₁/(s−λ₁)] [1+(λ₂−1)/(s−λ₂)] /[(s−λ₃)(s−λ₄)].
The product gives F=K s(s−1)/D. Each division acts at a zero still available, and the resulting density g satisfies |g|≤Mp for M=A²(1+(2+γ)A)^2. F is real and symmetric; by Fourier uniqueness g/p is real and even (the central tilt makes both densities even). F(0)=0 and F has all critical jets. Hence g/(Mp) is a functional of norm ≤1 annihilating the indicated generators. Its value at the target function is F(2)/M, with |D(2)|≤(2+γ)^4. This proves the bound even if there were infinitely many other exterior orbits. Under RH, every real even annihilator bounded in L∞(ν) produces a density g=p h of the space V, which is zero. By Hahn–Banach the distance is zero.

Finite application: any FINITE real combination of those generators with certified integral error below the threshold of the formula evaluated at H excludes all exterior zeros of height ≤H. Only the jets used by that combination are needed; it is not necessary to have enumerated all critical zeros up to H to validate the implication. The global obligation is to exhibit approximations with error tending to zero. The positive distance in the case of a quartet is a lower bound, not an already proven procedure for reaching those errors.

### Least squares that do keep the global criterion

Write v(x)=exp(x/2)p(x) for the even density of ν. Use the real even space L²(w dx), w=(1+x²)v², with the same generators and target function as in the preceding entry. Cauchy–Schwarz gives ||r||_{L¹(ν)}≤√π ||r||_{L²(w)}. Hence a quadratic distance tending to zero suffices for RH. Conversely, under RH the generators are dense in the WHOLE of this even space.

For the converse, if u∈L²(w) is even and orthogonal to the generators, its transform F(s)=∫exp((s−1/2)x)u(x)w(x)dx is entire, symmetric, has F(0)=0 and the prescribed critical jets. With σ=Re s,
    |F(s)|² ≤ ||u||² sup_x[exp(σx)p(x)] · ∫(1+x²)exp(σx)p(x)dx.
By the theta tails |p′|≤C exp(2|x|)p, also on the compact by increasing C. The total variation of exp(σx)p bounds its supremum and is ≤|σ|K(σ)+C(K(σ+2)+K(σ−2)). In the second integral use 1+x²≤C(exp(x)+exp(−x)). By Stirling on the line and the symmetry of K, for a=1,2 one has K(σ+a)+K(σ−a)≤C_a(1+|σ|)^(a/2)K(σ). Consequently |F(s)|≤C||u||(1+|σ|)^(3/4)K(σ). These bounds also justify holomorphy by domination on compacts. Under RH, F/K is entire and the rigidity argument in cones applies with exponent 3/4 even for this signed transform: the quotient is constant. F(0)=0 annihilates it and Fourier gives u=0.

For a finite independent list with Gram G and vector b of products with the target f, the squared distance is ||f||²−bᵀG⁻¹b. Its limit along an exhaustive enumeration of the generators is zero if and only if RH. A first exploratory computation of the RELATIVE residual in norm (without squaring) was obtained. Always including cosh(x/2), on adding 0,1,2,4,8 cosines of the first positive ordinates the results were 0.0348271, 0.0317314, 0.0306306, 0.0290754, 0.0272189. Method: weighted least squares by SVD at 220 Gauss–Legendre nodes of [0,2], using parity, eight theta terms and numerical ordinates from mpmath. These are exploration numbers in double precision without rounding certificate or extrapolation. Unconditional convergence remains open.

### Exact tail threshold and necessary slowness in the extreme weight

For a>0 fix w_a(x)=exp(a|x|)v(x)^2. The transfer to L¹(ν) costs (2/a)^(1/2). Under RH, the transforms of the even annihilators in this Hilbert space are exactly K(s)P(y), y=s(s−1), with P(0)=0 and 8 deg P<a for nonzero P. Indeed, the previous Cauchy–Schwarz argument now uses ∫exp(a|x|+σx)p≤K(σ+a)+K(σ−a) and produces polynomial growth of degree 1/2+a/4 relative to K(σ). Rigidity in cones makes the quotient polynomial; symmetry expresses it in y. The two-sided density of KP is q=P(∂²+∂)p, and the exact condition for membership in the dual is ∫|q/p|² exp(−a|x|)dx<∞. If j=deg P, the leading term of q/p in both tails has asymptotic modulus const·exp(4j|x|), by differentiation of the first theta term (the terms n≥2 are negligible up to any fixed order). Thus the case 8j=a also diverges. The converse is obtained using this same density. For 0<a≤8 convergence of the projections of the target is equivalent to RH. For a>8 the functional with P=y exists unconditionally and its value at the target is 2K(2), so there is never convergence to zero.

At a=8 one also obtains a quantitative floor for a finite prefix. If a critical ordinate γ≥1 is omitted entirely, even keeping the other critical jets, the Hilbert distance of the target to the space used is ≥c/√log(2+γ), with c fixed. Put L=γ²+1/4, D=y+L and F=yK/D. It is entire and keeps all the required jets at the other ordinates. Its real density q satisfies uniformly
    |q(x)|/p(x) ≤ C min(1, exp(4|x|)/γ²).
To justify it, for f=p or f=p″+p′, divide its transform by D. The inverse density in the right tail is the integral from v=0 to ∞ of exp(v/2) sin(γv) f(x+v)/γ (by two divisions, or partial fractions). In the left one the analogous formula with x−v and exp(−v/2) is used, by the cancellation at both zeros. One integration by parts bounds the modulus by γ⁻² times the absolute value at the endpoint plus the total variation of the amplitude. In both tails the amplitude is positive and decreasing in v for both f: this follows from the differentiated asymptotics of the first theta term up to order three. For compact x its variation is uniformly bounded and p has a positive minimum. The result is ≤Cγ⁻²p for f=p and ≤Cγ⁻² exp(4|x|)p for f=p″+p′. The second gives a bound for q directly; by F=K−LK/D, the first gives the other. There is no dependence on separation from any other ordinate.

Consequently ∫|q/p|²exp(−8|x|)dx≤C γ⁻⁴ log(2+γ), splitting at |x|=(log γ)/2. The functional equals F(2)=2K(2)/(2+L) at the target and annihilates the mass; normalizing gives the floor. It does not apply if the chosen ordinate was included. Therefore in the extreme weight, not even under RH can one hope, for prefixes with first omitted ordinate γ, for a rate o(1/√log γ). It is a restriction on an approximation norm, without window enlargement.

### Explicit approximation on growing intervals; cost of the tail

For each x interpolate y↦B_x(y)=cosh(x√y) (defined by its power series) at y=1/4 and at −γ² for positive critical ordinates, and evaluate the polynomial at y=9/4. Repeated nodes up to the available multiplicity are admitted through Hermite interpolation. With m nodes counted with repetition one obtains an allowed combination S_m(x), with coefficients independent of x: at γ>0 the derivatives in y up to j become combinations of the derivatives in γ up to j by the chain rule.

For all x the error satisfies
    |cosh(3x/2)−S_m(x)| ≤ B_m(x) := cosh(3x/2) |x|^(2m) ∏_j|9/4−y_j| /(2m)!.
Indeed, for U on [−1,1] with density proportional to (1−u²)^(m−1),
    B_x^(m)(y) = (m! x^(2m)/(2m)!) E cosh(x√y U).
This is checked through the series and the beta moments, E U^(2k)=(1/2)_k/(m+1/2)_k. On the real interpolation interval the modulus of the expectation is ≤cosh(3x/2), even for y<0 through the cosine. Apply the real Hermite remainder.

Without RH, select the first m−1 simple critical zeros: by P122.003, γ_j≤C j/log(2+j) adjusting C. Stirling or a sum of logarithms gives [∏|9/4−y_j|/(2m)!]^(1/(2m))≤C′/log m. Hence for c>0 sufficiently small the uniform error on |x|≤c log m is O(exp(−ηm)) for some η>0, absorbing the polynomial factor cosh(3c log(m)/2). One obtains an explicit sequence that does converge on growing intervals using critical zeros unconditionally.

Audit of the global step. Even under RH and taking ALL ordinates with multiplicity (the most favourable option in density), the previous integrated majorant grows. By Riemann–von Mangoldt γ_j∼2πj/log j, whence
    [∏|9/4−y_j|/(2m)!]^(1/(2m)) ∼ π/log m.
Here the mean of log log j is log log m+o(1) and the contribution of the fixed node is o(1) in the normalized logarithm. Moreover [∫|x|^(2m)cosh(3x/2)v(x)dx]^(1/(2m)) ∼ (log m)/2. For the lower bound integrate over a unit interval from (1/2−ε)log m, using the theta tail exp(−O(exp(2x))) there. For the upper bound cut at (1/2+ε)log m: outside the cut the bound exp(−c exp(2|x|)) dominates |x|^(2m) with integral o(1), and inside the mass of the tilted weight suffices. Let ε↓0. Hence (∫B_m dν)^(1/(2m))→π/2>1. This proves the failure of this global majorant even in the favourable hypothesis; it does not prove divergence of the approximants. The unresolved step is keeping the cancellation of the remainder on integrating, or building other coefficients with a global bound.

### Exact signed error and certified falsifier of the sign of the remainder

For these interpolants the signed integral is exactly
    ∫(cosh(3x/2)−S_m(x))dν = π/3 − ∏_{chosen γ}(γ²+9/4)/(γ²+1/4),
with repetition for each included jet. Indeed the integrals of the critical nodes and their jets are zero. The integral of the generator cosh(x/2) is K(1)=1, its Hermite coefficient is the product shown (the cardinal of the simple node 1/4), and K(2)=π/3.

The difference is positive at each prefix. To see this, the entire function B(y)=K(1/2+√y) has order ≤1/2 by parity and the O(r log r) growth of the logarithm of the envelope of K. Its canonical product in y has genus zero. In the quotient B(9/4)/B(1/4) each critical zero contributes the factor of the finite product, and an exterior quartet contributes |(9/4−z²)/(1/4−z²)|² with z=ρ−1/2. The latter is >1 because Re(z²)<1/4. Thus the signed error only measures the omitted factors of the Hadamard product. Under RH, using all jets of height ≤H, the signed error is asymptotic to (log H)/(3H): the logarithm of the remaining product is asymptotic to 2Σ_{γ>H}γ⁻² ∼ (log H)/(πH) by partial summation. This argument about the product does not control the absolute error.

Counterexample at the prefix of the first 16 ordinates, one cosine per ordinate plus cosh(x/2). With Arb ball arithmetic at 128 bits, the remainder at x=17/20 lies in (−8.351,−8.350) and at x=2 in (7.388,7.389); the signed integral lies in (0.01636,0.01638). Reproduction: use g_j=acb.zeta_zero(j).imag, j=1,…,16, y=(1/4,−g₁²,…,−g₁₆²); compute each weight as the product of (9/4−y_k)/(y_j−y_k) for k≠j, with ctx.prec=128. Evaluate cosines and hyperbolic cosines on balls, with exact rational arguments. This rules out proving that the remainder has a single sign for every prefix. By continuity and positivity of the weight, the absolute integral is strictly larger than the signed one for this prefix. Global convergence of the absolute residuals is not ruled out.

### Certified measurement of the global norm, with free weights as a control

The script verify_195_hermite_l1.py (python-flint, 160 bits) encloses ∫|cosh(3x/2)−S(x)|dν over the WHOLE line. Outward-rounded intervals: Hermite with 8 cosines (0.02070,0.02242), with 16 (0.02323,0.02556), with 32 (0.05379,0.05986). An independent fit with 16 cosines and rational coefficients of denominator 10⁷ gives (0.01746,0.01938). Hence the growth among those three Hermite prefixes is strict, while the same space of 16 cosines admits an error smaller even than Hermite with 8. None of these comparisons determines the limit of the sequence.

Details of the certificate. On x≥0 use the unnormalized density exp(x/2)Σ(2a²−3a)exp(−a), a=πk²exp(2x), and divide by the integral with cosh(x/2), since K(1)=1. On [0,2] integration is by interval inclusion over 2048 cells. The combined cosine is evaluated by cubic Taylor around the centre with absolute remainder of order four. The tail k≥9 costs <10⁻⁴⁸ pointwise since 2a²exp(−a)≤5exp(−a/2). For x≥2 the density is ≤10exp(x/2)exp(−πexp(2x)/2) by geometric sum. Against cosh(3x/2), its integral is ≤(10/π)exp(−πexp(4)/2)<10⁻³³. Multiplying by one plus the ℓ¹ norm of the coefficients covers the whole residual. Only the search for the free coefficients used optimization on a mesh; its final certificate uses the exact rationals and covers the continuous integral. It is a finite upper bound, with no new window nor certified exclusion of zeros.

### Cost of an exterior quartet after keeping the four oscillations

Let γ≥1 be the height of an exterior quartet and D(s) the monic product of its four linear factors. For the L¹(ν) approximation test of entry 3227 the floor is improved from c(1+γ)^−6 to cγ^−2.
