For the Hilbert weight w_a of 3249 one obtains distance ≥c_a γ^(−2+a/4) if 0<a<8 and ≥c/√log(2+γ) if a=8. All these bounds are independent of the horizontal distance of the quartet to the line. They are lower bounds in the presence of a hypothetical zero, not an upper estimate of the residuals.

The same functional F(s)=s(s−1)K(s)/D(s) is used, whose value F(2)≥cγ^−4 and which annihilates the mass and the critical jets. Write f=p″+p′ and q for the density with transform F. For x≥0, by successive two-sided division and Fubini,
    q(x)=∫_[0,∞)^4 exp(Σ λ_j v_j) f(x+Σv_j) dv.
For x≤0 use the four integrals to the left, with signs inverted in the exponents and in the shift (the global sign is positive). Each necessary cancellation persists on dividing by the previous roots, since the four are distinct.

Put t=|x| and B=exp(2t). For large t and r≥0 the theta tails give p(x±r)/p(x)≤exp(−cBr) outwards, integrating the logarithmic slope. For 0≤k≤4, |f^(k)(x±r)|≤C_k p(x±r) B^(k+2) exp(2(k+2)r) by the differentiated series. Taking absolute values in an integral over k variables with Σv_j=r, the remaining exponential product is at most exp(r), and the simplex measure gives r^(k−1)dr/(k−1)!. Hence the integral with f^(l) is bounded by C p(x) B^(l+2−k) for k≥1, l≤4. The case k=0 is the pointwise bound. On a compact set of x the constants are enlarged by the doubly exponential decay and the positive minimum of p. With k=4,l=0 one obtains |q|/p≤C B^−2.

Now integrate by parts ONCE in each of the four variables, using the complete exponential as primitive and |λ_j|≥γ. In each term, the k variables that did not end up on the boundary are accompanied by exactly k derivatives of f. By the preceding bound l=k cancels the power of B that those derivatives cost. The boundary terms at infinity vanish by the tails. One obtains uniformly
    |q(x)|/p(x) ≤ C min(B^−2,γ^−4 B²) ≤ C γ^−2.
No division by differences between roots was made. The real even quotient q/p normalized by its supremum gives the new L¹ floor. In the dual of w_a its squared norm is computed with exp(−a|x|)dx: splitting at t=(log γ)/2, it is ≤C_a γ^(−4−a/2) for 0<a<8 and ≤C γ^−8 log(2+γ) for a=8. Dividing F(2) by the norm bounds concludes.

Asymptotic operational consequence: an L¹ certificate with error <c/H² would exclude quartets up to H (γ≥1), and in the extreme norm error <c/√log(2+H) would suffice. The constants here have not been evaluated numerically. The previous rational certificate with 16 cosines does not become, through this improvement, an exclusion at a numerical height.

### Upper bound for the best fit from a finite verification

Assume only that all nontrivial zeros with |Im ρ|≤H are on the critical line and that all their jets are included in the prefix. With the original weight w=(1+x²)v², the best error in Hilbert norm of the target cosh(3x/2) using that prefix and cosh(x/2) satisfies, for H sufficiently large,
    dist_H ≤ C (log log H / log H)^(5/4).
The constant and the threshold are independent of the zeros above H. By Cauchy–Schwarz the same rate holds, with factor √π, for the L¹ error of these coefficients. It is the projection fit, not the Hermite interpolation rule. Under RH this gives an upper rate for the sequence. Without RH the implication applies only to verified complete prefixes.

Proof by duality. For an even annihilator u of the prefix with norm ≤1, use the F of the least-squares entry. One has F(0)=F(1)=0 by mass and symmetry, and |F(σ+it)|≤C(1+|σ|)^d K(σ), d=3/4. Q=F/K is holomorphic in |s|<H by the finite hypothesis. Uniformly over these u, log⁺ M_Q(H/4)≤C H log H: on a circle of radius between H/2 and 3H/4 free of boundary zeros apply the mean bound log⁺|F|+log⁻|K|, Jensen at K(0)=1 and then Poisson in the inner disc. The same argument at fixed radius bounds Q on compacts, uniformly in large H.

In the cones near both real half-axes the Stirling bound of the rigidity entry gives |Q(s)|≤C(1+|s|)^d exp(C (Im s)²/(1+|Re s|)), with uniform constants (use the compact bound near the origin). Put θ=10 log log H/log H, r=1/θ, R=H/4. In the upper sector θ≤arg s≤π−θ, |s|≤R, consider J(s)=Q(s)exp(iAθs)/(s+i)^d, with a holomorphic branch. On the rays |J|≤C for A absolute and large. On the arc log⁺|J|≤C H log H. The harmonic measure of the arc from |s|=r is ≤C(r/R)^k, k=π/(π−2θ): the power that straightens the sector takes it to the unit half-disc and the measure of the semicircle is O(|z|) for |z|≤1/2 (by the harmonic sine series with data 1 on the semicircle and 0 on the diameter). Hence log|J|≤O(1)+C H log H (r/R)^k=O(1). Indeed k−1≥2θ/π and H^(1−k)≤(log H)^(−20/π), while r^k≤(log H)^2 eventually. Undoing the exponential loses at most exp(Aθr)=exp(A). The lower sector is covered by conjugation; in the remaining horizontal cones Stirling applies directly. Thus M_Q(r)≤C r^d. Since Q(0)=Q(1)=0, the maximum of Q(s)/[s(s−1)] on that disc is ≤C r^(d−2). Evaluating at s=2 gives |F(2)|≤C θ^(2−d). Taking the supremum of the pairings over unit annihilators ends the proof. The finite verification is an input: it has not been proved that it extends to all heights nor has a new window T been computed.

### An auxiliary moment tolerates one missing critical condition

Keep the target cosh(3x/2) fixed and add exactly the generator cosh(5x/2) to the mass and the critical jets. It still holds that zero distance, both in L¹(ν) and in the Hilbert weight (1+x²)v², is equivalent to RH. Under RH the previous generators already sufficed. For any exterior quartet with polynomial D, use F=K y(y−6)/D with y=s(s−1). Its density is dominated by p by two-sided division and partial fractions, also if there are other quartets. It annihilates mass and the auxiliary generator (y=0,6) and equals −8K(2)/D(2)≠0 at the target. The cost of the detector changes on adding the generator; the previous floor cγ⁻² does not transfer automatically.

In a prefix up to H, allow one missing condition: all zeros up to H are critical, but at one of the ordinates the last jet may have been omitted (this includes omitting a simple ordinate entirely). It is not necessary to know which one in order to compute the fit. With the same Hilbert norm, the best error is O(θ^(5/4)), θ=10 log log H/log H, uniformly in the location of the omission. With a complete prefix the ceiling improves to O(θ^(13/4)). Indeed for the unit annihilator F, multiply F/K by D₀=(s−ρ)(s−conjρ)/|ρ|² corresponding to the omitted pair, or by 1 if nothing is missing. Holomorphy on the disc is recovered; |D₀|≤C(1+r)² uniformly by the fixed lower bound on the first ordinate and D₀(2)≥1. The truncated-sector proof holds for this modified quotient with d=3/4+deg D₀. The boundary mean gains at most O(log H) and the exponent of the divisor (s+i)^d in the sector changes accordingly. There are now four real zeros 0,1,3,−2 by symmetry and orthogonality. Dividing by their four factors on the disc r=1/θ gives O(r^(d−4)) at s=2, proving both rates. It does not cover an unknown number of omissions.

First approximant in the new class, with no ordinate as input. Take S=(2/3)cosh(x/2)+(1/3)cosh(5x/2). Since y↦cosh(x√y) is convex for y≥0 by its series, S≥cosh(3x/2) on all of R (9/4 is the combination with those weights of 1/4 and 25/4). Hence the integrated ABSOLUTE ERROR is exactly
    2/3+K(3)/3−K(2)=2/3+ζ(3)/π−π/3 ∈ (0.00209571,0.00209572).
Evaluated with Arb at 140 bits. The small bound is for the enlarged criterion, and a single fixed error does not prove convergence. The possibility of adding a generator rests on the two deformation directions of a quartet; adding two independent moments would absorb both if there were only one simple quartet.

### The fixed-sign error has a floor even if RH holds

Write f=cosh(3x/2), L=∂²+∂, y=s(s−1). Let P₋(y)=y(y−6) and P₊(y)=y(y−6)(y−3). For each choice the density p_±=p+εP_±(L)p is positive for one and the same sufficiently small ε>0. Indeed, if j is the degree, P_± is monic and the leading term of P_±(L)p/p is positive and of order exp(4j|x|) in both tails, by the differentiated theta series. On compacts the quotient has a finite minimum. The transform is K(s)(1+εP_±(y)); the integrations by parts are justified by the decay of the derivatives. Normalization, symmetry, the values at s=1,3 and all imposed critical jets are kept. Therefore the even measures ν_±=exp(x/2)p_±(x)dx integrate each generator exactly like ν. However ∫f dν_±=K(2)(1±8ε).

Consequently every majorant S≥f in the spanned space has ∫(S−f)dν≥8εK(2), by integration against ν₊. Similarly every minorant S≤f has ∫(f−S)dν≥8εK(2) via ν₋. These are unconditional barriers for ALL finite combinations, with no limit on the height or on the number of cosines. Also, if S_n→f in L¹(ν), no common lower bound −C exp(A|x|) can hold for all S_n−f: extract an almost everywhere convergent subsequence and apply Fatou against ν₊, where the integral of the residual tends to −8εK(2). The same argument with ν₋ forbids a common upper envelope of that type.

Quantitative cost in amplitude. For any approximant put E=∫|r|dν, r=S−f, and B=max(1,sup_x |r(x)|exp(−3|x|)). It is finite for each finite combination even with jets. With dη=exp(x/2)P₋(L)p dx one has |∫r dη|=8K(2) exactly and |dη|≤C exp(8|x|)dν. On |x|≤R the variation of this pairing is ≤C exp(8R)E. In the tail it is ≤CB exp(−c exp(2R)) by the theta density and the definition of B. Choose exp(8R)=4K(2)/(CE) for small E. Then log(2+B)≥c′ E^(−1/4), or E≥c″/[log(2+B)]⁴ adjusting constants for E not small. With only cosines, mass and auxiliary, B is bounded by one plus the sum of the moduli of the coefficients. Thus a rule claiming decreasing error must allow growing amplitudes; perfecting the previous convex majorant does not suffice. This result does not give a convergent upper bound.

### Reduction of the global norm to an interval of radius (log m)/2+O(1)

Let r be an exponential polynomial (including the residual f−S), with m exponents counted with repetition and |Re λ|≤3. For an absolute constant C and m sufficiently large, put R_m=(log m)/2+C. Then
    ∫_{|x|>R_m}|r|dν ≤ exp(−m) ∫_{|x|≤R_m}|r|dν.
There is no condition on the coefficients, the separation of ordinates or the imaginary frequencies. In a prefix of n cosines without jets, plus the mass, the auxiliary and the target, one can take m=2n+6. Therefore minimizing the norm on this single interval produces an approximant whose GLOBAL error is at most (1+exp(−m)) times the global optimum. The statement presupposes control of the continuous integral on the interval, not only of a mesh.

Proof. Reuse the recurrence of the optimal-diameter quadrature (entry 3146), now with seed of length l=(log m)/4 and step h=l/m. For translation in either direction the moduli of the characteristic roots are ≤exp(3h). The expansion of the reciprocal of the denominator as a product of m geometric series gives, at the cell at distance y=kh, a bound for the unweighted integral by the unweighted integral of the seed [0,l] (or its reflection), multiplied by
    m (1+exp(3h))^m binom(k+m,m) exp(3kh)
    ≤ exp(C₁m log(2+y/l)+3y).
Indeed the integral over the initial phase of the largest of m initial amplitudes is dominated by the sum of their integrals. The lower theta bound on the seed is ≥exp(−C₂ exp(2l)) by the first positive summand and parity, so converting the initial integral into its weighted norm costs at most exp(C₂√m). On a tail cell the density is ≤C₃ exp(−c exp(2y)). For y≥R_m−h, the exponent c exp(2y)/2 dominates C₁m log(2+y/l)+3y+C₂√m+2m if C is fixed sufficiently large: at the endpoint y/l→2 and afterwards the quotient of the exponential by the growing terms is increasing. The remainder exp(−c exp(2y)/2) is summed over the mesh at cost O(1+1/h), absorbed by exp(m). Including the cell touching R_m allows using exactly the indicated radius. The two seeds lie inside the interval. The result for the minimizer follows by taking infima; local existence is that of best approximation in finite dimension.

The coefficient 1/2 in the radius is necessary for a uniform statement about this general class: take r=x^(m−1), the exponent zero repeated m times. For 0<b<b′<1/2, the integral over |x|≤b log m is ≤ν(R)(b log m)^(m−1), while over [b′log m,b′log m+1] it is ≥(b′log m)^(m−1) exp(−O(m^(2b′))). The interior/exterior quotient tends to zero. This does not prove optimality for the actual ordinates of ζ. The previous interpolant already converges on |x|≤c log m for small c. To close by this route control over the rest of the norming interval is still missing. The need to estimate separately the ℓ¹ norm of the coefficients to certify the infinite tail has been removed.

### Uniform approximation by the critical count actually used

Let e(R,H) be the best UNIFORM error for cosh(3x/2) on |x|≤R, with the cosines and critical jets chosen up to H (adding mass or the auxiliary only improves it). For any A>√(H²+9/4),
    log e(R,H) ≤ 3R/2 + 2RA/π − 2Σ_{chosen γ} log(A/√(γ²+9/4)).
Repetitions of an ordinate require its consecutive jets. The formula uses only the included list; it does not presuppose that all zeros are critical. By uniform duality on C[0,R], it suffices to prove it for every signed measure η of variation ≤1 annihilating the generators. F(z)=∫cosh(zx)dη(x) is entire, even and satisfies |F(z)|≤exp(R|Re z|). The jets become zeros at ±iγ with the indicated multiplicities. Apply Jensen with centre 3/2 and radius A: the mean of log|F| on the boundary is ≤3R/2+2RA/π and each pair of zeros contributes the subtracted summand. If F(3/2)=0 the bound is immediate. Then take the supremum over η. This proof obtains coefficients by best approximation, not by Hermite interpolation.

If the COMPLETE prefix on the line with its multiplicities has been verified up to H, put A=H+2. The subtracted sum is H/π [log(H/(2π))−2]+O(log² H): replacing √(γ²+9/4) by γ costs O(Σγ⁻²), and A by H costs O(log H). Integrate the count twice in the sense of counting both signs, that is, use 2∫₀ᴴ N(t)dt/t and the Riemann–von Mangoldt formula. For fixed δ>0, the radius
    R = (1/2)log(H/(2π)) − 1 − δ
gives e(R,H)≤exp(−2δH/π+O(log² H)), with no hypothesis on higher zeros. Even without complete verification, the classical proportion of simple critical zeros of P122.003 gives for every η₀<1/5 and large H error ≤exp(−c H log H) on |x|≤η₀ log H, using only the simple ones (choose a proportion strictly between 2η₀ and 2/5 in the lower asymptotic count).

In the complete-prefix case m≈(H/π)log H and the distance between the radius proved for uniform approximation and the radius sufficient to control the global norm is (1/2)log log H+O_δ(1). The leading coefficients relative to log H coincide, but that strip grows and the coefficients of the interior minimizer have no bound on it here. The result does not transfer the local exponential error to the global norm.

### Unconditional global convergence on dilating the weight, and barrier in the opposite direction

Keep the test functions and change only the norm to L¹(v_d dx), v_d(x)=v(dx), d>0 fixed. The weight of the sign criterion is exactly d=1. For d>5/2 the cosines of the simple critical zeros up to height H suffice, without RH, to approximate cosh(3x/2) on the WHOLE line with error ≤C_d exp(−c_d H log H). For 0<d<1 even the enlarged family with mass, auxiliary and all critical jets has strictly positive distance, independently of RH. Under RH and with all jets, global convergence with that rate extends to every d>1. None of the constants is claimed to be uniform as the threshold is approached.

For the ceiling, the norm reduction is carried over by x'=dx: the order m of the residual is kept and the exponents are divided by d. For d>1 they still satisfy the same bound on real parts. The sufficient radius in x is R=(log m)/(2d)+O_d(1). Let α be an available lower asymptotic proportion of simple critical zeros among all zeros (or of critical jets using multiplicities). If dα>1, choose 1/(2d)<η<α/2. Since m≪H log H, for large H R<η log H. The Jensen proof for uniform approximation, applied to the selected count up to H, gives error ≤exp(−c H log H) there: the sum of zeros contributes at least (α′/π)H log H+O(H) for any 2η<α′<α, while the boundary costs (2η/π)H log H+O(log H). Take the best approximant on that interval and apply the norm reduction to the SAME residual. The integral of the weight is finite. With α=2/5 the old theorem audited in P122.003 suffices. Under RH one can use α=1 with jets. The argument also works for any fixed target cosh(bx) with real b, changing only constants; it does not require Hermite interpolation.

For the floor, take the signed measure η with density exp(x/2)P(L)p with P(y)=y(y−6), from the one-sided discard. It annihilates all generators and its integral of the target equals −8K(2). For d<1, |dη/dx|≤C exp(8|x|)v(x)≤C_d v(dx), since log v(x)=−πexp(2|x|)+O(1+|x|) and exp(2d|x|) grows more slowly. By duality the L¹(v_d) distance is ≥8K(2)/C_d. Thus d<1 would be an excessive demand even if RH holds. The positive proof, for its part, uses strict slack in dα>1; there is no passage to the limit d↓1 without uniform control. In particular the dilated-weight theorem does not certify a new window of the paper.

### Location instability under positive perturbation preserving the moments

There exist positive probabilities p_Γ with ||p_Γ/p−1||∞ of order Γ⁻², with normalized and symmetric transform and with the same moment K(3), for which two pairs of simple critical zeros of ξ are replaced by a quartet at horizontal distance 1/4+o(1) from the line. The statement is unconditional about the perturbed laws. The transform is explicit and the change of divisor is exact, counting multiplicities.

Choose pairs of simple critical ordinates Γ−h,Γ+h with Γ→∞ and h→0. They exist by N₀,simp(T)≫T log T: if consecutive gaps had a positive floor the count would eventually be O(T). Put y=s(s−1), A=(Γ−h)²+1/4, B=(Γ+h)²+1/4, D=(y+A)(y+B), ε=1/(4Γ²), and define
    W_Γ=K · [D+ε y(y−6)]/D.
The symmetry in s is exact; the rational factor equals one at y=0,6. The quotient is removable in the product with K at the four removed points.

To prove uniform positivity, apply the four two-sided divisions to the transformed numerator of f=L(L−6)p. One has |f(x)|≤C exp(8|x|)p(x). In each tail, the four integrals are taken outwards, and the four exponential moduli together are ≤exp(r), r the sum of shifts. With B₀=exp(2|x|), the theta slope bound gives p(x±r)/p(x)≤exp(−c B₀ r); the integral of r³exp(−(cB₀−9)r)/6 is O(B₀⁻⁴). It cancels the four powers of B₀ of f. On compacts use the doubly exponential integrability and the minimum of p. Thus the real density q with transform Ky(y−6)/D satisfies |q|≤C p with C independent of Γ,h, without dividing by differences of roots. Therefore p_Γ=p+εq is strictly positive for large Γ. Moreover ||p_Γ/p−1||∞≥ε because on the real axis W_Γ(x)/K(x)→1+ε as x→+∞, and that quotient is a weighted average of p_Γ/p.

The discriminant of the new quadratic in y is (A+B−6ε)²−4(1+ε)AB. Divided by Γ² it tends to −1, since (A−B)²/Γ²=16h²→0. Its roots have real part −Γ²+O(1+h²) and imaginary part ±(Γ/2)(1+o(1)). At s=1/2±√(y+1/4) one obtains the quartet with |Re s−1/2|→1/4 and |Im s|/Γ→1. The rational formula keeps the rest of the divisor of K and adds the new points, even if they coincided with previous zeros. A fixed prefix of critical data and the two real moments cannot distinguish these witnesses for Γ sufficiently large. This does not preserve the two deliberately removed pairs of jets nor the arithmetic formula proper to ξ.

### What the arithmetic cell observes of the perturbation

For K and W_Γ of the previous subsection use the centred error of the cell r=1/2 of 3124 with multiplier G_v(s)=exp(v(s²−s)/2), 0≤v≤1. Here v denotes the variance, not the theta density. It is legitimate to take v=0 for THESE two laws: K already decays exponentially in vertical strips and W_Γ is its product with a rational quotient with removed singularities. Let Δ_v(y) be the difference of both errors, each with its own centring. Write ρ_j=1/2+iγ_j, γ₁,₂=Γ±h. For y≥1,
    Δ_v(y)=2√y Re Σ_{j=1,2} a_j exp(iγ_j log y) + O(Γ^−2/y),
    a_j=−(1−r^ρ_j)G_v(ρ_j)W_Γ(ρ_j)/ρ_j.
It is the four old annihilations that were lost which give the residue. They are simple, W_Γ(ρ_j)≠0, and the new zeros of the witness contribute no poles to −ζ′/ζ. The cell factor removes the possible term at s=0. On Re s=−1, |W_Γ−K|=ε|K y_s(y_s−6)/D| with y_s=s(s−1). If |Im s|≤Γ/2, the rational quotient is bounded; elsewhere the distances to all poles are ≥1 and a polynomial in |Im s| suffices, absorbed by the decay of K. The logarithmic derivative on that line grows at most logarithmically. This justifies the uniform contour bound and the usual shift of the explicit formula (also without Gaussian using heights avoiding zeros).

For each η>0 and Γ→∞ along the construction,
    sup_{0≤v≤1, 1≤y≤exp(vΓ²+(π/2−η)Γ)} |Δ_v(y)| = o(1)
when the interval is nonempty. On the circle of radius 2 centred at 1/2+iΓ, the upper factors of D have modulus ≥1 for large Γ and the lower ones ≫Γ. By Stirling and polynomial growth of ζ, |K/D|≤Γ^C exp(−πΓ/4) on the boundary, and by removability and maximum also inside. At the residues |G_v(ρ_j)|≤exp(−vΓ²/2+o(Γ)) uniformly, since h→0. With the previous bound for |W_Γ(ρ_j)| and the factor √y a margin exp(−ηΓ/2+o(Γ)) remains. This is an indistinguishability bound at FIXED absolute tolerance for the specified observable; it is not a limit for exact observations.

On the other hand for each fixed Γ and v the mean over 0≤t≤U of |exp(−t/2)Δ_v(exp t)|² tends to 2Σ|a_j|²>0 by orthogonality of the four distinct frequencies. Thus the perturbation is detectable at arbitrarily high scales. There is here no uniform lower bound for those coefficients nor an estimate of the first detection. Removing the Gaussian removes the term quadratic in Γ from the indistinguishability bound, but the linear exponent contributed by the gamma factor of ξ remains. It is not inferred that the observations without Gaussian detect the change right after that scale.

### Return to the Weil form: the change is visible in norm in any fixed window

For T>0 in L²[−T,T], consider only the finite difference J_Γ between the spectral sums of the perturbed and the original divisor, with the convention F(z)=∫f(x)exp(zx)dx and summands F(z)conj(F(−conj z)). No prime formula for the perturbed divisor is presupposed. Let M_Γg=exp(−iΓx)g, c(x)=cosh(x/4), a(x)=sinh(x/4) and
    B=2(c⊗c−a⊗a−1⊗1),
where u⊗u is g↦u〈u,g〉. Then in operator norm
    J_Γ=M_Γ B M_Γ* + M_Γ* B M_Γ + o_T(1).
Indeed the new height is at distance O(1/Γ) from Γ by the quadratic formula, the two old heights are at distance h=o(1), and the horizontal displacement tends to 1/4. On the fixed interval the evaluation vectors can be replaced by their limits after demodulating, with error o_T(1) in L². In each carrier the two new points give the cross pairing between exp(x/4) and exp(−x/4), and the two old ones subtract two constant evaluations. This gives B.

The blocks decouple: on the six modulated vectors of 1,c,a the Gram matrix tends to the direct sum of two identical Grams by Riemann–Lebesgue. On orthonormalizing (each triple is independent for T>0), the nonzero eigenvalues converge to those of two copies of B. In particular ||J_Γ||→||B||>0, even though J_Γf→0 for each FIXED f by Riemann–Lebesgue. A smooth real odd g with ∫ga≠0 gives J_Γ[M_Γg]→−2|∫ga|². If the primitive moments at ±1/2 are required, use −Γ⁻²(∂²−1/4)M_Γg with g smooth of interior support: the two moments are exactly zero and the L² difference from the modulated one is O_g(1/Γ), preserving the limit.

This detects the change of the divisor at constant order but not the sign of the complete form. Indeed for that same packet with fixed nonzero g, the archimedean part of the original form grows like a positive multiple of ||g||² log Γ. The digamma symbol is log|τ|+O(1) at high frequency and bounded below; integrating against the translated Fourier profile of g (rapid decay) gives the leading term. The primitive correction is a combination of the same packets with profiles g′,g″ and coefficients O(1/Γ), O(1/Γ²), so it does not change that order. The prime translations for n≤exp(2T) form a finite sum bounded by C_T||f||² and the poles are also bounded in the window. Thus on this packet the complete value grows positively even after adding J_Γ. The proof rules out using the mere detection of a negative block in the difference as a global negative test of paper 46.

### Analytically verifiable negative windows for the high artificial divisor

For every η>0 the surgeries of the previous subsections can be chosen at heights Γ→∞ so that the COMPLETE spectral form of the modified divisor has a negative primitive test at radius (2+η)log log Γ+O(1), without presupposing RH for the original divisor. The background of the modified form instead converges to the original background in each fixed window. These are two statements for the perturbed model. Distinct antecedent: R166_102 compared thresholds in an exchange flow parametrized by s; here heights are chosen avoiding exceptional zeros of the real divisor in order to bound the spectral background of the packet.

Selection. Fix small b>0 such that 2(1/4−b)(2+η)>1. By density of simple critical zeros there are infinitely many dyadic blocks [X,2X] with ≫X log X simple ordinates. By Ingham (entry 230), the zeros in [X/2,3X] with |Re ρ−1/2|≥b number O(X^(q+o(1))) with q<1, using symmetry. Delete their neighbourhoods of radius 2X^κ with 0<κ<1−q. By the O(log X) count of zeros per unit interval, o(X log X) ordinates are deleted. There is still a unit cell with ≫log X surviving simple zeros; choose two at distance O(1/log X). The heights Γ of the midpoint and Γ′ of the new quartet (Γ′−Γ=O(1/Γ)) are at distance at least X^κ from the exceptional ordinates. The new relative abscissa δ tends to 1/4.

Test. Choose φ smooth real even nonnegative, nonzero, supported in (−1,1), L=(2+η)log log Γ. Modulate by exp(−iΓ′x) the odd profile φ(x−L)−φ(x+L), and apply −(∂²−1/4)/Γ² to impose the two primitive moments without enlarging the support. Its transform before the correction is 2sinh(L(z−iΓ′))Φ(z−iΓ′), with Φ the two-sided transform of φ. At the points z=±δ+iΓ′ the Weil pairing is negative and the sum is −8 sinh²(Lδ)Φ(δ)². The primitive factor multiplies the signed summand by (z²−1/4)²/Γ⁴; its modulus is |z²−1/4|²/Γ⁴. On pairing the two points conjugate by reflection, the real part of the multiplier tends to one there. The conjugate pair at negative height costs o(1) by rapid decay of Φ uniformly in the strip.

For the original divisor bound the sum in absolute value. Within |Im z−Γ′|≤X^κ the abscissas have modulus <b, and the cost is O(exp(2bL)log Γ) by decay of Φ and counting by unit intervals. Outside, exp(L) and decay of arbitrary order in |Im z−Γ′| suffice, absorbing the primitive factor of degree four and the count, giving o(1). Suppressing the old critical evaluations only subtracts nonnegative terms. The new negative term dominates, since (2δ−2b)L−log log Γ→+∞. The negative sign of the model on that test is proved. Optimality of the radius is not claimed.

At fixed radius T the conclusion of stability of the background is uniform over functions. For each modulated evaluation vector of the exact blocks, the transform of its envelope (exponential of bounded parameter restricted to [−T,T]) is O_T((1+|τ|)^−1). After modulation, its squared norm in the reciprocal weight of log(2+|τ|) is O_T(1/log Γ), separating |τ|<Γ/2 from the rest. Cauchy–Schwarz and the fixed number of vectors give |J_Γ[f]|≤C_T/log Γ · ∫log(2+|τ|)|f̂(τ)|²dτ. By the archimedean symbol and the window boundedness of primes and poles, that integral is ≤C_T(W[f]+C_T′||f||²). Taking infima over the unit sphere, in the same domain (also in the primitive one), implies that the variation of the background is O_T(1/log Γ). In particular, any fixed strictly positive floor survives for large Γ. Positivity of the original background in new windows has not been established.

### Sufficient radius to detect a real exterior zero without internal separation

Let δ+iΓ be a zero of E(z)=K(1/2+z), with 0<δ<1/2 and large Γ. Put U=Γ+log(2+Γ)log(2/δ). In the Weil form of ξ itself there is then a smooth complex primitive test that is strictly negative at radius
    T ≤ (1/2) log U + C,
with an absolute constant sufficiently large. In particular (log Γ)/2+O_d(1) suffices when δ≥d>0. The height is not chosen and no minimal distance to the other zeros is imposed. Antecedent in this same round: division by a zero produced cardinal tests and a finite radius without this estimate; the change here is interpolating a whole group by contour.

Circles. Take a radius in [δ/4,δ/2] for the disc centred at δ+iΓ avoiding the distances to all nearby zeros by ≥cδ/log(2+Γ). It exists because there are O(log Γ) zeros in the neighbourhood of bounded height, with multiplicity. Use the mirror disc under z↦−conj z, disjoint from the first. On their circles |E|≥exp(−CU). Detail: for ζ in the variable s use a disc of centre 2+iΓ and radius in [4,5] without boundary zeros. There are O(log Γ) zeros inside. Divide ζ by its Blaschke factors in the disc, of modulus one on the boundary. The quotient B is holomorphic without zeros, |B|≤Γ^C by the polynomial strip bound, and |B(2+iΓ)|≥|ζ(2+iΓ)|≥c by Euler. Harnack for log(Γ^C/|B|) gives |B|≥Γ^−C′ on the subdisc of radius 3. Each removed factor has modulus ≥cδ/log Γ on the chosen circles by its distance to the zeros and the formula for the disc factor. Stirling costs exp(−CΓ); the loss O(log Γ log log Γ) is absorbed in CΓ. The two circles lie in the indicated subdisc.

Cardinal. For a positively oriented circle C₀ build outside the disc the function
    F₀(z)=E(z) ∮ dw/[2πi (z−w)E(w)].
Inside the disc one has to add 1 to that expression to obtain the entire continuation (residues at the zeros and at w=z). At every zero of E it equals exactly the indicator of the disc, also in the presence of multiplicity. Its inverse density is the integral over the same contour of exp(−wx)∫_x^∞ exp(wt)v(t)dt divided by 2πi E(w), by integration by parts first in Re z>max Re w. For negative x one can use minus the integral from −∞ to x: the integrated difference is ∮exp(−wx)dw/(2πi)=0. By the theta tails and the differential equation of the primitive, for the first six orders the derivatives of this density are ≤exp(CU)exp(−c exp(2|x|)); the polynomial factors in Γ and in exp(|x|) are absorbed into the constants of the exponent. Take the difference of the cardinals of the two discs: their values at the zeros are +1,−1 and 0 elsewhere.

Cutoff. Multiply the density by a smooth cutoff equal to one on [−T+1,T−1] and zero outside [−T,T], with uniform derivatives, and apply −(∂²−1/4)/Γ² to satisfy the two primitive moments. With T=(log U)/2+C and C sufficiently large, the discarded part and its first six derivatives, even with weight exp(|x|), have integral O(exp(−U)). Integrating by parts in Fourier, the error between transforms after the primitive correction is O(exp(−U)(1+|Im z|)^−3) on the whole strip of zeros (increase C if needed). Its ℓ² norm over the zeros with multiplicities is O(exp(−U)) by the unit count. Before the cutoff, after the primitive correction, each zero of the discs contributes −(z²−1/4)²/Γ⁴, with real part ≤−1/2 for large Γ, and the others contribute zero. The discs contain at least the reflected pair and O(log Γ) zeros; the ℓ² norm of the exact data is O(√log Γ). Cauchy–Schwarz in the Weil involution keeps negativity after the cutoff. It is a conditional detection radius for any hypothetical exterior zero; it neither proves a positive sign in those windows nor the existence of the zero.

### Direct quantitative detection in POWER matrices with prescribed real exponents

If ξ has a zero ρ=1/2+δ+iΓ, Γ sufficiently large, 0<δ<1/2, the complete matrix of POWER_CONE_001 at the anchor a=32 and ANY set of m distinct real nodes of [Γ,2Γ] has a negative eigenvalue provided that
    m ≥ C Γ log Γ log(2/δ)/δ
with C absolute and sufficiently large. No separation between nodes is required and no estimate of ξ′(ρ) is used. The nodes may be taken equally spaced. This quantifies the Pick bridge already identified in R162_803 and POWER; the Pick mechanism is not new. Here one bounds how many powers force detection starting from the hypothetical position, without quantifying the cost of certifying the spectrum in finite arithmetic.

Proof. If the real matrix [(L(a_i)+L(a_j))/(a_i+a_j−1)] were positive semidefinite, the finite Nevanlinna–Pick theorem (including the singular case, via Cayley) would give P holomorphic with nonnegative real part on Re s>1/2 with P(a_i)=L(a_i), L=ξ′/ξ. By Schwarz–Pick between half-planes, using P(32)=L(32)>0 fixed, |P(s)|≤C(1+|s|)^2/(Re s−1/2). Put Z=(s−1)ζ(s); on Re s≥1/2, |Z|+|Z′|≤C(1+|s|)^3, by Euler summation with floor at 1 and its derivative (or Cauchy on a slightly larger strip). Moreover LZ=Z′+[1/s+ψ(s/2)/2−(log π)/2]Z. On Re s>α=1/2+δ/4,
    A(s)=(L(s)−P(s))Z(s)/(s+2)^7
is holomorphic, bounded by C/δ, and vanishes at each of the m high nodes. Factorization by its Blaschke factors in that half-plane, or iterated Schwarz, gives |A(s)|≤(C/δ)∏|(s−a_j)/(s+a_j−2α)|. On all of |s−ρ|≤δ/2 each factor has modulus ≤exp(−cδ/Γ), by the identity for one minus its squared modulus.

Choose r∈[δ/4,δ/2] such that on the WHOLE circle |s−ρ|=r one has |Z(s)|≥exp(−C log Γ log(2/δ)). Use the local disc of ζ centred at 2+iΓ and the Harnack estimate of the previous subsection. For its O(log Γ) local factors, each distance |s−λ| has floor |r−|λ−ρ||. The uniform average in r of log⁻|r−u| is ≤log(4/δ)+C uniformly in u, by rescaling and integrability of log⁻|x| on intervals of length one. Sum before choosing r. The denominators of the disc factors cost constants, and |s−1|≥1. This avoids any loss from internal separation.

Therefore on that circle |L−P|≤(C/δ)(CΓ)^7 exp(C log Γ log(2/δ)−cmδ/Γ). With the declared dimension this bound can be made <1. But (2πi)⁻¹∮(L−P)ds counts the interior zeros of ξ with multiplicity and is at least one, whereas by the length of the circle it would have modulus ≤r<1. Contradiction. The diagonal change by ζ(a_i)>0 of the POWER coordinates preserves inertia, so the negative value corresponds to a REAL combination of the powers. For fixed δ order O_δ(Γ log Γ) suffices. No uniform margin for the eigenvalue nor proof of semidefiniteness of the blocks was obtained.

### A single real vector per order and exact negativity rate in L² norm

Fix u=63/2 and φ_j(t)=√(2u)exp(−ut)L_j(2ut) on t≥0, the real orthonormal basis of POWER_014. Put s_w=1/2+u(1+w)/(1−w), L=ξ′/ξ and L(s_w)=Σ c_n w^n at the origin. The Laguerre generating function and the full kernel of POWER_001 give, for small real w,v,
    Σ W[φ_j,φ_k] w^j v^k = (L(s_w)+L(s_v))/(1−wv).
Indeed the physical generating functions are √(2u)exp(−(s_w−1/2)t)/(1−w); inserting both into the two-exponent formula, the prefactors cancel the denominator down to 1−wv. One may differentiate in the weighted norm of POWER_014 for w,v near zero. One obtains diagonal 2c₀ and entry c_n at distance n>0.

It suffices to prove W[(φ₀+φ_n)/√2]≥0 for each n≥1, with fixed PLUS sign. Indeed that unit energy equals exactly 2c₀+c_n. If all of them are nonnegative, L(s_w)+2c₀/(1−w) has nonnegative coefficients (the constant one is 3c₀>0). A pole of L in Re s>1/2 would be a pole in |w|<1. By Pringsheim's theorem a series with nonnegative coefficients and radius r<1 would have a singularity at w=r. But there s_r is real >1 and ξ(s_r)≠0. This excludes all interior poles. The converse follows from the full sign under HR. For the same reason eventual nonnegativity suffices, modifying a prefix by a polynomial. These are two Laguerre modes at fixed rate; φ_n contains a polynomial of degree n and is NOT an individual power of the family of distinct exponents. The reduction uses the known Pick object and a positive-series argument; no novelty of Pringsheim's principle is claimed.

More precisely, if HR fails, let r be the smallest modulus of (ρ−1/2−u)/(ρ−1/2+u) for Reρ>1/2. It is <1 and attained, since in each compact interior disc there are only finitely many poles. The poles on |w|=r are simple even for multiple zeros. Subtract their principal parts and use Cauchy up to a radius between r and the next pole (and less than one): c_n r^n differs by o(1) from a finite real sum Σ b_j exp(−inθ_j) with nonzero amplitudes and distinct phases without zero frequency. It has mean zero and strictly positive mean square, by orthogonality of the frequencies. On the compact closure of the phase group generated by one step, its continuous function takes strictly positive and strictly negative values. Returns to each of two sign zones with margin are relatively dense: the inverse translates of the open set by the positive orbit cover the group and a finite subcover suffices. Consequently there is an integer J, depending on the divisor, such that in every stretch of J sufficiently high indices some unit vector (φ₀+φ_n)/√2 has value ≤−c r^(−n), and another has value ≥c r^(−n).

If λ_N is the minimum of the full matrix of the first N modes in this orthonormal basis, eventually λ_N<0 and (−λ_N)^(1/N)→1/r. For the lower bound use the negative subsequence with bounded gaps up to N−1. For the upper one the maximal row sum is ≤C N r^(−N) by the pole expansion. This gives the rate in the physical norm for the confluent blocks; no such rate is claimed for the Euclidean eigenvalue in the ill-conditioned coordinates of nearby exponents. It remains to prove 2c₀+c_n≥0 for unbounded n.

### Positive sign of the two-mode sequence up to quadratic order in the verified height

Fix u=63/2. There are constants c_u,k_u>0 such that if all zeros up to height H are on the critical line, for H sufficiently large and 1≤n≤c_u H² one has
    W[(φ₀+φ_n)/√2] ≥ k_u log(2+n)/√(1+n).
The full prefix is a finite hypothesis; nothing is imposed on the higher zeros. It is the sign of one unit vector per order, not semidefiniteness of the block of that size.

Write z=ρ−1/2, w(z)=(z−u)/(z+u), b(z)=2u/(u²−z²). The Hadamard product of ξ in the centred variable (pairing z and −z) gives the exact real value E_n=Σ_z b(z)[1+w(z)^(−n)], with multiplicities. Indeed the constant terms 2/(u−z) can be averaged with 2/(u+z), giving b(z); the coefficients of degree n≥1 of 1/(s_w−ρ) are b(z)w(z)^(−n). The paired sums are absolutely convergent for fixed n. Projecting all zeros to z=iγ, keeping their ordinates and multiplicities, one obtains the positive sum of weights 2u/(u²+γ²) times 1+cos(nθ(γ)), θ(t)=2 arctan(u/t) for γ>0, with the conjugate contribution for γ<0.

This projected sum has floor ≫_u log(2+n)/√(1+n) without HR. For large n take A=B√n with B fixed large depending on u, and use only A<γ≤2A. In the unweighted count the sum of 1 over the band is asymptotic to A log A/(2π). For cos(nθ) the contribution of the main Riemann–von Mangoldt density is O_u(A² log A/n) by one integration by parts, since |θ′|≍_u A⁻² and is monotone on the band. The contribution of the remainder of the count is O_u(log A (1+n/A)) by Stieltjes integration by parts. The latter is an arbitrarily small fraction of the mass term once B is fixed large, and the main oscillatory one is o(A log A). Since 1+cos≥0 and the minimal weight on the band is ≫_u A⁻², the floor follows. For the finitely many small n the projected sum is strictly positive because of the large heights, where cos(nθ)→1.

Error of the horizontal shift. For |γ|>H, −1/2≤Re z≤1/2 one has |b|≪_u γ⁻², |b′|≪_u |γ|⁻³ and |w′/w|≪_u γ⁻². Starting from |w(iγ)|=1, the modulus of w(z)^(−n) is ≤exp(C_u n/γ²). Integrate the derivative of the summand along the shift of length ≤1/2 and sum by Riemann–von Mangoldt. The total projection error is bounded by
    C_u (H⁻¹+n/H²) exp(C_u n/H²) (log H)/H.
There is no error below H by hypothesis. For n≤c_u H² the projected floor is at least a constant times (log H)/H for c_u≤1 and H large, by eventual monotonicity of log n/√n. Choosing c_u small and then H large leaves at least half the floor over the whole range. Numerical constants remain to be determined if a concrete certified index is wanted, and control of the tail at all orders without prior verification is missing.

Later deduplication of the eventual-sign argument: paper 37, Fejér section, already uses Pringsheim to exclude Cayley poles from an eventual sign. POWER_007 records the Toeplitz bands. The application here is the energy of the vector with fixed plus sign and the preceding quantitative positive estimate; no novelty is attributed to the general eventual-sign argument.

### Positivity of the same vector up to order H² log H

Under the same hypothesis of complete verification up to H, the range is improved to n≤c_u H² log H and the floor to k_u [log(2+n)]^(3/2)/√(1+n), with unevaluated positive constants and H sufficiently large. Two estimates acting on different variables are combined.

Horizontal tail. In a band Y<|γ|≤2Y, let d=|Re ρ−1/2|. For f_n(z)=b(z)(1+w(z)^−n), the symmetry between +d+iγ and −d+iγ cancels the linear term of the shift. Differentiating twice on the segment between the two points, one obtains
    |f_n″| ≤ C_u Y⁻²(Y⁻¹+n/Y²)² exp(C_u nd/Y²).
Indeed b^(j)=O_u(Y^(−2−j)) for j≤2, (log w)′=O_u(Y⁻²) and (log w)″=O_u(Y⁻³). For a=C_u n/Y²≤c₁ log Y with c₁ sufficiently small, one has Σ d²exp(ad)≪Y/log Y. To see it, integrate the derivative of t²exp(at) against Selberg's uniform bound N(1/2+t,2Y)≪Y log Y exp(−t log Y/4) of 413. For t≥1/4 it suffices to use the bound at t=1/4, since exp(a/2) leaves a power saving. After summing the bands Y=2^jH, the projection error is
    ≪_u (H⁻¹+n/H²)²/(H log H).
The zeros of height ≤H do not contribute to this error.

Projected floor. Take A=B√(n/log n), ℓ=D/log A, with D fixed large and then B fixed large according to D,u. The classical Fujii–Tsang second moment gives ∫_A^(2A)|S(t+ℓ)−S(t)|²dt≪A log(2+D). By the counting formula, except on a set of measure O(A log(2+D)/D²), the interval (t,t+ℓ] contains at least D/(4π) ordinates with multiplicity (increase D if needed). On the other hand on [A,2A−ℓ] an absolute positive proportion of t satisfy cos(nθ(t))≥1/2: the monotone phase runs through ≫n/A periods and its maximal speed is at most five times the minimal one. On each of those intervals of length ℓ the phase varies by at most C_u D/B², so 1+cos(nθ(γ))≥1 for all its zeros. Choose D so that the preceding exceptional set occupies less than half of that proportion, and B so that the variation is <π/6. Integrating the number of zeros over the good starting points gives ≫AD; each ordinate counts over length at most ℓ. There are therefore ≫A log A favourable ordinates and the weight of each is ≫_u A⁻². This gives the claimed projected floor; the finitely many small n are absorbed into the constant. External input used only for the variance: Tsang, *Some Ω-theorems for the Riemann zeta-function*, theorem 4 (https://doi.org/10.4064/aa-46-4-369-395), also stated in Trudgian, theorem 5.1.

Comparison. For H²≤n≤c_u H² log H put X=n/H². The ratio between the tail error and the new floor is ≪_u X^(5/2)/(log H)^(5/2). Choosing c_u small controls that ratio and guarantees the hypothesis on a in all bands. For n≤H² the tail costs O(1/(H log H)) and is again less than half the floor for H large. Simplicity is not assumed and no new window T is deduced. The density application here sums weighted shifts; it does not estimate the position of each individual zero.

### Sparse blocks of Laguerre modes with all crossings

Fix the number k≥2 of modes and u=63/2. Let j₁<…<j_k be nonnegative indices of diameter N=j_k−j₁. There are constants c,k₀,C>0 depending only on k,u such that, with complete verification of the zeros up to H sufficiently large, if
    1≤N≤c H² log H,    min_{i<k}(j_{i+1}−j_i)≥C√(N/log(2+N)),
then for any complex coefficients a_i the full form satisfies
    W[Σ a_i φ_{j_i}] ≥ k₀ [log(2+N)]^(3/2)/√(1+N) · Σ|a_i|².
For k=2 ALL jumps 1≤N≤c H² log H are covered, absorbing the finitely many small ones as indicated below; there is no bound on the initial index j₁. The orthonormal basis and the Toeplitz identities make the L² normalization literal.

Proof. Normalize Σ|a_i|²=1 and remove j₁ from all indices by Toeplitz. In the projection of all zeros to the line, the value of the matrix is the discrete integral of |P(t)|² with weight 2u/(u²+γ²) per ordinate, P(t)=Σ a_j exp(i(j−j₁)θ(t)) (use both signs of ordinate). For N large fix A=B√(N/log N). On A≤t≤2A the first derivative test for the phase (j−l)θ(t) gives integral O_u(A²/|j−l|). Hence ∫|P|² ≥3A/4 if the minimal separation is ≥C_{k,u} A, using Σ_{j≠l}|a_j a_l|≤k. Since |P|≤√k, the region with |P|≥1/2 has measure ≫A/k. Removing the final strip of length ℓ=D/log A is harmless. The Fujii–Tsang moment used before guarantees ≥D/(4π) zeros per interval of length ℓ except for starting points of measure O(A log(2+D)/D²). Choose D large according to k and then B large according to k,D,u so that ℓ sup|P′|≤1/4, since sup|P′|≪_u √k N/A². Finally fix C in the statement according to that B. Integrating over the good starting points and dividing by ℓ one counts ≫_{k,u} A log A ordinates with |P(γ)|≥1/4. Thus the projected floor has the declared order.

The true/projected discrepancy of each Toeplitz band of distance h≤N is ≪_u(H⁻¹+N/H²)²/(H log H) by the symmetric estimate of the preceding entry. For the diagonal one uses b(z) directly, or the constant case of the same computation. The cost in operator norm is at most k times that bound. The previous comparison with c small leaves half the floor. For bounded N there are finitely many configurations after translation. Their projected matrices are positive definite: a nonzero trigonometric polynomial does not vanish at the infinitely many distinct phases accumulating at zero. The discrepancy tends to zero and the constants are adjusted. This includes small jumps when k=2, since for N large the single jump N automatically satisfies the separation. The result is for Laguerre modes of arbitrary degree, distinct from the simple powers of 073, and does not allow k to grow without control.

### Positivity of the spectral tail for full blocks of growing dimension

In the coordinate z=ρ−1/2, consider a causal test function with rational transform F(z)=P(z)/∏_{j=1}^m(u_j−z), deg P<m, u_j>1/2, repetitions allowed. For H sufficiently large, the part of the Weil sum with |Im z|>H is positive definite on that WHOLE space if m≤cH^(1/3), with c absolute and independent of the rates. If all u_j equal u=63/2, m≤c_u√H suffices. The first conclusion about the tail is unconditional. If all zeros up to H are on the line, a sum of squares is added and the same positivity holds for the full form. In particular this covers any combination of m simple powers with exponents a_j=u_j+1/2>1 in the first range, and the consecutive Laguerre block of dimension m in the second. For these rationals the spectral formula is obtained directly by polarizing the POWER kernel through the Hadamard product; repetitions by differentiation in the parameters. The sum converges absolutely by the rational decay of at least 1/|γ| for each test factor.

Arbitrary rates. Split each band Y<γ≤2Y, Y≥H, into m cells of length Y/m. In a cell with lower endpoint a put t=(γ−a)m/Y∈[0,1] and τ=t−iδm/Y, where z=δ+iγ. In the new variable, F(i(a+tY/m))=p(t)/D(t) with p of degree <m. The poles of D in the variable t lie horizontally at distance at least m from [0,1], since their real part is −am/Y. Hence |D′/D|≤1 on the rectangle with real part [0,1], also for the reflected coordinate. On the whole cell |D(t)| is comparable to |D(0)| with absolute constants, and D(t)/D(τ)=1+O(m/Y).

On that cell, for any polynomial Q of degree <m, the sample norm Σ_γ |Q(t_γ)|² is comparable to (Y log Y/m)||Q||² in L²[0,1] if m³≤cY. Indeed the main term of the count has density comparable to Y log Y/m. The error by parts is O(log Y)(||Q||∞²+∫|(|Q|²)′|)≤C log Y·m²||Q||². One uses ||Q||∞≤m||Q|| and ||Q′||₂≤Cm²||Q||₂; both follow from the orthonormal Legendre basis by Cauchy–Schwarz, using |L_j|≤1 for the usual Legendre polynomials and ∫_{−1}¹(L_j′)²=j(j+1). Half-open intervals avoid duplicating nodes.

Even though the complex shift changes from sample to sample, finite Taylor and the preceding inequality applied to each derivative give
    ||p(τ_γ)−p(t_γ)||_{samples} ≤ C (Y log Y/m)^(1/2)||p||₂ [exp(Cm³/Y)−1].
Here each differentiation in L² costs at most Cm². Dividing by D and using its controlled variation proves that the two lists F(δ+iγ), F(−δ+iγ) differ from the common list F(iγ) in relative norm O(exp(Cm³/Y)−1+m/Y). For c small, the scalar product of the two lists has real part ≥half the reference squared norm, by Cauchy–Schwarz. The argument includes multiplicities and also applies to negative heights by reflecting the coordinate. The reference cannot be zero on a cell for nonzero p, by the lower sampling inequality. Summing proves the first claim.

Fixed rate. On γ>H use at once t=H/γ∈(0,1], τ=H/(γ−iδ), |τ−t|≤t²/H. Then F(δ+iγ) is a constant times (t/H)(τ/t)p(τ)/(1+iuτ/H)^m, deg p<m. In the case considered the denominator and τ/t are 1+O_u(m/H) uniformly. For the samples with weight t² one has
    Σ_{γ>H} t_γ² |Q(t_γ)|² ≍ H log H ||Q||₂²
if m²≤cH. Indeed the main integral is H/(2π)∫ log(H/(2πt))|Q|²dt. Its lower bound is immediate; for the upper one separate t<1/H and use ||Q||∞²≤m²||Q||² there. The Stieltjes error is bounded by C log H·m²||Q||² using t²log(H/t)≪log H and t log(H/t)≪log H in the integral of the derivative of t²|Q|². The boundary at zero disappears. Taylor with step ≤1/H gives relative error O_u(exp(Cm²/H)−1+m/H) with respect to the same samples of the polynomial p, with the common factor t/H. With c small one concludes as before. The floors obtained are relative to the evaluations of the reference on the tail; they are not absolute margins uniform in all power coefficients. The results do not allow arbitrary m for fixed H.

### Explicit full block: up to 10 000 arbitrary powers a>1

Strict positivity of POWER_CONE_001 is obtained for any list of up to 10 000 distinct real exponents >1 and any nonzero combination. One uses the rigorous published verification of Platt–Trudgian up to H=3·10¹² (https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.09765) and the explicit count of Bellotti–Wong, v2 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.15470). The improvement over the cell argument is to approximate the inverse of the denominator with RELATIVE error on a whole dyadic band. The result is not inferred from a numerical diagonalization.

On Y<γ≤2Y, Y≥H, use t=(γ−Y)/Y. Evaluation at δ+iγ changes t into τ=t−iδ/Y, with |τ−t|≤1/(2Y). Up to a nonzero constant the rational transform of the previous entry is p(t)/D(t), deg p<m, with D(1/2)=1; all roots of D lie at distance at least 3/2 from 1/2, since their real part is −1. For |t−1/2|≤1 one has |1/D(t)|≤3^m, factor by factor. Let S be the Taylor polynomial of 1/D up to degree 4m+12 and Q=pS. For |t−1/2|≤0.51, Cauchy gives
    |1−D(t)S(t)| ≤ (1+0.51/1.5)^m 3^m 0.51^(4m+13)/0.49 < 0.001.
This relative bound includes all relevant t and τ and does not depend on the coefficients nor on the closeness between poles. In particular p/D and Q differ by ≤0.0011|Q| there. It suffices to work with polynomials of degree ≤K=50012.

For every polynomial q of degree ≤K, let V(q) be the list q(t_γ) of the band counting multiplicities. Then
    0.1 Y log Y ||q||₂² ≤ ||V(q)||² ≤ 0.25 Y log Y ||q||₂²
with the continuous norm on [0,1]. Indeed on [Y,2Y] the count differs from the main function T log(T/(2πe))/(2π) by ≤log(2Y) by Bellotti–Wong, since 0.10076 log T+0.24460 log log T+8.08344≤log T for T≥H. The main density relative to Y log Y lies between 0.14 and 0.18. The absolute relative error in the Stieltjes integral is ≤6(K+1)² log(2Y)/(Y log Y) times ||q||₂², including both endpoints. Here ||q||∞≤(K+1)||q||₂, ||q′||₂≤2(K+1)²||q||₂ by Legendre, and ∫|(|q|²)′|≤2||q||||q′||. The error factor is <0.006 on Y≥H. The intervals are half-open as in the previous proof.

For variable shifts |τ_γ−t_γ|≤1/(2Y), the exact polynomial Taylor expansion and the upper sample bound for each q^(j) give
    ||(Q(τ_γ))−V(Q)||/||V(Q)|| ≤ √(0.25/0.1) [exp((K+1)²/Y)−1] < 0.002.
p is assumed nonzero, so V(Q) is not zero by the floor. Restoring the rational increases the discrepancy with V(Q) to less than 0.004 in relative norm. This holds both at the zeros and at their reflections −δ+iγ. By Cauchy–Schwarz the real part of the scalar product of both lists is at least (1−2·0.004−0.004²)||V(Q)||²>0 (restore the common normalization constant if applicable). For negative heights the same proof is used reversing the sign of i. Thus the entire tail is strictly positive on the whole block; the heights up to H add squares. The convergence of the sum and the identification with the full form were justified in the previous entry. For repeated powers the coefficients are combined before asserting strict positivity. The number 10 000 leaves slack and is not optimal. The same computation, keeping (5m+13)²/Y small, also improves the general order of the dimension bound to c√H uniformly in the rates.

### Arbitrary number of powers with up to 9999 sign changes

Order the distinct exponents, combine repetitions and omit zero coefficients. If the real coefficients change sign k≤9999 times, the full form is strictly positive on the nonzero combination, independently of the number m of powers. The positive diagonal change of coordinates preserves signs. Write F(z)=Σ d_i/(u_i−z), with u_i increasing. On each interval between two consecutive poles whose coefficients have the same sign, F tends to infinities of opposite sign at the interior endpoints. Choose a zero v_i in that interval. There are m−1−k intervals of this type. Define I as the disjoint union of [u_i,v_i] and A(z)=∏(v_i−z)/(u_i−z). By cancellation F=A R with R having numerator of degree ≤k and denominator formed by the k+1 remaining poles. It does not matter where the remaining zeros are.

For Im z≠0 one has A(z)=exp(∫_I dx/(x−z)). Thus |(log A)'(z)|≤π/|Im z|. On the line, −d log|A(iγ)|/dγ is the integral over I of 2xγ/(x²+γ²)², between zero and the integral over the whole positive half-axis, equal to 1/γ for γ>0. On each band (Y,2Y] the max/min ratio of |A(iγ)| is therefore ≤2. For |δ|≤1/2, |A(±δ+iγ)/A(iγ)−1|≤exp(π/(2Y))−1=:η.

Apply the previous block to R and call V its common normalized reference with the constant of the rational restored. Each list of R at the two shifts differs from V in norm by ≤0.004||V||. For F use W_γ=A(iγ)V_γ. By the max/min ratio, both lists of F differ from W in norm by ≤[2(1+η)0.004+η]||W||<0.01||W||. The real part of the scalar product is ≥(1−2·0.01−0.01²)||W||²>0. Conjugation covers negative heights and the zeros of the verified prefix contribute squares. Thus any finite real witness of negativity requires at least 10000 alternations between ordered coefficients. The class of inputs covered is not a subspace and the theorem gives no upper bound for the alternations of a possible witness.

### Global reduction to strict alternation with almost equal amplitudes

Fix any 0<ε<1. It suffices to prove semidefiniteness for alternating residues of modulus in [1−ε,1+ε], in lists of even length. One can even impose that the distance within each pair be smaller than any prescribed positive bound. Proof: by homogeneity normalize any finite real list d_i so that |d_i|≤2ε. Replace each pole u_i by u_i,u_i+h with residues 1+d_i/2 and −1+d_i/2. Choose h positive smaller than all original separations. The ordered list alternates strictly and in the coalescence limit the two residues add up exactly to d_i. The form converges by entrywise continuity of the real Pick kernel on u,v>1/2, even on the diagonal (the denominator u+v is positive). Positive diagonal congruence allows the proof to be formulated in residues. A negative form remains negative for all sufficiently small h by continuity. The converse by restriction and the bridge theorem give equivalence with the global target. For each fixed ε the normalization is nonzero on every nonzero witness; one cannot fix ε=0 in this argument. The same reasoning allows the two residues of each pair to be multiples of a common step by prior rational approximation if one only seeks to detect strict negativity.

Operational consequence: neither strict alternation nor an arbitrarily small relative contrast between amplitudes simplifies the universal problem by itself. The information surviving the collapse of pairs lies in the small signed imbalances. This density argument does not extend the proved sign to new inputs.

### Positivity per zero for residues with one-signed partial sums

Let u_i>1/2 be ordered and S(x)=Σ_{u_i≤x} d_i. If S≥0 for all x (or S≤0 by global inversion) and the real list is nonzero, each spectral summand of the POWER form has strictly positive real part. This includes alternation of exactly constant amplitude and allows nonzero partial sums after the last pole. By integrating each step, F(z)=∫ S(x)/(x−z)² dx. Let γ>0 and δ=|Re ρ−1/2|. For −δ≤s≤δ put y=x−s and J_s(x)=2yγ/(y²+γ²)², the imaginary part of the kernel. It is positive on the support of S. If δ=0 one obtains directly |F(iγ)|²>0.

For γ>H=3·10¹² use the zero-free region of Mossinghoff–Trudgian–Yang and symmetry to have r=1/2−δ≥1/(6 log γ) (https://doi.org/10.1007/s40993-023-00498-y). For any two positions of the segment, the corresponding y differ by ≤1 and are ≥r. Their ratios are ≤1+1/r. Moreover the derivative of log((y²+γ²)²) in y is bounded by 2/γ. Hence J_s≤B J_t for any s,t of the segment, B=(1+6 log γ)exp(2/γ). By differentiation,
    |∂_s Re (x−s−iγ)^(−2)|/J_s = |y²−3γ²|/[γ(y²+γ²)] ≤ 3/γ.
Write F(±δ+iγ)=a_±+ib_±. Integrating the inequality in s and in S(x)dx, |a_+−a_-|≤(3B/γ) min(b_+,b_-). Since a_+a_-≥−(a_+−a_-)²/4, the real part of the reflected product is ≥[1−(3B/(2γ))²] b_+b_->0; log(γ)/γ decreases and the factor 3B/(2γ) is <10^(-8) for γ≥H. On the verified prefix δ=0; for negative heights use conjugation. Convergence is that of the original rational. Consequently a real witness of negativity requires that its ordered partial sums take both signs, in addition to the previous bound on the alternations of the residues. The result does not extend by continuity to every small imbalance independent of the separation between poles, by the previous reduction.

### An arbitrary crossing of the partial sums: sign per zero

If S changes sign only once at c, invert the sign globally so that S(x)(c−x)≥0. For G(z)=(c−z)²F(z) the integrand with respect to S(x)dx is K=((c−z)/(x−z))². At z=s+iγ, |s|≤δ, we write C=c−s, X=x−s. Then
    Im K = 2(c−x)γ(CX+γ²)/(X²+γ²)².
The integral has strictly positive imaginary part even when passing through the crossing. For γ>H one has r=1/2−δ≥1/(6 log γ). The ratio between the moduli of Im K at two positions of the segment (x≠c) is ≤B=(1+6 log γ)² exp(2/γ): C and X change by factors ≤1+1/r, and the denominator is compared as in the previous lemma. For the derivative of the real part, ∂_s K=2(c−x)(c−z)/(x−z)^3. Consequently
    |∂_s Re K|/|Im K| = |CX(X²−3γ²)+γ²(3X²−γ²)|/[γ(X²+γ²)(CX+γ²)] ≤3/γ.
At x=c the derivative is zero. The integrals also converge for S constant on the tail. Let G_±=a_±+ib_± be the reflected evaluations. One obtains b_+/b_- between 1/B and B and |a_+−a_-|≤(3B/γ)min(b_+,b_-). Replace a_+ by a_- in G_+: the normalized real scalar product of (a_-,b_+) and (a_-,b_-) is ≥1/B, since one is obtained from the other through a positive diagonal of condition ≤B (divide the spectral floor by the ceiling). Restoring a_+, the unit vector changes in norm by ≤6B/γ, by the triangle inequality for normalization and the lower bound b_+ for both norms. Going back from G to F the additional difference of arguments has modulus ≤2/γ, by integrating the derivative of the argument of (c−s−iγ)². Thus the cosine of the final angle is ≥1/B−(6B+2)/γ>0. Indeed B≤40(log γ)² for γ≥H, and 8·40²(log γ)^4/γ<1 already at H and decreases. For verified heights δ=0 and G has positive imaginary part. Conjugation covers negative heights.

The number of poles, the separation, the location c and the magnitudes of S are not restricted. Combined with the sign without crossings, every negative witness requires at least two sign changes of the partial sums, omitting zeros. Multiplying by a second quadratic factor does not automatically preserve the argument: the sign of the imaginary part of the product also depends on the real parts.

The one-crossing threshold is optimal for the per-zero argument. At any height γ≥H take F(z)=(z²+γ²)/∏_{j=1}^4(j−z). The residues in the previous convention are (1+γ²)/6, −(4+γ²)/2, (9+γ²)/2, −(16+γ²)/6; their partial sums have signs +,−,+,0. For any 0<δ≤1/2, the product of the reflected numerators is (δ²+2iδγ)² (with conjugation of the second), whose argument is within δ/γ of π. The difference of arguments of the denominators is ≤8δ/γ by integrating in s for the four factors. The reflected product therefore has strictly negative real part. It is an algebraic falsifier at any hypothetical exterior height, not the existence of an exterior zero. The total form of this same vector is strictly positive by the four-pole theorem. Already with two crossings compensation between heights is indispensable for an argument admitting exterior zeros.

### Per-band compensation for any fixed number of accumulated crossings

For each fixed integer k there is a finite Y_k such that the real contribution of every band Y<γ≤2Y, Y≥Y_k, is strictly positive simultaneously for all nonzero real lists whose S has at most k sign changes. The poles and their number are arbitrary. The mechanism is an interpolation bound in the pole variable that admits two or more crossings and compensates between heights.

Rescale w=Y/(x+Y) and transport S(x)dx/(x+Y)² to a finite real measure ν on [0,1]. Then F(YZ)=∫[1−(1+Z)w]^(−2)dν(w). Let m_j=∫w^j dν and P the monic product of the factors w−t at the ℓ≤k change points, one per crossing (a null stretch allows choosing any interior point). Since Pν has fixed sign, ∫|P|d|ν|=|∫P dν|. This is positive for a nonzero test, since the measure has a density and is not concentrated at the nodes. Normalize max_{0≤j≤k}|m_j|=1. Now ∫|P|d|ν|≤2^ℓ. For a smooth function f on [0,1], its Newton interpolant of degree <ℓ at the nodes has Newton coefficients bounded by ||f^(j)||∞/j! (integral formula for divided differences, also for complex f); the absolute sum of monomial coefficients of the product of j factors is ≤2^j. The pointwise remainder is ≤|P| ||f^(ℓ)||∞/ℓ!. Hence |∫f dν|≤Σ_{j=0}^ℓ 2^j ||f^(j)||∞/j!. For ℓ=0 this is the total variation bound. The control is uniform even if the positions of the crossings come together.

The normalized transforms form a locally bounded family of holomorphic functions on the plane slit along [0,∞): apply the preceding inequality to the kernel, whose w-derivatives are uniformly bounded on each compact subset of that domain. Their derivatives of order j at Z=−1 are (j+1)! m_j. No locally uniform limit can be identically zero, because the maximum of the moduli of those normalized derivatives for j≤k equals 1. By Montel and the identity theorem there is c_k>0 such that ∫_1^2 |F(iYt)|²dt≥c_k in the chosen normalization. The interior Cauchy bounds give a uniform bound M_k for the function and its first derivative in Z, on a fixed neighbourhood of the segment i[1,2].

Apply the zero count of the 10000-block entry to the function |F(iYt)|². The main integral is ≥c'_k Y log Y and the error by parts is O_k(log Y), including the endpoints. Shifting each point Z=it to Z=it±δ/Y changes each reflected product relative to the reference square by O_k(1/Y); summing O(Y log Y) zeros the change is O_k(log Y). For Y sufficiently large the main integral dominates. Rescaling restores the sign. The proof does not give Y_2≤3·10¹² nor uniformity in k. Hence it does not yet certify the full form with two crossings; it does prove that for each fixed k every negative per-band contribution is confined to heights bounded in terms of k alone.

### Up to eight accumulated crossings: explicit threshold H=3·10¹²

Use the previous normalization of the first k+1 moments with k≤8 and write f(Z)=F(YZ) normalized. The map h=(√(−Z)−1)/(√(−Z)+1), with the root of positive real part, takes the slit domain to the disc. On |h|≤0.9, p=√(−Z) has |p|≤19 and Re p≥1/19. For x≥0, b=(x+1)/|x+p²|≤600000: if x≤1500, both factors |p±i√x| are ≥1/19; otherwise use |x+p²|≥x−361. This bounds the inverse of the denominator |1−(1+Z)w| for w∈[0,1]. The previous Newton bound applied to the kernel gives |f|≤Σ_{j≤8}(j+1)b_max²(2·362·b_max)^j<10^84, with b_max=600000. On the other hand the maximum of |f| on |Z+1|≤0.05 is ≥0.05^8 by Cauchy and the normalization of the moments. There |h|=|Z+1|/|1+p|²<0.03 since Re p≥√0.95.

Take 500 equispaced nodes Z_j on i[1,2], including the endpoints. Their images h_j satisfy |h_j|≤0.5 (substitute p=(1−i)√(t/2), 1≤t≤2). They are at mutual distance at least 1/(48·500) because |dZ/dh|≤48 on the convex disc |h|≤0.5. If all |f(Z_j)| were ≤exp(−6100), their Lagrange interpolant L in h would have norm ≤exp(−6100)·500·(1.4·48·500)^499<exp(−100) on |h|≤0.9. The difference f−L vanishes at the 500 nodes. Divide by the 500 Blaschke factors of the disc of radius 0.9 and apply the maximum principle: on |h|≤0.03 each factor has modulus ≤0.9·0.53/(0.81−0.015)<0.61. On that disc |f|≤exp(−100)+(10^84+1)0.61^500<0.05^8, a contradiction.

Now approximate f by its Taylor polynomial Q of degree 12000 at 1.5i. On |Z−1.5i|≤1 again |f|≤10^84: |Z|≤2.5, Im Z≥0.5, and (x+1)/|x−Z|≤12 separating x≤5 and x>5. By Cauchy the error on |Z−1.5i|≤0.51 is ≤10^84·0.51^12001/0.49<exp(−7800). Consequently the maximum of Q on the segment exceeds exp(−6100)/2. Its L² norm on that segment is ≥exp(−6100)/(2·12001) by the Legendre inequality of the 10000-block. Use the sampling of that entry on Y≥H: ||V(Q)||≥√(0.1Y log Y)||Q||₂ and the number of points is ≤0.25Y log Y by the same lemma for constants. At each shifted evaluation, the absolute Taylor error therefore costs less than 0.001||V(Q)|| in list norm. The shift of Q itself costs less than 0.002||V(Q)|| by the previous polynomial lemma. The two lists of f have scalar product with positive real part on every band by the relative bound 0.003 with respect to the same reference. Add the verified heights, which contribute squares. This proves strict positivity of the full form for up to eight accumulated crossings and any number of poles. It allows negative individual contributions already with two crossings.

### Negative band: exponential cancellation of moments even with unbounded crossings

Let Y≥H and K=⌊√Y/40⌋≥43301. Keep the compactified measure ν and the moments m_j of the previous entry. If the real contribution of the band is ≤0 for a nonzero test, then
    max_{0≤j≤K/250}|m_j| < exp(−0.01K) ||ν||_TV.
Moreover such a band requires more than K/1300 accumulated crossings. In particular, the full sign is obtained for up to 33 crossings, with no limit on the poles.

Common proof. Use alternatively ||ν||_TV=1, or the normalization max_{j≤k}|m_j|=1 when k≤K/1300. On the disc |h|≤0.9 and on the disc |Z−1.5i|≤1 the bound M=exp(28+22k) holds in the second normalization: in the Newton sum bound Σ(j+1)A^j≤(k+1)²A^k, A=2·362·600000, and (k+1)²≤4^k. In the first, M=exp(28) suffices, by total variation. In both cases M≤exp(0.018K). The Taylor polynomial Q at 1.5i of degree K has error E≤M·0.51^(K+1)/0.49<exp(−0.65K) on the disc of radius 0.51.

If the supremum of the transform on i[1,2] exceeded exp(−K/2), one would have ||Q||₂≥exp(−K/2)/(2(K+1)). The same polynomial sampling inequalities keep the constants 0.1 and 0.25 since (K+1)²/Y<0.000627 on Y≥H (Stieltjes error <0.004). The relative shift error is <0.002 by Taylor and the relative discrete approximation error is bounded by √2.5 E/||Q||₂<0.001. As before this forces strict positivity. Hence a nonpositive band implies sup≤exp(−K/2).

Put n=⌊K/20⌋ and interpolate at n+1 equispaced nodes as before. The distance between nodes j,l in h is ≥|j−l|/(48n). On |h|≤0.9, the sum of moduli of the Lagrange basis is ≤(1.4·48n)^n 2^n/n!≤(134.4e)^n<exp(6n). Thus ||L||≤exp(−0.2K). On |Z+1|≤0.05, dividing f−L by Blaschke gives
    |f| ≤ exp(−0.2K)+(M+1)0.61^(n+1).
With total variation one the right-hand side is <exp(−0.023K), since K≥43301. By Cauchy, |m_j|≤20^j exp(−0.023K)/(j+1), less than exp(−0.01K) for j≤K/250. With normalized moments and k≤K/1300 the right-hand side is <exp(−0.006K), while Cauchy and the normalization require sup≥0.05^k≥exp(−0.003K). This contradiction proves the second statement. The first condition applies even if the number of crossings is arbitrary. A strongly oscillating measure can cancel its first moments; it is not proved that the necessary cancellation is impossible.

### The moments on any finite list of bands can vanish while preserving negativity

Antecedent: rational inner factors are used at the beginning of this same memo for causal projection. Here the application is to decide whether the multiscale cancellations of the previous entry are incompatible with a negative witness. For real poles and real residues the contribution is evaluated through F(z)F(−z). Given any finite list Y_l>1/2 of distinct scales and integers n_l≥1, multiply F by B(z)=∏[(z+Y_l)/(z−Y_l)]^{n_l}. Since B(z)B(−z)=1, EACH reflected term is preserved exactly, and F B vanishes to order ≥n_l at −Y_l. For the measure ν_l compactified at that scale, m_j=Y_l^j F^(j)(−Y_l)/(j+1)! (use the unnormalized transform); hence this imposes all the prescribed moments, from j=0 to n_l−1.

To return to simple poles the numerator is kept and the repeated poles of the denominator are separated into distinct real poles >1/2 tending to the initial ones, avoiding all other poles. The prescribed zeros remain exact. At every spectral point the products converge, and uniformly over sufficiently small perturbations the transforms are O_F,B(1/(1+|γ|)) by degree and compactness of the pole configurations, first for large height and then at the finitely many remaining points. The series of products converges dominatedly. Thus, if there was strict global negativity (or on some finite list of bands), it persists for simple poles and exactly vanishing moments at all chosen scales. Therefore no global contradiction can rest solely on the impossibility of realizing a finite number of such cancellations. This conditional result does not construct a negative witness for ζ.

### Alternative normal form at fixed poles

Related to the reduction to real roots of the entry on the translated block. For F=N/D with N,D real, the spectral product depends linearly on the polynomial A(y)=N(z)N(−z), y=−z², with fixed denominator D(z)D(−z). A is nonnegative on y≥0. It is decomposed explicitly as a sum with positive coefficients of terms y^e∏(y−r_i)² with r_i≥0: the positive real roots have even multiplicity; each negative root contributes y+|r|; a nonreal pair a±ib contributes (y−a)²+b² if a≥0 and y²+2|a|y+a²+b² if a<0. Expand these factors, keeping the permitted squares unexpanded. The leading coefficient is positive. Each term of the sum equals exactly the spectral product of a numerator z^e∏(z²+r_i), of degree ≤deg N, with the same D (absorb the coefficient by a square root). This reduces any negative witness to one with all numerator zeros on the imaginary axis, without altering the poles or increasing the degree. At the positive poles these numerators have a single sign, so the residues alternate strictly on the original list of simple poles. Unlike the previous reduction by coalescing pairs, no additional poles are introduced. Neither the factorization nor the phase identity decides the sign of the functional on these normal forms.

### Compensation of poles and roots distributed over scales, without degree bound

Let F(z)=(v−z)^(-1)∏_j (z²+t_j²)/[(u_j−z)(w_j−z)], with distinct real poles >1/2, t_j>0 and u_j,w_j in [t_j,2t_j]. Assume at most L=100 centres t_j in each [b,2b), for all b>0. The full form is strictly positive, with no restriction on how many octaves are occupied. This geometric condition admits alternations of the residues at all poles. The lacunary comparators of 212-84 act in a circuit basis; here one uses the cancellation of the degree of each quotient in the logarithmic derivative.

On a band Y≥H rescale all positions by Y and write Z=z/Y. On |Z−1.5i|≤1 separate the rescaled centres t into low (<1/8), middle ([1/8,8)) and high (≥8). For the low ones, the logarithmic derivative of each quotient is a signed sum of four 1/(Z−a); subtracting 1/Z from each term preserves the sum because there are two roots and two poles. Its modulus is ≤48t since |Z|≥1/2, |a|≤2t and |Z−a|≥1/4. The low t sum to ≤L/4 by dyadic intervals. For the high ones, the logarithmic derivative has modulus ≤4/(t−2.5)≤6/t and the sum of 1/t is ≤L/4. There are ≤6L middle centres. Extract from them only their numerators, forming a polynomial P of degree d≤12L. The two poles of each middle factor cost ≤4 in logarithmic derivative and the extra pole costs ≤2 by vertical distance. Thus for f(Z)=F(YZ)=A(Z)P(Z), the factor A is holomorphic without zeros on the disc and |A'/A|≤38L+2=:D. Normalize |A(1.5i)|=1 by a scalar; on the whole disc e^(−D)≤|A|≤e^D.

Let U=max_{1≤t≤2}|f(it)|>0. Then max_segment |P|≤e^D U. Interpolating P at d+1 equispaced nodes of the segment, the sum of moduli of the basis on the disc is ≤(1.5d)^d 2^d/d!≤(3e)^d (for d=0 it is 1). Thus max_disc |f|≤e^(2D)(3e)^d U≤exp(102L+4)U. The Taylor polynomial of f up to degree 50000 at 1.5i has error ≤exp(102L+4) U·0.51^50001/0.49<exp(−20000)U on the disc of radius 0.51. Its continuous norm on the segment is ≥U/(2·50001) by Legendre. Apply the sampling and shift of the 10000-pole entry to the polynomial; the absolute approximation error costs <0.001 in relative norm of the reference by the point count. The reflected product on every band has strictly positive real part. The verified prefix adds squares. The pairing and the local density are sufficient hypotheses; the previous normal form does not guarantee them for an arbitrary witness.

### Arbitrary concentration in one octave: cubic cost for the low factors

In the normal form write N(z)=z^e∏_{j=1}^n(z²+t_j²), D(z)=∏_{l=1}^m(u_l−z), and d=m−e−2n≥1. For γ≥H with t_j≤γ/2 for all j, a sufficient condition for strict sign at that height is
    max{ 2d/γ, (4Σ_j t_j² + 2Σ_l min(u_l²,γ²))/γ³ } < π/2.
Neither pairing nor separation of the factors is required. If it holds at H and all t_j≤H/2, it holds above by monotonicity of each term (including min(u²,γ²)/γ³). Consequently the full form is strictly positive. If some poles exceed H the cost of each saturates at 2/H, without magnitude restriction.

Proof. Write y=−(δ+iγ)²=a+ib; a=γ²−δ²≥0.99γ² and |b|≤γ. By conjugation take b≥0. The exact reflected product is W=y^e∏(y−t_j²)²/∏(y+u_l²). With θ=arg y, a continuous argument of W is −dθ+E, where E=2Σ(arg(y−t_j²)−θ)+Σ(θ−arg(y+u_l²))≥0. Since θ≤2/γ, the first term has modulus ≤2d/γ. By the contraction of arctan, each root difference is bounded by bt_j²/[a(a−t_j²)]≤2t_j²/γ³. The pole difference is ≤min(θ,bu_l²/[a(a+u_l²)])≤2min(u_l²,γ²)/γ³. The two terms of −dθ+E have opposite signs, so the indicated maximum suffices. On the verified prefix squares are added. The criterion measures the phase of the full product; applying absolute values separately to the derivatives of F would lose the cancellation of the first-order terms in u_l.

For example, for odd m ≤10^36, e=0, n=(m−1)/2 and ALL t_j and u_l in [1,2], the second quantity is ≤16m/H³<0.60 and the first is 2/H. Repetitions among the centres and distinct poles as close as desired are allowed. These are combinations with residues determined by the numerator; it is not semidefiniteness for all numerators of the block. At this scale the difficulty cannot be attributed merely to the accumulation of many factors in one octave: what matters is their position relative to the spectral heights and the degree deficit.

### Radial count without pairing, for arbitrary real numerators

Let F=N/D be strictly proper, with N real nonzero, and D with distinct positive poles >1/2. On each band Y≥H form the list of ALL zeros and poles divided by Y, with multiplicities, and split it by modulus into low (<1/8), middle ([1/8,8)) and high (≥8). Let Δ be the number of low roots minus that of low poles, p the number of middle poles and d that of middle roots. Put
    D_Y=2|Δ|+6Σ_low |a|+2p+2Σ_high 1/|a|,   K=⌊√Y/40⌋.
If 2D_Y+d log(3e)≤K/2, the band has strictly positive contribution. It suffices to check this at Y=H·2^j to conclude the full sign. No normal form is imposed on the numerator nor any correspondence between the factors.

On the disc |Z−1.5i|≤1 take out the polynomial of all middle roots. The remainder A has neither zeros nor poles on the disc. In its logarithmic derivative the low terms contribute Δ/Z plus errors ≤|a|/(|Z||Z−a|)≤6|a| each; this includes roots at zero. The high ones cost ≤2/|a| and each middle pole ≤2. Thus |A'/A|≤D_Y. The same interpolation argument of the scales entry bounds the maximum of the rational on the disc by exp(2D_Y)(3e)^d times its maximum U on the segment. Taylor at the centre up to K has error ≤U exp(K/2)0.51^(K+1)/0.49. On the disc of radius 0.51 this is less than 0.0001 U/(K+1) already for K≥43301 (and the quotient decreases). By Legendre the polynomial has continuous norm ≥U/(2(K+1)); the sampling and shift for that K were justified in the entry 'Negative band'. The sign follows by common reference.

Example of a global condition: at most L=400 nonzero roots and poles IN TOTAL in each octave [b,2b), and absolute accumulated discrepancy ≤400 between counts of roots and poles of modulus <r for all r>0 (including zero). Then Σ_low|a|≤L/4, Σ_high1/|a|≤L/4 and p+d≤6L. Hence 2D_Y+d log(3e)≤4·400+4L+max(4,log(3e))·6L=12800<K/2. The family includes for example pairs of roots ±iR followed by poles at R²,2R², repeating at successive scales R larger than 10R² of the previous one, plus an initial pole at 1, initial R >10. The scale ratio between each root and the nearest pole in multiplicative scale can be made arbitrarily large by choosing the sequence sufficiently spaced. The per-band hypothesis is more flexible than these two global bounds; the criterion is only sufficient.

### Full blocks of arbitrary dimension on geometrically separated rates

For each q>1 there is U(q) such that the full form is strictly positive for ALL coefficients, real or complex, when the rates u_j=a_j−1/2 satisfy u_1≥U(q) and u_{j+1}≥q u_j. The floor after normalizing the diagonal depends only on q, even if the block length tends to infinity. It is a statement about entire linear subspaces. POWER_FIXED_BLOCK_ASSEMBLY_OBSTRUCTION §4 treats the obstruction by node confluence to diagonal dominance; here the relative separation is fixed and the inverse of the reference Cauchy matrix is used.

By POWER_CONE_001, put l(u)=L(u+1/2)>0. After normalizing the diagonal, the exact kernel is C_ij cosh((log l(u_i)−log l(u_j))/2), with C_ij=2√(u_i u_j)/(u_i+u_j). Let h=log q. By explicit Cauchy inversion, |(C^−1)_ij|=C_ij p_i p_j, p_i=∏_{r≠i}(u_i+u_r)/|u_i−u_r|. Each p_i≤P_h=∏_{r≥1}coth(rh/2)^2<∞ by exponential decay. Moreover the rows of C sum to at most S_h=1+4Σ_{r≥1}exp(−rh/2). The matrix C is the Gram matrix of normalized exponentials in L²(0,∞); the row control of the inverse gives λ_min(C)≥b_h=1/(P_h² S_h)>0 for every length.
