For smooth tests H on fixed support translated to R→∞, the linear Weil form, or its distributional identity on t>0 (193), gives ∫H(t−R)dμ(t)=−Σ_z m_z exp(zR)∫H(y)exp(zy)dy + O_H(exp(−R/2)). The remainder is the trivial archimedean kernel and the polar term decaying away from the origin. The zeros with Re z<σ cost O(exp(σR)) by two integrations by parts and unit count. The two points w and its conjugate jointly contribute to the oscillating real test the number −m_w Re(exp(iα+wR)Q(w)); choose α according to R to make it positive with modulus m_w exp(bR)|Q(w)|. Hence the two integrals have opposite signs and magnitude ≫exp(bR).

Interpolate H_±(t−R) linearly at the nodes rh of the table, with R=C log L. The tent coefficients are nonnegative values with sum O(1/h). The error has L¹ norm O(h²), and its distributional second derivative has total variation O(1), since the slope differences of the interpolant sum in modulus to at most a constant times the L¹ norm of H''. These bounds and those of the first derivative give, at each zero, a transform error ≤C exp((Re z)R) min(h²,(1+|Im z|)^−2). Interpolating the two majorants gives C exp(ΔR)√h/(1+|Im z|)^(3/2), summable. The explicit formula extends to the interpolation by mollification and domination with this regularity (for each fixed L). The total error is o(exp(bR)) by the choice of b. In each of the two sums with nonnegative coefficients some tent contributes, in the desired direction, a discrepancy ≫h exp(bR)=L^(Cb−1) up to a constant factor. Removing O(1) for powers and absorbing constants gives the statement.

### How many cells and which prime intervals would have to fail

Assume Δ>0 and fix C>3, 0<p<CΔ−1. On the band of centres C log L+O(1) of 4044 there are, for each ε>0 and dyadic L sufficiently large, at least L^{d−ε} cells with prime discrepancy >L^p and at least L^{d−ε} with discrepancy <−L^p, where
    d=1−3(1/2−Δ)/(3/2−Δ)=2Δ/(3/2−Δ)>0.
A fixed proportion of those cells with disjoint interiors can be chosen, separately for each sign. If Δ=1/2 the exponent is one, without requiring the supremum to be attained.

The individual bound complementing the signed average of 4044 uses the density count, not the mere count of all zeros. In the centred variable put q(v)=3(1/2−v)/(3/2−v). By Ingham's density theorem used in 2244, for 0<v<1/2 the number up to height U with abscissa ≥v is O_{v,δ}((2+U)^{q(v)+δ}) for all δ>0. For v=0 use the total count. The moment of a tent centred at t is exp(zt)h [sinh(zh/2)/(zh/2)]², bounded in modulus by C exp((Re z)t)h min(1,(L/|Im z|)²). The sum of the last minimum over the zeros of abscissa ≥v is O(L^{q(v)+δ}) by dyadic bands, taking δ small. For Re z≤0, O(L log L) suffices. Divide [0,Δ] into finitely many mesh pieces ≤η and use the density at the left endpoint and the exponential factor at the right one. Since Cv+q(v) is increasing for C>3 (|q'|≤3), choosing η and δ sufficiently small one gets, on every fixed band around C log L,
    max |prime discrepancy| ≤ O_ε(L^{CΔ−1+q(Δ)+ε}).
Here the linear explicit formula of 4044 and the O(1) bound for the removed powers are used. The endpoint Δ=1/2 is handled with the last piece from the left.

Fix σ between 0 and Δ in the previous construction. The support of the annihilator g is fixed; dividing by each chosen zero keeps the support within the same interval, so the same bandwidth D can be chosen for all targets b close to Δ. The height of the majorants and the constants may depend on b. The values of H_± used as coefficients are individually bounded. By 4044, before dividing by the sum of weights, each sign contributes mass ≫_b L^{Cb}. The correction for composite powers costs O_b(L) in that mass. All cells of modulus ≤L^p contribute jointly O_b(L^{1+p}). Choose b arbitrarily close to Δ with Cb>1+p and C(Δ−b)<1/2. Dividing the remaining mass by the previous individual bound and absorbing constants gives the claimed exponent. Thus a number of cells is controlled, not a uniform positive proportion.

Translation without the triangular weight: write X=L^C. On each selected cell, the nonnegative function w(u)=u^(−1/2)(1−|log u−rh|/h)_+ is unimodal for h≤1 (differentiate on each flank); its maximum is O_D(X^(−1/2)). Its superlevel sets are intervals contained in the cell, of length O_D(X/L). The discrepancy is ∫w(dθ−du), where θ sums log prime. By layers, a discrepancy >L^p forces on some superlevel set (x,y] θ(y)−θ(x)−(y−x) ≫_D √X L^p, and similarly with negative sign. For almost every level the endpoints are not primes. Choosing a class of indices modulo three within the cells of each sign gives disjoint intervals of the same sign with the same counting exponent (adjust ε to absorb constants). Their exact length is not prescribed. Antecedent 2244 treats a different Gaussian average; the zero density is used here in addition to limit cell-by-cell concentration in unsmoothed prime counts.

### Intervals of prescribed additive length and moments of each sign

For any 0<α<1 fix H=X^α and E_H(x)=θ(x+H)−θ(x)−H. If Δ>0, there are constants 0<A<B such that, for EVERY sufficiently large X and for the two signs separately,
    ∫_[AX,BX] (E_H)_± dx/X ≥ H X^{Δ−1/2−o(1)},
    ∫_[AX,BX] (E_H)_±² dx/X ≥ H² X^{2Δ−1−o(1)}.
The intervals have exactly length H in the x coordinate, including those of the same average. For α=1−1/C with C>3 and 0<p<CΔ−1 the count of 4056 is moreover attained, now by disjoint intervals of that length with ±E_H(x)>√X L^p, where L=X^(1/C). X may range over the reals.

Proof. Use the tests H_±(y) of 4044 with R=log X and w(v)=v^(−1/2)H_±(log v); w is nonnegative, smooth with support in a fixed compact subset of (0,∞), with uniform bounds as the phase varies. Put δ=H/X and w_δ(s)=δ^(−1)∫_[s−δ,s] w(v)dv. The exact Fubini identity is
    ∫ w(v)E_H(Xv)dv = δ∫ w_δ(u/X)(dθ(u)−du).
Replacing w by w_δ, the difference of the profile in the variable y is exp(y/2)(w_δ−w)(exp y), of C² norm O_w(δ) and fixed support. By the explicit formula of 4044 and two integrations by parts, its effect before the exterior factor δ is O_w(√X δ X^Δ), with error from composite powers O_w(√X δ): on a fixed band the weighted mass of powers is O(1). For w itself, the main term before the exterior factor is ±c_w √X X^b+O_w(√X(X^σ+1)), with 0<σ<b, according to the choice of the positive test in 4044. Choose b arbitrarily close to Δ with Δ−b<1−α. The perturbation does not cancel the main term. By nonnegativity of the weight and its upper bound uniform in X, the unweighted integral of each part over a common band is ≫_b H X^{b−1/2}. As there, A,B can be kept fixed while b approaches Δ. Cauchy–Schwarz gives the second statement; −o(1) means here the eventual inequality with loss of any power ε>0.

For the additional count take L=X^(1/C). In the fixed band one has uniformly |E_H|≤√X L^{CΔ−1+q(Δ)+ε} up to a constant depending on ε, with q from 4056. Indeed, round the endpoints to half-integers at cost O(log X), apply the truncated explicit formula of 235 at height comparable to X, and subtract. Each zero contributes, in modulus and after dividing by √X, at most a constant times X^{Reρ−1/2} min(1/L,1/(1+|γ|)). The small variation in H due to rounding does not affect the bound; the truncation error is polylogarithmic. For Reρ≤1/2 or the first piece of the partition of 4056 the sum of the weights up to height O(X) costs O(log²X); for every left endpoint v>0 the exponent q(v)<1 makes the dyadic sum above L converge with the loss ε. Removing prime powers costs O(√X log²X), absorbed because CΔ−1>p>0. This justifies the ceiling. The lower mass bound for b close to Δ, discarding the contribution ≤√X L^p, forces a set of starting points of measure ≥X L^{−q(Δ)−ε} for each sign (adjust ε). A maximal family of starting points separated by at least H covers that set with intervals of radius H, so it gives ≥L^{1−q(Δ)−ε} disjoint intervals for each sign after absorbing constants. Joint disjointness between the two families does not follow.

Quantitative implication: a ceiling H X^{o(1)} for the second moment of ONE single part, in the indicated band or in bands covering it with that same ceiling, along a subsequence of X, forces Δ≤(1−α)/2. Analogously a ceiling √H X^{o(1)} for the one-sided first moment suffices. To infer global closure by this path one would need these ceilings for α arbitrarily close to one, with coverage of the required bands. The PNT for almost all intervals of 2454 only controls error relative to the term H and does not provide those ceilings.

### One part of the upper bound for additive lengths

Let x∈[AX,BX] with 0<A<B fixed and 1≤H≤X. In the explicit formula for E_H of 4070, the sum of ALL zero terms with Reρ≤1/2, plus the correction for composite prime powers and the trivial term, has mean square O_{A,B}(H log⁴(2X)) with measure dx/X. It is an unconditional ceiling for that specific contribution. The grouping principle is already in 2460 for multiplicative increments; for additive length one must estimate the shifted endpoints and the low-frequency terms separately.

Put Y=X/H. For |Imρ|≤Y use ((x+H)^ρ−x^ρ)/ρ=∫₀ᴴ(x+s)^{ρ−1}ds. For each s, enlarge (x+s)/X to a fixed compact subset of (0,∞) and majorize with a smooth non-negative cutoff. In the logarithmic coordinate, two integrations by parts bound the cross terms between ordinates γ,γ' by C(1+|γ−γ'|)^(−2) times the sizes of the coefficients. The constant is uniform in the real parts in [0,1]. Grouping by integers and the count O(log(2+Y)) per unit give a bound for the square of the norm by C log(2+Y) times the sum of squared moduli of the coefficients, counting multiplicities. Here each coefficient costs ≤X^(−1/2) and there are O(Y log(2+Y)) points. Minkowski in s gives squared norm ≤CH² X^(−1)Y log²(2+Y).

For U<|γ|≤2U, U≥Y, separate the two endpoints of the increment. On each one the same grouping applies with coefficients of modulus ≤√X/U, so that the squared norm is ≤CX log²(2+U)/U. Summing the norms over U=2^jY costs O(√(X/Y) log(2+Y)); the tails converge in L² and coincide with the series of the explicit formula in the distributional sense. The correction for composite prime powers in any interval (x,x+H] has modulus O((1+H/√X) log²(2X)): for each k≥2 there are O(1+H X^(1/k−1)) integers whose k-th powers fall there, and only O(log X) values of k. This ceiling is O(√H log²(2X)). The trivial-zero term is bounded by the explicit formula away from the origin for large X. This proves the claim. By the Lipschitz property of the positive and negative parts, for the one-sided target of 4070 it suffices to control the same part of the sum of the remaining terms (with the sign of the explicit formula). That control has not been proved in the presence of right zeros.

### The mean-square ceiling includes the right tail above X/√H

Let X≥2, H=X^α, 2/3≤α≤1. In the same fixed interval of 4085 one can additionally include ALL terms with Reρ>1/2 and |Imρ|≥U₀=X/√H. Their mean square is O_{A,B}(H log^8(2X)). The same bound holds for the sum of that tail and the pieces already treated. The arithmetic input used is Ingham's uniform density estimate already employed in 2460, not a hypothesis on the position of the zeros.

In the block U≤|γ|<2U, for either of the two endpoints x,x+H the Gram bound of 4085 gives, with measure dx/X, squared norm at most C log(2U) U^(−2) Σ X^(2Reρ). The band-change factor for the second endpoint is uniform because H≤X. For v=Reρ−1/2>0 decompose X^(2Reρ)=X(1+2 log X ∫₀ᵛ X^(2s)ds). Use N(1/2+s,2U)≪U^{q(s)}log^5(2U), q(s)=3(1/2−s)/(3/2−s), uniformly up to the endpoint (at s=0 the total count suffices). Thus it suffices to bound X^(1+2s) U^(q(s)−2) for all s from 0 to 1/2. Put k=1−α/2≤2/3. For U=U₀=X^k one has
    1+2s+k(q(s)−2)−α = k q(s)−2(1/2−s) ≤ 0,
because 3k≤2(3/2−s). For U=2^j U₀ one gains in addition 2^(−j) since q≤1. Hence the norm of the block is O(√H·2^(−j/2) log³(2U)√log(2X)); summing over j and squaring one even keeps O(H log^7(2X)). The exponent eight of the statement leaves room. The sum is understood in L². The same argument allows selecting any subset of the tail without changing the constants.

Consequence for 4070: it suffices to prove the one-sided ceiling H X^{o(1)} for the FINITE sum of the terms with Reρ>1/2 and |Imρ|<X/√H, with the sign of the explicit formula. The inequality |u_±−v_±|≤|u−v| controls the remainder without presupposing independence. The cutoff grows with X and eventually includes any fixed right zero from some scale on. Therefore the unconditional bound for the tail does not extend the window T nor bound the remaining finite contribution.

### A prescribed additive partition detects both signs without averaging the shift

For H=X^α with 0<α<1, in 4070 one can use only the partition (a+jH,a+(j+1)H], with a arbitrary, even chosen separately for each X. If Δ>0 there is a fixed band [AX,BX] such that on its complete cells, for all sufficiently large X, the discrete average of each part of E_H is ≥H X^{Δ−1/2−o(1)}. Its second moment is ≥H² X^{2Δ−1−o(1)}. The threshold is uniform in a. The count of 4056 for α=1−1/C, C>3 and 0<p<CΔ−1 is preserved, now OVER the cells of that single partition. In particular cells of opposite signs are also disjoint. This refinement did not follow from the count over free starting points nor from an average over translations.

Proof. Put δ=H/X, R=log X and fix the smooth non-negative real weight w of the argument of 4070 for each sign and phase, with norm and support uniform in X. In the variable v=u/X replace it by its value at the center of each cell, giving a weight w_m≥0. It has total variation O_w(1) and ||w_m−w||₁=O_w(δ), including the boundary cells by extension by zero. Enlarge the fixed band to include all cells of nonzero weight. For the proof of the truncated formula move each endpoint in the variable u to the nearest half-integer. Since H≥1, the resulting weight is still an ordered step function; its L¹ distance in v to the original is O_w(1/X) by summing jumps. The change in the integral against dθ−du is O_w(log X), since one only pays the jumps times the mass in a strip of length ≤1 at each endpoint, not the number of cells separately.

For the rounded weight apply, by summation by parts, the truncated formula of 235 at its endpoints, with a common good height T in [X,2X] and cost O_w(log² X) by total variation, initially for ψ. For the smooth weight use the full explicit formula, which can be truncated at the same T with error O_w(1) by repeated integration by parts in the moment. The total cost of removing composite prime powers from both is O_w(√X log² X) in the fixed band. For each zero the error between the two moments in the formula for ψ is
    O_w(X^{Reρ} min(δ,1/(1+|γ|))).
Indeed the integral is X^ρ∫(w_m−w)(v)v^{ρ−1}dv with the rounded weight; the variation bound and the L¹ bound are preserved when multiplying in log v by exp((Reρ)log v) on the fixed compact set. Zeros with Reρ≤1/2+s cost O_w(√X X^s log² X) when summed up to T. For fixed s>0, the sum of the minimum over Reρ>1/2+s is O_{s,ε}(δ^{1−q(s)−ε}), q(s)=3(1/2−s)/(3/2−s), separating |γ|≤1/δ and higher dyadic bands via Ingham; take ε<1−q(s). This summability of the moments of the jump cells makes it possible to fix the partition.

First choose 0<s<Δ, then ε as above and an exterior point at distance b arbitrarily close to Δ, with b>s and Δ−b<(1−α)(1−q(s)−ε). This makes all errors o(√X X^b). By 4044 and the change of variable of the weight w in 4070 the smooth weight gives ±c_w √X X^b in leading magnitude and sign. In the original partition the sum is exactly Σ w_j E_H(a+jH); since w_j≥0 and bounded, each sign has mass ≫_b √X X^b. Divide by O(X/H) cells and apply Cauchy–Schwarz. The bandwidth stays fixed when letting b→Δ as in 4056. If the count is required, discard the threshold √X L^p as in 4070 and divide the mass directly by the per-cell ceiling proved there. The origin of the mesh is not changed in order to pick the two signs.

Thus a one-sided bound of the desired size on ONE partition per X would suffice for the criterion of 4070, always with coverage of the indicated band. That upper bound is not proved.

### Comparison between neighbouring cells without main term

Fix k≥1, 0<α<1 and H=X^α. In the partition of 4103 let P_j=θ(a+(j+1)H)−θ(a+jH) and let D P_j=P_{j+1}−P_j. If Δ>0, in a fixed band of sizes comparable to X the per-cell average of each part (D^k P_j)_± is at least
    (H/X)^k H X^{Δ−1/2−o(1)}.
This holds for all sufficiently large X and any origin a; k stays fixed in the limit. Consequently the ceiling H X^{o(1)} for the second moment of ONE part of D^k P along a subsequence would force Δ≤(k+1/2)(1−α), with the same band coverage as in 4070. The criterion uses only differences of sums of logarithms of primes and is invariant under adding to P_j any polynomial in j of degree <k. For k=1 the price relative to 4103 is a factor H/X in the mean signal.

Proof. Put δ=H/X, v_j the scaled center of the cell, and take the non-negative weight w(v)=v^{k−1/2}H_±(log v) with compact support in (0,∞), with H_± from 4044. The phase of the test will be chosen at the end. The sum Σ w(v_j)D^k P_j is, by discrete summation by parts, the integral against dθ of the step weight whose values are Σ_{l=0}^k (−1)^{k−l} binom(k,l)w(v_j−lδ). Its integral against du is exactly zero: the cells have equal length and the coefficients sum to zero. After dividing by δ^k these values are averages of (−1)^k w^(k) over k independent translations in [0,δ], by the fundamental theorem of calculus. Hence the normalized weight approximates g=(−1)^k w^(k) with error O(δ) in L¹; its total variation is O(1) by the bound on the derivative of the averages and common support. This also holds near the endpoints by smooth extension by zero.

The smooth moment in the formula for ψ is computed exactly by k integrations by parts:
    ∫g(v)v^(ρ−1)dv = [(ρ−1)…(ρ−k)] ∫ H_±(y)exp((ρ−1/2)y)dy.
The zeros of the annihilator are preserved; the polynomial factor does not vanish at the chosen exterior point. Rotate the phase so that the contribution of that point and its conjugate has the desired sign. The contribution of abscissae smaller than 1/2+s for the smooth test costs O_w(X^(1/2+s)), by its vertical decay of arbitrary order. For the step error it suffices to apply the BV and L¹ bounds directly to the normalized weight, without including the polynomial factor in the error. The half-integer, truncation, prime-power and density argument of 4103 gives o(X^(1/2+b)) choosing b close to Δ and s fixed between 0 and b. Hence the ORIGINAL weighted sum has magnitude ≫_b δ^k X^(1/2+b) with each sign according to the chosen weight. Since the original weights are non-negative and bounded and there are O(X/H) cells, the two-sided statement on the parts follows. Dividing the band only by the mesh length does not affect the endpoints: a common band is chosen with margin for the k following cells. For the second moment use Cauchy–Schwarz. The detection mechanism remains that of the positive filter of 4044; the change is the arithmetic observable and the explicit loss due to differencing. The one-sided ceiling for that observable has not been proved.

### Arithmetic upper bound for the divisors up to (XH)^(1/3) in the adjacent difference

Take H integer, √X≤H≤X, and integer starting points n in a fixed band [AX,BX]. In the difference between the sums of Λ over (n+H,n+2H] and (n,n+H], replace Λ(m) by its exact component
    Λ_{≤R}(m)=−Σ_{d|m, d≤R} μ(d) log d.
The second moment of this component, averaged over n, is
    ≪_{A,B} R log⁴(2R) [1+R² log(2R)/X].
With R=⌊(XH)^(1/3)⌋ it is O(H log⁵(2X)), with no hypothesis on zeros or on prime correlations. For H>√X by a power of X, the cutoff exceeds √X by a power. Antecedents: divisor splitting in 164 and 505 for other tests, and the large sieve in 2854. The bound here is for the two contiguous boxes of 4117 with unsmoothed edges and for both signs jointly.

Let e(t)=exp(2πit), A_H(t)=Σ_{H<j≤2H}e(jt)−Σ_{1≤j≤H}e(jt). By exact orthogonality in Z/d, the datum at starting point n equals Σ c_{a/q} e(na/q) over reduced fractions with denominator q≤R, with c_{a/q}=−A_H(a/q)Σ_{q|d≤R}μ(d)log(d)/d. The constant mode vanishes exactly. For q≥2 the arithmetic factor costs ≤C log²(2R)/q. By geometric summation |A_H(t)|≤C/dist(t,ℤ); summing its square over a=1,…,q−1 gives O(q²). Thus Σ|c_{a/q}|²≤C R log⁴(2R). In the Gram matrix of those exponentials over n, the diagonal is O(X) and each cross term costs ≤C/dist(a/q−a'/q',ℤ). Distinct fractions have circular separation ≥1/R²; ordering by distance in both directions, the off-diagonal rows sum to O(R² log(2R)). Schur's inequality and division by the number of starting points give the ceiling. With the chosen R, R≤H and R³/X≤H. No Möbius cancellation has been used to control this range.

By Λ=−(μ log)*1 what remains is exactly the term of divisors d>R. To return to P_j one removes composite prime powers at cost O(√H log²X) per difference as in 4085. By Lipschitz and Minkowski the one-sided bound of the required size for the difference of the tail d>R, averaged over those same starting points, would suffice. The average over all integers controls the average of the partitions of each class modulo H and allows choosing one with good second moment of the full observable if that ceiling for the tail is obtained. With H integer and scales H=⌊X^α⌋ the argument of 4117 is preserved because H/X=X^{α−1}(1+o(1)); the argument does not give a ceiling for each individual origin. In the tail the cofactors m/d are O_{A,B}(X/R); what remains to control is the signed sum over those cofactors.

### Sharpness of the divisor cutoff and pairs of the tail that can be paid in absolute value

Let K_d(n)=⌊(n+2H)/d⌋−2⌊(n+H)/d⌋+⌊n/d⌋. Always |K_d|≤1. The ceiling of 4129 cannot be extended by a power of X if uniformity for arbitrary sublists is required, even keeping the TRUE coefficients −μ(d)log d on the sublist. Fix 1/2<α<1, (1+α)/3<β<α, H=⌊X^α⌋, D=⌊X^β⌋. There is a sublist S⊂[D,2D] such that the mean over n∈[X,2X] of the square of its contribution is ≫D³(log D)²/X, larger than H by a power factor. The list is chosen once for that entire average.

Indeed there are ≫D squarefree integers d∈[D,2D] with {H/d}∈[1/4,1/3]. The real preimage is a union of O(H/D) intervals of total length ≫D by the change y=H/t: on [H/(2D),H/D] the Jacobian H/y² is comparable to D²/H and ≫H/D complete periods remain. In each interval the error in counting squarefree integers against length/ζ(2) is O(√D) by summing μ(m) over square divisors m². The joint error O(H/√D) is o(D) because β>2α/3. For v={H/d} in that range, K_d=1 if {n/d}∈[1−2v,1−v), and K_d=−1 if {n/d}∈[1−v,1). Both strips have measure ≥1/4. For each d use the strip that makes −μ(d)K_d positive and remove 1/12 of its length in fractional coordinate from the right end (i.e. remove a piece of measure 1/12). Thus for ≫X starting points n₀∈[X,3X/2] that sign is kept for each integer n between n₀ and n₀+D/16, since d=o(X). By averaging there is a single n₀ suitable for ≫D divisors. Freeze those divisors as S. On the whole range each one contributes log d, which proves the lower bound. The analogous argument, reversing the strip, also builds a sublist with a negative plateau. Nothing negative is claimed about the full list: the example establishes the need to control compensations between divisors in a uniform extension of the method.

In the REAL tail d>R there is indeed a part of the second moment that is controlled without signs, even for d≫H. In the square of Σ_{d>R}−μ(d)log d K_d(n) consider ALL pairs d≤e with d/gcd(d,e)≤J. The sum of the absolute values of their averaged contributions is O_{A,B}(J H log⁴(2X)), uniformly for 1≤H≤X (the reverse order costs another factor two). It includes the diagonal and ALL divisibility pairs with J=1. To prove it truncate e≤(B+2)X, since there are no relevant multiples beyond. For n∈[AX,BX], if e>2H, K_e≠0 requires some multiple in (n,n+2H], and the proportion of such n is ≤C H/e by periodicity or by counting the O(X/e+1) multiples. Together with |K_d|,|K_e|≤1 one obtains E|K_d K_e|≤C H/e also for e≤2H, adjusting the constant. For fixed e it suffices to choose g|e and an integer d/g≤J, at most J τ(e) possibilities. With |μ(d)log d μ(e)log e|≤C log²(2X) and Σ_{e≤Y}τ(e)/e≤(1+log Y)² the ceiling follows. Hence for J=X^{o(1)} this part already satisfies H X^{o(1)}; the remaining quadratic residual contains pairs whose reduced ratio has both terms larger than J. To apply criterion 4117 through the two-sided second moment a signed ceiling for that remaining sum would suffice; it does not follow from the example with sublists.

### Exact covariance over the period and localization of the error in the arithmetic window

For the two adjacent cells of 4129 write g=(d,e), l=[d,e]. Over a complete cycle of n modulo l, exactly
    C_per(d,e)=mean K_d(n)K_e(n)=2g²/(de) min({H/g},1−{H/g}).
Indeed, conditioned on n mod g, the classes of n mod d and n mod e are independent by the Chinese remainder theorem, even in the degenerate case d=e. For each position j in the two cells the probability of d|n+j on that fiber is g/d if g|n+j and zero otherwise. Thus the conditional expectation is (g/d)K_g(n). The second floor difference K_g takes each of ±1 on a fraction min({H/g},1−{H/g}) of the period, as one checks by separating {H/g}≤1/2 or >1/2. Both marginals have mean zero. In particular, for ALL pairs of divisors up to CX, even restricted to any sublist, the sum of the moduli of the complete covariances with weights μ(d)log d μ(e)log e is O_C(H log⁵(2X)). It suffices to write d=ga,e=gb, sum 1/(ab) and use Σ_{g≤CX}min(1,H/g)≪H log(2X). No compensation between different pairs is needed for this part. It is the modulus of the mean of each product; replacing it by the mean of its modulus would change the statement.

For the ceiling of the second moment in the window of 4117 it suffices to study the mean with weight χ(n/X)/X, where χ≥0 is smooth with compact support in (0,∞), and χ≥1 on the required band. One may take it Gevrey of order two (convolve a larger interval with a compact Gevrey bump of mass one); |χ̂(t)|≤Cexp(−c√|t|). Normalize the period term by ∫χ. For l≤X/log³(2X) the error of replacement by (∫χ)C_per, even summed in modulus over all those weighted pairs, is O_N(X^(−N)) for each fixed N asymptotically. When expanding the l-periodic product in Fourier all its coefficients have modulus ≤1. By Poisson the nonzero frequencies (including replicas of the zero class) are bounded in total by Σ_{k≠0}|χ̂(kX/l)|≪exp(−c'√(X/l)). The number of pairs is O(X²). Removing the smooth weight in each pair separately is not justified; its use as a majorant requires the full second moment to be a non-negative square.

A range of the physical expansion of the product K_d K_e can also be paid in absolute value. Let m,m' be the multiples appearing in the two differences, both in (n,n+2H]. The terms with |m−m'|≤Jg, including m=m', jointly cost O_C(H(1+J) log⁶(2X)) for J≥1. Each pair m,m' belongs to O(H) windows. For fixed g write m=gu, m'=g(u+k), |k|≤J; the options for d/g and e/g are at most τ(u)τ(u+k). With 1≤u,u+k≤CX/g, Cauchy bounds the sum in u by Σ_{v≤CX/g}τ(v)²≪(X/g)log³(2X), by the elementary count of divisor pairs (Σ_{a,b≤Y}1/[a,b]≪log³(2Y)). Sum over k and g, divide by X and pay the two logarithms of the coefficients. In particular the whole product is included when g≥2H/J, and for g≥2H only the same multiple can occur. This extends the trimming of small index differences (first-cell criterion 2875) to small differences in units of the common divisor.

Therefore, for a two-sided ceiling it suffices to bound the bias relative to the period of the pairs with l>X/log³(2X); among those pairs one can remove at cost H X^{o(1)} the configurations with reduced distance |m−m'|/g≤X^{o(1)} and the pairs with reduced ratio already paid in 4141. The period bound cannot be used to replace the remaining pairs by periodicity: their periods may far exceed the observed length. The balance of that residual has not been bounded.

### First harmonics of the correlations of long periods

In the divisor sum of 4129, even truncated to an arbitrary sublist up to CX, expand the datum in reduced frequencies θ=a/q. For each pair θ,θ' write the difference modulo one as k/l, with l=[q,q'] and −l/2<k≤l/2. Here k is the index over THIS common period, without cancelling additional factors of k/l. The contribution of ALL pairs with 0<|k|≤J costs in absolute value O_C(H J(1+J) log⁷(2X)), uniformly for 1≤H≤X and J≥1. No small upper bound on l is required. With J=X^{o(1)} this is already of sufficient size. The statement refers to reduced frequencies of the collected divisors, not to the least common multiple of the original divisors coinciding with l.

Proof. The coefficients of 4129 satisfy |c_θ|≤C log²(2X) W(θ)/q, with W(θ)=min(H,1/dist(θ,ℤ)); the zero frequency is missing. Order q≤q' and put g=(q,q'), u=q/g, v=q'/g. If θ−θ'=k/l modulo one, the distance from θ to an integer is ≤dist(θ',ℤ)+J/l≤(1+J/u)dist(θ',ℤ), since dist(θ',ℤ)≥1/q' and q'/l=1/u. Hence W(θ')≤(1+J)W(θ). For fixed q,a,g and k, av≡k mod u. Since (a,u)=1, in a block V≤q'<2V with q'≥q there are O(1+V/q)=O(V/q) options for v, including u=1. With q' fixed, b in θ'=b/q' is unique modulo q' since ub≡av−k mod l and l/u=q'. The coprimality checks can be omitted when majorizing the count. Summing moduli of the products in this block row by row gives ≤C log⁴(2X) τ(q)(1+J)W(θ)²/q². Moreover Σ_{a*} W(a/q)²/q²≪min(1,H/q): sum min(H²/q²,1/r²) over the distances r/q to an integer. Finally Σ_{q≤CX}τ(q)min(1,H/q)≪H log²(2X) by divisor counting. Summing O(log X) blocks and 2J indices proves the bound, even without exploiting the sign of the coefficients or the oscillation in n. In the smooth average of 4149 the multiplier of each cross term is uniformly bounded, so the same ceiling applies.

Application. In that expansion the zero harmonic costs O(H log⁵(2X)) by the sum of squares of the coefficients using the same bound for W. By Poisson and the Gevrey cutoff of 4149 the pairs with dist(θ−θ',ℤ)>log³(2X)/X cost jointly O_N(X^(−N)), since there are at most O(X⁴) pairs and coefficients bounded by a polynomial. Therefore for J=X^{o(1)} the only thing still pending, in this representation, is the signed sum over
    J<|k|≤l log³(2X)/X.
This includes an improvement in range over the use of complete cycles: taking for example J=exp(√log X), one can pay all frequencies of common reduced period l≤X exp(√log X)/log³(2X) at cost H X^{o(1)}. The upper limit of this band of periods already exceeds X. The residual sum has not been majorized; the upper bound of the full moment does not follow.

### What the full Möbius list cancels when marking common divisors

In the identity Λ(m)Λ(m') via two divisor sums, fix the intersection of the prime supports of d|m and e|m'. If some side has at least two distinct primes that do NOT divide the integer on the other side, the contribution of EACH fixed intersection is zero. If each side has exactly one private prime p,q, the polynomial of all intersections is
    log p log q ∏_{r prime common to m,m'} (y_r−1).
The factorization exponents of m,m' may be arbitrary. The cancellations are exact, before averaging over starting points and with the real Möbius weights.

Indeed, introduce the product of −μ(d)log d and −μ(e)log e via the mixed derivatives in s,t of Σ μ(d)μ(e)d^s e^t ∏_{r|gcd(d,e)}y_r, where e^t in the summand means the divisor e raised to t. The sum factorizes: the private primes of the first side contribute 1−p^s, those of the second 1−q^t, and each common prime r contributes 1−r^s−r^t+y_r r^(s+t). Evaluating at s=t=0 after differentiating once in each variable gives both statements coefficient by coefficient. Arbitrarily deleting divisors destroys this factorization.

The cancellation reaches macroscopic size with the true coefficients. For m=2p, m'=2q, p≠q odd primes, the stratum gcd(d,e)=1 gives exactly −log p log q and the stratum gcd(d,e)=2 gives +log p log q. In the first cell (n,n+H] of 4129, averaging over integers n between X and 2X, each stratum over these ordered pairs has mean of magnitude ≫H² for H=o(X), H/log²X→∞. Indeed S_n=Σ_{n<2p≤n+H}log p has mean ≫H: it suffices to keep the primes with 2p between 1.2X and 1.8X, each counted H times, and apply PNT. The mean of S_n is also O(H) by Chebyshev after interchanging sums. Jensen gives mean of S_n² ≫H² and the diagonal costs O(H log X). The joint contribution of both strata is exactly zero. This computation describes the block of pairs within a single cell; it does not attribute size H² to the square of the difference between the two cells.

**Route decision.** The example exhibits a compensation of order H², relevant against the budget H X^{o(1)}, absent when the two strata are separated. Applying it to all divisors recovers the identity Λ(m)Λ(m'). For m=p,m'=q distinct primes, from the start a single nonzero term survives: d=p,e=q, without marker. Hence pairing terms of the same pair of integers via their common primes yields no saving at all in that main block. What is missing would require comparing distinct pairs of integers with each other or changing representation. Do not use the cancellation of semiprimes as a new floor for the form.

Additional independent cross-check: paper 44 §8bis (8bis.2b) and its correction K1 §12 already record a dependence via prime intersection in another coefficient; R140_004_CONFIRMATION, H3 confirms it. They are not the differentiated Möbius identity computed here, but they are an antecedent of the marking operation. Do not reopen this mechanism without an identity between distinct pairs.

### Distinct pairs between the two cells: the congruence term and a falsifier for uniform relative errors

Let a_i=−1 for 1≤i≤H and +1 for H<i≤2H. Write S(d) for the singular series of prime pairs with difference d≠0, normalized to mean density one. The model contribution Σ_{i≠j}a_i a_j S(j−i) is O_ε(H^{1+ε}), in modulus, for each ε>0. It is a computation on the congruence term; it does not assume the prime pairs conjecture for θ. The real diagonal coefficient in the average of 4129 costs O(H log X) by Chebyshev. What remains is the signed average of the real deviations of pairs from S, with the same weights and the same averaging endpoints as in the original square.

Elementary detail. The expansion S(d)=Σ_q μ²(q)c_q(d)/φ(q)² is obtained by multiplying the local factors, since c_p(d)=−1 or p−1 according as p∤d or p|d. It converges absolutely for each d≠0. For q≤2H, temporarily incorporating the diagonal turns the Ramanujan sum into Σ_{b mod q}^*|A_H(b/q)|², with A_H from 4129. It is O(q²) by geometric summation, including the mode q=1 which vanishes. The diagonal to be subtracted is 2Hφ(q) for q before the weight. With φ(q)≫_ε q^{1−ε}, both parts sum to O_ε(H^{1+ε}), readjusting ε. For squarefree q>2H use |c_q(d)|≤(q,d) and Σ_{1≤d≤2H}(q,d)≤2Hτ(q). Each difference appears O(H) times. The sum of the tail is bounded by C H² Σ_{q>2H}τ(q)/φ(q)²=O_ε(H^{1+ε}). If the average of the observed pairs were exactly S(d), the comparison between the cells would already have the desired size.

**Quantitative obstruction.** Not even replacing that equality by relative errors O(exp(−√log X/2)) in EACH difference suffices, as an inference based only on these moments. Fix H=⌊X^α⌋, 0<α<1, z=exp(√log X), Q the product of the primes ≤z, V=φ(Q)/Q. Take, independently, a uniform shift modulo Q and a uniform phase U in [0,2π]. Among the integers coprime to Q after the shift, keep n, independently given both parameters, with probability
    [1+a cos(πn/H+U)]/(V log X),   a=exp(−√log X/4).
On the other integers put zero. By Mertens' product V is comparable to 1/log z, so this is a probability for large X. Let Y_n equal log X at the retained points and zero elsewhere. The law is stationary by the uniform shifts and the independence of the draws. One has E Y_n=1, E Y_n²=log X, and for 1≤|d|≤2H
    E Y_n Y_{n+d}=S_z(d)[1+(a²/2)cos(πd/H)],
where S_z is the truncated local product. For odd d both products are zero. For even d the logarithm of the ratio of S_z to S is O(Σ_{p>z}1/p²+Σ_{p|d,p>z}1/p)=O(log(2X)/z). Therefore all positive correlations coincide with S(d) with the declared relative error, much smaller than any inverse power of log X. The diagonal was calibrated exactly in the model; for the real primes its average has log X as main term.

However, conditioning only on U one has E(Y_{n+i}|U)=1+a cos(π(n+i)/H+U). By conditional Jensen and averaging over U,
    E |Σ_i a_i Y_{n+i}|² ≥ (a²/2)|A_H(1/(2H))|² ≫ H² exp(−√log X/2).
The difference between the two geometric sums at that phase has modulus 2/sin(π/(2H)). Also each one-sided part squared has expectation at least a²|A_H|²/4 by convexity. For H=X^{α+o(1)} this exceeds H X^{o(1)} by a power. These are expectations of a model that varies with X; it does not assert simultaneous empirical estimates for any realization nor describe an arithmetic counterexample. Diagnosis: the known local term satisfies the ceiling; relative approximations by shift, even with this uniform error and respecting the local prohibitions, allow a coherent error precisely at the frequency at which the two cells have response of order H. Signed control across different separations, or a stronger precision, is required, not a new subdivision of divisors.

Cross-check: 1192 already uses the variance of a shifted primorial sieve and 2873 detects a signed sum of correlations in another cell. The combination here preserves the mean, a diagonal of prime size and the local prohibitions while quantitatively exhibiting the defect of a relative approximation uniform in differences. No novelty is claimed for the Ramanujan expansion nor for its use for model moments.

### Single macroscopic comparison at integer powers and its positive inverse

Write F(x)=θ(x)−x and C(x)=θ(4x)−3θ(2x)+2θ(x). C compares the mass of (2x,4x] with twice that of (x,2x]; both terms have the same main term. For C_+=max(C,0), C_−=max(−C,0), and each fixed integer k≥1 one has, for each sign separately,
    lim_{N→∞} log( N^{k/2} + (1/N) Σ_{j≤N} C_±(j^k) ) / log(N^k) = 1/2+Δ.
Thus ONE orientation, ONE k (for example k=4) and ONE subsequence with mean ≤N^{k/2+o(1)} suffice. There is no family of lengths tending to an extremal exponent. The comparison changes the length when the cell start changes. Antecedents: bounds at powers and Landau in 195, modal probing in 235, positive filter of 2244/4044 and sampling of 4103. The factorial alternating average of 2762 contains a factor ζ that annihilates the zeros; the multiplier appearing here is (2^ρ−1)(2^ρ−2), nonzero in the open strip.

Proof. The ceiling via the explicit formula for θ of 235 is |C(x)|≪_ε x^{1/2+Δ+ε}, with the main term cancelled. For Δ=0 the explicit summand N^{k/2} already gives the lower bound. If Δ>0 take the non-negative weight w(v)=v^(−3/2) H_±(log v) of 4044 for a zero at distance b close to Δ. In the continuous average of C(Xv) against w(v) the term of each zero is
    −(X^ρ/ρ)(2^ρ−1)(2^ρ−2) ∫ H_±(y) exp((ρ−1/2)y)dy.
It is obtained by applying the explicit formula to θ (first ψ; removing prime powers costs O(√X log²X)), or by integrating by parts in the linear formula for the density. The factor at the target point is nonzero since 1<|2^ρ|<2. Adjusting the phase and using the positive annihilation as in 4044 gives magnitude ≫_b X^{1/2+b} for each orientation in a fixed band and for all large X.

To preserve the signal at the powers j^k, put Y=X^{1/k}. Replace the integral by the Riemann sum in j/Y, step 1/Y, with non-negative coefficient Y^(−1) k(j/Y)^(k−1) w((j/Y)^k). On the fixed compact set the additive relative error of the moment of v^ρ, before the factor 1/ρ and X^ρ, is O_w(min(1,(1+|γ|)/Y)), by variation and by the direct ceiling. To justify the computation with the jumps use the truncated formula of 235 at the three integer endpoints c j^k rounded up to the half-integer at distance 1/2, with a common good height T in [X,2X]. The displacement after dividing the argument by X is O(1/X), and its moment error is included in the same minimum, since Y≤X. The correction of the main term at the three evaluations is O(1); the truncation and prime-power costs are O(√X log²X) on average. The original smooth integral admits truncation there with error O(1) for ψ. For abscissae ≤1/2+s the combined moment error costs O_w(X^{1/2+s} log²X). For larger abscissae it costs O_{w,s,ε}(X^{1/2+Δ}Y^{−(1−q(s)−ε)}) by Ingham and the sum of min(Y^(−1),1/(1+|γ|)) as in 4103. Fix 0<s<Δ and ε<1−q(s); then take b close to Δ with k(Δ−b)<1−q(s)−ε. Both errors are o(X^{1/2+b}). The coefficients of the samples are bounded by O_w(1/Y); since they have a common sign, the sum of C_± over the band gains ≫_b Y X^{1/2+b}. To pass to all j≤N, take Y=N/B with B fixed larger than the upper endpoint of the support in the coordinate j/Y. The bands can be kept fixed while varying b as in 4056; even a B depending on b does not change the exponent. Letting b tend to Δ proves the limit.

Elementary complement, distinct from the sampling step. For all x>0 there is the exact identity
    F(x)=−Σ_{m<0}C(2^m x)−Σ_{m≥0}2^(−m−1) C(2^m x).
The first sum is finite after omitting zeros. With T the dilation by 2, C=(T−1)(T−2)F. By telescoping, the sum over negative indices is (T−2)F(x), since F(y)=−y near zero. The sum over non-negative indices is −(T−1)F(x) since (T−1)F(y)=o(y) by PNT; its convergence is in the written order. This gives the identity. For 0<σ<1 a global ceiling C_+(x)≤M x^σ implies F_−(x)≤M x^σ/[(2^σ−1)(2−2^σ)], and with the signs reversed the other one-sided direction holds. One sums the two geometric series of the majorant; absolute convergence of the original series is not required. The pointwise inversion uses data from the whole orbit; it is not presupposed in the criterion via subsequential averages. The arithmetic ceiling for the comparison between the two products of primes is still missing.

### Arithmetic floor after removing right zeros of logarithmic height

For x→∞, m=⌈log x⌉, let B be the finite sum of log p times (1−p/(2x))_+^m−2(1−p/x)_+^m. Put c_m=Γ(3/2)m!/Γ(m+3/2) and K_m(s)=m!/[s(s+1)…(s+m)]. Then
    B + Σ_{Re ρ>1/2, |Im ρ|≤8m} (2^ρ−2)x^ρ K_m(ρ) ≥ (0.34−o(1)) c_m √x.
The sum counts multiplicities and conjugate pairs. It is an unconditional inequality for the corrected expression. It does not establish the sign of B by itself.

Proof. For ψ, integrate the truncated weight twice by parts against dψ, using I(y)=∫₀ʸ ψ(t)dt=y²/2−Σ y^(ρ+1)/[ρ(ρ+1)]+O(1+y). For each scale z=x,2x the kernel on I is m(m−1)(1−t/z)^(m−2)/z² on [0,z]. The beta integral gives z/(m+1) for the main term, −z^ρ K_m(ρ) for each zero and error O(1+m/z). The main term cancels. To return to θ, ψ(t)−θ(t)∼√t by the prime number theorem applied to squares; the higher exponents contribute O(t^(1/3)log²(2t)) for t≥2. Integrating ψ−θ with density m(1−t/z)^(m−1)/z gives (1+o(1))c_m√z. Indeed the integral of √t is exactly c_m√z, which diverges, while the part below any fixed cutoff is bounded. The net bias in B is thus (2−√2+o(1))c_m√x.

For σ=Re ρ≤1/2, separate the first factor j=1 and use |j+ρ|≥j+σ for j≥2. Thus |K_m(ρ)|≤C m^(−σ)/(|ρ||1+ρ|), uniformly via the gamma quotient for 0≤σ≤1. Strictly left zeros are o(c_m√x) by dominated convergence with Σ(1+γ²)^−1. On the line one obtains directly |K_m(ρ)|≤(3/2)c_m/|ρ|². The Hadamard identity 2Σ Re(1/ρ)=2+γ_E−log(4π)<0.047 implies Σ_line |ρ|^−2<0.047 by positivity of each term. Above 8m, |K_m(ρ)|≤8^(2−m)m²/(|ρ|γ²); even with x^σ≤x this tail is o(1). What remains is 2−√2−(2+√2)(3/2)(0.047)>0.34.

Scope: the cutoff grows with x. The Riesz integral, the bias from squares and the filtering of zeros have antecedents; the computation quantifies their combination for this finite sum. Global positivity requires controlling the removed contributions or obtaining the arithmetic sign by another argument. Without an effective bound for the o(1) no numerical interval of positivity follows from a finite table of zeros.

### Positive transfer to the exponential sum and sieve test

Let E(t)=Σ_p log p (exp(−pt)−2exp(−2pt)). For every integer m≥1, if U has density u^m exp(−u)/m!, then E(t)=E_U[B_m(U/(2t))]. Indeed E[(1−a/U)_+^m]=exp(−a) by translation in the integral. This allows a sufficient arithmetic proof of HR: it suffices that B_m(z)≥0 for all sufficiently large m and m exp(m−1)/32 ≤ z ≤ 8m exp(m). No uniform margin in that sign is needed.

Proof: take m=⌈log(1/t)⌉. If m/16≤U≤16m then z=U/(2t) lies in the indicated interval. Outside, |B_m(z)|≤Cz by θ(y)≪y. The truncated first moment of U is (m+1) times the tail probability of a gamma of shape m+2. By the exponential Chernoff bound at both ends, this probability is O(exp(−1.7m)): the limiting rate for the ratio a is a−1−log a, larger than 1.8 for a=1/16 and for a=16. Thus E(t)≥−o(1). For Re s>1 its Mellin transform is Γ(s)(1−2^(1−s))Σ_p(log p)p^(−s). The prime series differs from −ζ′/ζ by a function holomorphic in Re s>1/2 (powers ≥2). The real pole at 1 cancels, but the multiplier does not vanish in 1/2<Re s<1. Apply Landau to the integral over (0,1) of E(t)+1, eventually positive; integrating over (1,∞) and cutting off a compact set only changes entire functions, and adding 1 on (0,1) only adds 1/s. Being regular at every real s >1/2, its abscissa is ≤1/2. This excludes right zeros. Conversely, under HR the floor of 4219 holds uniformly on these intervals: z/m→∞, there are no zeros off the line, and the squares argument, the error O(1+m/z) and the bound on the line are uniform. Therefore the sign on those intervals is equivalent to the target. Antecedent for the use of Landau: 3130. The bridge via a positive average allows transferring a one-sided bound without inverting the smoothing.

Arithmetic test: replace the prime weights by the integers coprime to a primorial M>1, with any constant positive normalization. Before normalizing, the exponential sum is exactly Σ_{d|M} μ(d)/(1+exp(dt)), by inclusion–exclusion and geometric series. Its main term at zero is −(t/4)Π_{p|M}(1−p), with absolute error ≤(t³/48)Π(1+p³), by |v−tanh v|≤v³/3. For t=M^(−2) the relative error is ≤(1/12) M^(−4)Π[(1+p³)/(p−1)]≤9/(96M) since (1+p³)/(p−1)≤p³ for p≥3 and the factor for 2 is 9 instead of 8 (hence the correct final bound with 2 is 9/(96M)). The sign alternates even as the number of exact local restrictions increases indefinitely. This example rules out deducing E(t)≥0 solely from the density and the exclusion of multiples in that regime. Its small magnitude does not contradict a constant lower bound nor rule out sieves with additional information.

Control of the atom 1 (independent check). The periodic sieve above includes n=1. To require zero weight at 1 and preserve the mass, move that weight to the first prime q not dividing M. For g(u)=exp(−u)−2exp(−2u), |g′|≤5, so the change is ≤5qt. If M is the product of the first r primes, q≤2p_r by Bertrand and q/φ(M)→0 since φ(M)=(p_r−1)Π_{i<r}(p_i−1). The main term has modulus tφ(M)/4: the alternation persists for large r with this correction and after normalizing by M/φ(M). Removing the unit without moving it does add a term of order one and destroys the example.

### Moving threshold of the semiprime leakage in the exponential comparison

Let g(w)=exp(−w)−2exp(−2w). Denote by R(X,z) the sum of (log n)g(n/X) over n≥2 with all prime factors >z, and by D(X,z) its subtotal over composites. In this test the sieve includes the real weights log n and excludes the unit.

For z=λ√X, λ>0 fixed, D(X,z)∼(2X/log X)∫_{λ²}^∞ (exp(−w)−exp(−2w))dw/w. In particular no fixed λ kills the first term. Indeed three factors require n>z³ and their tail is negligible even summing over integers. For two factors p,q the count of ordered pairs introduces 1/2 off the diagonal (the diagonal correction is O_λ(√X log X)). By PNT in p/√X and q/√X one gets the double integral of g(uv) over u,v≥λ with prefactor 2X/log X. One can truncate in dyadic boxes: for u≈2^i λ,v≈2^j λ the normalized contribution in absolute value is O_λ((1+i+j)2^(i+j)exp(−λ²2^(i+j))) by Chebyshev. Changing to w=uv gives the weight log(w/λ²); integrating by parts gives the announced integral, strictly positive.

Closer to the required precision there is an explicit threshold. For fixed real b, L=log X, s=L−2log L+b, z=√(Xs), h=X/z, one has D(X,z)→2exp(−b). To prove it, it suffices to take z<p,q≤2z, since integers n>2z² have tail O(X log(Xs) exp(−2s))=o(1); those with three factors too. The diagonal correction is O(z log z exp(−s))=o(1). Write p=z+hu,q=z+hv. Then pq/X=s+u+v+uv/s. The prime counting measure in u, divided by h/log z, converges to du on each compact subset of [0,∞). In fact the PNT with remainder O_A(z/log^A z) on [z,2z] allows subtracting primitives because h=z/s; the same argument uniformly bounds the normalized mass in each interval of length one up to s. This justifies domination by exp(−u−v), and g(pq/X)/exp(−s) tends to exp(−u−v). The weight log(pq)/(2log z) tends to one uniformly on the box. The subtotal is thus asymptotic to exp(−s)h²/log z, which tends to 2exp(−b).

On the other hand Σ_{p≤z}(log p)g(p/X)=−θ(z)+(3/2)s+o(1): g(w)=−1+3w+O(w²), Σ_{p≤z}p log p=z²/2+O_A(z²/log^A z) by PNT and the quadratic remainder costs O(z³/X²). Consequently
    E(1/X)=R(X,z)−θ(z)+(3/2)s−2exp(−b)+o(1).
This eliminates the composite leakage with constant precision and computes the cost of removing small primes, keeping θ(z) exact. The surviving arithmetic obligation is the floor R(X,z)≥θ(z)−(3/2)s−O(1) for large X. It is not proved. Replacing θ(z) here by z via PNT does not preserve constant precision. Antecedents in 934 (Buchstab profile with fixed logarithmic scale) and 4231 (periodic sieve); here the cutoff is moved to the two-factor edge and the exponential weight makes its remaining contribution measurable.

### A sign without subtraction for the moving sieve

There is an important simplification of the obligation of 4241. It suffices to prove R(X,√(X log X/2))≥0 for all large X. Constant precision, and in particular the subtraction of θ(z), were unnecessary for the global target. Indeed Landau in 4231 works equally with E(1/X)≥−C_ε X^(1/2+ε) for each ε>0: adding C_ε t^(−1/2−ε) on (0,1) only adds a real pole at 1/2+ε. Hence there are no zeros further to the right for any ε>0.

Put L=log X. For s→∞, s≤L, the box argument of 4241 gives
    D(X,√(Xs)) ∼ exp(−s) X/(s log(√(Xs))).
Tail precision for this range: three factors cost O(X log(Xz³)exp(−z³/X)); for pairs outside the box z<p,q≤2z, the bound via integers O(X log(Xs)exp(−2s)) suffices if s≫log L. This is the only range we use below. For slower s that tail of pairs can be bounded via boxes of side h=X/z in p,q. By the PNT with remainder of any logarithmic power, each one-dimensional box up to 2z has O(h/log z) primes, and for p>2z the same bound is used up to p≤zL² (the PNT remainder there is absorbed by increasing the saving power); beyond that the exponential decay allows summing over integers. In these boxes pq/X≥s+i+j for indices i,j≥0, and outside the square of side z one index exceeds s−1, giving relative o(1). The diagonal over the whole zone is negligible at the same normalizer (in the box O(z log z exp(−s)) suffices). The rest of the proof is the local limit of 4241.

For s=L/2 one obtains D=o(√X), θ(z)∼√(XL/2), and Σ_{p≤z}log p·g(p/X)=−θ(z)+O(L). Thus a simple positive sign for R gives E≥−O(√(XL)); this implies HR by the first paragraph. Conversely, under HR the Riesz floor of 4219 and the gamma transfer of 4231 imply E≥−o(1), and R=E+θ(z)+D+O(L)>0. The cost of ignoring the correction even has optimal scale: inf_{z≥√X}(θ(z)+D(X,z))∼√(XL/2). In this range all counted composites have n>X and g(n/X)>0, so D decreases as z increases. Below z²/X=(1/2−ε)L its value is at least that at the endpoint, of order X^(1/2+ε)/L². Above it θ(z)≥(1+o(1))√((1/2−ε)XL) suffices. Taking ε↓0 and comparing with the cutoff L/2 proves the claim.

Unconditional range at the same sieve scale. PNT with classical remainder gives E(1/X)=O(X exp(−c√L)) with some c>0, by integration by parts against g, whose integral is zero (separate p≤√X and p≥XL²). For any 0<d<c, at the cutoff s=d√L the positive main term of D dominates that error. Thus R(X,√(Xd√L))>0 for all sufficiently large X. Also for √X≤z≤√(Xd√L), by monotonicity of D and because the removed primes lie below X log 2, where g<0. The pending jump is to prove this same sign with s=L/2. This comparison does not measure a Weil window T.

### The jumps of the sieve change sign only once

For large X and √(2X)≤z≤X/10, R(X,z) decreases and then increases, as a step function of z. All its minimizing cutoffs in that interval satisfy
    z²/X = (log X)/2 − (3/2)log log X + log(4√2) + o(1).
The monotonicity of the normalized jumps follows directly from the admitted integers. The estimate of their position uses PNT. This statement determines the most demanding cutoff for simultaneous positivity in that range, although the value at the minimum remains open. Unlike 4253, here the exact jump of R is studied, not only the order of the minimal cost.

On crossing a prime p exactly n=p and n=pm with m≥p and smallest prime factor ≥p are removed. Dividing the jump R(X,p)−R(X,p−0) by (−g(p/X))log p>0 one obtains 1−J(p), where J is the sum over those m of
    (1+log m/log p) g(pm/X)/(−g(p/X)).
J decreases strictly between primes of the interval. The set of m decreases by inclusion, and each surviving term decreases: the first factor decreases, and the logarithmic derivative in p of the quotient is ≤(−0.6m+5)/X<0 for large X. Indeed (log g)'(w)=−1+2exp(−w)/(1−2exp(−w))<−0.6 for w≥2, while |(log(−g))'(v)|≤5 if 0≤v≤0.1. The signs of the jumps are thus exactly ordered, including prime powers and composites of any order.

For p²/X=s=(log X)/2−(3/2)log log X+O(1), put h=X/p=p/s. In [p,2p] the admitted m are primes, and at m=p+hu the weight is (2+o(1))exp(−s−u) for u in compact sets. PNT with remainder O_A(p/log^A p) gives density h/log p in this variable and O(h/log p) in boxes of width one up to s. The tail m>2p costs O(h exp(−2s)) even summing integers, since 1+log m/log p≤1+m/p and the exponential is geometric. Thus J(p)∼2h exp(−s)/log p. At s=(log X)/2−(3/2)log log X+b the limit is 4√2 exp(−b). Quantitative PNT guarantees primes in every interval of length εh for fixed ε>0, which translates into gaps o(1) in s in this band. Taking b on both sides of log(4√2) and using monotonicity proves the localization even if a jump equals zero.

Diagnosis: by changing z within the critical band one can order the entire profile of R via the sign of its increments. The term E(1/X) is common to all those values and disappears exactly in each increment. The height of the minimum is not obtained from this. For scaling by a zero-free region with a sieved mass and its prior calibration, see 2400–2414; moving that region to another weight does not constitute a distinct mechanism.

At any cutoff s=a log X with 0<a<1/2 fixed, R≥0 eventually would already exclude zeros with Re ρ>1−a: the cost D+θ(z) is O_a(X^(1−a)) by 4253 and the Landau floor applies with that exponent. In particular a first step of size proportional to log X would already require a fixed zero-free strip.

### Mixtures of profiles: finite separation and exact reduction to a multiple pole of the same order

Separator for the family of 3607. Fix Y≥1 and measure V_F(t)=|F(iYt)|². Take 101 equally spaced nodes between 1.4 and 1.6 inclusive, and t*=1.65. For every member of 3607, and for every positive mixture of its profiles with arbitrary poles, V(t*)≤K² Σ_j V(t_j), K=exp(7604)300^1200. Indeed in units of Y there are at most 100 centers in [1,2). Each one discards at most one node at distance <0.0009. At a surviving node all linear factors of the mean polynomial of 3607 have distance ≥0.0009 from their root, since the centers outside [1,2) and the negative roots are even at distance ≥0.4. Each factor grows by a ratio at most 1+0.25/0.0009<300 when passing to the target. The analytic remainder grows by a ratio ≤exp(2·3802) by 3607. The mixture preserves the inequality by linearity. An admissible test with centers at the 101 nodes and 203 distinct poles strictly violates it. With up to 100 distinct nodes in the same interval one can put centers at all of them and choose pairs of poles in their intervals: no ceiling of the same type at an additional point holds for that sample. It separates in the topology of finite values, without inferring the sign of the form of ζ from the separating functional.

Alternative positive reduction. Let m be poles u_j>1/2, a real numerator N of degree <m, and Q the full form of the bridge. There is an identity of averages *at fixed degree*:
    Q(N(z)/Π_j(u_j−z)) = mean_τ Q(N(z)/(U(τ)−z)^m),
    U(τ)²=Σ_j τ_j u_j²,
where τ is uniform on the simplex τ_j≥0, Στ_j=1 (total mass one). It is the classical Feynman parameter identity applied to the reflected product, with a target distinct from the density of POWER_014 and from the growing blocks of 3933. Proof: for y≥0 write each 1/(y+u_j²) as an exponential integral in r_j≥0. Passing to radius Σr_j and proportions τ leaves the radial Jacobian r^(m−1), whose integral gives (m−1)!/(y+Στ_j u_j²)^m. The identity extends to y outside the ray (−∞,−min u_j²] by holomorphy. Multiply by N(z)N(−z) and put y=−z² at each spectral point z=ρ−1/2; there the extension always holds (even a real z in the strip would give y>−1/4). The quotients are O((1+|Im ρ|)^−2) uniformly on the simplex by the degree, the compactness of the centers and the separation of poles at the low points. The series over zeros allows the interchange. A negative test with m poles forces a negative test with a single pole of multiplicity m, with exactly the same numerator and center between the original poles. By continuity of the average there is even a relatively open set of negative parameters. Conversely a strictly negative confluent value persists when slightly separating the poles.

This reduces, at each individual order, the problem for all denominators to blocks in a single real variable, without losing the order or moving the zeros of the numerator. The check of semidefiniteness of those blocks, uniformly in the order, remains open. The integration formula is classical; no bibliographic novelty is attributed to the reduction without a specific search.

Verified reinforcement: the same identity at z=iξ exactly averages the squared physical norm by Plancherel and Tonelli. Therefore the quotient Q/‖f‖² is an average of the confluent quotients with weights proportional to their squared norms; at some center the quotient is ≤ the original one. On a compact interval of poles with nonempty interior, the Rayleigh infimum at formal order m coincides exactly for simple and confluent poles, also when fixing the same N≠0: the reverse direction approximates any center by m distinct poles of the interval, with dominated convergence in both forms. Formal order allows cancellations if N(U)=0; the normal forms with imaginary roots do not suffer that cancellation at U>1/2.

### Up to degree 32 in the numerator, with no restriction on the number or relative position of the poles

Let N be a nonzero real polynomial of degree d≤32. For all t>0 the sum
    S_N(t)=Σ_ρ exp(tλ²)N(λ)N(−λ),   λ=ρ−1/2,
is strictly positive. Consequently the full form is positive for N(z)/Π(u_j−z), for ANY number m>d and any rates u_j>1/2, even repeated. The coefficients of N are arbitrary. Antecedents: 1700 controls scalar derivatives of the heat trace; 3517 gives polynomial sampling and shifting; 3607 pairs poles and roots. Here the cross terms of an entire polynomial are controlled jointly by multiplying the trace by a Gaussian weight.

Proof. Fix H=3·10¹² from the certificate used in 3517, and B the first 2^k H, k≥0, with tB²≥1000. Treat first the positive heights (the negative ones give the conjugate). The prefix γ≤H contributes non-negative squares. In every band Y<γ≤2Y of the dyadic partition between H and B, tY²<1000. Let f(Z)=N(YZ) exp(tY²Z²/2). The two lists are evaluated at Z=±δ/Y+iγ/Y, with δ=Re λ. Their product with conjugation is exactly the summand of S_N. Approximate the exponential factor by its Taylor polynomial of degree 12000 centered at 1.5i. On the disk of radius 1 its modulus is ≤exp(3125); on radius 0.51 its inverse is ≤exp(2021). The Cauchy bound exp(5146)0.51^12001/0.49<0.001 controls the relative error, including the shifted nodes. The product of N with the Taylor polynomial has degree ≤12032. By 3517 the shifted lists of the polynomial differ from the central one in relative norm <0.002; returning to f the extra error is <0.002. Their scalar product has real part ≥0.98 times the squared norm of the central polynomial list. The sampling lower bound of 3517 and the approximation on the segment give a real contribution ≥0.08 Y log Y ∫₁² |N(iYv)|²exp(−tY²v²)dv.

Use as reference Y=B/4 and M=max_{1≤v≤2}|N(iYv)|. If this band lies below H, one evaluates on the line and it suffices to sample the polynomial N after minorizing the weight by exp(−tB²/4). The lower bound of 3517 holds for degree 32 down to Y≥H/4: the relative error of the integrated count ≤6·33² log(2Y)/(Y log Y) and the same main density >0.14 ensure the factor 0.1. If it lies above H the previous paragraph applies. In both cases, using ||N||∞≤33||N||₂ on the unit segment, this band contributes at least 0.01 B log B exp(−tB²/4) M²/33².

In the tail 2^j B<γ≤2^(j+1)B, interpolate N at d+1 equally spaced nodes of the reference band. In units Y=B/4 the distance factors when evaluating at both shifted positions are ≤11·2^j; the sum of the basis polynomials is bounded by (22e·2^j)^d using d!≥(d/e)^d (for d=0 it is one). Hence |N(±δ+iγ)|≤M(64·2^j)^32. The count of 3517 for constants gives at most (j+1)2^j B log B points, and |exp(tλ²)|≤exp(−0.99tB²4^j). Dividing the sum of the moduli by the reference floor gives at most
    100·33²·64^64 Σ_{j≥0}(j+1)2^(65j) exp(−tB²(0.99·4^j−0.25)) < 1.
Indeed 4^j≥1+3j and tB²≥1000. Strict positivity is proved even if the entire tail opposes.

To obtain the rational denominators integrate S_N(t) with positive weight t^(m−1)exp(−U²t)/(m−1)! and apply the average of 4281. The absolute interchange after integrating costs O(|γ|^(2d−2m)) per zero in the tail; m≥d+1 suffices. Alternatively, for different poles the direct convolution of the weights exp(−u_j²t) gives the same argument. No sparsity, pairing or condition on the signs of the residues is required. The proof does not give unbounded numerator degree.

### Growing thermal degree and physical length: the threshold is √(2td)

Write h_{n,t} for the orthonormal Hermite functions of scale √t, with h_{0,t}(x)=(πt)^(−1/4)exp(−x²/(2t)). Fourier/Laplace takes the block n≤d precisely to exp(tz²/2)N(z), deg N≤d (also over the reals). Let μ(t,d) be the infimum of the quotient of the full form by the squared physical norm on this block. For A>0 and d=⌊A/t⌋, any 0<T₋<√(2A)<T₊ satisfies
    λ_W(T₊) ≤ liminf_{t↓0} μ(t,d) ≤ limsup_{t↓0} μ(t,d) ≤ λ_W(T₋).
The centered windows [−T,T] are used. Continuity in T is not presupposed. In particular, for each positive A<3.92, all numerators of degree ≤⌊A/t⌋ have S_N(t)>0 for all sufficiently small t. The threshold in t is not effective here. Conversely, a strictly negative window of radius T is detected in all these blocks for A>T²/2. Antecedents: 3933 and the reciprocal-mass bridge for rational blocks; here the scale and the constant come from the thermal Hermite basis.

Detail of the uniform localization. Put ||v||_* = ∫ exp(|x|/2)(|v|+|v′|) dx. The spectral sum defines a bilinear form bounded by C||u||_*||v||_*: integration by parts gives |F_v(δ+iγ)|≪||v||_* /(1+|γ|) for |δ|≤1/2 and the sum of (1+|γ|)^−2 converges. For ||v||₂=1 in the block, Cauchy–Schwarz and the classical Mehler diagonal give, for any 0<r<1,
    |v(x)|² ≤ r^(−d)[πt(1−r²)]^(−1/2) exp(−x²(1−r)/(t(1+r))).
For v′ the same ceiling is used at order d+1 with a factor O((d+1)/t) in the square via the ladder relation. Choose T₀ between √(2A) and T₊. There is a fixed r close to 1 such that T₀²(1−r)/(1+r)>A log(1/r), since the quotient log(1/r)(1+r)/(1−r) tends to 2. Outside T₀ an exponential margin exp(−c/t) remains in the weighted integrals, keeping part of the Gaussian decay for integration. A smooth mask equal to one up to T₀ and supported in (−T₊,T₊) changes v by O(exp(−c′/t)) in the * norm. The total * norm grows only polynomially in 1/t: inside T₊ Cauchy–Schwarz and ||v′||₂≤C√((d+1)/t) suffice; outside the tail serves. The L² norm of the cutoff tends to one uniformly by the same ceiling. The window lower bound gives the first endpoint.

For the upper endpoint, take a real smooth test f compactly supported in (−T₋,T₋) and approximate it by its convolution with the Gaussian of variance t, which converges in the * norm and in L² (also for the derivative by translation). Each Gaussian translated to a is an O(t^(−1/4)) multiple of h_{0,t}(x−a), whose coefficients in this basis have squared moduli exp(−b)b^n/n!, b=a²/(2t); this follows from the generating function of the Hermite polynomials. Uniformly in |a|≤T₋ one has b≤q A/t with q<1. The projection onto n≤d loses O(exp(−c/t)) even in the * norm. Indeed, for arbitrarily small η>0 the Mehler diagonal with r=exp(−η), integrated after taking the square root and applied also to the derivative via the ladder, gives ||h_{n,t}||_*≤C_η t^(−C)(1+n)exp(η n/2) for 0<t≤1. For the tail of coefficients use Cauchy–Schwarz with exponential weights: for a Poisson Z with mean b, E[exp(3ηZ)1_{Z>d}]≤exp(−kd+b(exp(k+3η)−1)). First choose k>0 with q(exp(k)−1)<k and then small η>0; the polynomial factors are absorbed in the slack between η and 3η. The L² estimate is immediate from the same tail. Integrating in a against f produces a vector of the block that converges to the test in both norms. Taking the infimum using the smooth kernel of the window form proves the upper endpoint.

Scope: there is no longer a fixed ceiling on the degree, but the product t·degree is restricted. To reach a larger physical radius by this path one needs an independent sign bound that controls blocks beyond the corresponding threshold.

### Thermal monomials of unbounded order and detection by slope

Let H=3·10¹² and w=−(ρ−1/2)²=a+ib. The pure-numerator test N(z)=z^n has thermal form M_n(t)=Σ_ρ w^n exp(−tw). For ALL integers n≥0 and all t>0 with tH²≥4n one has M_n(t)>0. No maximum is imposed on the order of differentiation. Conversely, if there is an exterior zero, there is an open interval of slopes s>0 and, shrinking it if necessary, a single dominant exterior conjugate pair. For a rational slope in that interval and three fixed shifts h_j≥0, for each sufficiently large n there is a j with M_n(sn+h_j)<0. Thus the obstruction in the heat trace can be seen with a single monomial of each large degree; the temperature is varied, not the polynomial coefficients. Substantial antecedents: 1700 already proves the sign for n≤10⁹ at all t, 1959/1985 study saddles and signs for moments of auxiliary cutoffs, and 1684 isolates dominant products in shifted determinants. The following detection acts on the full trace.

Floor in the wedge. For n≤100 apply 1700. Take n>100 and s=t/n≥4/H². There is a critical zero of ordinate γ₀ between H/3 and H/2 by the explicit count of 3517 (the difference of main terms dominates 2log H) and the verification up to H. Its contribution is [γ₀² exp(−sγ₀²)]^n. For γ>H in modulus, put y=γ²/H²≥1. One has |w|≤γ²+1/4 and a≥γ²−1/4. The ratio of bases in modulus relative to the critical node is at most
    9(y+1/(4H²)) exp(−4y+1+1/H²) ≤ 0.46/y.
The last inequality uses that y(y+1/(4H²))exp(−4y) decreases for y≥1. Summing over all high zeros, their relative cost is ≤0.46^n H² Σ_ρ 1/γ² <1 by the bound 0.049 of 1700. All other zeros contribute positive terms. This proof uses only one verified node to dominate the tail and does not assume HR.

Detection. If w₀=a₀+ib₀ with b₀≠0, at s₀=1/a₀ one has |w₀|exp(−s₀a₀)>1/(es₀), the maximum of x exp(−s₀x) for x>0. The strict inequality persists on an interval, so no real node can maximize |w|exp(−sa). On a compact set of positive slopes the candidates for the maximum form a finite set by Gaussian decay. Distinct lines log|w|−sa cross only at isolated points: identical coincidence implies the same a and modulus, i.e. the same conjugate pair. Choose a subinterval without crossings and a rational s in it. If w=a+ib is the winner, V=|w|exp(−sa), the remainder is O(V₂^n) with V₂<V, for each fixed non-negative h, by summability of the bases. The dominant term is 2m V^n exp(−ha) cos(n(arg w−sb)−hb), where m counts the occurrences of w. At h=0,2π/(3|b|),4π/(3|b|) one of the three cosines is ≤−1/2 for each n. A small fixed perturbation of those h even allows rational shifts (with margin −1/3). Under HR all summands are positive. The wedge argument implies that the detecting slopes lie below 4/H². The sign has not been proved for all those slopes.

### Phase cancellation at the dominant height: all monomials at small time

For EVERY integer n≥0 and EVERY 0<t≤10^(−4), M_n(t)>0. In particular S(t)=Σ exp(tλ²) has derivatives of ALL orders with alternating signs on the same interval, even if the dominant height exceeds H without bound. The mechanism of 4324 (dominating by a verified zero) only covers R=√(n/t)≤H/2; here the positive contribution is obtained at the same unknown heights. The total count of zeros with multiplicity is used. This statement does not imply positivity of the moment matrices of arbitrary order.

By 1700 and 4324 it suffices to take n>10⁹ and R>H/2. Put W=1/√t≥100, R/W=√n. For positive height γ write ρ=1/2+δ+iγ and w=(γ−iδ)², |δ|≤1/2. The modulus of the term w^n exp(−tw) is exp(2tδ²) f(r), with r=√(γ²+δ²), f(v)=v^(2n)exp(−tv²). A real phase of the term is 2tδγ−2n arctan(δ/γ). For γ≥R/2 its modulus is ≤3t|γ−R|+t/R: use |x−arctan x|≤|x|³/3 and |2δ|(γ+R)/γ≤3. Thus all terms with |γ−R|≤10W have positive real part (phase <0.31). The two terms linear in δ cancel at the center of the band.

On [R,R+W], r≥R and r−R≤W+1/2. Since log f has zero derivative at R and second derivative ≥−4t for v≥R, one has f(r)≥exp(−3)f(R). The count in that interval is ≥0.1W log R: the derivative of the Riemann–von Mangoldt main term exceeds 0.14 log R, and the error at both endpoints is ≤2 log(2R) by the explicit bound used in 3517 (valid here also from H/2 on). Thus the real part of the core is ≥0.004 W log R f(R).

On the whole half-line (log f)″≤−2t, so f(r)≤f(R)exp(−t(r−R)²). Outside the positive core group the heights into strips jW≤|γ−R|≤(j+1)W, j≥10, with |r−γ|≤1/2. Each strip, counting both sides, has at most 10(j+2)W log R zeros. To verify the ceiling the explicit counting formula of 3517 for endpoints ≥100 suffices (the error there is ≤4log(2+v)); smaller endpoints are cut at 100 and the fewer than 100 zeros of the prefix are added. For v≤R+(j+1)W one uses W≤R and log(2+v)≤(j+2)log R. Integrating the main term over length ≤W per side and summing the endpoint errors gives the indicated ceiling. The total cost relative to W log R f(R) is at most 10exp(t/2)Σ_{j≥10}(j+2)exp(−(j−0.005)²)<10^(−38) (successive ratios are <1/2). The contribution of negative heights is obtained by conjugation. The core strictly dominates.

Combined with 4324, every monomial failure must simultaneously satisfy n>10⁹, t>10^(−4) and n/t>H²/4. The detecting converse of 4324 still enters that region by making n large with a fixed small slope. Hence the new simultaneous sign for all orders at small time does not yet give the global sign.

### Arithmetic floor of the monomials when temperature and dominant height grow together

For each 0<ε<2 there is R_ε such that M_n(t)>0 whenever R=√(n/t)≥R_ε and 0<t≤(2−ε)log log R. In particular, for EACH fixed temperature t>0 all sufficiently large degrees have positive sign. It is a bound on the full form obtained by controlling the prime term, independent of the abscissae of the high zeros. Internal antecedent: 4334 treats all degrees at small temperature by direct estimation of the zero side; 3411 uses a doubly logarithmic scale for another test and a modified divisor.

Proof. By 4334 it suffices to take t≥10^(−4). For n≥1 normalize the even Weil test function to h(v)=(v/R)^(2n)exp(n−tv²), with maximum 1 at v=±R. The sum Σ h((ρ−1/2)/i) has the same sign as M_n(t), with factor exp(n)R^(−2n)>0. On the real axis h≥0. For fixed b>1/2 and R≥4b,
    ∫_ℝ |h(x+ib)| dx ≪ exp(2tb²)/√t.
Indeed the integrand is exp(2tb²)h(r), r=√(x²+b²), and h(r)≤exp(−t(r−R)²) by concavity of log h with second derivative ≤−2t. Where r<R/2 the integral without prefactor costs O(R exp(−n/4))=O(1/√t); for r≥R/2 the inverse Jacobian per half-axis is ≤2. Shifting the Fourier transform without 2π in the frequency u gives |ĥ(u)|≪exp(−b|u|+2tb²)/√t. The prime terms of the explicit formula thus cost O_b(exp(2tb²)/√t) in modulus, since ΣΛ(k)k^(−1/2−b) converges.

The archimedean term has density (Re ψ(1/4+iv/2)−log π)/(2π), with ψ the digamma function; it is bounded below and equals (log |v|+O(1))/(2π) when |v|≥2. On [R,R+1/√t], h≥exp(−2) by (log h)″≥−4t for v≥R. Moreover ∫h≪1/√t by the same Gaussian bound. The result is a floor (c log R−C)/√t with absolute c>0. The poles at ±i/2 cost in total ≤2exp(n+t/4)(2R)^(−2n), o(1/√t) uniformly in the given regime (n=tR² and t≥10^(−4)). The sign is decided as soon as exp(2tb²)=o(log R). For each ε choose b>1/2 close enough to 1/2 that 2b²(2−ε)<1. This proves the announced band. R_ε is not quantified. In particular the fixed detecting slopes of 4324, with R bounded and t growing, remain outside this argument.

### Exact rate of the negative part at each large temperature

Write Δ=sup_ρ |Re ρ−1/2|. Choose C(t)≥1 with C(t)→∞ as slowly as desired and log log(3+C(t))=o(t); for example C(t)=log(3+t). For t≥1 define the finite observable
    D(t)=1+max_{1≤n≤⌊t C(t)⌋} [−exp(n)(t/n)^n M_n(t)]_+ .
Then lim_{t→∞} (log D(t))/t = 2Δ². The ordinary limit persists along any sequence of temperatures that diverges. Under HR D(t)=1. Under an exterior zero there is a negative degree at EACH large temperature, among the indicated degrees, with the above rate. In particular a subexponential bound for this maximum along a subsequence suffices. This measures the obstruction that remains; it does not prove the ceiling. Antecedents: 4324 chooses three temperatures per degree; 4203 obtains another rate for the error of a macroscopic prime comparison.

Proof. With u=n/t, R=√u and w=a+ib=−(ρ−1/2)², the modulus of each normalized term is exp(t g_w(u)), where
    g_w(u)=u(1+log(|w|/u))−a.
Its maximum over u>0 equals |w|−a=2δ² and is attained at u=|w|=γ²+δ². More precisely, with r=√|w|, concavity in the radial variable of 4334 gives exp(t g_w(u))≤exp(2tΔ²) exp(−t(r−R)²). By counting in intervals of length one the moduli are summed at cost O(log(2+R)) for t≥1: |r−|γ||≤1/2, and in each strip at distance j from R there are O(log(3+R+j)) nodes with multiplicities; the Gaussian tail is uniformly summable. For the finite maximum, the logarithm of the additional cost is o(t) by the condition on C. This gives the ceiling and covers Δ=0.

For the floor take an exterior w₀, δ₀≠0. Near u₀=|w₀| the maximum of g_w is at least 2δ₀²−η for any sufficiently small η>0, while every real node gives ≤0. On a nearby compact set only finitely many w can compete: a grows like γ², |w| like γ² and u stays bounded. After subtracting the common part u(1−log u), the remaining functions are lines u log|w|−a. Avoiding the finitely many crossings allows fixing u where there is a single dominant conjugate pair (grouping multiplicities), with uniform positive advantage on a compact neighbourhood of u. For all large t test n=⌊tu⌋+j, with j in a fixed list of consecutive integers from 0 to ⌈2π/|arg w|⌉+1 for that pair. The cosine cos(n arg w−tb) is ≤−1/2 in at least one: 0<|arg w|<π/3 because |γ|>14 and |δ|<1/2. The progression goes around a complete circle with steps smaller than the arc where the cosine is ≤−1/2. The bounded change of n changes the exponent t g_w(n/t) only by O(1). The remaining sum loses exp(−ct) relative to the dominant term by the uniform advantage and the uniform summability of exp(g_v(n/t)) (a time factor 1 is reserved). The proposed degrees eventually enter the chosen cutoff even if C diverges very slowly. Therefore liminf (log D(t))/t≥2δ₀²−η. Letting η↓0 and taking the supremum over zeros proves the statement without requiring Δ to be attained.

### The prime sum has two parts of size exp(t/2) along the same thermal slope

Fix R₀≥4, even larger than the verified height. For n=⌊t R₀²⌋, R=√(n/t), h from 4346 and ĥ(u)=∫h(v)exp(−iuv)dv, define P_±(t)=Σ_p (log p)/√p [±ĥ(log p)]_+. One has
    P_±(t) ∼ 4 (R₀²/(R₀²−1/4))^(1/4) exp(t/2)
for each sign. The weight concentrates at log p=2t+O(√t) in the sense that outside |log p−2t|≤K√t the relative limsup tends to zero as K→∞. Prime powers with exponent ≥2 cost in total O(1) in modulus. Therefore a term-by-term estimate, even discarding one of the signs, pays the exponent 1/2 along every fixed slope of this class. The smaller rate sought requires cancellation among true primes within the main zone or between that zone and its complement. The equivalence of the leading terms does not give an exponential saving.

Proof. By the Fourier transform of the Gaussian and 2n differentiations, Y(u)=exp(u²/(8t))ĥ(u)/ĥ(0) is the even Hermite function of index 2n evaluated at u/(2√t), normalized to Y(0)=1. It satisfies Y′(0)=0 and Y″+qY=0 with q=(4n+1)/(4t)−u²/(16t²). On 0≤u≤4t, q lies between two positive constants depending on R₀, with q≥1 for large t. The energy E=Y²+(Y′)²/q satisfies 0≤E′≤−(q′/q)E; thus Y and Y′ are uniformly bounded. More precisely
    Y(u)=(q(0)/q(u))^(1/4) cos(∫₀ᵘ √q(v)dv)+O_{R₀}(1/t).
The approximating function has the same initial data and residual in the equation O(1/t²) by q′=O(1/t), q″=O(1/t²); the term proportional to the sine cancels when differentiating the factor q^(−1/4). The same energy bound from any point shows that the homogeneous propagation is bounded in norm, so integrating the residual up to 4t costs O(1/t). By gamma integration or Laplace at ±R, ĥ(0)∼√(2π/t).

For log p>4t, use the shift b=1 of 4346 (also for R≥3b: in r≥R/2 the Jacobian r/√(r²−b²)≤3/√5). That shift and Chebyshev give cost O(exp(2t)/√t Σ_{p>exp(4t)}log p/p^(3/2))=O(1/√t). For log p≤4t the previous Gaussian envelope, Chebyshev on unit intervals and the identity u/2−u²/(8t)=t/2−(u−2t)²/(8t) give the indicated concentration and allow first restricting to |u−2t|≤K√t. There one can replace dθ(exp u) by exp(u)du with error o(exp(t/2)) for each sign: by PNT the difference of primitives is o(exp u) uniformly, and integration by parts against exp(−u/2−u²/(8t))[±Y(u)]_+ costs at most that relative bound times O_K(ĥ(0) exp(t/2)√t), including boundary terms. The positive parts are Lipschitz and |Y′| is bounded.

In that zone q(u)→R₀²−1/4 uniformly. The mean of [±cos φ]_+ over a period is 1/π. It can be replaced by its mean in the integral with error O_K(1) before the factor ĥ(0)exp(t/2): the periodic difference has bounded primitive, φ′=√q≥1, φ″=O(1/t), and the weight exp(−(u−2t)²/(8t)) has bounded variation. As K→∞ the integral of the weight is asymptotic to √(8πt); multiplying the factors gives the announced constant. Finally, the shift b=1/√t gives for the prime powers cost O(t^(−1/2)Σ_{p,k≥2} log p·p^(−k(1/2+1/√t)))=O(1) by Chebyshev at k=2 and absolute convergence for k≥3. No information on the position of zeros was used in this comparison of the two masses.

### Sign and cancellation at larger temperatures outside a sparse set of heights
