Let S(x)=Σ_{n≤x}μ(n)/n and B(x)=xS(x). For each zero ρ there are, in every annulus [Y/√(2log Y),Y√(2log Y)], excursions of B of both signs and magnitude ≫ρ Y^Reρ, for Y sufficiently large (round the integers at the cuts). Indeed, partial summation and Σ μ(n)/n=0 give

    B(x)=M(x)−∫₁^∞ M(xw)dw/w².

The last value of the reciprocal series and the absolute integrability of M(u)/u² are obtained from the quantitative PNT used in 5309. The identity also holds for x<1. Fubini with h or k_ρ is absolute: the integral with |M(xw)| is ≤Cx, and the kernel has a finite absolute first moment. In 5610 the mean of B against h is therefore O(1); in 5636 its mean against k_ρ is

    (F(ρ)/ρ)Y^ρ (1−1/(1−ρ))+Oρ(1).

The previous remainder is uniform for every positive argument. Since 0<Reρ<1, the multiplier is nonzero. Use |k_ρ|≤Cρh and |B(x)|≪x to cut both tails as before. In particular, in each large annulus there are two consecutive prefixes whose values S have opposite signs or one is zero, with nonzero jump. At the second index n one can take a fraction θ=−n S(n−1)/μ(n) of its coefficient to obtain a prefix a^(n) with Σ a^(n)_d/d=0. There is also an integer endpoint with |S|≤1/(2n) by the length of the jump.

In 5762 fix X, R=√(2log X), q=⌈log X⌉. Choose that upper cut n_+=D strictly above Y₀=√(3XR), but with D≤Y₀ polylog X: it suffices to apply the return with centre Y₀ log X. The support of μ−a^(D) begins at D or later; D²>3XR. The convolution identity of 5699 remains exact with this a, since it is algebraic for any sequence. The short term of the hyperbola still cancels, since D≤v/2 throughout the annulus. One obtains T(v) as a pure remainder: the reciprocal mass of a^(D) is exactly zero.

Now take U₀=X/(100qRD) and look for another cut n_−=E in the annulus with centre U₀/log X. Thus E≤U₀ and E≥U₀/polylog X for large X. Form b=a^(D)−a^(E). This sequence lies in [E,D] with the original signs and coefficients throughout its ENTIRE interior. Only its two endpoints may have a fractional coefficient between zero and the original label. One has

    Σ b_d/d=0,   and   T(v)=−Σ_{E≤d,e≤D} b_d b_e G_q(de/v) + O(X^(−2))

uniformly in the annulus. To justify the trimming, first apply the centred kernel of 5714 to a^(D). In each interaction with a^(E) one has v/(de)≥100q, even against any site of the upper cut. Its total cost in the centred kernel is O(X polylog X exp(−4q)). Once a^(D) is replaced by b one can use the complete kernel again by the pointwise identity G_q(x)=1/x−xK_q(1/x)/4 and the new zero reciprocal mass. In particular the indices below the lower cut no longer appear, not even in an external square.

If only integer coefficients are required, ignore the two fractions and keep only the interior. The additional error in the complete form is O(√X polylog X), since there are D=√X polylog X columns, at most two rows and two columns are changed and in this rectangle G_q(de/v)≪1+v/E²≪polylog X. The exact balance and the error O(X^(−2)) correspond to the fractional endpoints. Neither version bounds the remaining sign of the form in the annulus.

### Common cuts suppressing a growing number of reciprocal moments

Fix N=√X, t=log N, k=⌊t^(1/3)⌋, m=k+2 and r=√(100(k+1)t). One can choose two convex mixtures of at most k+3 genuine prefixes each, using the same weights for ALL the moments, so that their difference b satisfies

    |Σ_d b_d (N/d)^j| ≤ N^(−2+o(1))     (−1≤j≤k, j integer).

The support lies between N exp(−O(k log t)) and N exp(O(k log t)); b_d=μ(d) in the central zone between both transition bands, and at the edges it keeps the sign with modulus ≤1. For fixed k the loss of width is only polylogarithmic. Unlike the cut in 5800, the equalities are approximate and there may be many fractional coefficients.

Proof. Write S_j(x)=Σ_{n≤x} μ(n)n^(−j). Take independent variables V_i, −1≤i≤k, with density y^i h(y)dy/(y ξ(i)), positive and normalized by 5610. For each j and x>0 one has the exact identity

    E S_j(x V_j) = (1/ξ(j)) ∫_{1/x}^∞ z^(j−1) f(z) dz.

Expand h into f(ly), integrate from n/x, substitute z=ly and group by nl: μ*1 remains, which only contributes at 1. The sums of moduli converge by the Gaussian from 1/x on for each fixed x. Since |f(z)|≤C z² for all z>0, the error relative to the constant C_j=F(j)/ξ(j) (by continuity where appropriate) is ≤C x^(−j−2)/((j+2)ξ(j)); j=−1 and j=0 are included.

Put W_j=∏_{i≠j} V_i. Conditioning on W_j and then integrating gives error ≤Y^(−j−2) exp(O(k² log(2+k))) for the prefix with endpoint Y∏V_i. Indeed ξ(i)≥c>0 for all indices using the integral over [1,2], and ξ(s)≤exp(O((1+|s|)log(2+|s|))) on the real line by both Gaussian tails. Apply this to E W_j^(−j−2)=∏_{i≠j}ξ(i−j−2)/ξ(i).

Use centres Y_+=N r^(2m) and Y_−=N r^(−6m). Condition the product on the event that ALL its factors lie between r^(−1) and r. The excluded probability is ≤exp(−r²+O(k log(2+k))) by Gaussian domination at both ends and a union bound. To check the error even in the coordinates multiplied by N^j, use |S_j(u)|≤2(1+u²), Cauchy–Schwarz and E(∏V_i)^4≤exp(O(k² log(2+k))). With r as above the error of that conditioning, multiplied by N^j, is O(N^(−3)) uniformly. Also N^j Y_±^(−j−2) exp(O(k² log(2+k)))≤N^(−2+o(1)), since k² log t=o(t). The truncated expectation is a convex combination of vectors of integer prefixes in a finite band; by Carathéodory in dimension m, m+1 suffice. Subtracting the two representations cancels the same constants C_j. The bands, with integer roundings, lie in [N r^m,N r^(3m)] and [N r^(−7m),N r^(−5m)].

To apply this to T(v) use the upper mixture as a in the algebraic identity of 5800. The difference μ−a begins beyond √(3XR), and the short term cancels uniformly. The square of that mixture is negligible: C₁=0, and its reciprocal mass is O(N^(−3+o(1))). On removing the lower mixture, each interaction containing it has z=v/(de)≥r^(2m)/R up to constant factors, and the bound of 5714 against all harmonics costs O(X^(−2)) even with the new upper endpoint N^(1+o(1)). Reintroducing the complete kernel for b costs v|Σ b_d/d|²≤N^(−4+o(1)). The same form still detects each zero with its previous excursions. In particular, every part of its kernel that is a combination of (N/d)^i(N/e)^j, −1≤i,j≤k, with sum of moduli of coefficients N^o(1), contributes only N^(−4+o(1)). The rest of the kernel remains unbounded. It has not been shown that degree k approximates the whole form to root precision in the widened band.

### Adverse test for using the balanced moments while paying the remainder in absolute value

With the same k,m,r,N as in 5822, fix v=X=N² and W=r^(4m). For any combination P(d,e) of (N/d)^i(N/e)^j with −1≤i,j≤k, even with arbitrarily large real coefficients, the sum

    Σ |b_d b_e| |G_q(de/v)−P(d,e)|

admits no power saving over N². Precisely, for each δ>0 and every sufficiently large N it is >N^(2−δ), uniformly in P. It already suffices to restrict e to [.99N,1.01N] and w=N/d to [.1,W]. In both ranges the genuine Möbius coefficients are present by 5822, far from both transition bands. The upper bound of exponent 2 for the infimum is obtained with P=0 from the size of the support and of the kernel.

Suppose a cost ≤N^(2−δ) on that rectangle (δ<1/2 suffices). By the squarefree count, for some squarefree e the row sum is O(N^(1−δ)). Fix an absolute small η>0. Discard the Oη(N^(1−δ)) sites of that row with error >η. The remaining squarefree sites cover the interval in d with mesh Oη(N^(1−δ)+√N), endpoints included: any gap of length H there contains H/ζ(2)+O(√N) squarefree integers. In w the mesh is therefore h≤N^(−δ+o(1)), since W=N^o(1).

Put a=N/e and write p(w) for the Laurent polynomial of the row. At those nodes |p(w)−G_q(1/(aw))|≤η. Since G_q(1/(aw))=aw−K_q(aw)/(4aw) and |K_q|≤1, the ordinary polynomial Q(w)=w p(w)−aw² is bounded by O(1+η W) on the mesh, without any hypothesis on its coefficients. If its degree n=max(2,1+upper degree of p) is ≤W^(1/3), Markov on the interval of length W−.1 gives n² h/W=o(1), transferring that bound to the continuum with a factor ≤2. If it exceeds that threshold the sought degree floor already holds.

Take good nodes near .10,.20,.30,.80. At the first three the kernel is exactly zero: for all 1≤s≤3 one has s a w<1. At the last the kernel has an absolute floor, since on the last half-interval of [Z,Z+1] one has s a w>1 for all Z∈[1,2]. Hence the third divided difference of w p(w) at those nodes has modulus ≥c−Cη, with uniform constants. Subtracting aw² does not change it. By the mean value theorem and Markov applied three times,

    c' ≤ sup |Q'''| ≪ n⁶(1+η W)/W³.

Hence n≳W^(1/3). This contradicts n≤k+1, since W=r^(4(k+2)). The conclusion uses both the specific widening of the band and the exact tent kernel; in 5327 Taylor treated a weight on microcells, with a different geometry.

Since N=√X, the minimal absolute remainder has exponent 1 in X, whereas the sufficient ceiling has exponent 1/2. Even allowing enormous coefficients and discarding a power fraction of bad sites in a row does not rescue the approximation. The lower bound concerns the absolute cost of the remainder. It does not estimate the signed sum with μ(d)μ(e).

### Diagonalization by logarithmic frequencies in the widened band

The obstruction of 5842 changes with the basis. In the same block b of 5822 the complete form has a representation by O(q k loglog X) complex squares, with error O(X^(−1)) uniform in the annulus. There are no products of moments of different frequencies. The squares keep their phase.

Put H(u)=G_q(exp u)−exp(−u). By 5714 and 5737, H(u)=−exp(u)K_q(exp(−u))/4; for u≥log 3 it is exactly −exp(−u). Thus |H(u)|≪exp(−|u|). With the convention M_H(s)=∫H(u)exp(su)du one obtains in −1<Re s<1

    M_H(s)=(1−2^(−s))ζ(s) E[(Z+1)^(s+1)−Z^(s+1)]/[s(s+1)].

In Re s>1 first integrate G_q(exp u) using the count of odd numbers and then integrate t between Z and Z+1. To continue, subtract exp(−u) for u<0 and add the term 1/(s−1); in the interior strip the latter coincides with the integral of −exp(−u)exp(su) over u>0. At s=0 the limiting value −(log 2)/2 is used. For large |τ| integrate q times in the q uniform variables: E(a+ΣV_i)^(1+iτ) is q^q times the forward difference of order q, step 1/q, of a^(q+1+iτ), divided by ∏_{j=2}^{q+1}(j+iτ). For a=1,2 its modulus is ≤3(6q/|τ|)^q. By Euler–Maclaurin of order two, ζ(iτ)=O((1+|τ|)^2) for |τ|≥1. These bounds give, after dividing by the period, a tail of the Fourier series smaller than X^(−5) when cutting at Cq, for example with C=10000 and X sufficiently large.

Take U as a bound for |log(de/v)| over the support and the annulus, with U=O(k loglog X) by 5822. Choose P a multiple of log 2, the smallest exceeding U+log(100q)+log 3+2. In the periodization Σ_l H(u+lP), the copies l≥1 are exactly −exp(−u)/(exp P−1) in total. On summing with b_db_e they produce only −v(Σ b_d/d)^2/(exp P−1), of modulus N^(−4+o(1)). For l≤−1 one has exp(−u−lP)≥100q, and the damping of 5714 bounds the error by O(exp(−4q)) pointwise after summing the geometric progression of the prefactor exp(u+lP). Since Σ|b_d|≤N^(1+o(1)), the negative copies and the Fourier tail cost O(X^(−2)) for large X. Also the difference between G_q and H is the reciprocal term already bounded.

With τ_j=2πj/P and B_j=Σ b_d(d/N)^(iτ_j), one gets

    T(v)=−(1/P) Σ_{|τ_j|≤Cq} M_H(−iτ_j) exp(iτ_j log(X/v)) B_j² + O(X^(−1)).

The periodized series converges absolutely by the tail bound and represents the continuous function. The coefficients have modulus O(1/P) by the integral norm of H. The zero term is negligible by the moment j=0 of 5822. All nonzero τ_j that are multiples of 2π/log 2 can also be suppressed exactly, by the factor 1−2^(−s). The result is a real form on pairing j and −j. Its list of frequencies and all the B_j are common to the whole annulus. Compare with the sampling of 5465: there a second moment of moduli is controlled for a different sieved sum; here the signed form of the balanced block and its explicit Mellin symbol are obtained. The approximation avoids the polynomial barrier of 5842; it remains to estimate the real part of the arithmetic sum of squares with their phases.

### Sublogarithmic one-sided sampling by two moments with the same positive nodes

Let G(w)=exp(−w²/4)/√(4π) and F_X(u)=∫G(w−u)M(X exp w)dw. Use the Gaussian observable instead of interpolating by values of T: an interpolation formula with weights of both signs would not by itself transfer a one-sided ceiling. For large t=log X put l=log√(2t), m=⌈12t/log t⌉ and use the m+1 nodes of Gaussian quadrature for the measure h(exp u)du on [−l,l]. They are the roots of the orthogonal polynomial of degree m+1 for that measure. At EACH large centre, for both orientations separately,

    log(1+max_j (±F_X(u_j))_+) / log X → Θ.

Hence to close the sign a one-sided ceiling X^(1/2+o(1)) on this list along a divergent sequence of centres suffices. The rule is fixed without using zeros or values of M. The sampled values are Gaussian averages in the logarithm: explicitly F_X(u)=Σ μ(n) erfc((log(n/X)−u)/2)/2. The same sampling is not claimed for unaveraged M.

Proof. By 5610 and 5636, the complete integrals of F_X(u) against h(exp u) and k_ρ(exp u) are respectively O(1) and (F(ρ)/ρ) exp(ρ²) X^ρ+Oρ(1). Apply Fubini and average the identities at centres Xexp w against G(w); the error of the second identity is bounded at all positive centres. The absolute interchange follows from |M(x)|≤x and the tails of the kernel. By |k_ρ|≤Cρh and Cauchy–Schwarz, the mean square against h is ≥cρ X^(2Reρ). The estimate |F_X(u)|≤eX exp u shows that outside [−l,l] the integrals with h of |F_X| and of F_X² cost o(1): the Gaussian tail in exp(|u|) contributes exp(−2πt) up to powers of t. Thus the same floor and the ceiling O(1) of the signed mean hold on the interval.

The entire continuation F_X(z) satisfies |F_X(z)|≤eX exp(Re z+(Im z)²/4), by the modulus of G. Taylor at zero, Cauchy on radius √m and l=o(√m) give a real polynomial of degree m with uniform error ≤2eX exp(√m+m/4)(l/√m)^(m+1)=X^(−5+o(1)). Its square approximates F_X² with error o(1) using the trivial ceiling on the interval. The same positive rule is exact for both polynomials, since m+1 nodes integrate up to degree 2m+1. The sum of weights is ≤1/2. Thus both the signed mean O(1) and the quadratic floor are preserved, with error o(1).

To see why this gives BOTH signs at the nodes, put H=max_j |F_X(u_j)|. The classical bound |M(x)|≪ε x^(Θ+ε) and the Gaussian moment give H≤X^(Θ+ε+o(1)). The weighted sum of moduli is at least the sum of squares divided by H. The difference between the positive and negative masses is O(1). For each s<Θ, choose a fixed zero with β=Reρ sufficiently close to Θ and ε>0 with 2β−Θ−ε>max(s,0). Each sign must exceed X^s at some node eventually. The ceiling via H proves the limit. The two-moment argument allows common nodes without adapting the quadrature to any k_ρ, which does depend on a zero. As an antecedent, 1051 gave one-sided sampling via a mesh of step H^(−3) for another prime detector. Here the positivity of a single quadrature, the bounded theta mean and the entire smoothing reduce the list to O(log X/loglog X) unconditionally. The arithmetic ceiling on that list has not been proved.

### One-sided sampling by finite sums of μ, without a Mertens prefix

Let t=log X, l=log√(2t), λ=(log t)^4/t and m=⌈12t/loglog t⌉, for t sufficiently large. Freeze λ throughout the list. Take the m+1 Gauss nodes of 5880 with this new degree. At each node u use Y=X exp u, Gλ(v)=exp(−v²/(4λ))/√(4πλ) and compute

    S(Y)=Σ μ(n) Gλ(log(n/Y)),   |log(n/Y)−2λ|≤3√(λ log Y).

For each orientation one has log(1+max_j (±S(Y_j))_+)/t → Θ. In particular it suffices to bound by X^(1/2+o(1)) the positive part of these sums along a single sequence X→∞. Now the arithmetic input is only integers in finite intervals; the ratio of endpoints in each interval is exp(O((loglog X)^2)). The number of nodes grows somewhat faster than in 5880.

Proof. Before the cut, the sum D(u) is the derivative in u of the average of M(X exp w) against Gλ(w−u), by Stieltjes integration. Integrating D against h(exp u) and kρ(exp u) on the line is equivalent by Fubini to averaging B(X exp w) and I(X exp w) against −Gλ′(w). In 5642 the remainder of I is globally bounded, and so is B. The first mean costs O(λ^(−1/2)); the second equals F(ρ) exp(λρ²) X^ρ+Oρ(λ^(−1/2)), by integration by parts of the exponential mode. For each fixed zero the coefficient tends to F(ρ)≠0. The domination |kρ|≤Cρ h gives the quadratic floor ≫ρ X^(2β). The trivial bound by integration against |Gλ′| is |D(u)|≪λ^(−1/2) X exp u. The tails of both moments for |u|>l still cost o(1) as in 5888.

To justify the quadrature first use the entire average of M. Its modulus at z is bounded by X exp(Re z+λ+(Im z)²/(4λ)); Cauchy for its derivative on a circle of radius √λ gives on |z|=r=√(mλ) the ceiling λ^(−1/2) X exp(r+2+m/4+O(√m)). Since log(r/l)=(1+o(1))loglog t, the Taylor remainder of D on [−l,l] after degree m is ≤exp((−11+o(1))t). This allows squaring and applying the same positive quadrature to both moments with error o(1). The classical bound of M against |Gλ′| gives max|D|≤X^(Θ+ε+o(1)). As in 5892 the quadratic floor divided by that maximum gives an absolute mass of exponent at least 2β−Θ−ε−o(1). Subtracting the polylogarithmic cost of the signed mean recovers both signs.

Finally each discarded tail can be paid for even using |μ|≤1. At both ends the profile is monotone; by sum-integral comparison the discrepancy for the majorant without μ is O(Gλ(2λ±3√(λ log Y))). The continuous integral over each tail is Y exp(λ) erfc(3√(log Y)/2)/2, completing the square in the variable log(n/Y). Thus the total loss is Y^(−5/4+o(1)) uniformly over the nodes. The spectral identity is used before the cut; afterwards this absolute estimate suffices.

Direct internal antecedents: 5465 smooths another detector with the sieved prime factors and 5880 samples a prefix sum with erfc weight. Here differentiating, reducing the variance and jointly adjusting the degree eliminates the prefix and retains both orientations. The signed cancellation inside the bands is still pending.

### Unconditional ceiling for the finite list itself

With the parameters of 5894, t=log X and Q(t)=(log t)^(2/3)(loglog t)^(1/3), there is an absolute c>0 such that, at all nodes and in both orientations,

    |S(Y)| ≤ Y exp(−ct/Q(t)).

This estimate does cancel part of the arithmetic mass of the list. Its mass in moduli is asymptotic to Y exp(λ)/ζ(2): integrate the count Q₂(x)=x/ζ(2)+O(√x) by parts against Gλ(log(x/Y)); the error is O(√Y/√λ) by the moment of |Gλ′| with weight exp(v/2). Removing the tails costs o(1) by 5894.

In the untruncated sum invert the Gaussian on Re s=1+1/t. The integrand, omitting the inversion factor, is Y^s exp(λs²)/ζ(s) by the identity μ*1=δ₁. Cut at height H=t. The Vinogradov–Korobov zero-free region already used in 2414 gives a zero-free rectangle up to height H+2 and from 1−2b/Q(t), with b>0 sufficiently small. In the interior rectangle from 1−b/Q(t) to 1+1/t and up to height H, the reciprocal costs at most exp(O((log t)^2)). Indeed, away from bounded heights use the local expansion of ζ′/ζ over the O(log t) zeros at vertical distance ≤1 and remainder O(log t); each horizontal distance needed when approaching from the left is ≥b/Q(t). Integrate from 1+1/t, where |1/ζ|≤ζ(1+1/t); on the low compact set use continuity of 1/ζ including its zero at 1. This argument for the reciprocal already appears with another width in 593.

The new vertical costs Y exp(−b log Y/Q(t)+O((log t)^2)); log Y=t+O(log t). The horizontals cost O(Y exp(−λH²+O((log t)^2))) and the tail on the original vertical admits the same ceiling by |1/ζ|≤ζ(1+1/t) and the Gaussian integral. Here λH²=t(log t)^4, so these errors and the absolute error of 5894 are absorbed. Reducing b gives the announced c.

The zero-free region mechanism is already indexed; this application quantifies its reach on the exact observable of 5894. The guaranteed exponent 1−c/Q(t) tends to one. It does not exclude any zero of fixed real part less than one.

### Four positive means to test a barrier of exact size at the nodes

For any fixed zero ρ=β+iγ there are four lists with O(log X/logloglog X) nodes in total, on which BOTH signs of the finite sums S of 5894 reach at least cρ X^β for each sufficiently large X. The factor cρ is independent of X. Unlike the limiting exponent in the universal list, here no X^ε is lost and Θ need not be known. The price is that the four lists depend on the zero under test.

Construction. In the variable u, write h₀=h(exp u), k=kρ(exp u), and choose C>0 with |k|≤C h₀ by 5640. For q=Re,Im and η=±1 use the measure h₀+η q(k)/(2C), restricted to [−l,l]. Its density lies between h₀/2 and 3h₀/2. Apply to each one Gaussian quadrature with the degree of 5894. Call A(q,η) the sum of S with those unnormalized positive weights. Then uniformly as X grows,

    A(q,η) = η q(F(ρ) exp(λρ²) X^ρ)/(2C) + Oρ(λ^(−1/2)).

Indeed the identity of 5894 gives this formula for the complete integral of D. Domination by 3h₀/2 allows removing the tails with error o(1). The uniform polynomial approximation of D already proved serves without changing the degree for the four measures; each total mass is ≤3/4. The finite cut for S again costs o(1). This proves the formula without squaring or dividing by an unknown maximum. One of the two coordinates of the complex number has modulus at least its modulus divided by √2, and exp(λρ²)→1. The two choices of η for that same coordinate give means of opposite signs and size ≫ρ X^β. The positivity and bounded mass of the quadrature transfer both bounds to individual values.

Comparison with 5636, 5894 and the positive weights of 1051: the continuous detector and the idea of two orientations have antecedents. The concrete change in the discretization is to incorporate the per-zero kernel components into the positive Gauss measures. In particular an arithmetic proof could now allow dependence on ρ in the constants: to exclude a candidate zero, a ceiling o(X^β) for the positive maxima of its four lists along some divergent sequence would suffice. The formula also shows why proving only a ceiling Oρ(X^β) produces no contradiction.

### One positive measure at dyadic centres and the cost of averaging the phases

Fix a supposed zero ρ=β+iγ and C from 5924. Take ONE measure with density h₀+Re(αk)/(2C), where α=conj(F(ρ))/|F(ρ)|, independent of the scale. Use its positive quadrature and the finite sums of 5894 at the centres X_j=2^j. Denote by A_j its unnormalized mean and by P_j the maximal positive part of S at its nodes. Then, with K=|F(ρ)|/(2C)>0 and θ=γ log 2,

    A_j / 2^(jβ) = K cos(jθ)+oρ(1),       (A_j)_+ ≤ (3/4) P_j.

The first equality is obtained by applying the proof of 5924 to Re(αk); the factor exp(λρ²) tends to 1 and λ^(−1/2)2^(−jβ) tends to zero. The second uses the total mass ≤3/4. Hence there is a fixed integer Lρ such that in EACH block of Lρ sufficiently large dyadic centres one has

    (1/Lρ) Σ P_j / 2^(jβ) ≥ K/5.

Proof without an irrationality hypothesis. For x in [−1,1], x_+≥(x²+x)/2. If exp(iθ)≠1, the mean of cos(jθ) over any block of L indices is O(1/(L|1−exp(iθ)|)), by the geometric sum. If exp(2iθ)≠1, that of its square is 1/2+O(1/(L|1−exp(2iθ)|)); if exp(2iθ)=1 it is exactly 1. Thus the average of the positive part is at least 1/4−oρ(1) as L grows, uniformly in the start of the block. When exp(iθ)=1 it equals 1 at all indices. Choose Lρ to obtain at least 1/5 before applying the factor 4/3, and absorb the oρ(1) into j. This proves the inequality.

Consequence for the arithmetic side: it suffices that, for each candidate, the average of P_j/2^(jβ) tends to zero along some sequence of blocks of consecutive dyadic indices with start and length tending to infinity (split into pieces of Lρ and ignore the rest). Only one measure is used and an exceptional set of centres is allowed if its normalized contribution to the average is small. On the other hand, in the non-resonant case exp(iθ)≠1, the SIGNED average of A_j/2^(jβ) does tend to zero on all those blocks, even under the zero hypothesis: replacing the positive parts by that signed mean would be a false criterion. The dependence of Lρ on the candidate allows phases close to resonance; there is no uniform claim in height. The aliasing antecedent in 2054 concerns multiple fronts; here the kernel of 5640 isolates a single mode before averaging. The one-sided arithmetic ceiling is still missing.

### Which part of the square is paid without cancellation between reduced quotients

In S(Y)² of 5894 write the two integers as da,db, with (a,b)=1. For fixed 0<α<1 and A=Y^α, the ABSOLUTE mass of all terms with max(a,b)≤A has exponent exactly 1+α in Y. More precisely, for A in any interval of powers Y^δ≤A≤Y^(1−δ), it lies between constants times YA/(log Y)^2 and YA. The same floor is already attained on a set of terms of positive sign. Therefore, for any candidate β>1/2, the sector max(a,b)≤Y^(2β−1)/log Y can be removed at cost o(Y^(2β)). To compare with X^(2β) at all nodes, use instead A=X^(2β)/(Y log X). It still falls in the interval of powers because Y=X^(1+o(1)). This cut includes the entire diagonal. For any fixed increase of exponent, payment in moduli fails.

Upper proof. Extend to all positive d and remove the signs and the cuts. The product of the two Gaussians factors into exp(−log²(a/b)/(8λ)) times a Gaussian in log(d√(ab)/Y), of parameter λ/2 and with factor 1/√(8πλ). Comparing the unimodal sum over d with its integral plus twice the maximum gives, apart from the first exponential, O(Y/√(abλ)+1/λ). For b≤a, on [a/2,a] the sum of the exponentials divided by √(ab) is O(1/a+√λ) by comparison with the Gaussian sum in (a−b)/(a√λ). In the blocks a/2^(k+1)<b≤a/2^k, k≥1, the contribution is O(2^(−k/2) exp(−(k log 2)^2/(8λ))) by summing b^(−1/2). Summing over a, doubling and paying the discrete error by A²/λ gives O(YA+Y log(2A)/√λ+A²/λ)=O(YA) in the indicated range.

Genuine floor. Split [A/2,A] into O(1/√λ) cells of length ≤A√λ. By the prime number theorem and Cauchy there are ≫A²√λ/(log A)^2 pairs of distinct primes a,b in the same cell (the removed diagonal costs O(A)). For each pair take d in [Y/a,(1+√λ)Y/a]. There are ≫(Y/A)√λ values that are squarefree and coprime to ab: the elementary formula Q₂(z)=z/ζ(2)+O(√z) gives the density in that interval, and the multiples of a or b cost O((Y/A)√λ/A+1). Both logarithms log(da/Y),log(db/Y) are O(√λ), inside the cut of 5894. Each product of weights is ≫1/λ and each Möbius product equals +1. The reduced representation prevents duplications for ordered pairs. Multiplying the three estimates proves the floor.

The antecedent 4870 controls a different square by signed inversion in the common divisor and uses Θ. Here the upper cost is absolute and the floor uses genuine primes in both cofactors, without hypotheses on zeros or twin primes. At the nodes where a zero would impose S(Y)≥cρ X^β, the signed complement with cofactors larger than the cut must contribute ≫ρ X^(2β). There is no upper estimate of that complement.

### Signed saving when passing the absolute cut of the cofactors

Denote by V_A the SIGNED contribution to the square of 5950 from max(a,b)≤A. For A in [Y^δ,Y^(1−δ)] with fixed δ>0, and every fixed N,

    |V_A| ≪_{δ,N} YA/(log Y)^N + Y^(1/2+o(1)) A^(3/2).

In particular for each 1/2<β<1 and each fixed K one can remove up to A=(X^(2β)/Y)(log X)^K at cost o(X^(2β)), uniformly over the nodes. This crosses the absolute threshold by any fixed power of log X. For the second term, at this cut its exponent with respect to X is 3β−1<2β.

Write w(n)=∏_{p|n}p/(p+1), f(n)=μ(n)w(n). For (a,b)=1 the sum over d carries the indicator μ²(d)1_{(d,ab)=1} multiplied by μ(a)μ(b). Its count up to z is z w(ab)/ζ(2)+O(τ(ab)√z): expand μ² by square divisors and count the remaining integers coprime to ab by inclusion-exclusion; complete the main series with tail O(√z). It also holds for 0<z<1. On integrating by parts against the product of Gaussians of 5950, the error per pair is ≪τ(ab)√Y (ab)^(−1/4)/λ. Indeed, with z=Y exp(v)/√(ab), the moment of exp(v/2) against the modulus of the derivative of exp(−v²/(2λ)) is O(1); the prefactor is O(1/λ). Summing up to A gives the second term. Using uncut Gaussians costs o(1) in the sector: the mass removed in one factor is Y^(−5/4+o(1)) and the other absolute mass is O(Y). The resulting main term is

    Y exp(λ/2)/(ζ(2)√(8πλ)) · Σ_{a,b≤A,(a,b)=1} f(a) f(b) exp(−log²(a/b)/(8λ))/√(ab).

To bound the sum use the representation of the exponential as a mean of (a/b)^(iτ) with τ normal of variance 1/(4λ). Expand the coprimality via divisors e. For each squarefree e the summand after separating factors is μ(e) w(e)^2/e times the mean of the squared modulus of Σ_{n≤A/e,(n,e)=1} f(n)n^(−1/2+iτ). For e>(log Y)^B its total contribution in modulus is O(A/(log Y)^B) by the trivial bound O(√(A/e)). The range |τ|>log Y costs less than any inverse power of Y by λ(log Y)^2≫log Y and the same trivial bound.

For e≤(log Y)^B with B fixed, write f(n)1_{(n,e)=1} as μ*g_e. The quotient of local factors at p∤e is (1−w(p)p^(−s))/(1−p^(−s)), and at p|e it is 1/(1−p^(−s)). Hence Σ|g_e(n)|/n^(3/4)≪(1+e)^C with C absolute (the product outside e converges). The classical Mertens bound |M(x)|≪_J x/(log(2x))^J for every J, convolving and splitting the index of g_e at √x, gives a bound ≪_J (1+e)^C x/(log(2x))^J for the prefix sum. Abel, also splitting off n≤√(A/e) if necessary, gives for the twisted sum the ceiling ≪_J (1+|τ|)(1+e)^C √(A/e)/(log(A/e))^J. Choosing first B and then J sufficiently large absorbs all logarithmic factors, even λ^(−1/2) from the main term. This proves the statement.

Compared with 4870, which already used inversion in the common divisor and the unknown exponent Θ, the estimate here is unconditional at the cut of the candidate β and keeps an explicit density formula in the cofactors. The gain is logarithmic; the remainder with larger cofactors remains open.

### A family of genuine pairs with strictly negative balance

Fix 0<α<1, A=Y^α and L=log A. Inside the square of 5950 take exactly the pairs whose TWO reduced cofactors belong to [A/2,A] and have the form rp with p prime and r∈{1,2,3}. Keep the original weights and ALL admitted common divisors. Their signed contribution W is

    W ∼ −[(log 2)/4+(log 3)/6] YA / [ζ(2) L³].

The positive mass of the prime-prime pairs alone has order YA/L². Here it is compensated within an explicit family that also contains semiprimes and whose balance favours a ceiling. This family can be omitted when majorizing the square even in bands with α>2β−1, beyond the cut of 5960.

Proof. The density substitution of 5960 holds for any subset of pairs of cofactors with the same absolute error O(Y^(1/2+o(1)) A^(3/2))=o(YA/L³). For large A the representation rp is unique. If a=rp,b=sq, the coprimality condition requires (r,s)=1 and p≠q, since p,q>3. In the main expression of 5960, restoring p=q and replacing w(p),w(q) by 1 cost O(Y polylog Y): there are O(A) pairs with equal prime, each with weight O(Y/(A√λ)), and the relative change of weights is O(1/A). The remaining constant factor for passing from summing over primes to integrating in x=rp and y=sq is v_r v_s, where (v₁,v₂,v₃)=(1,−1/3,−1/4) incorporates μ(r)w(r)/r.

By the PNT with remainder O_J(z/(log z)^J) for every J, the continuous density in x is dx/log(x/r) after extracting 1/r. The substitution in the two factors costs o(YA/L³). Indeed in the variables x/A,y/A∈[1/2,1] the kernel (ab)^(−1/2) exp(−log²(a/b)/(8λ)) and its partial derivatives of orders (0,0),(1,0),(0,1),(1,1) cost O(A^(−1)(1+λ^(−2))). A Stieltjes integration by parts in each variable absorbs this polylogarithmic loss and the prefactor λ^(−1/2) by taking J sufficiently large.

Write C_rs=1_{(r,s)=1}. Then Cv=(5/12,3/4,2/3), and vᵀCv=0. On expanding 1/log(x/r) in powers of 1/L, the terms depending on log(x/A) and log(y/A) at order L^(−3) also vanish by that same identity. Uniformly on the square there remains

    Σ C_rs v_r v_s / [log(x/r) log(y/s)] = −[(log 2)/2+(log 3)/3]/L³ + O(L^(−4)).

Finally the double integral of the kernel exp(−log²(x/y)/(8λ))/√(8πλxy) over [A/2,A]² is (1+o(1))A/2: after scaling by A and putting y=x exp u, the Gaussian density in u tends to the point mass at zero, with factor exp(u/2) and the indicator of the interval. The boundary has measure zero and the Gaussian moment is bounded. Multiplying by Y exp(λ/2)/ζ(2) proves the asymptotic. For prime-prime alone, the same computation keeps coefficient 1 at order L^(−2).

The ceiling of the complement does not follow from the balance of this sector. The novelty relative to using the PNT for a bound in moduli is that the coprimality and the densities of the multipliers 1,2,3 exactly cancel the first term and determine the sign of the next.

### Persistence with a growing primorial and change of sign on completing the factor 6

In the band of 5978 take L=log A, z=L/10 and P=∏_{5≤q≤z, q prime}q. Admit in each cofactor all numbers rdp with d|P, r in R={1,2,3} and p prime >z. Let W_R be the joint contribution of those pairs. With H=∏_{q|P}(1−2/(q+1)) and c₀=(log 2)/4+(log 3)/6, one has

    W_{1,2,3} ∼ −c₀ H YA/(ζ(2)L³).
    W_{1,2,3,6} ∼ H YA/(12ζ(2)L²).

Here H≍1/(log z)². The first result simultaneously admits any subset of all primes between 5 and z in each multiplier, whose number of possible factors grows without bound. The second result completes the same family by allowing 6 in either coordinate. The additional joint contribution changes the sign and exceeds the initial negative balance by a factor of order L.

Proof. By PNT, 6P≤A^(1/4) eventually, so the prime p completing the cofactor is unique and ≫A^(3/4). Use the density of 5960 with the same absolute error. For each multiplier m=rd the continuous weight is v_m=μ(m)w(m)/m, with denominator log(x/m). The rows and columns carry the matrix C_mn=1_{(m,n)=1}. At each prime q|P there are two options, 1 and q, and only the pair (q,q) is excluded. Its factor in the quadratic sum of coefficients is 1−2/(q+1). The condition (r,s)=1 is treated in a separate block. In R={1,2,3} the main contribution is zero by 5978; in the next coefficient any insertion of log d or of log(x/A) remains multiplied by that zero, whereas inserting log r gives exactly the coefficient of 5978 times H. For complete R the block of 2 and 3 factors and equals (1−2/3)(1−2/4)=1/6. Mertens and the convergence of Σ_q q^(−2) give the estimate of H.

Uniform details. The sum of |v_m| is O(log z) by Euler product. With weights proportional to |v_d| the inclusions of q are independent, with probability 1/(q+2); by Chebyshev and partial summation the mean of log d is O(log z) and its second moment is O((log z)²). For x in [A/2,A], log(x/m)≥L/2 eventually. The expansion of the two denominators up to L^(−3) has remainder ≤C(1+log²m+log²n)/L⁴. Summed in modulus it costs O((log z)^4/L⁴)=o(H/L³). Thus even the small negative term is preserved.

In replacing the prime sums by integrals, the counting discrepancy in the coordinate x/A costs O_J(A/(m L^J)) before normalizing, uniformly in m. The proof by parts of 5978 is summed with the weights 1/m, whose sum is O(log z), and the derivatives of the kernel cost only powers of L. Replacing w(p) by 1 has relative error in moduli O(A^(−3/4)) against a gross mass O(YA polylog Y). Coincidences of the large prime cost O(Y A^o(1)) since there are at most O(A) primes, 2^ω(P)=A^o(1) choices of d and each pair weighs O(Y/(A√λ)) in the density. These errors and that of 5960 are negligible at the scale YA H/L³. Integrating the kernel as in 5978 gives both asymptotics.

Scope. The negative sign is indeed stable when introducing new primes via the complete set of their squarefree divisors specified here. Completing the only incomplete local block, that of 2 and 3, restores a positive main term. Therefore extending this cancellation simply by completing the multipliers does not by itself produce the global ceiling.

### Recovering a negative balance including 6 via semiprimes with an adjusted cut

Fix 0<α<1, A=Y^α, L=log A, η=1/(1+exp(1)). Let U=log v for v uniform on [1/2,1], b=E U+log 2+(log 3)/2 and B=exp(η(L+b)). In each reduced cofactor of [A/2,A] admit all numbers m n with m|6 and n a prime >B or a product of two DISTINCT primes >B. Thus 6 is included completely. The signed contribution W of the pairs of this sector satisfies

    W ∼ YA [Var U−(log 2)²−(log 3)²/4] / [12 ζ(2) (1−η)² L⁴].

The coefficient is strictly negative: Var U≤(log 2)²/4 by the range of U. This reverses the positive sign of the single-large-prime sector with the same four multipliers. It does not include three large primes.

Proof of the density. For n of size comparable to A, the one-prime list contributes signed density −1/log n. For two primes, order the smaller p first and replace the prime counts by the PNT integrals. The density obtained is ∫_B^√n dp/[p log p log(n/p)]. Integrating in log p, the sum of the two densities is

    D(n)=[log((log n−log B)/log B)−1]/log n.

More precisely, on any subinterval of the range [A/12,A] the counting discrepancy relative to this integral is O_J(A/L^J) for each fixed J. In the cumulative count of pairs use Σ_{B<p≤√n}(π(n/p)−π(p)); the PNT with arbitrary saving of logarithms allows replacing the inner sum with error O_J(n/L^J), since p,n/p≥B and Σ_{B<p≤√n}1/p=O(1). For the outer one, integrate by parts the weight li(n/p)−li(p), vanishing at √n, with derivative O((n/p²+1)/L); the error of π(p) costs O_J(n/L^J) by increasing the initial saving by one order. The derivative of the continuous integral has no boundary term at √n by the same vanishing. This justifies the density even after integrating against the kernel of 5960 by the derivative bounds of 5978. The factors w of the large primes can be replaced by 1 at cost O(YA polylog(Y)/B). Excluding pairs with a common large prime costs the same order: there are at most Σ_{k>B}^{A}⌊A/k⌋²≪A²/B possible pairs counting multiplicity, each density weight is O(Y/(A√λ)). The small coprimality is preserved exactly. The density substitution in the common divisor has the error of 5960, also o(YA/L⁴).

At x=Av, n=x/m, the numerator of D vanishes at log n=L+b. Uniform Taylor for m|6, 1/2≤v≤1 gives D(x/m)=(log v−log m−b)/[(1−η)L²]+O(L^(−3)). The Jacobian and the factors of m leave the same v_m=μ(m)w(m)/m as in 5998. The normalized Gaussian in log(x/y) tends to the diagonal as in 5978; the rescaled profiles are bounded and converge uniformly. It remains to average the product of the two linear factors over a single variable U, with weights 1_{(m,m′)=1}v_m v_m′.

The total of these weights is 1/6. Normalize them algebraically to mass one. For each prime q=2,3 the only divisibility configurations between m,m′ are (0,0),(1,0),(0,1), with weights proportional to 1,−1/(q+1),−1/(q+1). Each indicator has mean −1/(q−1); the product of the two at the same prime is zero. The configurations of distinct primes factor. Hence the mean of log m is −log 2−(log 3)/2 and the signed covariance of log m and log m′ is −(log 2)²−(log 3)²/4. By the choice of b the average of the normalized product gives exactly the announced bracket. Multiplying by the length A/2, the mass 1/6 and the density prefactor proves the asymptotic. The negativity comes from excluding the same prime in both cofactors, after cancelling the main density of primes against semiprimes.

### Completing all the large primes restores a positive balance for every fixed power cut

In 6015 now admit in n ALL squarefree products of primes >B, keeping m|6 and x=mn in [A/2,A]. For any B with log B/log A→η fixed in (0,1), the contribution W of this sector to the square is

    W ∼ YA D(1/η−1)² / [12 ζ(2)(log A)²] > 0,

where D is the Dickman function, defined by D=1 on [0,1] and uD′(u)=−D(u−1) for u>1. At the threshold of 6015, 1/η=1+e lies strictly between 3 and 4: it suffices to incorporate the pairs in which at least one cofactor has three large primes to reverse the balance. For any other fixed exponent the leading coefficient of the complete sector cannot be tuned to zero either.

Proof. Put h=log B, k(v)=1_{v≥1}/v and g(u)=Σ_{j≥1}(−1)^j k^{*j}(u)/j!, a locally finite sum (additive convolution). In the continuous approximation dp/log p, each prime p=B^v has measure exp(hv)k(v)dv. After taking the product of j primes, the common exponential factor is the product itself, so the density with respect to the real product n is k^{*j}(log n/h)/h. Dividing by j! orders the distinct tuples and μ contributes the sign. To justify the passage from the prime sums on any subinterval, only a bounded number of factors depending on η intervenes. Replace one coordinate at a time by the PNT integral, fixing the product d of the others: its interval has endpoints between B and A/d and the error is O_J(A/(d L^J)), L=log A. Integrating or summing 1/d over those coordinates costs O_η(1), since Σ_{B<p≤A}1/p and its integral analogue are bounded. Tuples with repetitions cost O_η(A/B) in the count, by divisors p² and bounded multiplicity. The atom n=1 falls outside the interval. Collisions between coordinates of the two cofactors, the weights w(p) and the integration against the Gaussians are handled as in 6015, with errors o(YA/L²).

The sign of the complete density is decided without numerical approximation. By symmetry u k^{*j}=j (1_{[1,∞)}*k^{*(j−1)}), with zeroth power equal to the mass at 0. For u>1 this gives u g(u)=−[1+∫₀^{u−1}g(v)dv]. Then D(u)=1+∫₀^u g is precisely the above function. Integrating the equation gives uD(u)=∫_{u−1}^u D(v)dv for u≥1 (equality at 1 and equal derivatives). A first zero would be impossible because that integral would be strictly positive. Hence g(u)=−D(u−1)/u<0 for each u>1.

Uniformly for m|6 and x in the band, g(log(x/m)/h)/h=−[D(1/η−1)+o(1)]/L. The continuity used here also holds when 1/η is an integer greater than 1. In the square, the product of both densities has positive coefficient. The coprimality matrix of the divisors of 6 gives 1/6, and the integrated kernel gives A/2, as in 6015. This proves the asymptotic for the original arithmetic weights.

The Dickman function is classical; the conclusion here is the quantitative obstruction for the exact family of 6015. The Buchstab computation in 905 and 932 sums convolutions without these alternating signs. This result concerns fixed η: a cut with η→0 would require uniform estimates against the decay of D and the growth of the number of factors. For a fixed cut, a compensation at root size must involve the complement of the complete sector.

### Nested moving cuts: signed compensation of almost all the previous balance

Write L=log A and fix c>0. Put U=c log L/loglog L, h=L/U and B_c=exp(h). Keep m|6 and all squarefree products of primes greater than B_c, with both cofactors in [A/2,A]. The balance W_c of this sector in the genuine square satisfies, for A=Y^α, 0<α<1 fixed,

    W_c ∼ YA D(U−1)²/[12 ζ(2)L²] = YA L^(−2−2c+o(1)).

Hence for c₂>c₁>0 the sectors are nested and the balance of ALL the added pairs is W_c₂−W_c₁ ∼ −W_c₁. The positive residue relative to the previous one is L^(−2(c₂−c₁)+o(1)). The claim includes the mixed pairs, with only one of the cofactors newly admitted.

Arithmetic uniformity. In the tuple approximation of 6033 keep the divisor j! in all errors. On [B_c,A] both the prime sum of reciprocals and the integral of reciprocals against dx/log x are bounded by H=log U+O(1), by Mertens. For an interval of products, replacing one coordinate at a time gives total discrepancy, summing over j, at most O_J(A h^(−J) Σ_{j≥1} j H^(j−1)/j!)=O_J(A h^(−J) U). The PNT is applied at both endpoints ≥B_c of each nonempty section. For repeated tuples already divided by j!, the mass of each integer is ≤1 because the number of its orderings is ≤j! and its number of factors determines j. Then the repetition error costs O(A/B_c) by multiples of squares. The discrepancy is O_K(A/L^K) for every fixed K. The continuous masses in moduli are O(A exp H) by the reciprocal majorant, and the discrete mass is O(A). Thus the integration by parts in the two coordinates and the derivative bounds in 5978 preserve precision O_K(YA/L^K) for every K. The errors from shared primes and from w are negligible at that scale: each integer has ≤U large factors and B_c grows faster than any power of L. The error of the common-divisor density of 5960 saves a power of Y.

Uniformity of the main term. The integral identity of 6033 and the decrease of D give D(v)≤D(v−1)/v. For large v and ε=1/log v one has, for 1≤s≤v, D(s)≥(ε/v)D(s−1+ε), integrating only the first stretch of length ε. Iterating the two bounds gives log D(v)=−(1+o(1))v log v. In particular D(U−1)=L^(−c+o(1)). For |s−(U−1)|≤1/2, the logarithmic derivative in modulus D(s−1)/(sD(s)) is L^o(1), by the same estimates at both arguments, uniformly by monotonicity. Now log(x/m)/h differs from U by O(U/L) for m|6. Integrating the bound on the logarithmic derivative shows that the complete continuous density is −(1+o(1))D(U−1)/L uniformly in the band. The coprime sum over m keeps the coefficient 1/6 and the kernel the length A/2. Taking K>3+2c in the previous errors concludes the proof.

The compensation of the added sector is arithmetic and one-sided. The remainder W_c, although it is reduced by any prescribed LOGARITHMIC power by choosing c, still has exponent 1+α with respect to Y. This proof is not uniform when c grows with A up to the scales needed to save a power of Y.

### Residual fraction smaller than every inverse power of log A at two explicit cuts

In 6049 now put Z=L^(3/8)(log L)^(1/4) and U=κ Z/log L, with κ>0 fixed sufficiently small. With B=exp(L/U), the COMPLETE sector of cofactors m n, m|6, P⁻(n)>B, in [A/2,A] still satisfies

    W_κ ∼ YA D(U−1)²/[12ζ(2)L²],
    log(W_κ/(YA)) = −(3κ/4+o(1)) Z.

For 0<κ₁<κ₂ sufficiently small, the enlargement cancels everything except a fraction exp(−(3(κ₂−κ₁)/4+o(1))Z) of the initial balance. This is a gain larger than any fixed power of log A, but Z=o(log A).

Proof. Use the classical Vinogradov–Korobov PNT remainder, |π(x)−li(x)|≪x exp(−c(log x)^(3/5)/(loglog x)^(1/5)). In each section ≥B of the coordinate substitution of 6049 the maximal relative loss is E=exp(−c h^(3/5)/(log h)^(1/5)), h=L/U. Summing over the numbers of factors, the total cost in counting is O(A U E), by the same factor j/j! and the reciprocal mass log U+O(1). In the two-coordinate integration against the kernel, the mass of the measures and the rescaled derivatives cost only fixed powers of L. Hence the PNT error in W is O(YA L^C E). The costs of repeated squares, shared primes and weights w are O(YA L^C/B) by increasing C, and the density estimate of 5960 saves a fixed power of Y.

For the continuous density RELATIVE precision in D is needed even though D is now much smaller than every inverse power of L. By the positive integral identity, D(v)≥D(v−1/2)/(2v) for v≥1. Using it twice gives D(v−1)/D(v)≤4v² for v≥2 and by the differential equation |(log D)′(v)|≤4v. The change O(U/L) in the argument across the band and the four multipliers alters the logarithm of D by O(U²/L)=o(1). The density and the factor 1/6 transfer with relative error o(1).

By 6049, log D(U−1)=−(1+o(1))U log U=−(3κ/8+o(1))Z. Meanwhile h^(3/5)/(log h)^(1/5)∼(8/5)^(1/5)κ^(−3/5) Z. Choose κ so small that the constant in the exponent of the error E exceeds 3κ/4 by a fixed margin. Thus the PNT error, even after the polylogarithmic losses, is o of the main term. The other errors are too. This proves both statements.

Quantitative limitation of this particular estimate. To obtain a fixed gain A^(−δ) via the profile D one would need U log U of order L. That forces h=L/U of order log L. In that range, paying separately for the PNT error in each coordinate with the ceiling E above no longer certifies an error of order exp(−δ L). No lower bound on the effective error has been proved: there could be cancellation between the substitutions for different numbers of factors.

### Completing the band down to the prime 3 without replacing the prime counts

In the band [A/2,A]² of reduced cofactors, A=Y^α, 0<α<1 fixed, let W(B) be the exact balance with cofactors m n, m|6, P⁻(n)>B, including the weights and cuts of 5894. For fixed C, uniformly in 3≤B≤(log A)^C,

    |W(B)| ≪ YA exp(−c L^(3/5)/(log L)^(1/5)),    L=log A,

with c>0 which may depend on α,C. For B=3 every squarefree pair of the band enters. In particular the balance added from the cut of 6063 to the WHOLE band is asymptotic to the negative of W_κ, with residual fraction in modulus ≤ exp(−c′ L^(3/5)/(log L)^(1/5)). No sign is assigned to the residue.

Uniformity lemma. Let F=L^(3/5)/(log L)^(1/5). For an integer q≤Y^4, removing from μ the primes ≤B and the prime divisors of q is equivalent to convolving μ with the indicator of the integers supported on that set of primes P. For x with log x between L/3 and 2L, the resulting prefix sum is O(x exp(−c₁F)), uniformly in q,B. Indeed take δ=F/L. One has ∏_{p∈P}(1−p^(−1+δ))^(−1)≤L^O(1): up to L^K with K>max(C,3) use p^δ≤2 and Mertens; above that only divisors of q intervene and there are O(L) possible primes, each of weight O(L^(−K(1−δ))). In the convolution, for auxiliary divisors v≤√x use the Mertens bound of 5309 at x/v and sum the reciprocals; for v>√x pay by moduli with Σ 1/v≤x^(−δ/2)∏(1−p^(−1+δ))^(−1). Both ranges give the lemma.

To apply the lemma keep the EXACT sum over d=gcd of the two original indices. By the finite cut there are O((Y/A) exp(O((log L)^2))) possible d. For cofactors a=m n and a′=m′n′ fix m,m′|6 coprime to each other and to d, and omit non-squarefree d. The remaining condition (n,n′)=1 is expanded by Σ_{e|n,n′} μ(e); write n=e k and n′=e k′. The large factors of e must exceed B, and (e,d)=1. Each separated sum in k carries μ(k), excludes the primes ≤B and those of de, and is restricted to [A/(2me),A/(me)] with the Gaussian weight in log(dmek/Y) and the original cut. The extracted Möbius constants have modulus ≤1. For e≤√A, the endpoints have logarithm between L/3 and 2L eventually; also de≤Y^4. The cut weight has variation and supremum O(λ^(−1/2)), by unimodality. Abel and the lemma give O(λ^(−1/2)(A/e)exp(−c₁F)) per sum, including any subinterval of the support. For e>√A the trivial bound is O(λ^(−1/2) A/e), since e≤A. After multiplying both sums, summing e via Σ e^(−2) and then d, the total cost is O(YA exp(O((log L)^2)) λ^(−1)(exp(−2c₁F)+A^(−1/2))). This implies the bound. Since F/Z→∞ relative to the exponent Z of 6063, it gives the claim about the complement.

The dependence on Mertens marks the scope: for the complete band the saving is still subpower. Unlike 6063, here the exact balance is controlled down to the endpoint B=3, including all intermediate primes. The global sum has not been controlled at root scale.

### Reconstruction without sieving the integers: minimal weights for sharing 2 and 3

Keep the Gaussian weights of 5894 BEFORE the cut, freezing λ across all shifts. Let D_λ(x)=Σ μ(n)Gλ(log(n/x)). Form C_λ(x,y) as the product of those two sums, weighting each pair by θ(gcd(n,m)), with θ multiplicative on squarefree numbers. Take θ_p=0 for p≥5, θ₂=2√2−2, θ₃=2√3−3. No integer is removed from the input sums. Only the common divisors 1,2,3,6 are allowed. There are coefficients h(i,j)≥0 independent of the Gaussian such that

    D_λ(Y)² = Σ h(i,j) C_λ(Y/i,Y/j),
    Σ h(i,j)/(ij)^σ < ∞ for EVERY σ>1/2.

The two weights are the smallest possible, coordinate by coordinate, among the multiplicative weights 0≤θ_p≤1 that allow such a formal inversion with finite norm throughout that region. This quantifies the obstruction of the small primes to extending 4880, which removed them from the input integers.

Indeed, in the formal variables u,v of a prime, the quotient of the two factors is

    (1−u)(1−v)/(1−u−v+θ_p uv) = 1+(1−θ_p)uv/(1−u−v+θ_p uv).

The reciprocal of the denominator has nonnegative coefficients by the geometric expansion around (1−u)(1−v), subtracting (1−θ_p)uv. Evaluated at u=v=r=p^(−σ) it converges if (1−θ_p)r²<(1−r)². For p≥5 this holds down to σ=1/2 and the factor differs from 1 by O_σ(p^(−2σ)). For p=2,3 and every σ>1/2 it is equivalent, taking the limit at the boundary, to θ_p≥2√p−p. If any of these weights is decreased, the denominator vanishes at some r<1/√p, with nonzero numerator. Already the single formal factor of that prime prevents the required norm. The case θ_p=1 has quotient identically 1. The product of the series gives the identity coefficient by coefficient. The substitution into the Gaussians converges absolutely, for example by majorizing each weight Gλ(log(n/x)) by a λ-dependent constant times (x/n)^2 and using the norm at σ=2.

One-sided consequence for the finite lists. For each σ>1/2 it would suffice that along a sequence X→∞, for all its nodes Y of 5894 and all integer shifts i,j, one had C_λ(Y/i,Y/j)≤X^o(1)(Y²/(ij))^σ with uniform loss (it may depend on σ). Summing against h one obtains |D_λ(Y)|≤X^(σ+o(1)); the cut of 5894 transfers the ceiling to S. Take σ arbitrarily close to 1/2 and apply the detection at each centre. One may restrict to i,j≤X² with error o(1) in the reconstruction: the previous Gaussian majorant with fixed exponent k has constant O(λ^(−1/2) exp(k²λ)). In the coordinate with i>X² use k=6 and extract i^(−4)≤X^(−8); in the other use 2. The bound Y^8 X^(−8) alone does not suffice, but with k=8 the same computation gives Y^10 X^(−12)=X^(−2+o(1)), and the norm at σ=2 remains. This reduction covers pairs between different bands; the arithmetic ceiling of C is still pending. The optimality concerns only the specified positive multiplicative inversion.

### Cost at root exponent and power tolerance in unequal rectangles

In the inversion of 6094 one may concede a power loss in the ratio of sides without paying for it in the final exponent. Allow the common divisors 2 and 3 without penalty (θ₂=θ₃=1), keeping θ_p=0 for every p≥5. The support of common divisors is still exactly {1,2,3,6}. Put b₅=log((1+√5)/2)/log 5. For the new h, the rectangles i,j≤R satisfy, with r=max(i/j,j/i),

    Σ h(i,j) r^b /√(ij) ≪_b log(2R)              (0≤b<b₅),
    Σ h(i,j) r^b₅/√(ij) ≪ (log(2R))².

Therefore a bound C_λ(x,y)≤X^o(1)√(xy) max(x/y,y/x)^b₅ at the finite shifts of 6094, with uniform o(1), would suffice. It is a genuine power tolerance for sides of different scales, keeping the root target on the reconstructed square. The sum of shifts outside the trimming is still o(1) by the same moment of order 2. The arithmetic ceiling on the rectangles remains open.

Proof. In the Euler norm evaluate u=p^(−1/2−s+b), v=p^(−1/2−s−b) for s>0 and also use the symmetric orientation, whose sum dominates r^b. For p=2,3 the factor is 1. For p≥5 it equals 1+uv/(1−u−v). At s=0 the critical condition is p^(−1/2+b)+p^(−1/2−b)≤1. Since b<1/2, the left-hand side decreases in p; equality at 5 is equivalent to 5^b+5^(−b)=√5 and gives b=b₅. For p≥7, after extracting the factor (1−p^(−1−2s))^(−1), the remaining product converges uniformly down to s=0: each correction is O_b(p^(−1−(1/2−b))), apart from finitely many bounded factors. This costs O_b(1/s) by ζ(1+2s). The prime 5 costs O_b(1) in the interior and O(1/s) at the boundary by 1−5^(−s). Take s=1/log(2R) and use (ij)^s≤exp(2). For b>b₅ the factor of the prime 5 alone diverges for some s>0 near zero (or one of u,v≥1); no polylogarithmic bound in R can survive, since by dyadic summation it would imply convergence for every s>0.

With the minimal weights of 6094 and b=0 the truncated cost is instead of order (log(2R))³. Indeed as s↓0 the complete norm at σ=1/2+s is asymptotic to K/s³, K>0: the factors of 2 and 3 have simple poles by differentiation of the denominator and the others give ζ(1+2s) times a positive convergent product. The truncated ceiling is deduced as before. For the floor, take s=M/log R with M fixed and large. The mass of ij>R in the damped norm is ≤exp(−M/2) times the norm at s/2; the ratio between both norms tends to 8. Thus a positive fraction remains on ij≤R, contained in the square. With these minimal weights any b>0 already breaks the threshold at 2, since u+v increases strictly and uv does not change when tilting the exponents. The change of weights therefore has a verifiable effect on the tolerance of the criterion.

### The larger side suffices with a moving cut of common primes; optimal cost

Put R=X², t=log R and z=log t. In 6094 leave all common primes ≤z unpenalized and exclude the larger ones (θ_q=1 or 0 respectively); freeze this cut for all shifts. Denote the positive coefficients by h_z. For p the smallest prime >z,

    log Σ_{i,j≤R} h_z(i,j)/min(i,j) ∼ t/(p log p).

This costs R^o(1). Consequently a one-sided ceiling C_{λ,z}(x,y)≤X^o(1) max(x,y) on the finite rectangles of 6094 along a sequence suffices for each precision scale X^ε (or directly with uniform subpower loss along a sequence). Indeed max(Y/i,Y/j)=Y/min(i,j). The cost outside the trimming is uniform: on passing from θ=0 to θ=1, local factors with nonnegative coefficients disappear, so the norm at 2 is majorized by that of 6111. On the diagonal the requirement is still the root scale on each side of the product. Rectangles with smaller side ≤exp(√log X) already satisfy the pointwise ceiling, since Σ_n Gλ(log(n/x))≪x/√λ uniformly by integrating the count ⌊n⌋≤n against the derivative in modulus. Thus |C|≪xy/λ.

Proof of the cost. By symmetry it suffices to estimate the sum with weight 1/j: it lies between half and all of the stated sum. Fix ε>0 and s=(1+ε)/(p log p). In the first variable introduce i^(−s), paying R^s. For q≥p the local factor is 1+q^(−1−s)/(1−q^(−s)−1/q). The denominator is ≥c_ε min(s log q,1): at q=p one has (1/p)/(1−p^(−s))→1/(1+ε) and that quotient decreases in q. Hence the logarithm of the product is O_ε(1/s+log(1/s)+1), by Σ_q 1/(q log q)<∞ and log ζ(1+s)=O(1+log(1/s)). Since p∼z by PNT, this cost is o(t/(p log p)). The ceiling is obtained with constant 1+ε in the exponent.

For the floor use ONLY powers of the first excluded prime. For k=⌊t/log p⌋ and 1≤l≤k, one has h_z(p^k,p^l)=binom(k+l−2,l−1)≥binom(k−1,l−1), by the factor uv/(1−u−v). The sum with weight 1/p^l is ≥(1+1/p)^(k−1)/p. Its logarithm is (1+o(1))t/(p log p). Letting ε↓0 proves the asymptotic. In particular any fixed cut of this type would require a power loss for this norm, already by the same floor with p fixed. On the other hand any cut tending to infinity allows subpower loss by monotonicity and the Euler bound with any fixed s>0 once the first prime exceeds a threshold depending on s.

This improves the tolerance in the geometry relative to 6111 at the price of admitting common divisors formed by small primes up to z. The optimal cost characterizes the reconstruction; it does not by itself give a bound for the arithmetic balance when both sides are large.

### At a maximum of a finite list, common divisors of bounded size suffice

For each 1/2<σ<1 and each δ>0 there is a fixed K=K(σ,δ) such that the square of the sum at a selected scale is preserved, with relative error ≤δ, counting only pairs with gcd≤K. Here the VALUE of the common divisor is limited, even if all its primes are small. The selection uses only finite sums of μ without sieving. It does not require rectangles with different sides.

Fix X and the universal nodes Y_j of 5894. For ALL descendants x=Y_j/k use the same profile φ(v)=Gλ(v)1_{|v|≤4√(λ log X)}. Denote D(x)=Σ μ(n)φ(log(n/x)). At the original nodes the difference from the uncut detector is o(1), by the sum-integral comparison of 5894 (the cut contains the one with coefficient 3 for large X). The common profile allows exact dilations even after the cut. Put M=max |D(x)|/x^σ over all lists x=Y_j/k, k an integer ≥1, and choose a maximizer x*. It suffices to take k≤max_j Y_j exp(4√(λ log X)), because beyond that all sums vanish. If M=0 the claim about the square is trivial.

Let B_d(x) be the contribution of multiples of d to D(x). It vanishes if d is not squarefree. Otherwise
    B_d(x)=μ(d) Σ_{h: p|h ⇒ p|d} D(x/(dh)).
This is the convolution identity for μ with the primes of d removed; the dilations at x* remain in the list. Hence |B_d(x*)|≤M (x*)^σ ∏_{p|d}(p^σ−1)^(−1). For the contribution E_d of the pairs with gcd EXACTLY d, inclusion-exclusion gives E_d=Σ_e μ(e)B_{de}(x*)². Summing in moduli from d>K on one obtains

    Σ_{d>K}|E_d| ≤ D(x*)² Σ_{k>K, k squarefree} τ(k) ∏_{p|k}(p^σ−1)^(−2).

The complete series has finite product ∏_p(1+2/(p^σ−1)²). Thus the announced fixed K exists; the tail is even O_{σ,η}(K^(−η)) for 0<η<2σ−1, inserting k^η into the product. The approximation is relative to the REAL signal of the maximum, without using Θ for the error.

If there is a zero of abscissa β>σ, choose σ<s<β. The detection of 5894 and the common cut imply M≥X^(s−σ−o(1)) for every large X. Moreover x* grows at least like a positive power of X: by the absolute majorant |D(x)|≪x/√λ of the previous subsection, (x*)^(1−σ)≫M√λ. Take δ=1/2. At least one of the K common-divisor classes contributes ≥D(x*)²/(2K). Consequently, for each σ, a one-sided ceiling O_σ((x*)^(2σ) X^o(1)) for the sum of those K classes at the single selected maximum, along a divergent sequence of X, would suffice. It would exclude every β>σ. Each class is computed on a single diagonal; after dividing by d they are strictly coprime pairs with both indices coprime to d. Even removing the terms with equal indices the detection conclusion is preserved, since in the first K classes they can only be (d,d), outside the support at x* for large X.

The antecedents 4870 and 4890 already control large divisors in Möbius tails and use contraction. The change here is to obtain an absolutely summable tail of exact CLASSES, with prescribed relative error at a finite maximum of the unsieved detector and K independent of X. The ceiling of the small classes at that maximum has not been proved.

### A single statistic of exact classes recovers the spectral distance to the line

Prescribe any integer K=K(X)→∞ with log K=o(log X), however slowly it grows. Put ε=1/√log K, σ_X=1/2+ε for X sufficiently large, and select x* as in 6138 with this moving exponent. σ is not chosen according to a candidate zero. For the exact balances E_d at that centre define

    V(X)=max_{1≤d≤K}(E_d)_+ / x*.

With Θ=sup Reρ one has unconditionally

    log(1+V(X))/log X → 2Θ−1.

Consequently the ceiling V(X)≤X^o(1) along a divergent sequence suffices, with a single protocol selected in advance. If Θ>1/2, the selected scale moreover satisfies log x*/log X→1. The maximum uses an exponent tending to 1/2; the same relative approximation is not claimed for the maximum defined exactly with 1/2.

Uniform control of classes. Insert k^ε into the majorant of 6138. Each prime term k=p of the product becomes 2 p^(−1−ε)(1−p^(−1/2−ε))^(−2). Its difference from 2 p^(−1−ε) is O(p^(−3/2)) uniformly, including the first primes with an absolute constant. Thus the product is O(ζ(1+ε)^2)=O(ε^(−2)). The tail of absolute balances beyond K is ≤ O(ε^(−2) exp(−√log K)) D(x*)²=o(D(x*)²). The total of moduli, without cut, is bounded by O(ε^(−2))D(x*)². Hence, when the maximum is nonzero,

    (1−o(1)) D(x*)²/(K x*) ≤ V(X) ≤ O(ε^(−2)) D(x*)²/x*.

To verify the exponent even if x* could be small, every point with D(x)≠0 satisfies x≥exp(−4√(λ log X))=X^(−o(1)). The classical Mertens majorant at exponent Θ+η, η>0 fixed, via Abel over the cut Gaussian gives |D(x)|≤X^o(1) max(1,x)^(Θ+η) (its upper support is x X^o(1) and its variation O(λ^(−1/2))). The centres of the lists are ≤X^(1+o(1)). This gives limsup ≤2Θ−1 letting η↓0. The detection of 5894 at the original nodes, valid for the common cut of 6138, gives max_j |D(Y_j)|=X^(Θ+o(1)). The normalized maximum then satisfies M≥X^(Θ−1/2−o(1)); and D(x*)²/x*=M² (x*)^(2ε)≥M² X^(−o(1)). Thus the lower limit is attained in the exterior case, while for Θ=1/2 V≥0 suffices. Finally if Θ>1/2, the inequality M≤X^o(1) max(1,x*)^(Θ−1/2+η) forces log x*/log X→1 on letting η↓0.

The control series at σ=1/2 diverges. The loss X^o(1) of the moving tilt allows quantifying how much of the square is localized by a list of classes of length chosen independently of Θ. The subpower arithmetic bound on V remains open.

### An indefinite block of almost linear size inside the cut gcd≤K

The small grouping of 6156 has no universal sign as a quadratic form, even restricting the support to squarefree integers in a fixed fraction of the central kernel. There is a quantitative obstruction with GENUINE Möbius SIGNS: at every x with X^a≤x≤X^2 (a>0 fixed), for the same K=X^o(1), K→∞, there exist two disjoint sets of integers of the band, each of cardinality x^(1−o(1)), whose INTERNAL contributions to Σ_{d≤K} E_d are respectively ≥x^(2−o(1)) and ≤−x^(2−o(1)). This applies also to the maximum x* of 6156 under Θ>1/2. The size of the complete balance is not inferred from it.

Construction. Take a prime P between K and 2K+2. Fix I=[x,x exp(√λ/2)] and consider the lists of primes q∈I and of integers P r∈I with r prime. By PNT with remainder smaller than any fixed logarithmic loss, their cardinalities are asymptotic to the lengths of I and I/P divided by log x and log(x/P), respectively. This is uniform because log(x/P)∼log x≍log X and the relative length is ≍√λ. In particular the second list has M=x^(1−o(1)) members and the first has at least 2M eventually. For large X, q,r,P belong to disjoint ranges, and q,r,P>K. Form a set N with M primes q and the M products Pr; reserve another M primes as a set Q. The common Gaussian cut admits all of I.

In N, pairs of distinct primes q are coprime, all pairs q,Pr are coprime and no pair of products Pr passes the cut (P>K). Nor does the diagonal of the primes. If U is the Gaussian mass of the q in N, V that of the Pr and J the sum of squared weights of the q, the internal balance is exactly U²−J−2UV. Each weight in I lies between exp(−1/16)Gλ(0) and Gλ(0). By equality of cardinalities, V≥exp(−1/16)U and the balance is ≤−(2exp(−1/16)−1)U². In Q the balance is the square of the mass minus the sum of squares, positive of order M²/λ. Both quantities have exponent two. The identity also shows that introducing the diagonal with a per-integer correction of size x^o(1) times its squared weight cannot turn the form into a positive semidefinite one: on N the correction costs only x^(1+o(1)). An analogous argument on Q prevents universally majorizing the form by that diagonal energy.

Concrete antecedents: 5950 used the positive contribution of primes in reduced cofactors; 5978 and 6015 computed asymptotic balances for complete families of fixed multipliers after averaging a common divisor. Here the excluded class P is chosen AFTER the cut K and the coprimality pattern directly gives both signs at exponent two inside the same window. The choice of subsets is not a proof of failure of the ceiling for μ on the complete support. It indicates that an estimate based only on the individual energy or the universal sign of the grouping would lose the cancellations between subsets.

### Compensating ALL the primes of the window in the coprime class of the maximum

With the cut profile φ and the K of 6156, fix X^a≤x≤X², a>0 fixed. Include all primes q of the support at x and, for each prime K<P≤H, all semiprimes Pr of the same support (r prime). Let U be the unsigned mass of the q, V_P that of the family Pr. Choose H as the first prime for which Σ_{K<P≤H}V_P≥U. Then H=K^(exp(1)+o(1)) and the INTERNAL balance of all these indices in the class of gcd one is

    −(1+o(1)) U²/(K log K),        U∼x/log x.

All its other classes up to K are empty. The positive term of ALL pairs of distinct primes, of order U², has been compensated, including both the prime-semiprime crossings and the admissible pairs of semiprimes. The selection only stops the list of factors P; it never trims a family internally. The result applies in particular to the centre x* under an exterior zero.

To verify the rule, uniformly for P≤K⁴ one has V_P=(1+o(1))U/P. Indeed replace the prime sum of the Gaussian centred at x/P by the PNT integral. Throughout the support log r∼log x because log P=o(log X) and the logarithmic width is O((loglog X)²). The main integral is (1+o(1))x/(P log x) since ∫exp(v)φ(v)dv→1. The remainder O_J(r/(log r)^J) by parts costs O_J((x/P)(log x)^(−J)∫exp(v)|dφ(v)|), including the two jumps; the last moment is O(λ^(−1/2)). The r are >K⁴, so the representation Pr is unique. By Mertens the sums up to K² and K⁴, divided by U, tend to log 2 and log 4. The first crossing exists, with excess ≤O(U/K). The same uniform Mertens formula gives log(log H/log K)→1.

In the expansion of the ordinary signed square all masses sum to (Σ V_P−U)². To pass to coprime pairs subtract all of Σ V_P², because two members of the same family share P>K. The other coincidences (q=q′, q=r, or r=r′ between different families) cost in total O(x^(1+o(1))) in moduli: there are at most x exp(O((loglog X)²)) options for the large prime and O(K⁸) pairs of labels, with product weights O(1/λ). All prime factors of these terms exceed K, so the only gcd allowed up to K is one. By PNT and partial summation, Σ_{K<P≤H} P^(−2)∼1/(K log K); the endpoint H≥K² is negligible. Thus Σ V_P²∼U²/(K log K). The square of the excess is O(U²/K²), and the coincidence error is also of lower order. This proves the sign and the asymptotic.

Difference from 6176: the population of primes is no longer thinned to manufacture a vector of negative sign. Difference from 6015: here the balance belongs directly to E₁ in the whole Gaussian window and the dominant loss is computed by the pairs sharing the label P. When majorizing E₁ this block of internal PAIRS can be removed; there remain, in particular, all crossings with indices outside the block, without a sufficient bound.

### Erasing all prime indices with their crossings to the precision of the root square

Choose the freedom of 6156 as K=⌊loglog X⌋. For every centre X^a≤x≤X², a>0 fixed, one can remove from the support ALL primes and a prefix of the semiprimes Pr of 6186, including ALL pairs touching them, with change O(x/λ) in E₁. The same operation leaves the classes E_d, 2≤d≤K, exactly intact. The selection uses only rows incident to the candidate indices. With a fractional weight on a single semiprime E₁ can be preserved exactly.

Let B(S,T) be the bilinear sum over ordered coprime pairs of the supports S,T with signed weights μφ; Ω is the whole support. The change on erasing A is R(A)=B(Ω,Ω)−B(Ω∖A,Ω∖A)=2B(A,Ω)−B(A,A). Let A₀ be the prime list and A₁ its balanced enlargement from 6186. At both extremes one has |B(A_i,Ω)|=o(U²/(K log K)). Indeed the row of q costs in balance, before multiplying by its own weight, D(x) minus the contribution of multiples of q. For Pr the same row is D(x)−B_P(x), with corrections at multiples of r, where B_P is the complete sum over multiples of P. All large q,r of the support are ≥x^(1−o(1)); the number of multiples of one of them in the window is x^o(1), and the number of rows is ≤x^(1+o(1)). Hence the total corrections even in moduli cost x^(1+o(1)), including any Gaussian weight.

Uniformly |D(x)|+max_{K<P≤K⁴}|B_P(x)|≪_a x exp(−c F), with F=(log x)^(3/5)/(loglog x)^(1/5). For D apply the classical Mertens bound of 5309 and Abel to the cut profile; the upper endpoint x exp(O((loglog X)²)) and the variation O(1/√λ) only reduce the constant c. For B_P use μ(Pk)=−μ(k)1_{P∤k}; the restricted prefix sum up to y is Σ_{j≥0}M(y/P^j). For P^j≤√y use Mertens and the geometric series of reciprocals; the rest costs O(√y). Then apply the same Abel at scale x/P. The absolute mass of A_i is O(U) by construction. Thus the bound on the rows implies the announced little-o for this K.

Now B(A₀,A₀)∼U², and B(A₁,A₁)∼−U²/(K log K) by 6186. Hence R(A₀)<0 and R(A₁)>0. Pass from one to the other by incorporating semiprimes one by one, by increasing P and then by increasing r. Each step changes R in absolute value by at most 2 sup φ Σ_{n∈Ω}|μ(n)|φ(log(n/x))≪x/λ, using the absolute bound of 6124. No monotonicity is needed: take the first zero crossing. One of its endpoints already gives the claimed precision with integer indices. Since the last index is >1, its pair with itself is not coprime; the dependence of the balance on its weight is affine. Interpolating the endpoints gives the exact version with a single fraction. Every removed index has all its factors >K. No incident pair with gcd>1 can enter the classes 2 to K.

Application to the maximum selected in 6156. Under an exterior zero x*=X^(1+o(1)); the error after dividing by x* is O(1/λ)=X^o(1), which does not hide a positive exponent of V. Thus all prime indices of the first K classes can be removed simultaneously at that maximum, without recomputing the maximum over the remaining indices. If a protocol defined at all centres is desired, keep the original support when x*<X^(1/2); under the exterior hypothesis this only happens on a prefix. The contribution of the remaining composite support has not been bounded. The additional step relative to 6186 is the control of the rows against Ω and the sign crossing of the TOTAL change on erasing indices.

### Simultaneous erasure of the primes in the linear sum and the coprime square

With K and the centre of 6200 one can erase ALL primes and a selection of products of two and three primes, so that the change in D(x) is X^o(1) and simultaneously that of E₁ is O(x/λ). The E_d for 2≤d≤K remain exactly intact. The centre is not recomputed. This avoids sacrificing the linear signal while preserving the square.

Construction with two disjoint sets of prime labels: P between K and K⁸, Q between K⁹ and K⁹⁰. Denote by a_p,b_q the weights 1/p,1/q normalized separately to sum one. The unnormalized sums tend to log 8 and log 10, both greater than one. Let U be the mass of all primes of the support. From each family pr take a prefix (in increasing r) with mass Ua_p up to error ≤g=Gλ(0). From each qr and pqr preselect in the same way masses Ub_q and Ua_p b_q respectively. There is capacity: for every label m=p,q,pq the complete mass of the mr with r prime is (1+o(1))U/m by the same uniform PNT of 6186, since m≤K⁹⁸. Each large r exceeds all labels and the representation is unique. The sum of all rounding errors is O(K⁹⁹ g)=X^o(1).

Start from the set A₀ with all primes and the selected pr. Reach A₁ by also incorporating the qr (positive sign) and the pqr (negative). Order these additions by taking the sign opposite to the accumulated signed mass whenever available. While both signs are available, each step brings the balance closer to zero or crosses it by ≤g; when one sign is exhausted, interpolate monotonically to the final balance. Both extremes have signed mass Δ=O(K⁹⁹ g), so that bound holds along the whole trajectory.

For the internal coprime square, if the large prime of each index is ignored, the exact formula is

    Δ² − Σ_p M_p² − Σ_q M_q² + Σ_{p,q} M_pq²,

where the M are SIGNED masses of removed indices containing the indicated labels. It is inclusion-exclusion; two indices can share at most one label from each set. Restoring the condition on the large prime costs x^(1+o(1)) as in 6186: for each large prime there are at most O(K⁹⁹) possible labels and each weight costs ≤g. At A₀ one obtains −U² Σ a_p² plus errors O(U K^O(1)g+K^O(1)g²+x^(1+o(1))). At A₁ all the marginal masses M_p and M_q vanish up to roundings, since Σ a_p=Σ b_q=1. What survives is +U² (Σ a_p²)(Σ b_q²) with the same type of error. By Cauchy the product of these two sums is ≥K^(−98). Both signs are strict with margin ≫U²/K⁹⁸.

At both extremes the bilinear form against Ω costs o(U²/K⁹⁸). For each row with labels p,q, include and exclude the multiples of p,q,pq in the total sum, using only the labels present. Each sum of multiples of m|pq is O(x exp(−c F)) with F from 6200: for squarefree m extract μ(m) and use at scale x/m the uniform estimate for coprime prefixes of 6080 (in that proof the set of primes dividing m suffices). Abel on the cut profile costs only exp(o(F)). Coincidences via the large prime imply x^o(1) multiples per row. The removed absolute mass is O(U), so K=⌊loglog X⌋ allows absorbing all these losses. Thus the total change R=2B(A,Ω)−B(A,A) is positive at A₀ and negative at A₁. Along the trajectory with controlled linear balance, stop at the first crossing. As in 6200, one step costs O(x/λ) in R. All removed indices have factors larger than K, so the classes 2,…,K remain intact.

Consequence. At the same selected centre one can impose simultaneously an entirely composite support, a linear signal preserved to subpower error and preservation of the coprime class to the precision of the root square. The construction only guarantees these estimates at that centre; it does not establish the dilation identities for the new selection at other centres nor a ceiling on the remaining support.

### A single integer selection of semiprimes for all linear scales

There is a FIXED set S of semiprimes of the forms 2r,3r,5r with r prime >5, independent of the centre, of the zero and of the Gaussian width, such that on erasing all primes and S from the coefficients of μ the change in the Dirichlet series continues holomorphically to Re s>0. In particular the new series, meromorphic there, preserves all principal parts of 1/ζ at the nontrivial zeros. Its term n=1 can also be erased (constant integer change), leaving an entirely composite support. The continuation does not claim ordinary convergence of the series throughout the half-plane.

Construction by blocks [N,2N), N a power of 2. Put L=log N, m=⌈L²⌉, v=log(n/N)/log 2. For large N one can choose weights 0≤t_n≤1 on the available semiprimes that reproduce exactly the moments of the primes of the block up to degree m. Indeed, the necessary and sufficient condition is that for every real polynomial P of degree ≤m,
    Σ_primes P(v) ≤ Σ_semiprimes max(P(v),0).
This is the support-function inequality for membership in the linear image of a compact convex cube, applied in all directions (including negative ones).

To verify it uniformly, in the coordinate x=N 2^v the density of the primes is dx/log x and that of the semiprimes dx Σ_{p=2,3,5}1/(p log(x/p)), with p in that set of three primes. The families are disjoint when r>5. The ratio of the densities is ≥31/30 for large x. In the continuous inequality, positive P leaves a margin ≥1/30 of its modulus and negative P leaves the full modulus, both with prime measure. Thus one gains ≫(N/L)∫₀¹ |P|dv. By PNT and Abel the discrete error is O_J(N L^(−J)(1+m²)‖P‖∞) also for P_+, whose variation does not exceed that of P. By Markov on [0,1], ‖P′‖∞≤2m²‖P‖∞, and by integrating around a maximum ‖P‖∞≪(1+m²)∫|P|. Taking J fixed and sufficiently large, the margin absorbs both errors.

Choose a vertex of the moment polytope. It has at most m+1 strictly fractional coordinates (otherwise there is a direction in the kernel supported on them). Round them to zero and keep the coordinates equal to one. The vertex can be fixed by lexicographic optimization to eliminate later decisions. Join the block selections and treat the initial blocks in any fixed way. For every complex function f on the block and any polynomial approximant P of degree ≤m, the discrepancy between the prime sum and the selected sum is at most O(N‖f−P‖∞+(m+1)‖f‖∞), using first the exact weights and only afterwards charging the rounding.

For f(v)=2^(−sv), its Taylor polynomial on the block has error less than N^(−3) for each compact set of s and N sufficiently large, by the factorial and m≥L².
